## 13. Request-validation, throttle-response and documentation-surface decisions

These rows were added by a later runtime review of the running service, which
raised four defects against behaviour the earlier sections had already delivered.
They cite row numbers from this log rather than that review's finding
identifiers, per the note at the head of this file.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 13.1 | Bound the paged-read `skip` parameter at `MAX_PAGINATION_OFFSET`, a single named constant equal to the largest signed 64-bit integer, imported by both paged reads | (a) A tighter policy ceiling, derived from the page-size cap or set at some round number; (b) a new validated `Settings` field so each deployment picks its own ceiling; (c) the literal number written at each call site; (d) catch the database error and translate it into a client error | The parameter carried only a lower bound, so an offset above the ceiling PostgreSQL binds an `OFFSET` parameter to reached SQL, and the driver's numeric-range refusal surfaced as an unhandled `500` for an unauthenticated caller. Bounding the parameter at the largest value the database can execute is the narrowest bound that closes the fault: every offset that returned rows before still returns them, and only offsets that cannot be executed at all are refused — by request validation, before a session is opened. A tighter policy ceiling would newly refuse offsets that currently succeed, a behaviour change wider than the defect. A configurable field would let a deployment name a ceiling the database still cannot execute, reintroducing the same `500`. The file's own specification forbids a hardcoded cap at the call site, so the bound lives in one constant that both routes import and the schema layer can be checked against. Catching the driver error leaves invalid input reaching SQL to be refused late, when the request-validation layer can refuse it first. | The published OpenAPI `maximum` renders as `9.223372036854776e+18`, because Pydantic v1 emits an integer bound through an IEEE-754 double. The runtime boundary is exact and was measured on both sides: the largest signed 64-bit value returns `200`, one above it returns `422`. A future move to a database with a narrower offset type would need this constant revisited. |
| 13.2 | Raise the saved-filter predicate ceiling to five, keeping the floor at one | (a) Leave the ceiling at one; (b) remove the ceiling; (c) a larger ceiling such as twenty or fifty; (d) derive the ceiling from the page-size cap | A ceiling of exactly one collapsed a one-to-many relationship — declared by the ORM, by the `List[Criteria]` response model and by the entity-relationship diagram — into exactly-one, so the shipped filter form's minimum-price and maximum-price pair could not be saved at all. Five is the ceiling already applied to the sibling collection on the same contract, so the two bounded collections stay symmetric and the derived per-filter child ceiling stays proportionate. Removing the ceiling reopens the resource-consumption class the bound exists to close. A larger ceiling grants capacity nothing in the product uses and widens the stored-object size for no purpose. Deriving it from the page-size cap would couple a request-body bound to an unrelated response-size bound. | Read literally, one line of the requirements document describes a single criteria; that tension is recorded as row 11.7. A deployment that had come to rely on the one-predicate refusal as a de facto limit loses it — it was never documented as one. |
| 13.3 | Answer a throttled request with the service's own `{"detail": ...}` envelope plus `Retry-After` and the three rate-limit headers, and answer a refused `Host` with that same envelope | (a) Enable the limiter library's header options on the stock limiter and keep the library's `{"error": ...}` body; (b) compose the headers by hand in the handler; (c) leave both refusals as they were and document the three envelopes; (d) keep the framework's plain-text host refusal | Two of the three refusal shapes the service could return diverged from the envelope every other status uses, so a client needed three parsers for one API, and a throttled client was given no indication of when to retry. Header emission is the limiter library's own feature, so it is enabled rather than reimplemented — but enabling it on the stock limiter turns every *successful* counted call into a `500`: the endpoint decorator injects headers after each counted call using the endpoint's `response` argument, which these endpoints do not declare, and the injector raises on a non-response outside its own `try`. A limiter subclass that returns unchanged when handed a non-response confines the change to the refusal path and leaves every success byte-identical, with no endpoint signature altered; the same subclass rounds the reset header to whole seconds, which the library emits as a fractional epoch. The refused-host answer is produced by a subclass of the framework's own host middleware that re-evaluates the framework's matching rules and substitutes only the body, so exact-host matching, suffix matching, the www redirect and the middleware order are untouched. | Both subclasses depend on library internals — the header injector and the host-matching rules — and could need revisiting on a dependency upgrade. The pins are exact, and the refusal bodies, headers and the unchanged success path are all covered by tests. Emitting the policy limit and the remaining count discloses the policy to a caller who has already been refused, which is what the standard headers are for. |
| 13.4 | Serve an HTML documentation response its own content-security policy — the pinned viewer origins, same-origin `connect-src`, `worker-src blob:` and the SHA-256 hash of that response's own inline script — while every API response keeps the strict `default-src 'none'` policy | (a) Permit `unsafe-inline` scripts on the documentation pages; (b) relax the single global policy for the whole service; (c) stop publishing the documentation routes; (d) serve the viewer assets from the application itself; (e) a per-response nonce | One global policy governed both the API responses and the HTML the service deliberately publishes for local use, so the viewer's stylesheet, bundle and inline bootstrap were all refused and the page rendered blank. Hashing the exact inline script of the response being sent restricts inline execution to the byte sequence the application itself generated, where `unsafe-inline` would admit any script injected into the same page. Relaxing the global policy would weaken every API response for the benefit of two HTML pages. Withdrawing the routes contradicts row 7.1, which publishes them locally on purpose, and the application-surface test that asserts them. Vendoring the viewer assets is new functionality and a supply-chain change of its own. A nonce needs a per-response random value and the same page rewrite, with no advantage over a hash for a body the application generates deterministically. | The digest is recomputed per response, so a viewer upgrade that changes the inline bootstrap needs no code change — but one that changes *where* the viewer fetches from does, because each permitted origin is named explicitly. Every named origin is a supply-chain trust decision, pinned to the versions the framework requests. A developer with browser tooling attached still sees one refused source-map fetch, recorded as row 12.8. |

## 14. Runtime QA findings — request correlation, webhook body type, ingestion isolation

Rows added for the QA testing round whose findings were numbered FINDING-1 to
FINDING-7 against the provider and observability runtime. That numbering is
per-review, so these rows cite behaviour rather than an identifier.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 14.1 | Attach the bound request identifier in `QueueDispatchHandler.prepare`, keeping the existing attachment in `RedactingFilter` as well | (a) Add the redacting filter to the queue handler as well as to the stream handler; (b) capture the identifier into the record at every call site; (c) drop the queue and emit synchronously | The identifier lives in a `contextvars` variable, which is per task and per thread. The only code that read it ran inside the filter installed on the *listener-side* stream handler, so it executed on the `QueueListener` thread and always read `None` — no record on the normal path carried a `request_id`, and correlation appeared only during queue overflow, which is worse than absent because it looks like it works. `prepare` is the last step that runs on the thread that logged, so reading it there is the smallest change that makes every path correct. Adding the whole redacting filter to the queue handler would have moved redaction, formatting and serialisation back onto the request path, which is exactly what the queue exists to prevent. Per-call-site capture would have to be repeated forever and would be forgotten once. | `prepare` no longer returns the record untouched. It sets one attribute and never raises, and the inline overflow path is covered because `emit` prepares before it enqueues. |
| 14.2 | Redact registered secret values literally, in addition to matching credential shapes | (a) Accept that a credential quoted in free prose survives; (b) read the configured secrets inside the logging module; (c) hash or fingerprint values instead of holding them | Shape matching needs a credential-shaped key name beside the value, so a provider that quotes a key inside an error sentence defeats it — measured with a provider error body reading `bad key <value> rejected`. A literal pass closes that. The logging module must not read configuration: it is imported from exception handlers and must stay leaf-level and cycle-free, which is why each module that *handles* a credential registers it instead. Fingerprinting cannot rewrite the value in text that already contains it. | Over-redaction if a registered value also occurs innocently. Bounded by an eight-character floor, a thirty-two value ceiling, and by registering only provider credentials. A value changed after import is not covered, so the registry is a safety net rather than the primary control. |
| 14.3 | Register the provider credentials from the three service modules that handle them, and not the signing key or the database URL | Register every secret setting from one place — the settings module or the application entrypoint | The settings module is deliberately leaf-level so that nothing it imports can cycle back into it, and the logging module reads no configuration; a single registration point would have to violate one of those two properties. Registering in the module that already holds the credential keeps both intact. The signing key and the database URL are handled elsewhere and their realistic leak shapes — an `Authorization` header, a `secret`-named field, a database URL carrying inline credentials — are already matched by shape. | Four values are registered rather than six. A future credential must register itself; the module that introduces one is the module that would. |
| 14.4 | Normalise the raw notification body once inside `verify_webhook_signature` | (a) Encode inside the postback builder; (b) remove the text branch from `webhook_body_object` so a text body is rejected | The two functions disagreed about the accepted type: one decoded text happily while the other raised `TypeError` on it, so a caller holding text got an exception from a function whose contract is that every failed check is *returned*. Normalising once means the bytes that are decoded are the bytes that are transmitted, which is the property the signature check depends on. Encoding inside the builder would have left the two functions still deciding the type separately; rejecting text would have made the tolerant function's own contract a lie. | A caller passing text now has it encoded as UTF-8. If that caller had decoded the request with another codec the re-encoded bytes would differ and PayPal would answer `FAILURE`, which is the correct outcome rather than a silent pass. |
| 14.5 | Write each provider record inside its own savepoint | (a) Keep one flush at the end of the pass; (b) de-duplicate identities in memory before writing; (c) open a fresh session per record | One flush at the end meant a single unwritable record discarded every other record in the payload — measured with a repeated address and with a NUL byte, each of which cost the whole pass — and it would keep costing every pass for as long as the provider returned that record. A savepoint per record also makes each write visible to the next record's identity lookup, so a repeated address is reconciled as a refresh, which is what the module's own premise says should happen; an in-memory de-duplication map would have handled that case only and left every other refusal fatal. A session per record would abandon the one-session, one-commit contract. | A 500-record payload now issues 500 savepoints and flushes rather than one batch. Measured at under one second for 500 records against real PostgreSQL. |
| 14.6 | Attribute only constraint, data and value-adaptation failures to the record; raise everything else | Isolate every exception the write raises | Isolating everything would turn a systemic failure — a revoked privilege, a dropped connection — into one refusal record per remaining record and a pass that still reported "Completed", which is a worse signal than the failure it replaced. A constraint violation, a value the column cannot hold, and a value the driver cannot adapt describe the record; a missing privilege describes the session. Verified by driving both: a real `CHECK` violation is counted and dropped while the pass commits, and a real `REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE` still ends the pass with rows unchanged and the pool released. | A failure class outside the three would end a pass that isolation could have survived. Preferred to the reverse, and the classification is a named constant rather than a scattered condition. |
| 14.7 | Report an ingestion failure by exception class and driver error class, carrying no message text | (a) Keep the driver message; (b) strip only the driver's `DETAIL` line; (c) redact the message by pattern | The module states that a failure record names how far the pass got and never a listing, and the driver message broke that: PostgreSQL's server-side `DETAIL` line repeats the value it refused, and `hide_parameters` does not suppress it. Stripping `DETAIL` alone is not enough, because a driver's *first* line also quotes values for some errors — `invalid input syntax for type … : "…"`. Pattern redaction cannot know which quoted fragments are provider data. The driver's error class — `UniqueViolation`, `CheckViolation`, `InsufficientPrivilege` — carries the diagnostic value without the data, so it is reported instead. | Less free text when debugging an ingestion failure. The exception class, its module, the driver error class and the progress counter remain, and the traceback is still available at `DEBUG`. |
| 14.8 | Name the failed contract fields on a discarded provider record | (a) Leave the discard record without context; (b) include the validation error message | A systematic discard was indistinguishable from any other: the record named no field, so an operator could not tell that, for example, every listing was being dropped for a date the contract cannot parse. The validation message would name the fields but is generated text and could carry a value in some cases, so the field names are taken from the error's locations and filtered against the contract's own declared field names — a closed set that cannot contain a provider value. | The record names which field failed. That is the intent; it is a contract field name, not provider data. |
| 14.9 | Refuse a listing address that is not an absolute `http`/`https` URL, and refuse NUL in either text field | (a) Leave the address bounded only by length; (b) also refuse other control characters; (c) sanitise the value instead of refusing it | The address field had a length ceiling and no shape, so `javascript:alert(1)` validated and was stored — and, measured through the admin write endpoint, answered `200`. A scheme allowlist with a host requirement and no user information refuses that class of value at the contract, which is where the other field bounds already live. NUL is refused because no text column can store it: the driver raised on it at write time, which cost the whole ingestion pass and answered `500` on the write endpoint; refusing it at the contract turns both into a named validation failure. Only NUL is refused, not every control character, because a provider address legitimately carries newlines and refusing those would drop valid records. Sanitising would store a value the provider never sent. | An address form outside the allowlist is now refused rather than stored. No client sends one: the write endpoint's own tests supply none, and the provider supplies web URLs. Free text in `street_address` is deliberately still stored as data. |

### Deliberate non-changes from this round

| # | Left unchanged | Why it was not changed | Risks |
|---|----------------|------------------------|-------|
| 14.10 | The full-replace refresh in `_refresh_listing`: a column the provider stops sending is set to `None` | This is the module's intended behaviour — the stored row states what the provider currently reports rather than accumulating values from earlier passes — and changing it would silently invent a merge policy for provider data. The QA round recorded it so it would not be mistaken for data loss, so the contract is now stated in the docstring instead. | A provider that intermittently omits a field will clear and restore it. Visible in `updated_at` and reported by the pass counters. |
| 14.11 | Free text in `street_address` — a value such as a script tag is stored verbatim | Storing text as data is correct; escaping belongs to whatever renders it, and the frontend is designated read-only and out of scope. Sanitising at the storage boundary would corrupt legitimate addresses and would still not make any renderer safe. | A renderer that interpolates the value without escaping would be vulnerable. Recorded as a consumer obligation rather than a storage one. |
| 14.12 | The three pre-existing `flake8` warnings in `backend/app/api/router.py` (`:8` E501, `:10` E501, `:10` W292) | AAP §0.6.1.1 designates that file REFERENCE and "deliberately unchanged", and its unchanged state is the AAP's own evidence that the four-prefix constraint is honoured. The two warnings sit on the `include_router(...)` prefix expressions themselves, and AAP §0.9.2 and §0.12.1 exclude reformatting and formatting-only change. | Three style warnings remain, so `flake8 backend` still exits 1. Resolvable by the owner of `router.py` or by a per-file ignore in `ci.yml`. |
| 14.12a | The two pre-existing `flake8` warnings in `backend/app/services/email_service.py` (E302, W292) | **Corrected**, not left. That file is an AAP §0.6.1.2 UPDATE and therefore in scope; the fix is whitespace only — one blank line before `send_email` and a trailing newline — with no semantic change. Row 12.6's count is superseded accordingly. | None. The full suite was re-run after the change: 796 passed, and `bandit -r backend/app -ll` still exits 0. |
| 14.13 | `run_listing_updater` is still not scheduled by the application lifespan | The QA round flagged it for confirmation rather than as a defect, and scheduling a background task in the entrypoint is neither a finding nor an AAP requirement for this work. The coroutine itself is exercised and correct. | The in-process loop runs only when something invokes it, and the lifespan does not — that half stands. **The claim that only something *outside* this repository can invoke a pass is WITHDRAWN &mdash; see rows 82.2, 88.2 and 92.7:** `infrastructure/kubernetes/65-ingestion-cronjob.yaml` invokes `update_listings` on a schedule from inside this repository, and row 92.3 records that a failed pass now exits non-zero so the schedule can see it. Reported, not fixed. |

## 15. Runtime QA findings — deployed startup, numeric contract, webhook concurrency

Rows added for the cross-cutting integration QA round, which drove the running
service against a real PostgreSQL database and a local provider stub and raised
four defects: the service could not start in any non-local environment, one
numeric value took the public listings read down permanently, an out-of-range
integer literal answered `500` instead of a validation refusal, and two
concurrent copies of one legitimate webhook deadlocked the event loop. That
round's finding numbers are per-review, so these rows cite behaviour and cite
row numbers from this log rather than that review's identifiers.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 15.1 | **Superseded in full by row 35.36. Row 2.5 is the controlling decision: every in-process store, the bounded one included, is refused outside `ENVIRONMENT=local`, and `backend/app/core/config.py` enforces that today. The position below was withdrawn once the shared store this row said nothing provisioned was provisioned — see rows 35.18 to 35.21. Do not act on the acceptance this row records.** Accept the bounded in-process rate-limit store outside a local environment, keeping the two unbounded in-process schemes refused there, and let `build_limiter` record the single-process caveat | (a) Pin a shared-store driver such as `redis` in `backend/requirements.txt`; (b) provision a shared store in Terraform and Compose and require it; (c) add a new opt-in setting by which a deployment declares it accepts per-process counting; (d) relax the rule for every in-process scheme including `memory` and `async+memory`; (e) leave the rule as it was and treat the unstartable image as a deployment concern | Three artefacts disagreed and the disagreement made every non-local configuration unstartable: `config.py` demanded a scheme whose counters are shared by every process, the manifest ships a driver for none of them, and `rate_limit.py` already contained a warning branch for exactly this combination that `config.py` refused before it could ever run. Accepting the bounded scheme reconciles all three at once and makes that branch reachable, so the caveat is stated at startup instead of being enforced as a refusal. Pinning a driver would add a runtime dependency the dependency manifest does not name and would still not start a deployment, because nothing in the infrastructure provisions a store for it to address — neither the Terraform configuration nor the Compose definition declares one, and the validator requires a scheme outside the in-process set to carry its store's address. Provisioning one is infrastructure work an order of magnitude wider than the defect. A new setting adds a configuration surface whose only purpose is to say yes to the thing the default already does. Relaxing the rule for every in-process scheme would readmit the two stores that hold one counter per caller address with no ceiling, which is the resource-consumption class the bounded store exists to close, so the two are kept apart by their own named set. Leaving the rule in place fails the requirement that the application starts. | A deployment running more than one process or replica enforces each credential-endpoint limit once per process rather than once per caller, so N processes admit N times each limit. It is recorded once at startup naming the setting, the scheme and the environment, and a deployment that needs one shared count still names a shared scheme here — it must then also install that scheme's driver in the image, which the library reports by name when it is missing. |
| 15.2 | Refuse a non-finite or unrepresentable number at the listing contract with one `pre=True` validator over `rent`, `broker_fee` and `square_footage` | (a) A plain validator after coercion; (b) an explicit `le=` ceiling on each field; (c) catch the serialisation failure in the response layer; (d) refuse the value in the endpoint rather than the contract; (e) store the value and omit the field from the response | One value took a frozen public endpoint down permanently and could not be undone by any code change: `1e400`, `1e999` and the bare token `Infinity` all decode to positive infinity, which satisfies the existing lower bound, which PostgreSQL stores in a `double precision` column, and which the JSON response layer then refuses to serialise — so the write answered `500` after committing the row, and every page containing that row answered `500` to anonymous and authenticated callers alike until the row was deleted by hand. A validator that runs *before* coercion is the only place one check closes both that fault and its sibling, an integer literal too large to convert to a double, because that conversion raises inside the coercion step and escapes request-validation handling entirely. Placing it on the creation contract closes the authenticated write path and the unauthenticated provider-ingestion path together, because the provider mapper builds the same model; the ingestion pass already counts a record its contract refuses as discarded. A ceiling expressed as a number would have to name a literal at the boundary of the type rather than the property actually required, and would not catch the pre-coercion overflow. Catching the failure at the response layer leaves the unusable row committed. Refusing in the endpoint leaves the contract able to produce a value the response cannot carry. | A provider record whose price is reported as infinity is now discarded rather than stored, and the discard is counted and recorded by field name. Nothing in the product sends such a value; the value could not be read back before either. |
| 15.3 | Give the listing response model the same finiteness constraint and project each row of a page on its own, recording and skipping a stored row the response cannot carry. **The skipping half was superseded by alternative (d) below — see row 28.5.** | (a) Rely on the contract guard alone; (b) widen the required `rent` field to optional and project a non-finite value as null; (c) exclude such rows in SQL; (d) keep failing the whole page | The contract guard stops a new row being written but does nothing about a row already stored — from a run before the guard, from a direct database write, or from any future path — and the requirement that the public read endpoint stays reachable is frozen, so it must not be breakable by stored data. Stating the constraint on the response model is honest about what that model can carry, and projecting row by row means one unusable row costs that row rather than the whole corpus: the remaining rows are served, ordering and repeat-stability are unchanged, and one record names the row so an operator can clear it. Widening `rent` would alter the eleven-field response contract that the read endpoint and the client schema depend on. A SQL predicate would be dialect-specific and would silently change what a page contains without saying so. | A page containing an unusable row returns fewer rows than its limit, which was already possible at the end of the corpus. The row is reported rather than repaired; repair is a data operation. |
| 15.4 | Run every blocking session call in the two `async def` subscription routes in a worker thread | (a) `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (transmission_id) DO NOTHING` and branch on the affected row count; (b) a short `lock_timeout` or `statement_timeout` on the session so the contended insert fails fast; (c) move the delivery record into its own committed transaction before the capture; (d) fix only the one contended statement and leave the rest of the route as it was | Two simultaneous copies of one legitimate notification — the case the uniqueness constraint exists to absorb, and one PayPal itself produces by redelivering — stopped the whole service permanently and lost the delivery. The mechanism is a circular wait between the event loop and the database: the second delivery's insert blocks on the first delivery's uncommitted row, and because that insert runs directly on the loop, the loop can no longer deliver the completion of the first delivery's provider call, so the first never commits and the second's wait never ends. No timeout applied, so nothing recovered without restarting the process. Moving the session work off the loop removes the cycle rather than bounding it, and it does so while keeping the exactly-once property intact: the waiter blocks on the index exactly as before, and learns the right answer either way — a commit gives it the constraint violation it reads as a repeat, a rollback lets its own insert succeed so the delivery is still settled. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` decides against an *uncommitted* row, so a first attempt whose capture then fails would leave the second having already acknowledged the notification, and PayPal does not redeliver an acknowledged one — the delivery would be lost, which is the same loss by a quieter route. A lock timeout leaves the deadlock in place and merely puts a clock on it. Committing the delivery record before the capture would break the rollback that currently lets a failed capture be settled by a redelivery. Fixing the single contended statement would close the measured case and leave the same class open at every other statement on those two routes, which is why the treatment is applied to both of them as one decision about where session work runs. | Each such call now costs a thread handoff, and a waiter occupies a worker thread for as long as the holder's provider call takes, which is bounded by the configured outbound timeout. The thread pool is shared with every other synchronous route, and the webhook route is rate limited per caller address and admits nothing before its signature is verified. The session is touched from a different thread than the one that opened it, sequentially and never concurrently, which the driver and the session both permit; the bound request identifier is carried into the worker thread with the context, so records emitted there stay correlated. One read on the same path is still issued on the loop — the ownership resolution inside the payment service — because it is a plain select that holds no lock and waits on none, so it cannot participate in the cycle; a future change giving that lookup a row lock would have to move it too, which is why the module states where each statement runs. |

### Deliberate non-changes from this round

| # | Left unchanged | Why it was not changed | Risks |
|---|----------------|------------------------|-------|
| 15.5 | `GET /health` still answers from the application alone and exercises no database read | The QA round observed, correctly, that the probe answered `200` throughout the listings outage and was the first thing to stop answering under the deadlock. Both of those defects are now closed at their cause, so the probe is no longer masking a live fault, and giving it a database read and a serialisation would change a route that passed every check for the sake of a signal about faults that no longer exist. A readiness probe distinct from a liveness probe is a deployment design decision, not a defect in this code. | A future fault in the read path or the session pool would not show in the probe. Recorded here so the next reviewer knows it is a choice. |
| 15.6 | The `[REDACTED]` value the startup caveat records for its tracked-key count | The redacting filter matches on field name, and this field's name ends in a credential-shaped word, so a plain integer is rewritten. Narrowing the name match to exclude it would weaken a control that exists to catch credential-shaped fields, for the sake of one diagnostic number that is also declared in `.env.example` and in the settings class. | The caveat record does not state the configured cap. The setting name it does state leads directly to the value. |

Rows added for the remediation of `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml`, the
file AAP §0.6.1.5 designates as closing C-4 and whose five enumerated settings
appear in the AAP §0.6.3 configuration table. Seven edits were authorised — four
lines modified, five deleted, none added — and every row below traces to C-4.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 16.1 | Reference both secrets with Compose's required-variable form `${VAR:?message}` rather than the soft `${VAR}` form | (a) Soft `${DATABASE_URL}`; (b) the unset-only form `${VAR?message}`; (c) an `env_file:` key; (d) a non-secret placeholder literal | The soft form's failure mode was measured on the adjacent line before the change: rendering the unmodified file emitted `JWT_SECRET: ''` together with `The JWT_SECRET variable is not set. Defaulting to a blank string.` A soft reference substitutes empty and proceeds, and because `backend/app/core/config.py` declares both `DATABASE_URL` and `SECRET_KEY` required with no default, that empty value surfaces only later as a container-startup validation error. The `:?` variant was chosen over `?` because it refuses an empty value as well as an unset one — measured in a directory with no `.env`: unset exits 1, empty exits 1, both values set renders and exits 0. `env_file:` is not enumerated in AAP §0.6.3 and would be scope creep; a placeholder literal would reintroduce a credential-shaped value into version control. | `docker compose config` and `up` now fail when either variable is unset. That is the intended loud failure, but it changes the verification procedure: the render gate must export both values or supply them through a Compose-visible `.env`. Compose reads `.env` from the compose file's own directory — `infrastructure/docker/`, which contains none — so the gate fails there by default, and a first probe run from the repository root passed only because it picked up the root `.env`. |
| 16.2 | Rename the compose variable `JWT_SECRET` to `SECRET_KEY` | (a) Keep the name and add a `JWT_SECRET` alias to the settings class; (b) supply both names during a transition; (c) keep the soft form on the renamed variable | `backend/app/core/config.py` declares `SECRET_KEY` and has no `JWT_SECRET` field, so the compose file was supplying a variable nothing reads while the value the application does read was never supplied by compose at all — it fell through to whatever `.env` held, historically the `your_secret_key_here` placeholder written by `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh`. Rendering the unmodified file confirmed this directly. An alias would widen the settings contract and edit a file outside this assignment; a transition period is unnecessary because `JWT_SECRET` has no reader anywhere in the codebase. The rename is the precondition for the startup key-strength check to see a compose-supplied key at all. | An operator whose environment exports `JWT_SECRET` must re-export it as `SECRET_KEY`; the required-variable form turns that from a silent weak-key deployment into a named render-time failure. `README.md:43` still documents `JWT_SECRET` — a separate agent's file, reported rather than edited here. |
| 16.3 | Remove the `./secrets` bind-mount and the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` path from the `db` service in favour of ambient credentials, pruning both now-childless parent keys | (a) Keep the bind-mount and rely on `.gitignore` covering `secrets/`; (b) move to Compose `secrets:`; (c) leave `volumes:` and `environment:` present but empty | The mount required a long-lived service-account key on every host running the proxy, and the key path is the second half of C-4. The Cloud SQL proxy supports Application Default Credentials, so on GKE or Cloud Run the workload identity supplies credentials with no key material at rest. No `secrets/` directory and no `google-credentials.json` has ever existed in this tree, verified by a recursive search, so nothing in-repo is lost by removal. Both parent keys were pruned rather than left childless because an empty `volumes:` parses as `null`, which states an intent the file does not have. | An operator running the proxy locally must supply ambient credentials rather than dropping a key file. `.gitignore` still covers `secrets/`, `**/secrets/` and `*credentials*.json` independently, as defence in depth. |
| 16.4 | Align the published port and the health-check URL to 8000 | (a) Leave 5000 and change the image to bind it; (b) publish 8000 but leave the health check on 5000 | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend` declares `EXPOSE 8000` and starts uvicorn with `--port 8000`, so nothing has ever listened on 5000 and the health check could never succeed — the mismatch is what made it unreachable and masked failures. The `/health` path was already present in the check and was not altered; the endpoint it names now exists in `backend/app/main.py`. | Anything addressing the backend on host port 5000 must move to 8000. `REACT_APP_API_URL` still names 5000 and is recorded in row 16.10. |
| 16.5 | Delete only the line instructing a reader to place `google-credentials.json` in `./secrets`, retaining the two preceding comment lines verbatim | (a) Delete the whole three-line comment block; (b) rewrite the note to describe ambient credentials | That single line is the mechanism by which a service-account key would enter the repository tree. The two remaining lines concern the `<INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME>` placeholder, are still factual, and deleting them would be a change untraceable to C-4. Rewriting the note to explain the substitution would place rationale in a configuration comment, which Rule 1 forbids. | None. The deleted instruction described a file that never existed in the tree. |
| 16.6 | Remove the exposed values from the working tree only, leaving revocation and rotation to the documented runbook | (a) Rotate as part of this change; (b) rewrite git history here | Removing a value from the current tree does not remove it from history, and every existing clone retains it, so both the database credentials and the expected service-account key must be treated as already compromised. This is why the runbook is Rule 3's highest-risk review entry. |
| 16.7 | Delete the final comment line while retaining the preceding line's terminator, so the file gains a trailing newline it did not have | (a) Drop that terminator too, preserving the original absence of a trailing newline; (b) restore the absence afterwards by a separate byte edit | The source file ended without a newline, so deleting its last line forces a choice. Retaining the terminator produces a one-line deletion in the diff; dropping it makes git rewrite the preceding line as well, yielding two deletions plus an insertion for an unchanged line. It also clears a real lint error: `yamllint` reported `no new line character at the end of file` against the original and does not against the result. The trailing newline is therefore a consequence of deleting the final line, not a reformatting choice. | The diff shows git's `\ No newline at end of file` marker against the deleted line, which can read as an unintended whitespace change. Recorded here so it is not mistaken for one. Verified that no other line's bytes changed. |
| 16.8 | Record these rows here rather than leaving the compose rationale to the owner of this log | (a) Record it only in the change description; (b) leave the rows to whoever next edits this log | Rule 1 makes this log the single source of truth for "why" and treats an unexplained deviation as a defect, and two entries were mandated for this file. No other author can supply this rationale, because the alternatives weighed and the measurements taken — notably the pre-change render that exposed the empty `JWT_SECRET` — exist only in the course of making these edits. AAP §0.11.4 states that creating documentation changes no application behaviour and so cannot breach the Minimal Change Clause. | A second file appears in a change whose assignment names one. The edit is strictly additive — 26 lines added, none removed, sections 1 to 14 byte-untouched — so it cannot conflict with existing content. |

Rationale for the file created under row 11.2. It is recorded here rather than in the file's own docstrings, which state only what each fixture provides.

(a) is refused because no `__init__.py` exists anywhere in this repository and the AAP authorises exactly one, `backend/tests/security/__init__.py`. (b) is refused because no pytest configuration file exists and the AAP authorises none. (c) does not fix CI. | The import block must stay below the bootstrap, so `# noqa: E402` is carried per line. The migration round trip is verified separately by `alembic upgrade head` and `alembic downgrade -1`, which is a distinct gate. `Base.metadata` carries the `UNIQUE` constraints on `subscriptions.paypal_order_id` and `webhook_events.transmission_id` that the replay and idempotency cases depend on, so nothing is lost. | The metadata and the migrations could drift apart. (b) is refused because `sqlite` is accepted by the settings validator only while `ENVIRONMENT` names `local`, which would couple two unrelated settings. The digest is identical either way, and `verify_password` is asserted against it. | Every seeded row shares one hash. No case depends on the rows having distinct hashes. |

The frozen `{access_token, token_type}` response shape is asserted unchanged. |

## 18. Price and entitlement tampering tests (`backend/tests/security/test_subscription_tampering.py`)

Rationale for the module that verifies findings H-2 (the client dictated the charge amount and the entitlement dates) and H-3 (payment capture accepted both identifiers from the caller with no ownership check). It is recorded here rather than in the module's own docstrings, which state only what each case asserts.

Rows 18.1 to 18.3 are deviations from the literal shape the module was described with. The description was written against the pre-remediation code; the delivered implementation had already moved on, and no field, function, route or plan entry was added to the application to make the described shape true.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 18.1 | **Deviation.** Assert that a `payment_method` field in the request body is *refused*, rather than sending it as part of the valid contract | Add `payment_method` to `SubscriptionCreate` so the described contract exists | The brief describes `SubscriptionCreate` as exposing "exactly `plan_id` and `payment_method`". The delivered schema exposes `plan_id` alone under `extra = "forbid"`, and row 6.7 is why: a field a client sends cannot influence the charge if the contract has no place for it. Adding the field back to satisfy a description would reopen exactly what row 6.7 closed, so the field is asserted refused instead — which is a strictly stronger claim than sending it would have been. | None. `test_h2_a_client_supplied_price_field_is_refused` pins the refusal, so restoring the field would fail the suite loudly. |
| 18.2 | **Deviation.** Assert `end_date is None` on the row that `POST /subscriptions/` opens, and assert the catalog-period window on the row a settlement activates | Assert both dates on the created row, as the brief describes | The brief expects creation to persist `start_date` **and** `end_date`. `_open_intent` deliberately writes `end_date=None` (rows 6.1 and 6.2): the window opens only once a charge has settled, so a row that exists across the approval window entitles nothing. Weakening the assertion to accept whatever creation writes would have made the case unable to fail; asserting the absence at creation and the derivation at activation covers the same requirement across the two states the row actually has. | The window assertion now depends on the activation path as well as on creation. Mitigated by `test_h2_the_opened_row_carries_no_entitlement_window`, which fails if creation ever starts writing an end date. |
| 18.3 | **Deviation.** Exercise the H-3 ownership binding by awaiting `capture_order` directly rather than through an HTTP capture route | Add a capture route that accepts an order identifier from the client | No such route exists: row 6.12 withdrew `POST /subscriptions/capture` and its request model precisely so that the service accepts no provider identifier from a client, and `test_api.py::test_the_webhook_is_the_only_additive_subscription_route` asserts the subscription surface is exactly the two frozen routes plus the webhook. A route taking a PayPal identifier from a client would be the vulnerability, not a way to test for it. Awaiting the service function reaches the same server-side lookup the webhook reaches. | The case does not exercise the HTTP layer. `test_h2_the_entitlement_window_is_the_catalog_period` covers the owner-bound capture end to end through `POST /subscriptions/webhook`, so the HTTP path is still asserted. |
| 18.4 | Read the refusal status from the application's own generated OpenAPI document, asserting it is the single non-success status declared for `POST /subscriptions/` | Write `422` as a literal in each case | The brief requires the exact status be read rather than guessed. Deriving it turns a change to the validation handler into one failure in `rejection_status` instead of a literal that silently disagrees with the service. The derivation also asserts that exactly one refusal status is declared, so an added error response is surfaced rather than absorbed. | If the document ever declares a second non-success status the helper fails for every case at once. That is the intended signal. |
| 18.5 | Read every monetary and period value from `get_plan`, and parametrize every price and window case over both published identifiers | Write `9.99`, `USD`, `30` and `365` as literals for one plan | A literal copy of the catalog passes even when the endpoint stops reading the catalog, because the test and the code would then hold the same constant independently. Reading through `get_plan` makes the assertion an equality with the single source of truth. Running both identifiers is what distinguishes a real period mapping from a coincidence that holds for one entry. | None. A catalog entry added later is covered by `test_h2_the_catalog_is_the_only_source_of_plan_identifiers`, which fails until `CATALOG_PLAN_IDS` is extended. |
| 18.6 | Install the payment stand-in at `paypal_service._client`, the transport boundary, and stand in `_bearer_credential` alongside it | (a) Patch `create_order` and `capture_order` at the endpoint module, as `test_payment_lifecycle.py` does for its own purposes; (b) patch `httpx.AsyncClient` globally | Patching the endpoint's view of the service would skip the ownership lookup that H-3 exists to prove, so the refusal cases would pass without the control being present. Patching at the transport boundary keeps every line of the service in the path and still guarantees no socket is opened. Standing in the credential accessor keeps the module-global grant cache out of the cases, so no case depends on or leaves behind a cached token. | The stand-in must track the shape the transport is called with. A drift would fail loudly rather than silently pass. |
| 18.7 | Assert "no state change" by comparing a snapshot of every mapped column, the subscription row count, the delivery-record count and both principals' stored roles | Assert only that the refusal raised | A refusal that raised after writing would satisfy an exception-only assertion, and the requirement is that the refused capture changed nothing. The snapshot is built from the model's own mapper, so a column added later is compared without the helper changing. | None. |
| 18.8 | Keep a positive control in which the owner captures its own order, and a further case in which the owner presents an identifier the service never stored | Assert the refusals only | A lookup that refused every capture would satisfy every refusal case, so without the positive control the suite could pass with the payment path broken. The unstored-identifier case pins that the lookup refuses an unmatched identifier on the same terms as another principal's row, which is the property that stops the refusal disclosing which orders exist. | None. Mutating the lookup to refuse unconditionally fails the positive control, which was verified. |
| 18.9 | Name every case `test_h2_*` or `test_h3_*` | Name them by behaviour alone | Rule 1's traceability clause requires 100% coverage with no gaps, and column 3 of `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` is the tests in this folder. A finding-prefixed name makes each of the two findings this module verifies locatable without reading the bodies, and the names are treated as a stable interface for the matrix. | The prefixes reference a per-review identifier set. The module docstring states which finding each prefix denotes so the names stay readable if the identifiers age. |
| 18.10 | Draw the two principals from the `registered_user` and `second_registered_user` fixtures rather than seeding an intruder locally | Seed a second account inside the module | `backend/tests/conftest.py` publishes the two as a pair of valid principals holding separate rows at the same role, which is exactly what this case needs, and OWASP's prescribed object-level test is two valid accounts that cannot reach each other's objects. A locally seeded account would duplicate the fixture and could drift from the password policy and the role baseline it applies. | None. |
| 18.11 | Stand in only the webhook signature check when the module drives a settlement, and assert nothing about signatures, certificate hosts or repeated deliveries | Assert those controls here as well | Rule 3's review entry 4 is validated against `test_paypal_webhook.py`, and duplicating its assertions here would create two places to update for one control. This module is scoped to price, entitlement and capture ownership. | The settlement path depends on a control this module does not assert. That control has its own module. |

position and the reason it was abandoned both stay visible.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 19.1 | **Reversal.** Revision 0002 now leaves **exactly one** administrator on every successful upgrade: it inserts the mandated account when the address is absent, and promotes it when the address is stored | (a) The previous tiered assertion — at most one always, exactly one when the target exists, **zero** with a warning when it does not; (b) raise and fail the upgrade when the target is absent | The tiered form allowed a state the AAP forbids in four separate places: §0.1.2 "Exactly one administrator is to be **seeded**, for `test@blitzy.com`", the §0.1.2 success criterion "Exactly one account holds administrative privilege after migration", §0.5.1.3 and §0.6.1.3 "asserts as a post-condition that exactly one administrative account exists", and the §0.8.2 gate "Exactly one, with every other account at `registered`". Measured on an empty PostgreSQL database, the previous revision exited 0 with `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE role='admin'` returning **0** — so the gate the AAP defines could not be met by a first deployment. (b) was rejected because a fresh database has no accounts, so raising would wedge `alembic upgrade head` for every new environment and for CI; `backend/app/main.py` no longer creates its own schema, which makes `upgrade head` against an empty database a normal, required operation. The AAP's own verb is "seeded", and the revision's filename is `0002_seed_single_admin.py`. | An `INSERT` in a data-only revision is a wider operation than the promotion it replaces. Bounded by the post-condition, which now refuses **any** state other than exactly one administrator holding exactly that address, raising and rolling the transaction back. Verified against PostgreSQL 13 and SQLite across empty, pre-existing-account, repeated-upgrade, downgrade and re-upgrade paths. |
| 19.2 | Store `!locked-no-password-set` in `users.hashed_password` for the account the revision inserts | (a) Generate a random password and log or print it; (b) copy a bcrypt hash of a known password; (c) leave the column empty | The column is `NOT NULL`, so some value must be written. (a) and (b) both create a live administrative credential — the exact outcome "no automatic grant path" exists to prevent — and (a) would additionally write a credential to a log. The chosen value carries no bcrypt prefix, salt or digest, so `security.verify_password` reaches its `ValueError` branch and reports a mismatch for every candidate, including the marker itself; `verify_credential` still performs its decoy comparison and pads to `MIN_CREDENTIAL_CHECK_SECONDS`, so the locked row is indistinguishable in time from any other. The account therefore holds the role and no means of authenticating until an operator deliberately stores a password. (c) is refused by the `NOT NULL` constraint. | An operator may be surprised that the seeded administrator cannot log in. That is the intended posture, and the marker is self-describing. Asserted by `test_the_seeded_administrator_holds_no_usable_credential`. |
| 19.3 | Compute the inserted `created_at` in Python as a naive UTC instant rather than with a SQL `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` | Let the database supply it | `users.created_at` is a naive `DateTime`, and the application writes timezone-aware UTC values that row 10.10's engine configuration keeps unambiguous. A SQL default would take the server's own clock and zone, which differs between PostgreSQL and SQLite and would make the stored instant dialect-dependent. Binding the value keeps the revision's behaviour identical on both. | The revision reads the clock of the host running the migration. That is the same clock the application writes with. |
| 19.4 | Read an injected connection from `config.attributes["connection"]` in `migrations/env.py`, falling back to the application engine | (a) Leave `env.py` bound to the application engine and have tests substitute the module's `engine` attribute; (b) point `DATABASE_URL` at the test database for the duration of a test; (c) call each revision's `upgrade()` directly with a hand-built `Operations` object | Without an injection point no test can run the revisions against an isolated database, which is why nothing exercised them. (a) works but reaches inside the module under test and cannot share a transaction with the test's own reads. (b) mutates process-wide state that `settings` has already validated and read. (c) bypasses `env.py` entirely, so the migration environment itself — the file the finding names — would still be untested. The chosen form is Alembic's own documented idiom, is inert when Alembic is driven from its command line, and keeps `env.py`'s online path on the tested path. A supplied connection is deliberately left open, so its owner keeps control of the transaction it belongs to. | `env.py` now has two connection sources. The command-line path is unchanged and is exercised by the `alembic upgrade head` gate. |
| 19.5 | Read `config.attributes["configure_logger"]` so a caller can leave the configuration file's logging section unapplied | Always call `fileConfig` | `fileConfig` replaces the handlers on the root logger and sets its level, which would displace the handlers pytest installs and make the grant's audit record unobservable by `caplog` — and would additionally perturb the logging-configuration cases in `test_settings_and_redaction.py`. The flag defaults to applying the section, so the command-line behaviour and the `[logger_alembic]` INFO level that makes the grant auditable are unchanged. | A caller could suppress logging configuration in a context where it was wanted. Only the test fixture sets it. |
| 19.6 | Verify the revisions against in-memory SQLite in the suite, and against PostgreSQL 13 through the `alembic` command line as a separate gate | (a) Run the suite's migration cases against PostgreSQL; (b) verify on SQLite only | (a) would make every migration case depend on a running database server, so a suite failure and an unavailable service would produce the same signal, and the cases could not run in an environment without PostgreSQL. (b) alone would leave the production dialect unexercised. Revision 0001 already uses `op.batch_alter_table` with explicitly named constraints, which is the portable form, and the installed SQLite is 3.50.4, which supports `ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN` — so the downgrade path is genuinely exercised rather than skipped. Both dialects were run: 15 suite cases on SQLite, and `upgrade head` → repeat `upgrade head` → `downgrade -1` → `downgrade -1` → `upgrade head` on PostgreSQL, ending with one administrator and no other account. | The two dialects could diverge on a future revision. The command-line gate is what detects that, and it is the gate AAP §0.10.1 already defines. |
| 19.7 | Supersede row 17.2: the suite now drives Alembic **in addition to** building the schema from `Base.metadata` | Replace the metadata-built schema with a migration-built one for every test | Row 17.2 kept the two signals separate so that a unit-test failure and a migration failure stay distinguishable, and that reasoning still holds — migrating for all 1100-odd cases would couple them and slow every test by a schema migration. What row 17.2 got wrong was treating the migration gate as adequate on its own: it was a manual command nothing asserted, so the additive defaults, the idempotence, the partial-schema path, the reversibility and the sole-admin post-condition were all claims rather than facts. The migration cases now assert them in one module, and the ordinary fixtures are untouched. | Two schema-construction paths exist in the suite. `test_upgrade_applies_over_the_schema_preceding_it` and the default-value cases are what keep the migrations and `Base.metadata` in agreement. |
| 19.8 | Add a `migrated_client` fixture and prove the three sole-admin properties together in `test_mass_assignment.py` | Prove the administrator count in the migration module alone and leave `test_mass_assignment.py` asserting only the fixture-seeded rows | Rule 3's review entry #2 assigns the Security reviewer three checks that belong together: exactly one administrative account exists after migration, every other account carries the default role, and a registration carrying a role field still yields the default. Split across two modules with two different databases, a reviewer cannot see them hold at once. Binding a test client to the migrated database lets one case assert all three against the state a deployment actually has. | The fixture overrides the application's session dependency, so a case may use `client` or `migrated_client` but not both. No case uses both. |
| 19.9 | **Name restated — see §27.2.** Rename `test_the_only_administrator_is_the_seeded_account` to `test_an_escalating_registration_adds_no_administrative_row` | Leave the name and add the migration case beside it | The old name claimed the sole-administrator post-condition while the body read back `admin_user`, a fixture row under `admin@example.com` that no migration produces — so the name asserted a property the case could not establish. The new name states what the body proves, and its docstring points at the case that proves the post-condition. | A reader following the old name finds nothing. The rename is recorded here for that reason. |

## 21. Rationale relocated out of application-source comments (second pass)

A re-review found rationale still embedded across the application source, at locations
§10 had not reached. The boundary test in §10.17 was applied again and **tightened**: a
purpose clause of the form "so <benefit or threat>" is now treated as rationale even
where the clause following it describes behaviour, because the connective asserts that
the behaviour is *the reason for* the construct. Each such clause was rewritten as a
plain statement of the behaviour, or the reasoning was moved here.

Each row names what the code now says and the reasoning that was removed from it.

| # | Location | Reasoning removed from the comment |
|---|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 21.1 | `backend/app/core/config.py` — `UNBOUNDED_RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_SCHEMES` | The bounded scheme is excluded from the unbounded set *because* `rate_limit.py` caps its tracked-key count; the exclusion is what makes the deployable set safe to widen. |
| 21.2 | `backend/app/core/config.py` — `MAX_PAGINATION_OFFSET` | The ceiling is the 64-bit signed maximum *so that* an offset above it is refused by request validation instead of reaching SQL and failing at the driver, where the error text would carry the bound value. |
| 21.3 | `backend/app/core/config.py` — `_check_rate_limit_sharing` | An unbounded in-process scheme is refused *because* it holds one counter per caller address with no ceiling, which is a memory-exhaustion path; and the in-process record exists *so that* an operator running more than one process can see that a limit of *N* has become *N × processes*. Row 2.5 is the decision. |
| 21.4 | `backend/app/core/security.py` — module docstring | The claimed role is recorded on `request.state` *so that* a refusal can name claimed-versus-effective, which is the audit signal for an escalation attempt; and `verify_credential` equalises its work *so that* the elapsed time discloses neither account existence nor the stored cost factor. Rows 4.2 and 5.2 are the decisions. |
| 21.5 | `backend/app/core/authorization.py` — module docstring | The entitlement is derived from the subscription row rather than read off the user *because* deriving it means the grant lapses with the row and nothing has to demote the account; a stored subscriber role is credited only at baseline *so that* a decision turning on such a role cannot be satisfied by a stale column; and the entitlement query is skipped when the credited role already suffices *so that* a route no entitlement can affect costs nothing extra. Rows 4.1 and 4.2 are the decisions. |
| 21.6 | `backend/app/core/plans.py` — module docstring | The status values live beside the catalog *because* both the endpoint that writes the column and the authorization module that reads it need them, and this module imports nothing from the application, so colocating them creates no cycle. |
| 21.7 | `backend/app/core/logging.py` — `MIN_SECRET_VALUE_LENGTH`, `MAX_REGISTERED_SECRETS` | A short value is refused *because* replacing it literally would rewrite text that merely contains those characters; the registry is capped *so that* the per-record replacement cost stays bounded. |
| 21.8 | `backend/app/core/logging.py` — `QueueDispatchHandler` | The identifier is read on the logging thread *because* it is bound per task and per thread while the listener runs on a thread of its own; the inline fallback bounds the queue's memory *at the cost of* the caller performing that one write itself, which is the trade accepted over discarding a record. |
| 21.9 | `backend/app/main.py` — `_documentation_policy` | Inline style is admitted *because* the viewers write their styles into the page as they render it; the blob worker is admitted *because* one viewer builds it from the page to index the schema for its search; same-origin connections are admitted *so that* the page can read the schema it documents. Each is an intentional narrowing of an otherwise deny-by-default policy, accepted for the documentation route alone. |
| 21.10 | `backend/app/api/endpoints/auth.py` — module docstring, `_lock_row`, `_abandon`, `_record_failed_attempt` | The unique constraint is the authority on a taken address *so that* a race ends with the loser answered exactly as an ordinary duplicate; the row lock serialises concurrent attempts *rather than* interleaving them; a persistence failure is rolled back rather than raised *so that* a database fault never discloses that the account exists. Rows 5.1a and 5.2 are the decisions; row 5.1, which described a conditional `UPDATE` instead of this lock, is superseded. |
| 21.11 | `backend/app/api/endpoints/listings.py` — read-route docstring | An unprojectable row is skipped rather than failing the page *because* a page is more useful than a refusal and the endpoint is reachable without a credential. **Superseded: the row now fails the page — see row 28.5.** |
| 21.12 | `backend/app/api/endpoints/filters.py` — module docstring, list-route docstring | The offset bound exists *so that* an offset the database cannot bind is refused by request validation; the children of a page are loaded by two statements *so that* the statement count does not follow the page size, which is the query-count property the route is designed for. |
| 21.13 | `backend/app/api/endpoints/subscriptions.py` — module docstring, webhook docstring | Statements run on a worker thread *because* the routes are `async` and the session is synchronous, and *so that* a statement waiting on a lock never occupies the event loop that must deliver another request's awaited provider call; a repeat delivery is answered `200` *because* PayPal redelivers anything not answered `2xx`; an uncommittable transition is answered `503` *so that* a charge PayPal has taken is never silently forgotten. Rows 12.7 and 6.x are the decisions. |
| 21.14 | `backend/app/services/paypal_service.py` — module docstring | The client is asynchronous *so that* no request blocks the API event loop; the ownership lookup goes through `load_owned` *so that* the decision, route and object are recorded by the one centralized authorization path; the raw bytes are transmitted verbatim *so that* PayPal checks the signature against the notification as it arrived; the error category exists *so that* a caller can answer a dependency failure differently from a rejected request; one shared client is used *so that* pooled connections and TLS sessions serve all four operations; and no database state is touched *so that* a caller's transaction is untouched. Rows 6.7 to 6.13 are the decisions. |
| 21.15 | `backend/app/services/zillow_service.py`, `email_service.py`, `paypal_service.py` — the `register_secret_values` comments | The literal value is registered *so that* it is removed from text that names no key, provider error prose included — the specific channel by which a credential embedded in an exception message reaches a log. Row 7.x is the decision. |
| 21.16 | `backend/app/services/zillow_service.py` — `fetch_listings` | The call performs no retry, stated as a design property rather than as the observable behaviour "one request is issued and no retry follows it". |
| 21.17 | `backend/app/tasks/listing_updater.py` — module docstring, `_write` | An identity-less record is discarded *because* it cannot be reconciled on a later pass and would otherwise be inserted again on every one; each record has its own savepoint *so that* one unwritable record is dropped while the rest of the payload is still recorded; a failure is reported rather than propagated *so that* a failing provider or database never ends the schedule; and no message text is carried *so that* no provider value travels with it. |
| 21.18 | `backend/app/db/models.py` — `locked_until`, `zillow_url` | The offset is stored *so that* the comparison against the server clock needs no zone assumption; the uniqueness covers present values *so that* a row carrying no provider address stays permitted, which is what lets an ingested record exist before it has been reconciled. **The `zillow_url` half describes a uniqueness the column does not carry and never should have — see row 28.1.** |
| 21.19 | `backend/app/db/database.py` — module docstring, `engine` | The session time zone is pinned *so that* a naive `TIMESTAMP` is read back as the same instant whatever zone the server carries, which is what makes the naive columns unambiguous; `Base` is re-exported *so that* one metadata registry serves the models, the Alembic environment and the application. Row 10.10 covers `hide_parameters`. |
| 21.20 | `backend/app/schema/listing.py` — `Listing`, `ListingCreate` | Measurements must be finite *because* a JSON body carries no representation for an infinity or a NaN; the write contract refuses them *rather than* storing them, which is what makes an unprojectable stored row reachable only from outside the contract. |
| 21.21 | `backend/app/schema/subscription.py` — `Subscription`, `SubscriptionCreated` | The checkout address *belongs to* the response that opens a subscription rather than to the read projection; `approval_url` is required *so that* a generated client is told the continuation is always present. Row 6.x is the decision on refusing an order with no allowlisted approval target. |

### 21.22 Constructs deliberately retained after the second pass

Nine occurrences of a flagged connective remain in the application source. Each was
examined against §10.17 and kept, so a re-reviewer can see they were considered rather
than missed.

| Location | Text | Why it is behaviour and not rationale |
|----------|------|--------------------------------------|
| `core/security.py:24` | "verification reports a mismatch rather than raising when a stored hash cannot be parsed" | §10.17 names this exact construct as permitted: it is the function's return contract. |
| `core/logging.py:1085` | "returns the record otherwise unchanged" | "otherwise" means "in other respects", not "or else". It states what the method returns. |
| `api/endpoints/auth.py:175` | "A persistence failure is rolled back and recorded rather than raised" | The caller's observable contract: the function does not raise. |
| `services/paypal_service.py:54` | "resolves to the same order and the same capture rather than to a second charge" | The observable outcome of a repeated call. |
| `services/zillow_service.py:77` | `"Refusing to call the listing provider because the "` | A runtime log message, not a comment. It records why *this call* was refused, which is the operational audit record AAP §0.12.2 requires. |
| `tasks/listing_updater.py:17` | "discarded rather than recorded" | Contrasts two observable dispositions of a record. |
| `tasks/listing_updater.py:27` | "reported rather than propagated" | States that the failure does not reach the caller. |
| `tasks/listing_updater.py:195` | "describes the session or the database rather than the record and is raised" | States which failures raise and which return. |
| `schema/subscription.py:69` | "refused rather than returned" | States that the response is not produced. |

### 21.23 Scope of the second pass, measured

The re-review cited specific line ranges in 23 files. Every cited range was brought to
zero flagged occurrences, apart from the nine constructs §21.22 records as behavioural.
The pass was then widened once, to remove **every** remaining `so that` construct from
those same 23 files: `core/config.py`'s rate-limit pattern comment, two in `main.py`
(the counted-request attribute and the `www.` redirect note), `tasks/listing_updater.py`'s
identity-column paragraph, `.env.example`'s chunk cap, and
`api/endpoints/subscriptions.py`'s status re-export comment. `so that` now appears in none
of the 23 files.

A whole-file scan across all 49 files this work touches still reports **262** lines
carrying a `, so ` consequence connective, the great majority in files and at lines the
re-review did not flag. They were left in place, and the reason is a scope judgement
rather than an oversight: the overwhelming majority state a consequence that is itself
observable behaviour — "The session is left clean, so the request can still be answered",
"Each member's value is the string the `role` column stores, so a padded value matches
nothing" — which §10.17 permits and which the AAP's CQ2 requirement to document
non-obvious logic depends on. Rewriting 262 comment lines across 50 files carries real
regression risk in exchange for no behavioural or security gain, and the boundary between
a consequence and a justification is the judgement §10.17 exists to make reviewable. The
count is recorded here so the residual is a measured quantity rather than an unexamined
one, and so a future reviewer who wants the sweep widened can see exactly how large it is.
