## 23. Planned-versus-actual file inventory, and the direct `limits` pin

Rule 1's traceability clause requires 100% coverage with no gaps, so the set of paths
this work actually touches has to be reconcilable against the AAP's planned mapping.
This section is that reconciliation, and it distinguishes a **planned** entry from a
**delivered** one.

> **Authority moved.** When this section was written it was the authority the
> traceability matrix drew its actual-changed-files figures from. It is no longer:
> [§35.28](#8228-the-rebuilt-planned-versus-actual-inventory) rebuilt those figures
> against the delivered tree and is now the only authority any other document should
> quote. This section is retained for the reasoning in §23.2 and §23.3, which still
> holds, and for the withdrawn measurement in §23.1, which Rule 1 requires stay
> visible rather than be edited away.

### 23.1 The counts

> **Superseded by [§35.28](#8228-the-rebuilt-planned-versus-actual-inventory).** Every
> figure in this subsection was measured mid-project and none of them describes the
> delivered tree: the count of changed paths, the planned-and-delivered count, the
> unplanned count, the pending count and the projected total are all stale, and the
> claim that all nine REFERENCE paths remain unmodified is false — one of them was
> modified by a later round, which §35.27 records. The subsection is kept unedited
> because Rule 1 requires a withdrawn measurement and the reason it was withdrawn to
> stay visible; §35.28 carries the rebuilt figures and is the only authority any other
> document should quote. The one statement below that still holds is the distinction
> the last paragraph of this box draws: 68 counts plan entries, not changed files.

Measured with `git diff --name-only <baseline> HEAD` plus the working tree and the
untracked set, against the 59 implementation and deliverable paths AAP §0.6.1.1 to
§0.6.1.6 enumerate:

| Quantity | Count |
|---|---|
| Paths the AAP plans (§0.6.1.1–§0.6.1.6) | **59** |
| Paths actually changed so far | **58** |
| — of those, planned and delivered | **47** |
| — of those, unplanned | **11** |
| Planned paths still pending | **12** |

The AAP's own headline of **68** entries is 59 planned changes plus the 9 REFERENCE
paths of §0.6.1.7, which are read and never modified. All 9 remain unmodified, verified
by their absence from the changed set. The two numbers are therefore not interchangeable,
and a traceability matrix must not present 68 as a count of changed files.

Landing all 12 pending planned paths with the 11 unplanned ones in place gives **70**
changed paths, not 59. That is the figure downstream documents must use.

### 23.2 The 11 unplanned paths

> **Extended, not superseded.** The eleven rows below are still accurate about the
> eleven paths they describe, and each remains in the delivered tree. Twenty-one
> further unplanned paths were added after this subsection was written — two by the
> round that wrote row 31.11 and nineteen by the round that wrote §35 — bringing the
> total to **32**. [§35.28](#8228-the-rebuilt-planned-versus-actual-inventory)
> enumerates all thirty-two in one place.

Each is recorded with why it exists and what carrying it costs. Reverting them was
considered as a whole and rejected: two are load-bearing at runtime, one is required by
a build, and eight hold passing regression coverage whose removal would lower assurance
to satisfy a count.

| # | Path | Why it exists | Risk of keeping it |
|---|------|---------------|--------------------|
| 23.2.1 | `backend/.dockerignore` | Row 11.3. The AAP names only the repository-root `.dockerignore`, but its own documented build command uses `backend/` as the context, and Docker reads the ignore file from the context root. Honouring only the literal path would leave INFRA-3 open for the documented build. | Two files to keep in agreement. Parity is verified by `diff`. |
| 23.2.2 | `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py` | The AAP requires a rate limiter on the credential endpoints and refuses unbounded in-process storage outside `local` (row 2.5). `slowapi`'s own `MemoryStorage` has no key ceiling, so the bounded storage the setting `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_TRACKED_KEYS` promises has to be built somewhere. Folding it into `auth.py` or `main.py` would put storage construction inside a route module or the application assembly, and `config.py` already documents this module by name at four places. | One module the AAP does not enumerate, and the direct dependency in row 23.3. Covered by `test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py` and `test_settings_and_redaction.py`. |
| 23.2.3 | `frontend/package-lock.json` | Created by environment setup, not by this work. `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend:11` runs `npm ci`, which fails without a lock file, and the CI workflow assumes one. AAP §0.9.2 lists the absent lock file as a flagged finding to report rather than fix — but it had already been generated and committed before this checkpoint, so the choice here is whether to *delete* it, which would reopen the finding it closes. | A frontend artifact inside a backend-scoped change. It is a lock file only: `frontend/package.json` is unmodified, verified by `git diff`. |
| 23.2.4 | `backend/tests/security/test_token_hardening.py` | Token forgery coverage beyond the planned `test_jwt_hardening.py`. | Suite runtime. No production code depends on it. |
| 23.2.5 | `backend/tests/security/test_authorization.py` | Unit-level coverage of `authorization.py` itself, which the planned `test_rbac_matrix.py` reaches only through routes. | As above. |
| 23.2.6 | `backend/tests/security/test_payment_lifecycle.py` | Order, capture and settlement coverage of the rewritten PayPal service. | As above. |
| 23.2.7 | `backend/tests/security/test_login_throttling_and_timing.py` | Timing-equalisation and rate-limiter coverage beyond the planned lockout module. | Deliberately accumulates limiter counts; see row 17.10. |
| 23.2.8 | `backend/tests/security/test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py` | Body-cap, pagination-bound and refusal-shape coverage, including `rate_limit.py`. | As above. |
| 23.2.9 | `backend/tests/security/test_settings_and_redaction.py` | Settings-validator and log-redaction coverage. | As above. |
| 23.2.10 | `backend/tests/security/test_application_surface.py` | Route inventory, security headers, CORS and health-endpoint coverage. | As above. |
| 23.2.11 | `backend/tests/security/test_migrations.py` | **Added by this round.** The re-review found that nothing executed either Alembic revision, so the additive defaults, the idempotence, the reversibility and the sole-admin post-condition were claims rather than facts. No planned module covers migration execution. See §19. | As above. Runs against in-memory SQLite and needs no service. |

### 23.3 The direct `limits` pin

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 23.3.1 | Pin `limits==4.2` directly, taking the manifest to **15** direct pins where the AAP §0.7.1 manifest lists **14** | (a) Import `MemoryStorage` through `slowapi` and leave `limits` transitive; (b) drop `rate_limit.py` and accept `slowapi`'s unbounded default storage; (c) implement bounded storage without the library | `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py:50` imports `from limits.storage import MemoryStorage` — a **direct** import, and a package that is directly imported belongs in the manifest at a pin, or an upgrade of `slowapi` can move the version underneath a subclass that depends on its internals. The package is already in the graph: `slowapi` declares `Requires: limits`, and the resolved version is 4.2 either way, so the pin adds no package and changes no resolution — `pip check` reports no broken requirements. (a) is refused because `slowapi` does not re-export the storage classes, so the import would reach into its namespace instead. (b) is refused by row 2.5. (c) would reimplement a windowed counter store, which is more code and more risk than a pin. | The manifest deviates from the AAP's stated 14-pin shape, which is why this row exists. A reviewer comparing the two counts sees the difference and the reason together. A `limits` release breaking `MemoryStorage`'s constructor would now be caught by the pin rather than absorbed silently. |

## 24. Compose runtime environment completion and build-path correction

Rationale for the changes to `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml`. Rows 24.4 and
24.5 **reverse** positions §16 took, and both §16 rows now carry a pointer here so the
earlier position and its reversal stay visible.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 24.1 | Name **12** settings as required interpolations (`${NAME:?message}`) rather than the 2 the file carried | (a) Mount a runtime `.env` into the container; (b) bake defaults into the compose file; (c) name only the 7 settings `Settings` declares without a default | `Settings` declares 7 fields with no default, so the file supplied 2 of 7 and the container could not start. Measurement then showed 7 is still not enough: `ZILLOW_API_URL` and `FROM_EMAIL` carry `example.com` defaults the validators refuse outside `local`, and `PAYPAL_RETURN_URL`/`PAYPAL_CANCEL_URL` carry plaintext-localhost defaults refused the same way (row 2.4). `ENVIRONMENT` is named too, because every one of those refusals turns on it and a deployment must declare which environment it is rather than inherit `development` by omission. (a) is refused because `backend/.dockerignore` correctly excludes `.env` from the image and mounting it would put a credential file back on the deployment surface. (b) would commit credentials, which is the C-4 finding itself. The `:?` form was chosen over `:-` for every one of the twelve so that a missing value ends the run with a named message instead of starting a container that fails validation later. | Twelve variables an operator must export or supply from a secret store. All twelve are documented in `.env.example`, and the failure is a named render-time error rather than a silent misconfiguration. |
| 24.2 | Give `PAYPAL_MODE` and `PAYPAL_API_BASE` overridable sandbox defaults | Leave them unset and let the settings defaults apply | The production guard refuses `ENVIRONMENT=production` while either still names sandbox. Without a way to set them from the compose environment, a production deployment could not start at all — the guard would be a dead end rather than a control. Naming them with sandbox defaults keeps the guard effective and makes satisfying it possible. Verified: `production` + `live` constructs, `production` + sandbox is still refused. | An operator could set the mode live while leaving live credentials unset. The credentials are required interpolations, so they cannot be absent. |
| 24.3 | Default `ALLOWED_HOSTS` to `backend,localhost,127.0.0.1` and `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` to `http://localhost,http://localhost:80` | Leave the settings defaults in place | `TrustedHostGateMiddleware` binds `settings.ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`main.py:1084`), whose default is `localhost,127.0.0.1`. The frontend container addresses `http://backend:8000`, so every one of its calls would have been refused on the `Host` header — the middleware would have looked like a fault rather than a control. `localhost` stays in the list because the compose health check sends it. The browser origin for a service published on port 80 is `http://localhost`, which the settings default did not carry. | Both are widened relative to the settings defaults, and both are overridable. Neither admits a wildcard. |
| 24.4 | **Reversal of the frontend half of row 16.10.** Replace `REACT_APP_API_URL=http://backend:5000` with `REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL=http://backend:8000`. **Both the address and the delivery form this row records were superseded — see row 27.8.** | Leave it, as row 16.10 ruled | Row 16.10 declined the change on the ground that the line sits in a frozen service block, is not security-relevant, and was already broken. The first two hold; the third is what makes the position untenable. `frontend/src/services/api.ts:6` reads `REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL`, so the old name was never read by anything, and the port named a listener that does not exist. Leaving a line that is both misnamed and misaddressed makes the deployment description of this system false, which Rule 2 requires it not be. The change is a name and a port; no service block key was added or removed. | Create-React-App inlines `REACT_APP_*` at build time and `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` declares no matching `ARG`, so the value still does not reach the bundle. That file is an AAP §0.6.1.7 REFERENCE path and is out of scope; the residual gap is reported, not fixed, and is unchanged from before. |
| 24.5 | **Reversal of row 16.11.** Point `dockerfile:` at `../infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend` and `../infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` | Leave `dockerfile: Dockerfile`, as row 16.11 ruled | Row 16.11 declined the change because the field is not enumerated in AAP §0.6.3 and blocks neither verification gate. Both remain true, and both are beside the point: the field names a file that does not exist, so `docker compose build` cannot build either service. A compose file that cannot build the images it describes is not a usable deployment description. Each new value resolves from its own build context — Compose resolves `dockerfile` relative to `context`, so from `../../backend` the value reaches `<repo>/infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend`. The build **contexts** are untouched, which matters because row 9.2 records that Docker resolves `.dockerignore` from the context root; changing a context would silently reopen INFRA-3. | The Dockerfile now sits outside its build context. That is supported — the client reads the Dockerfile itself and only the context is transferred — and it is the same arrangement the AAP's own documented `docker build -f` command uses. |

## 25. The administrative seed revision and its migration tests

Rows added for the review that raised two findings against the administrative seed: that `backend/migrations/versions/0002_seed_single_admin.py` could reach Alembic head with zero administrators, and that no test executed that revision at all. That review numbered its findings per-review, so these rows cite behaviour and other rows of this log rather than an identifier. The deviation from the revision's own implementation brief is row 11.8; the rows below are the implementation and test decisions that sit underneath it.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 25.1 | Provision the target address from inside the seed revision, immediately before the grant statement | (a) Seed it from a separate operator script or a one-off management command; (b) seed it from `0001` alongside the `role` column; (c) grant the role to whichever account happens to exist, such as the lowest identifier; (d) make the address configurable so a deployment names an account it has already created | (a) and (b) both break the property AAP §0.5.1.3 calls the control: "the grant lives in its own revision with its own log line and its own assertion". A script outside the migration chain is not applied by `alembic upgrade head`, so the postcondition would hold only when someone remembered to run it, and folding it into `0001` would put the grant in the same revision as the additive DDL, which is exactly what the AAP separates. (c) is an escalation route: it would grant administrative privilege to an account chosen by insertion order, which an attacker who registers first can influence. (d) is the configurable-target route AAP §0.5.1.3 forecloses, because anyone able to set an environment variable during a migration run could name their own address. Provisioning inside the revision keeps the grant, the address and the assertion in one auditable place and makes the postcondition hold unconditionally. | The revision writes a row on a table `0001` owns. It writes only the three columns `users` declares `NOT NULL` without a default, so it depends on `0001`'s `role` and `failed_login_attempts` defaults being in place — which the `down_revision` chain guarantees and which the migration tests assert. |
| 25.2 | **Superseded by row 19.2 — see §27.1.** Store a credential built from `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` that the module hashes and then discards | (a) A fixed placeholder password documented in the runbook; (b) a password generated and then logged or printed for the operator; (c) a sentinel that is not a bcrypt hash at all, such as `!`, so no candidate can ever parse against it; (d) leave `hashed_password` empty | (a) is a default credential: the value would live in version control and in every clone, which is the class of defect C-4 and C-1 exist to close. (b) writes a secret to a migration log, which the redacting logger and finding M-4 exist to prevent, and migration output lands in CI logs. (c) and (d) are both unusable in the right direction but introduce a **timing oracle**: `verify_password` returns `False` immediately for a hash bcrypt cannot parse, and `verify_credential` measures its floor from a real hash at the configured cost, so the one address whose stored value is unparseable would be distinguishable from every other address by how long a failed login takes — reopening half of M-1 for the single most interesting account in the system. A well-formed bcrypt hash over a discarded random value is unreachable by any password *and* indistinguishable in cost from a real one. Measured: the provisioned hash carries the `$2b$12$` prefix, and `verify_password` returns `False` for the address itself, for `admin`, for `password`, for the empty string and for the suite's own valid password. | The account cannot be signed in to until a password reset is performed out of band, and this revision provides no reset path. That is the intended posture — the grant creates a role, not an active session — but it must be stated to an operator, which is the rotation runbook's job. |
| 25.3 | **Superseded — see §27.1.** Moot once row 19.2 stands: the revision stores no bcrypt hash, so no cost factor is chosen. Let `bcrypt.gensalt()` supply the cost factor rather than reading `settings.BCRYPT_ROUNDS` | (a) Import the application settings and use the configured value; (b) import `get_password_hash` from `backend/app/core/security.py`; (c) hardcode a local cost constant | (a) and (b) both import `backend/app/**` into a revision, which the revision's brief forbids and which would couple a frozen migration to code that keeps changing — and (a) additionally pulls the whole settings validator chain into every migration run. Measured: `bcrypt.gensalt()` produces `$2b$12$`, and `Settings.BCRYPT_ROUNDS` is `Field(12, ge=10, le=15)`, so the library default already equals the application default. A local constant would be a third place to keep in agreement. `verify_credential` pads every check to a floor measured at the configured cost, so even a deployment that raised `BCRYPT_ROUNDS` sees no timing difference for this one row. | A future bcrypt release that changed its default cost would silently change this hash's cost. It would remain a valid, unreachable bcrypt hash, and the padding keeps the timing property either way. |
| 25.4 | Insert the row naming no `role`, and let the same single conditional `UPDATE` promote it | Insert the row with `role` already set to `admin` | Two write sites for the administrative value would mean two places a reviewer has to check, and the brief's whole legibility requirement is that the grant is one greppable statement. Letting the row take `0001`'s `registered` default also exercises that default, so a database whose `role` column somehow lacks it fails loudly on the `NOT NULL` constraint instead of silently accepting a null role. | The provisioned account exists at `registered` for the duration of one statement inside a transaction that has not committed, which no reader can observe. |
| 25.5 | Assert the exact identity postcondition — the addresses holding `admin` must equal `[ADMIN_EMAIL]` — in place of the three-way count tier | (a) Keep counting and add a separate "and the holder is the target" check; (b) assert the count alone, as the previous tier did | A count of one is satisfied by *any* single administrator, including one an attacker or a stray `UPDATE` created, and the review's requirement is literally "assert that the sole admin is `test@blitzy.com`". Reading the addresses answers both questions — how many, and which — in one statement, so there is no ordering between two checks to get wrong. It also subsumes the old at-most-one tier: two holders and one wrong holder both fail the same comparison. | The query returns addresses rather than a count, so its result grows with the number of administrators. That number is asserted to be one, and the comparison happens before anything is logged. |
| 25.6 | Name only the count and the target address in the refusal message, never the conflicting addresses | (a) List every address holding the role, which is what an operator debugging the failure wants; (b) name nothing at all beyond "post-condition failed" | (a) writes other users' addresses into migration output that lands in CI logs, and this repository redacts credential-adjacent values from application logs for the same reason. An operator holding the failure can run the query themselves against the database they are migrating. (b) leaves no way to tell a two-administrator conflict from a wrong-holder conflict. The delivered message states the count and whether the target is among the holders, which distinguishes every reachable failure. | An operator must run one query to learn which other account holds the role. Verified that the message names the count and the target and no other address. |
| 25.7 | `downgrade` demotes the account and never deletes it, including the row `upgrade` provisioned | Delete the row when this revision was the one that created it | A downgrade that deletes a `users` row destroys data: by the time anyone downgrades, that account may own filters and subscriptions through `ON DELETE`-less foreign keys, and the row may have been given a real password. AAP §0.6.1.3 specifies the downgrade as "demotes back to `registered`", and demotion is the exact inverse of the grant — the only thing this revision is authorised to have changed about an account that already existed. | `alembic downgrade -1` followed by `upgrade head` leaves one row rather than returning to an empty table. Measured on PostgreSQL: the round trip re-promotes the same row, skips provisioning and ends with exactly one administrator. |
| 25.8 | Log the resulting administrator count on the downgrade path too, and do not assert it | (a) Log the demotion alone, as before; (b) assert the count is zero after demoting | (a) leaves an auditor unable to confirm from the log that the demotion actually left no administrator. (b) would wedge a downgrade on a database where an operator had deliberately created a second administrator — a state this revision refuses to *create* but has no mandate to *destroy*, since its downgrade "touches no other account". Logging the count reports the outcome without taking that decision. | A downgrade can complete with a non-zero administrator count when another account holds the role. The count in the record is what makes that visible. |
| 25.9 | Cover the revision in a new `backend/tests/security/test_admin_seed_migration.py` rather than extending `test_mass_assignment.py` | (a) Add the cases to `test_mass_assignment.py`, which already holds the no-escalation negative; (b) add them to `test_api.py`; (c) leave the revision to the manual `alembic upgrade head` gate, as its brief assumed | The review asked for a dedicated module "preferably", and the reason it is the right call is unit boundaries: `test_mass_assignment.py`'s unit is the request contract and every one of its cases goes through the HTTP client, whereas these cases drive a migration against a bare connection and never build an application. Mixing them would give one module two harnesses and two units. (b) has the same problem at greater scale. (c) is what produced the finding: a gate nobody automated is a gate that reported zero administrators as a pass for two rounds. | One more module in a folder the AAP enumerated. The count is recorded here rather than treated as a silent addition. |
| 25.10 | Drive the revision's `upgrade` and `downgrade` in-process through `Operations.context(MigrationContext.configure(connection))` | (a) Shell out to `alembic upgrade head` against a real database from the test; (b) call `alembic.command.upgrade` with a programmatic `Config`; (c) copy the revision's SQL into the test and assert on that | (a) needs a live PostgreSQL server, which the folder's constraints forbid ("no external database, no network access"), and would make a unit failure and an unavailable server the same signal. (b) runs `migrations/env.py`, which builds the application engine from `settings.DATABASE_URL` and would connect to whatever that names — the same problem with more indirection. (c) tests a copy, which is the classic way for a test to pass while the code is wrong. Alembic's documented out-of-band operations context runs the revision's own functions against a connection the test owns, so every line under review executes and nothing outside the test does. | The harness depends on Alembic's operations-context API. The pin is exact, and the surrounding transaction is opened and rolled back by the test so the semantics match a real migration run. |
| 25.11 | Load the revision through `ScriptDirectory.from_config`, with the ini path built from the `REPO_ROOT` that `backend/tests/conftest.py` resolves from its own `__file__` | (a) `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` on the version file directly; (b) add the versions directory to `sys.path` and import by module name; (c) build the ini path relative to the working directory | The filename begins with a digit, so it is not importable by name — which rules out (b) and is why (a) would need a hand-built path. Going through `ScriptDirectory` additionally exercises the real wiring: it reads `backend/alembic.ini`, resolves `script_location`, and fails loudly if the revision identifier, the filename or the `down_revision` chain drift from what `alembic upgrade head` would use. (c) breaks under `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which runs pytest from `backend`; reusing the shared `REPO_ROOT` keeps one definition of where the repository is instead of a second one that could disagree with the `sys.path` bootstrap. | The tests fail if `alembic.ini` moves. That is the intended signal, and the chain assertion names it directly. |
| 25.12 | Build the test schema from `Base.metadata` and drive only revision `0002` | (a) Run `0001` first, then `0002`, so the chain is exercised end to end; (b) run `alembic upgrade head` against SQLite | (a) cannot work on the in-memory database this module uses: `0001`'s downgrade drops columns, and its `batch_alter_table` uniqueness work is written for a real dialect — a failure there would be a SQLite artefact reported against `0002`. (b) is (a) plus `env.py`. `Base.metadata` already carries the `role` column with its `registered` server default and the `failed_login_attempts` default, which is everything `0002` reads, and row 17.2 made the same choice for the same reason. The chain itself is asserted structurally by the head-and-`down_revision` case, and end to end by the PostgreSQL migration gate. | The metadata and `0001` could drift. The PostgreSQL `upgrade head` / `downgrade -1` gate is what detects that, and it is where this change was verified. |
| 25.13 | Read state back with parameterised SQL on the migration connection rather than through an ORM session | Query through a `sessionmaker` bound to the same engine, as the shared fixtures do | The subject under test writes SQL, and the properties being asserted are stored-column properties: which role each row holds, that a hash was not rewritten, that no row was deleted. Reading through the ORM would add identity-map and expiry behaviour between the assertion and the column, and would need `expire_all` bookkeeping around every migration run. Reading on the same connection also means the refusal cases observe exactly the state the rolled-back transaction left. | The module does not exercise the ORM mappings. Every other module in this folder does. |
| 25.14 | Assert the provisioned credential through the application's own `verify_password` | (a) Assert only that the stored value looks like a bcrypt hash; (b) call `bcrypt.checkpw` directly | (a) proves the shape and not the property: a hash of a known password looks identical. (b) tests bcrypt rather than the login path. `verify_password` is what `verify_credential` calls on every login, so asserting that it refuses a list of plausible candidates is an assertion about the door an attacker would actually try. | The case depends on the application module, so it fails if that import breaks — which is a signal worth having. |
| 25.15 | **Name restated — see §27.2.** Rename `SEEDED_ADMINISTRATORS` to `FIXTURE_ADMINISTRATORS` and `test_the_only_administrator_is_the_seeded_account` to `test_an_escalating_registration_adds_no_administrative_row` in `test_mass_assignment.py`, changing no assertion | (a) Leave both names and rely on the new module to supply the missing coverage; (b) change the case to assert against the migration's target address | The review recorded that the fixture-based case "creates false confidence because it cannot execute or detect migration behavior", and the word *seeded* is where that confidence came from: it reads as the administrator the seed revision grants, while the assertion is against `admin@example.com`, which `conftest.py` stores. (a) leaves the misleading name in place next to a module that now covers the real thing. (b) would be wrong — this case's subject is registration, not migration, and pointing it at `test@blitzy.com` would make it fail for reasons that have nothing to do with mass assignment. Renaming states what the case proves and leaves the proof itself byte-identical. | The names are a traceability-matrix input, and `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` is not written yet. It should cite the new names; both are recorded here so there is no ambiguity about which case verifies which property. |

## 26. Hardening the security regression suite itself

Rows added by a code review of the test files rather than of the service. It
raised ten findings: the two Alembic revisions were applied by no test, no
negative proved that an invalid setting stops real startup, one assertion
forbade response fields the AAP permits, the shared rate-limit counters were
cleared only on request, the SendGrid failure branch asserted nothing about what
it logged, the throttle assertion was indistinguishable from the account
lockout, one subprocess call carried no bound, the settings bootstrap inherited
whatever the machine exported, the concurrent replay branch was untested, and
`conftest.py` was executed under two module names. Every fix landed in
`backend/tests/**`; **no file under `backend/app/**` or `backend/migrations/**`
was changed in this round**, which row 26.17 records deliberately. That review's
finding numbers are per-review, so these rows cite behaviour and cite row
numbers from this log.

Two earlier rows are revisited here rather than edited in place, so the earlier
position and its reversal both stay visible: row 17.10 is corrected by row 19.3,
and row 17.2 is upheld and reconciled by rows 19.4 and 19.16.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 26.1 | Move every value the test modules share out of `conftest.py` into a new `backend/tests/support.py`, imported under exactly one name, and add a permanent case asserting one module object holds them | (a) Keep importing `conftest` and `backend.tests.conftest`, as five modules did; (b) add `backend/tests/__init__.py` so pytest imports the conftest under one package name; (c) add a pytest configuration file setting `importmode=importlib`; (d) duplicate the constants in each module | Measured, not inferred: a module doing `import backend.tests.conftest` during a real run left `sys.modules` holding both `backend.tests.conftest` and `conftest` as **two distinct objects**, with `SAME ForgedTokenFactory CLASS: False` — so a class imported directly was not the class the fixtures produced, and an `isinstance` or identity assertion could disagree with itself for reasons no case could see. (a) is the defect. (b) is refused for the reason row 17.1 gives: no `__init__.py` exists anywhere in this repository outside the one the AAP authorises. (c) is refused because no pytest configuration file is authorised. (d) copies a contract into ten places. `support.py` imports nothing from `backend.app`, which is what lets `conftest.py` import it *before* it applies the settings the application reads at import. | Two files now hold shared test state. The guard case is what stops a conftest import returning, and it asserts on `sys.modules` directly rather than on a convention. |
| 26.2 | **Deviation from row 17.3.** Assign all thirty-six settings unconditionally at bootstrap instead of `os.environ.setdefault`, and pin all thirty-six rather than ten | (a) Keep `setdefault`; (b) pass `_env_file=None` at each construction; (c) delete the offending names from `os.environ` at bootstrap | Row 17.3 chose `setdefault` so that a genuinely exported variable stays in place — "hermetic by default and overridable on purpose". Two measurements overturn that. First, the previous bootstrap does not merely absorb an ambient value, it **fails**: under a hostile environment exporting `ENVIRONMENT=production` the settings construction raised and the child exited 1, where the forced bootstrap exits 0 with `ENVIRONMENT='local'`. Second, only ten of the thirty-six fields were pinned at all, so the git-excluded repository `.env` was supplying nineteen of them — the suite's configuration was partly the developer's. A regression suite whose result depends on the machine it runs on cannot be the evidence that a control works. Assignment makes the suite's configuration the suite's own; the whole suite was then re-run with the repository `.env` renamed away and ten hostile values exported, giving a result identical to the baseline. (b) touches every construction site and leaves the ambient value visible to everything else. (c) has to enumerate what to delete, which is the same list, expressed as a subtraction. | A setting can no longer be overridden from the environment for a suite run, which is the point. A case needing a different value states it in the case; the startup harness of row 19.7 hands its child a complete environment of its own for exactly that reason. The thirty-six values must track the settings class — a field added without one fails construction at collection, loudly. |
| 26.3 | **Correction to row 17.10.** Clear the shared limiter counters from an autouse function-scoped fixture, and keep `reset_rate_limits` as a name a case can still declare | (a) Leave the reset opt-in and add the fixture to the modules that omitted it; (b) reset inside the `client` fixture only; (c) give each module its own autouse reset | Row 17.10 refused an autouse reset because `test_login_throttling_and_timing.py::TestRateLimiterEngages` "deliberately accumulates counts against it" and a parent-conftest reset "would clear them and make that case unable to fail". Re-measured: that module carries its **own** autouse counter reset which already clears before and after each case, and it accumulates only *within* one case body — which a function-scoped reset around the case never touches. The premise was wrong, and row 17.10's own stated risk — "a case that forgets the fixture can be throttled by an earlier one" — is precisely what the review found, as a result that changed with collection order. Proven by A/B on a two-case module: with the autouse reset both pass; with it shadowed out the second fails. (a) leaves the next module one omission away from the same defect. (b) misses cases that drive the limiter without the client. (c) is (a) restated per module. | A case that meant to inherit counts from a previous case cannot. None does, and the module that accumulates counts builds them inside its own body. |
| 26.4 | Cover the two revisions in a dedicated `backend/tests/security/test_migrations.py` with its own isolated file-backed databases, leaving `session_factory` untouched | (a) Change `session_factory` to run `alembic upgrade head`; (b) assert the revisions by reading their source; (c) rely on the AAP's command-line gate alone | Row 17.2 keeps unit-test schema creation off Alembic so that a migration failure and a unit-test failure stay distinct signals, and names its own risk: "the metadata and the migrations could drift apart. No automated gate existed — the review found the revisions applied by no test at all, and the administrative seed asserted only against a fixture-created row. A dedicated module supplies the missing gate without disturbing row 17.2's separation, so both properties hold at once. (b) proves nothing about what a revision does to a database. (c) runs one database in one state and asserts nothing about pre-existing rows, server defaults, uniqueness, idempotency, the absent-target path or the exactly-one post-condition. | The module needs a file-backed database and SQLite's `DROP COLUMN`, present since 3.35 and measured here on 3.50.4. Mutation-tested: changing the seeded address fails the case that names it. | A revision that renames a constant fails at attribute access rather than at an assertion. That is the intended signal, and the message names the attribute. |
| 26.6 | **Deviation.** Assert that a response carries its declared members, plus a recursive walk proving no stored hash appears at any depth, instead of exact key-set equality | (a) Keep exact equality; (b) drop the key assertion; (c) assert equality against a published field list | The AAP freezes the login shape three times over and each time adds "Fields may be added; none may be removed" (§0.8.1.3, §0.9.1, §0.12.1). Exact equality forbids the additions the AAP permits, so the assertion contradicted the contract it existed to protect — and `test_api.py` already asserted the same contract as a subset, so the suite disagreed with itself in two places. Mutation-tested in all four directions: a declared member renamed away fails; an added member passes; a hash disclosed under a declared name fails; a hash disclosed under an undeclared name nested at depth fails. (b) loses the removal signal, which is the half of the contract that is frozen. (c) is exact equality with an extra indirection. | An added field is no longer surfaced by this case. The recursive secret walk is what stops an added field carrying something it should not, and it now catches disclosure under a key no list would have named. |
| 26.7 | Prove that an invalid setting stops startup by importing the application in a **fresh child interpreter**, alongside the existing in-process construction cases rather than in place of them | (a) `importlib.reload` the configuration module; (b) keep only the existing `Settings(**values)` cases; (c) call an application factory with injected settings | The module's own brief forbids importing the constructed `settings` singleton and forbids forcing an in-process re-import; a fresh child interpreter is neither, and it is the only surface that can observe the gap the review named. The child runs in a temporary working directory, so the relative path `Settings.Config.env_file` names resolves to nothing and the repository's own file cannot rescue a case; it receives a complete valid baseline plus one hostile override, so each refusal is attributable to that override alone; and it prints its marker only after the import returns, so "did not start" is observed rather than assumed. Four further mutations of the configuration module were each caught by both surfaces, which is what shows the new cases are an independent dimension and not duplicates. | Thirty-two child interpreters are the slowest cases in the suite. | 26.8 | Give every subprocess wait a finite bound and convert expiry into an explicit failed-startup assertion naming the module and the bound | (a) Leave `subprocess.run` unbounded; (b) install `pytest-timeout`; (c) bound the whole session in CI | An unbounded child holds the suite open with no diagnostic at all, which is the one failure mode a test suite must not have. `pytest-timeout` is not installed, and adding a plugin is a dependency change no finding names. | 26.9 | Read what the SendGrid failure actually emitted by giving the real redacting handler a buffer of its own through the public `Handler.setStream` | (a) `capfd`; (b) attach a second handler carrying the same formatter; (c) assert on `caplog` records only | `capfd` was tried first and measured to be wrong for this handler: the queue listener writes to the stream object `sys.stdout` was bound to when the handler was built — at conftest import, during collection — which is pytest's *global* capture object, not the per-test file descriptor. (b) would assert against a formatter instance the application never uses, so a change to the real one would not be caught. | 26.10 | Spend the login allowance on logins that **succeed**, then assert the throttled request issues no statement against `users` and runs no credential check | (a) Keep spending it on wrong passwords; (b) widen `LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` or narrow `RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN` for the case; (c) spend it against a fresh unknown address per request | `RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN` admits five and `LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` locks at five, so five wrong passwords spend the allowance and lock the account at the same moment — and the neighbouring case already proves the **locked** handler leaves the count and the lock unchanged, which was the whole of what the throttle case asserted past its status code. The two controls were indistinguishable. A successful login returns the count to zero, so the row is provably unlocked when the throttled request arrives, and that request carries the correct password, so absent the throttle it would answer 200 rather than another 401. Measured contrast: the throttled request executes **no SQL at all** and makes no credential call, because the gate refuses it at the transport boundary before routing, where the locked path reads the row and runs one check and two comparisons. (b) would make the case prove something about a configuration the service does not run. (c) leaves no row to assert anything about. | The case depends on a successful login clearing the count, which its own neighbour asserts independently. |
| 26.11 | Reproduce a concurrent duplicate delivery with a controlled-session barrier that resolves the second flush the way the uniqueness index would, while driving the real route through the real ASGI stack | (a) Two real connections contending on the index; (b) run this module against PostgreSQL; (c) assert the concurrency at the `_in_session` unit level only; (d) leave the branch uncovered | Row 15.4 is the decision under test, and the branch it turns on — the waiter learning the right answer either way — had no coverage. (a) cannot be built on this suite's database: it is one in-memory SQLite held by a `StaticPool` single connection, so two sessions share one DBAPI connection, real contention cannot arise, SQLite reports `OperationalError: database is locked` rather than `IntegrityError`, and one session's rollback would reach the other. The barrier states exactly what the index states — refusing the waiter once the holder commits, admitting it once the holder rolls back — and everything else in the path is real: the route, the middleware stack, the signature verification, the session work and `run_in_threadpool`. The index itself is proven twice elsewhere, sequentially by the replay case and at the DDL level by the migration module's rejected duplicate insert, so nothing rests on the barrier that the barrier decides. (b) is an infrastructure change no finding names. (c) already exists for `_in_session` alone and says nothing about the route. | The barrier decides the outcome the index would decide, so a change to the constraint is not caught here — it is caught by the two cases that assert the constraint directly. Every wait is individually bounded, so a mistake in the choreography reports rather than hangs. |
| 26.12 | Drive the holder down its rollback path by failing its **commit**, rather than by failing the provider call | (a) Make the capture fail for the first delivery only; (b) deliver a notification whose application raises | The settled-capture event both deliveries carry issues no outbound capture at all — it reads the notification's own resource — so a provider failure cannot be produced on that branch without changing the event type and with it the branch under test. Making the transport diverge by call order would leave the two deliveries differing in more than one respect, and the case is about one difference. A failed commit is that one difference, it exercises a route path the service really has, and it leaves both deliveries otherwise identical. | The case depends on the reconciliation branch, which is covered on its own in `test_payment_lifecycle.py`. |
| 26.13 | Assert the contended insert waited off the event loop by **thread identity**, and bound each barrier step separately from the pair | (a) Assert only that both responses arrive; (b) measure elapsed time; (c) inspect the loop's ready queue | Both responses arriving also happens when the two deliveries never overlapped, so on its own it proves nothing about the property row 15.4 turns on. Thread identity states that property directly. Mutation-tested: with `_in_session` running its operation on the loop instead of in a worker thread, all three concurrent cases fail with the captured message "the first delivery was never released from its flush" after 30.5 seconds — bounded, never a hang, which is why each step carries its own bound rather than relying on the pair's. Elapsed time is a proxy that varies with the host. | The assertion names the worker-pool arrangement rather than the property in the abstract. A future change moving session work to a different off-loop mechanism keeps the property and keeps the case passing. |

## 27. Reconciliation of rows that no longer describe the working tree

This log accumulated over several rounds. A few rows record a position a
later round replaced, or one a later change made moot, and two rows
rename the same construct to two different names. Rule 1 requires an
abandoned position and the reason it was abandoned to stay visible, so no
row above is deleted: each is marked in place and reconciled here against
what the tree now does. Every claim below was read back from the tree
rather than carried over from the round that wrote it.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 27.1 | Row 19.2 stands: revision 0002 stores the sentinel `LOCKED_CREDENTIAL = "!locked-no-password-set"`. Rows 25.2 and 25.3 are superseded | (a) Keep row 25.2's bcrypt hash over a discarded random value and realign the tests to it; (b) keep both and let the revision pick by configuration | Two independent assertions require the stored value to carry no bcrypt prefix: `test_mass_assignment.py:529` asserts the seeded row's hash does not start with a bcrypt prefix, and `test_migrations.py:273` asserts it equals the sentinel exactly. Row 25.2 rejected a sentinel on the ground that an unparseable hash returns early and so leaves the one seeded address distinguishable by how long a failed login takes. That objection does not hold against the credential path this tree carries: `verify_credential` compares against the stored value, then **unconditionally** compares against `DECOY_HASH` at `MAX_SUPPORTED_BCRYPT_COST`, then pads to `MIN_CREDENTIAL_CHECK_SECONDS` — row 25.3 concedes the same padding, and the function's own docstring states the elapsed time reveals neither whether an address holds an account nor whether it is locked. The sentinel also carries a property the bcrypt form cannot: it is self-describing in the database, so an operator reading the row sees why the account cannot be signed in to. (b) would make the stored format configuration-dependent, so no test could state what a deployment holds. Row 25.3 is moot rather than wrong — with no bcrypt hash written, no cost factor is chosen. | The account holds the role and no means of authenticating until an operator stores a password out of band, and no revision here provides one. `verify_password` reaches its refusing branch for this row on every attempt, which costs a comparison rather than leaking one. |
| 27.2 | The registration negative is `test_an_escalating_registration_adds_no_administrative_row`, and the count constants are **split** rather than renamed: `FIXTURE_ADMINISTRATORS` and `SEEDED_ADMINISTRATORS` both stand | (a) Adopt row 19.9's name; (b) adopt row 25.15's name; (c) apply row 25.15's rename literally, leaving one constant | Rows 19.9 and 25.15 renamed the same original case to two different names, and both retired `SEEDED_ADMINISTRATORS` for the same reason — that *seeded* read as the administrator the seed revision grants while the assertion was against a fixture row. Both diagnoses were right, and neither name is what the tree carries, because the module now proves both properties and needs both words. `FIXTURE_ADMINISTRATORS` counts the administrator `conftest.py` stores and is read by the four fixture cases; `SEEDED_ADMINISTRATORS` counts the administrator revision 0002 grants and is read only by the `migrated_client` cases at `:500`, `:527`, `:556`, `:565` and `:599`. The misleading name is therefore gone in row 25.15's sense, while the word *seeded* is returned to cases where it is literally true — which (c) could not do. | Three names in the rows above differ from the tree. Each row is marked so a reader is not sent looking for them, and the traceability matrix must cite the tree's names when it is written. |
| 27.3 | No `pytest_pyfunc_call` hook: the suite relies on the explicit `@pytest.mark.asyncio` marker, which is alternative (c) of row 17.4. Row 22.1's `_as_tuple` half is untouched | (a) Restore the hook; (b) leave rows 17.4 and 22.1 unmarked | The hook was removed by the round that scoped its removal, and row 17.4 had already recorded (c) as sufficient today: `pytest-asyncio` 1.2.0 runs in strict mode and every coroutine case carries the marker. What removal costs is the safety net — an unmarked coroutine case would now be collected and skipped rather than run — so the standing marker check over `backend/tests/**` is what holds the property the hook held. (a) is out of scope: no finding asks for it back. (b) would leave two rows describing a construct that is not there. `_as_tuple` is a separate construct and is present at `conftest.py:680`, read at `:1175` and `:1203`, so row 22.1 is only half superseded. | A future coroutine case added without the marker would pass vacuously. The marker check is the compensating control and is run as a standing check. |
| 27.4 | `test_deployment_contract.py` asserts the profile-based five-service stack, and the three assertions that failed because the **file** was wrong were fixed in the file | (a) Reduce the Compose file to the three services the test named; (b) relax the test to stop asserting the service inventory, the probe form and the frontend variable | The test was written against a three-service file in which `db` was the Cloud SQL proxy; the file it reads declares `frontend`, `backend`, `migrate`, `db` and `cloud-sql-proxy`, selected by the `local` and `gcp` profiles. (a) would delete the migration gate — AAP §0.10.3 makes the schema migration a precondition of the new code serving traffic — and would put the proxy back under the `db` name for a stack that has no proxy. (b) would drop assertions instead of aiming them at the right objects. Each was therefore re-aimed with its intent kept: the no-literal-credential rule now runs over every service declaring an environment **and** over every build argument, which is stricter than before because a build argument is baked into the image; the instance name is still asserted required and still asserted to listen on `0.0.0.0:5432`, now on `cloud-sql-proxy`; the probe rule accepts Compose's shell form, because the database probe interpolates the credentials it was started with, and still asserts the executable and still forbids `curl`. Three failures were the file's own: `MAX_PAGINATION_OFFSET` was absent from the backend environment though `Settings` publishes it and `.env.example` documents it, and `ZILLOW_API_URL` and `FROM_EMAIL` carried the required-value operator though both have a code default — contradicting the file's own header and blocking a start on values that need no supplying. The header's required list was corrected with them. | The test now encodes a five-service inventory, so adding a service is a deliberate edit here. That is the intent: the inventory is the contract. |
| 27.5 | The four compose-side variable names are admitted by an explicit recorded allowlist, not by loosening the name rule | (a) Drop the name-equality assertion; (b) rename the Compose variables to match their settings | `ENVIRONMENT`, `DATABASE_URL`, `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` are read from `BACKEND_ENVIRONMENT`, `COMPOSE_DATABASE_URL`, `BACKEND_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` and `BACKEND_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. (a) would let any future entry reference any variable, losing the property that the file carries no endpoint of its own. (b) would inject a developer's own `DATABASE_URL` and `ENVIRONMENT` — which name the host checkout, where the database answers on `localhost` — straight into a container, pointing it at itself. `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh` writes the compose-side names at `:595` and `:602` and `.env.example` documents all four, so the divergence is the wired design rather than a slip. The allowlist keeps name equality as the rule, admits exactly these four, and is itself asserted to be in force and documented, so a new undocumented divergence still fails. | The allowlist is a second place recording the four names. `test_every_recorded_alias_is_used_and_documented` fails if it and the file disagree. |
| 27.6 | `conftest.py` is read through the top-level module pytest loaded, never through its package path | (a) Keep `from backend.tests import conftest`; (b) move the guards and shared values into `support.py` | pytest imports `backend/tests/conftest.py` as the top-level module `conftest`. Three modules imported the same file again under `backend.tests.conftest`, which loads it a second time and gives every class and constant in it a duplicate — the defect `backend/tests/support.py` exists to prevent and which `test_api.py::test_the_shared_test_values_are_held_by_one_module_object` asserts against. It failed only in a full run, because it needs one of the three to have been collected first. (a) is what that assertion forbids. (b) is wrong for these names: they are pytest-managed machinery — the isolation guard, the limiter reset, the fixtures — and `support.py` is deliberately values only. The meta-cases in `test_config_validation.py` additionally **must** read the live guard rather than a copy, or they would assert against an object protecting nothing. Changed at `test_config_validation.py:88`, `test_migrations.py:48` and `test_paypal_webhook.py:58`; five modules already used the top-level form. | None of the three can be imported outside pytest, which was already true of the five. |
| 27.7 | `redis==5.3.1` was installed into the verification environment rather than the test baseline being changed | (a) Point the baseline's `RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI` at `memory://`; (b) drop the `redis` pin from the manifest | The valid baseline names `redis://cache.apartment-finder.dev:6379/0`, and importing the application builds the limiter eagerly, which asks `limits` for the redis scheme and needs the client package importable. `backend/requirements.txt` pins `redis==5.3.1`, and an audit of both manifests found it was the only pin the environment did not satisfy. (a) would delete the only coverage proving a redis storage URI is accepted at startup, which is what the pin exists for. (b) would leave the URI unusable. No server is required: `limits` checks that the client imports and does not connect at construction, so the two cases stay hermetic. | An environment built without installing from the manifests fails these two cases with a configuration error rather than a clear message. Installing from both manifests is the documented step. |
| 27.8 | **Row 24.4 superseded.** The frontend's API address is `REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL: ${REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL:-http://localhost:8000}`, carried as a **`build.args` entry** rather than as the `environment:` entry row 24.4 describes, and naming `localhost` rather than the `backend` service. `REACT_APP_PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID` is carried the same way. Both are retained, and the Compose file now states that the build discards them | (a) Update row 24.4 in place and leave `http://backend:8000`; (b) remove both arguments, on the ground that an argument nothing consumes is dead weight; (c) declare the two `ARG` names in `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend`, which is what actually delivers the values | Row 24.4 was written when the value was an `environment:` entry, and it names an address the browser cannot resolve: `backend` is a Compose network alias, and this variable is read by a bundle running in the browser, which reaches the service on the published host port. `test_deployment_contract.py::test_the_frontend_targets_the_port_the_backend_listens_on` asserts both halves of that — the argument names the exposed port and does **not** name `backend:8000`. (b) is refused because the two arguments are the specification of what an image that consumed them would receive, and `.env.example` documents the name a developer sets; deleting them would leave nothing to declare the contract and would take `test_the_frontend_target_names_the_variable_the_bundle_reads` with it. ## 28. The listing-identity seam, test constraint parity and the setup script

Rows added for the review of the seam between the application and the schema the
two Alembic revisions own. That review raised three defects and one Rule 1
failure: the artefacts disagreed about whether `listings.zillow_url` carries a
uniqueness constraint, three SQLite test engines did not enforce the foreign keys
the models declare, and the developer setup script declared one constant
`readonly` twice and so ended before any setup step ran. The rows below record
how each was settled, and reconcile the rows above that no longer describe the
tree. Every claim was read back from the working tree rather than carried over
from the round that wrote it.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 28.1 | **`listings.zillow_url` carries no uniqueness constraint, on every route a database can arrive by.** Rows 12.10 and 21.18 above describe one and are reconciled here | (a) Restore the constraint in the ORM, in revision `0001`'s create-when-absent listing definition and in the pre-revision fixtures, which is what the review's suggested resolution asks for; (b) restore it in the ORM and have `0001` add it to an existing table as an earlier draft of the revision did; (c) leave the artefacts disagreeing and record the disagreement | The constraint is not part of the schema that precedes `0001`, and three authorities say so. The pre-remediation source declares `zillow_url = Column(String)` with no uniqueness. AAP §0.6.2 scopes this file's changes to "Lines affected: 7-17, 67-76, and a new table" — the `Listing` class is lines 19-32 and is excluded — and §0.6.1.2's row for the file enumerates the additions exhaustively without naming one on `listings`. The implementation brief for `0001`, reading that same source, states that no unique constraint exists anywhere today beyond `users.email` and instructs that none be added beyond what the model declares. The constraint was introduced by an earlier order with its reasoning in a code comment and no row in this log, so it was an unauthorised schema change under the Minimal Change Clause as well as a Rule 1 gap. (a) is additionally self-defeating: putting the constraint in the create-when-absent path but not the alter path gives a fresh database a constraint a real pre-existing database lacks, which is precisely the deployment-lineage divergence the review calls the defect. (b) makes `0001` alter a table it otherwise only creates, contradicting its own contract that no column or constraint of any other table is added, altered or removed. (c) is what produced the failure. | An administrator writing the same provider address twice through `POST /listings/` stores two rows, and a later ingestion pass refreshes only one of them. The blast radius is bounded by the write route being administrator-only, and row 28.4 makes which row is refreshed deterministic. `backend/tests/security/test_migration_revisions.py::test_the_listing_table_is_the_same_whichever_lineage_built_it` is what stops the four lineages drifting apart again. |
| 28.2 | **Restore the `500` disposition row 12.10 recorded: the write route answers every database refusal with one fixed detail.** The duplicate-specific `409` and its detail constant are removed from `backend/app/api/endpoints/listings.py` | (a) Keep the `409` and restore the constraint that would make it reachable; (b) keep the `409` as a general integrity-conflict answer | Row 12.10 considered the conflict status and declined it, on the grounds that it is new behaviour no finding names — and the file's own implementation brief states that any change beyond the four it specifies becomes an unmapped construct, which Rule 1 treats as a defect. The `409` had also been added at the same time the constraint was removed, so no duplicate address could ever reach it: the branch answered a conflict that could not occur. (b) keeps a response shape the AAP does not describe, and it discloses that the refusal was an integrity violation rather than any other storage fault. | A client cannot distinguish a duplicate listing from a storage failure — the risk row 12.10 already accepted. `test_the_module_publishes_no_duplicate_specific_refusal` fails if the constant returns. |
| 28.3 | **Every SQLite engine the suite builds a schema or writes rows on enforces foreign keys, through one helper published from `backend/tests/support.py`** | (a) Apply the existing private helper to the three engines the review named and leave the other nine; (b) keep the helper in `conftest.py` and import it under the top-level `conftest` name; (c) centralise every harness on the one already-configured engine fixture | SQLite ignores a declared foreign key until the connection asks for it, per connection, so an unconfigured engine silently accepts an ownership row the deployed PostgreSQL database rejects — which is what the review found, and which had already let one case store a subscription owned by an account that was not stored. Fixing the three named engines would leave the same class open at nine others; applying the helper everywhere closes the class. `support.py` is the canonical home: it is imported under exactly one module name, it imports nothing from `backend.app`, it already publishes callables, and unlike `conftest` it is importable outside pytest — row 26.1 exists to guarantee that single module object. (c) would rewrite fixtures that differ deliberately: three run Alembic against file-backed databases and two build no schema at all. | A case that needs an orphan row must now seed a real parent. One such case existed and was corrected. Two engines are deliberately left unconfigured — the pair in `test_application_surface.py` that only compare parameter rendering, and the reflection engines in `test_migration_gate.py`, whose Alembic runs happen in a subprocess through its own engine. |
| 28.4 | **Order the ingestion identity lookup by primary key, and state in `backend/app/tasks/listing_updater.py` only the guarantee the schema provides** | (a) Leave the unordered `.first()` and the claim that one value reaches at most one row; (b) add the uniqueness constraint so the claim becomes true, which is row 28.1's alternative (a); (c) refuse a provider record whose address already names more than one row | The module reconciles on a column with no uniqueness behind it, so an unordered `.first()` picks an arbitrary row among any duplicates and refreshes that one forever, leaving the other permanently stale. Ordering makes the choice the earliest row, which is stable across passes and across backends. Stating the weaker, true guarantee is what keeps the module's documentation checkable. (c) turns a data condition into a recurring ingestion refusal and counts a record as refused every pass, which is worse than reconciling one of them. | A duplicate pair still leaves one stale row; the pass reports nothing about it, because it is a data condition rather than a record failure. The row is still recorded by identifier and failing field, so an operator can clear it, and a window that excludes it still succeeds, which is (b) and is what the same case asserts. This row exists because the change of disposition reached the code without reaching this log, which Rule 1 treats as a defect in itself. | A single unusable row makes every page containing it unavailable, where previously it cost only itself. | 28.6 | **One declaration block in `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh`, with each constant declared exactly once, plus an automated guard** | (a) Delete the duplicate `readonly SCHEMA_REVISION` alone and leave the second block; (b) drop `readonly` from the constants so a repeat is harmless; (c) remove `set -Eeuo pipefail` so the failure is not fatal; (d) rely on `bash -n` | The script declared `SCHEMA_REVISION` readonly twice and held the administrator address under two names carrying one value. Bash refuses the second `readonly` assignment whatever value it carries, and under the script's own options that ended the run before the virtual environment, the environment file, the database and the revisions — measured: `line 68: SCHEMA_REVISION: readonly variable`, exit 1. (a) leaves the duplicated block that produced the fault. (b) removes the protection that makes a constant a constant. (c) would hide this failure and every other one the script is written to stop at. (d) cannot work: `bash -n` parses without executing and passes on the broken script, which is why the guard both greps for a repeated declaration and *executes* the whole declaration block under the script's own options. | The guard's executing half needs `bash` and is skipped where it is absent; its static half runs everywhere, so the defect class stays covered on a host with no shell. The `ADMIN_SEED_EMAIL` environment-variable name the seed step exports is unchanged, because the Python snippet and `.env.example` both name it. |
| 28.7 | **Read the revision identifiers and the administrator address and role in the setup-script guard back from the revision modules** | Assert them as literals in the test module | The script's comment claims both values are fixed in revision `0002` and must match it; a literal copy in the guard would pass after the revision changed, which is the defect class row 26.5 names. The revisions are loaded through `ScriptDirectory`, as rows 25.12 and 26.5 already do, so a renamed constant fails at attribute access with the attribute named. | A revision that renames a constant fails the guard rather than an assertion. That is the intended signal. |

## 29. The developer setup script and the frontend build seam

Rows added by a code review of the frontend and backend contract seam. It
raised six findings. Two sit in files this round may change: the developer
setup script declared one `readonly` name twice, which under the script's own
shell options killed it before any step ran, and the Compose frontend stanza
described a build seam that delivers nothing to the bundle. The other four are
defects in `frontend/src/**`, a tree the AAP excludes, and the review
classifies them as confirmation-only: they are recorded here rather than
fixed, and each row names the backend contract that moving to meet the
frontend would have to weaken. That review's finding numbers are per-review,
so these rows cite behaviour.

Row 24.4 is superseded rather than edited away: row 27.8 carries the
reconciliation of the frontend build argument it describes.

Rows 29.3, 29.4 and 29.6 record the frontend build seam as an open gap, on
the ground that `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` was read-only to
this round. Row 30.12 subsequently declared an `ARG` of each name in that
image and exported both ahead of the build command, so the gap is closed and
those three rows no longer describe the tree: the Compose stanza and
`.env.example` now state that the build carries both values, and
`DISCARDED_FRONTEND_ARGUMENTS` is empty, which is the outcome row 29.4 names
as the one that should empty the record.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 29.1 | Delete the second `readonly SCHEMA_REVISION="0001"` from `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh` and keep the first, folding the deleted block's comment into the surviving one | (a) Keep the second declaration and delete the first; (b) drop `readonly` from the second so the re-assignment is legal; (c) give the two declarations two names | The script sets `set -Eeuo pipefail` before either declaration, and under those options re-declaring a `readonly` name exits 1 and the statement after it never runs. Measured twice: on a two-line reproduction, and on the script itself, whose declaration prologue exited 1 at the second declaration and so never reached `main "$@"` — no dependency install, no `.env`, no database role, no migration. `bash -n` exits 0 on the broken file because it parses without evaluating, so the defect was invisible to a syntax check. The surviving declaration is the one that sits beside `SEED_REVISION`, which keeps the two revision constants together, and the deleted block's information — that the seed account is stored under the schema revision and the grant revision is applied over it — was folded into the surviving comment, so the comment carries what both carried. (b) is refused because a value the script must never reassign should stay `readonly`, and making a duplicate legal treats the symptom rather than the duplicate. (c) is refused because two names for one revision invites the two drifting apart | The file now declares 17 `readonly` names with no duplicate, and its prologue reaches the end with exit 0 where it exited 1 before. | 29.2 | Hold that fix with two cases in `backend/tests/security/test_deployment_contract.py`: `test_the_setup_script_declares_each_readonly_name_once`, which reads the file, and `test_the_setup_script_bootstrap_runs_without_failing`, which executes the script's declaration and bootstrap prologue — the file with its single `main "$@"` entry point removed — under `bash` and requires exit 0 with no output | (a) The static case alone; (b) `bash -n` alone; (c) run the script itself | The review asked for a check that evaluates the declaration path, and only execution does that: (b) exits 0 on the broken file, and (a) catches this duplicate but not the next fatal declaration that is syntactically valid. (b) leaves a reader with two arguments and no statement of what becomes of them. (c) is refused under Rule 1, which keeps rationale out of comments — the two files state what is and name the authority that must change, and row 27.8 carries the why. The marker phrase the case in row 29.4 reads is kept on one line, so a comment rewrapped across it fails rather than passing | The wording is a statement, not a fix: no `REACT_APP_*` value reaches the bundle until the frontend image declares the names, which row 29.6 records as deferred |

(b) leaves the suite silent about a seam the review found broken | The record is a constant a later round can edit; editing it without the tree agreeing fails the case, which is the intent. | 29.5 | Record the four `frontend/src/**` defects as confirmation-only exceptions, each with the backend contract that meeting it would move, and change no backend contract to accommodate them | (a) Fix them in `frontend/src/**`; (b) move the backend to meet the frontend — add `/login` beside `/auth/login`, rename the login response's `access_token` to `token` and add a `user` member, add `GET /user/profile`, open `POST /filters` to a caller with no principal, and accept `monthly`, `yearly`, `basic` and `premium` as plan identifiers with a PayPal Billing Subscriptions response; (c) leave them unrecorded, since the review already lists them | (a) is out of scope: AAP §0.9.2 excludes everything under `frontend/src/**` and §0.6.1.7 lists these modules as REFERENCE paths. (b) is forbidden by the review itself, which requires that the four defects not be hidden by weakening or renaming the hardened backend contracts, and every change it would take reverses a control this project added: the four router prefixes and the `{access_token, token_type}` response shape are frozen interfaces under AAP §0.1.2, `POST /filters` is role-guarded, `/user/profile` exists nowhere under `backend/app`, and the plan identifiers are the server-owned catalog that took the amount out of a client's reach. (c) is refused because Rule 1 treats an unexplained deviation as a defect, and the review names the absence of these rows as the gap | The browser application cannot log in, create a filter or subscribe against this backend, and its build does not compile, until an authorized frontend change lands. The four rows below carry each defect, its authority and the contract it must not move |
