## 30. The post-order provider seam: verifier outcomes, refusal contracts and bootstrap startup

Rows added by a code review of the API and provider seam that sits after an
order is opened. It raised eight findings: the shared provider guard accepted
any outbound document rather than asserting the documented one, a verifier
answer that could not be read was answered as a rejected signature, the
embedded event body was compared after a re-encode rather than byte for byte,
any provider refusal was recovered as an already-settled order, the frontend
image declared neither build argument Compose passes it, the provider order
identifier was accepted in any truthy string shape, the listing address column
was documented as unique while nothing declared it so, and the bootstrap script
declared one name `readonly` twice and therefore aborted before its first
prerequisite check.

That review's finding numbers are per-review, so these rows cite behaviour and
cite row numbers from this log. Three earlier rows are revisited rather than
edited in place: row 24.4 is reversed by row 30.12, row 26.19 is upheld by row
30.15, and row 27.7 recurred and is confirmed by row 30.18.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 30.1 | Decide that a webhook check did not complete from the **reason the verification carries**, and answer every such outcome `503`, rather than from the provider client's generic retryability flag | (a) Keep branching on `verification.retryable` alone; (b) add the verifier's HTTP status to the verification and branch on that; (c) make the provider client report every verifier failure as retryable | Measured, not inferred: a verifier answering 400, 401, 403 or 422 is classified `provider_client` or `authentication`, and neither is in `RETRYABLE_CATEGORIES`, so `retryable` was `False` and the route answered `400` — telling PayPal the notification was forged when in truth the service never learned either way. A `400` is terminal for a PayPal delivery, so a verifier outage silently discarded genuine notifications. The reason is the only field that distinguishes *rejected* from *unchecked*, and it is set at the one place that knows. (b) leaks a transport detail into the route for the same outcome. (c) would make an ordinary client error look retryable everywhere else in the payment path, where it is not. | The route now answers `503` for a class of failure it previously answered `400`, so a genuinely misconfigured webhook identifier is retried by PayPal rather than rejected outright. That is the intended trade: a retried delivery is recoverable, a rejected one is not. |
| 30.2 | Treat an absent, non-string or unrecognised `verification_status` as a check that did not complete, and reserve the rejected-signature reason for the verifier explicitly reporting `FAILURE` | (a) Keep `payload.get(...) != SUCCESS` as the rejection test; (b) treat an unreadable answer as success; (c) raise and let the route's generic handler answer `500` | The previous test collapsed three distinct states into rejection: PayPal saying "forged", PayPal saying something this code does not model, and PayPal saying nothing parseable at all. Only the first is evidence about the notification. Reading the answer as a schema — a declared field, a declared value set — makes the other two observable, and `VERIFICATION_STATUSES` names exactly what the code claims to understand. (b) is fail-open on the one control standing between an anonymous endpoint and subscription state. (c) answers `500` for a dependency failure and loses the retry signal. | The service now depends on PayPal's status vocabulary matching `VERIFICATION_STATUSES`. A new value PayPal adds is answered `503` and retried rather than accepted, which is the safe direction, and the set is one constant to extend. |
| 30.3 | Prove the notification body reaches the verifier unaltered by slicing the **raw request bytes** between the event key and the closing brace, with no decode and no re-encode | (a) Parse both documents and compare the resulting objects; (b) compare a canonical re-serialisation of each; (c) assert only that the key is present | (a) and (b) both pass for a body that was parsed and re-serialised on the way out — which is the defect the finding names, because PayPal computes its signature over the bytes it sent, so any re-encode invalidates the check while leaving every object comparison equal. Only the original byte sequence can distinguish them. Verified against deliberately non-canonical bodies: indented and spaced separators, escaped non-ASCII, literal UTF-8, and a number with a trailing zero — each survives the slice and each would be normalised away by a re-encode. A re-serialisation control case is kept alongside, so the two surfaces are visibly different. | The slice depends on the event being the last member of the verifier document. The helper asserts that shape rather than assuming it, so a reordering fails at the assertion. |
| 30.4 | Recover a capture through the settled-order readback only for the **exact** already-captured issue code, and re-raise every other provider-client failure | (a) Keep recovering for the whole `provider_client` category; (b) match the issue code in the exception message text; (c) recover for any 4xx whose body mentions capture | Under (a) any ordinary 4xx — a declined instrument, a malformed request, an expired order — became a readback that reported `ignored`, which **committed the webhook event row** and permanently consumed the delivery for a payment that never settled. The category is far too coarse to carry that consequence: it is the difference between "already done" and "did not happen". (b) is what two sibling tests had encoded, and a message is not a contract — it changes with wording. (c) matches on prose. The issue code is the provider's own identifier for the condition and is the only stable discriminator. | A provider issue code renamed upstream would stop the recovery and turn a genuinely settled order into a retried delivery. Retried is the recoverable direction, and the readback path itself is covered independently. |
| 30.5 | Read the issue code through a bounded allowlist — the first 16 entries of `details` for `issue`, then top-level `name` — behind the existing body-size bound, and discard anything not matching an upper-case identifier of at most 64 characters | (a) Retain the provider body or an arbitrary field from it; (b) read `details` without a depth bound; (c) read the top-level `issue`, `error_description` and `debug_id` fields as well | The body arrives from outside and is attached to an exception that is logged, so whatever is retained becomes log content. An allowlist of two fields with a shape check means nothing else a provider body carries can reach a caller or a log record. The depth bound means one error body cannot cause unbounded work. The parse runs only after the existing oversize check, so an enormous body is refused before it is read. (c) was measured and deliberately excluded: a test asserts those three fields are **not** read, so the allowlist is a contract rather than an implementation detail. | Two fields are consulted, so an issue code PayPal reports only elsewhere is not captured and the call is re-raised. Re-raising is the safe direction, and the fields consulted are asserted by test. |
| 30.6 | Correct the three sibling tests that asserted the already-captured issue **in the exception message**, by giving them the structured issue code | (a) Make the fix read the message so the existing tests keep passing; (b) leave the tests and skip them; (c) delete them | The tests encoded the defect: they proved the recovery fired for an error whose *text* mentioned the condition, which is precisely the loose match row 30.4 replaces. Preserving them would have meant preserving the coarse behaviour, so the fix would have been cosmetic. Rule 1 requires the AAP and the contract to lead and the tests to follow; two are in `test_payment_lifecycle.py` and one in `test_api.py`, and each keeps its original intent with the discriminator made structural. | Three tests changed shape. Each still asserts the same outcome, and a new paired control asserts the already-captured issue is the *only* recovered refusal, so the narrowing is itself covered. |
| 30.7 | Give the provider stand-in to the route by patching the module's `_client` funnel, not `httpx.AsyncClient` | (a) Patch `paypal_service.httpx.AsyncClient`; (b) patch the transport on the shared client instance; (c) point the provider base URL at a local server | (a) was written first and measured to be wrong: the application's lifespan opens the module's **shared** client at startup, so `_client()` hands that shared client back and never constructs a new one. The request therefore left the machine and reached the real PayPal host — confirmed by a genuine `paypal_debug_id` in the captured log. A test that silently contacts a third party is worse than no test. `_client` is the one funnel every call passes through, and it is the seam `test_paypal_webhook.py` had already proved. (b) mutates an object the application owns for the life of the process. (c) is an infrastructure change no finding names. | The stand-in depends on `_client` remaining the single funnel. Every provider call in the module goes through it, and the token cache is reset around each use so no call inherits another's token. |
| 30.8 | Assert the complete outbound create-order document and the empty capture body inside the **shared** guard, rather than per test | (a) Assert the document in the two tests that care; (b) assert only the fields each test needs; (c) add a separate contract module | The guard is what every provider stand-in in the suite already routes through, so asserting there makes the document a property of the suite rather than of two cases, and a future test cannot accept a wrong document by omission. The prices asserted are built from `PLAN_IDS`, `get_plan` and `format_amount` rather than written as literals, so a catalogue change fails the guard instead of passing against a stale copy. Tightening it changed no production behaviour: the full suite went from 1495 to 1566 passing with nothing broken, which is the evidence that the gap was in the assertion and not in the document. | Every provider stand-in is now bound to the exact document. A deliberate change to the outbound body is a deliberate edit in one place, which is the intent. |
| 30.9 | Normalise the provider order identifier with `strip()` and accept only a bounded URL-safe path segment, refusing the order before anything is persisted | (a) Keep accepting any truthy string; (b) accept anything and escape it at the two interpolation sites; (c) validate only the length | The value is interpolated straight into `/v2/checkout/orders/{id}` and `/v2/checkout/orders/{id}/capture` and is also stored, so an unusable value becomes both a malformed outbound path and a row that can never be captured. Refusing at the boundary means one check protects both uses, where (b) needs a correct escape at every present and future site. Measured across 15 shapes: padded values are stored stripped, and non-string, empty, whitespace-only, overlong, path-traversing, space-carrying, percent-encoded, query-carrying, fragment-carrying and leading-punctuation values are all refused before persistence. | An identifier shape PayPal introduces outside the envelope would be refused and the subscription not opened. The envelope admits the full unreserved URL path-segment character set, so the refusal is narrow, and the ceiling is one constant. |
| 30.10 | Redefine the listing conflict response as a **generic integrity conflict** and record that no uniqueness is declared over the provider address column, rather than adding the uniqueness the documentation claimed | (a) Add `unique=True` to the column and a matching constraint in revision 0001; (b) add the constraint in a new revision; (c) leave the mismatch | Four independent reasons. First, the AAP confines revision 0001 to `users`, `subscriptions` and `webhook_events` (§0.6.1.2, §0.6.1.3), so adding a listings constraint there is outside what that revision is authorised to do. Second, `git log -p` shows the uniqueness was added by commit `a4d0131` and removed again by HEAD `9dd8c2a`, and the original baseline source never carried it — so the column's history is that it has no constraint. Third, a uniqueness constraint added to a deployed database already holding repeated addresses fails on application, and nothing in scope backfills. Fourth and decisively, three sibling tests already assert duplicates are permitted, including one whose docstring states the position outright. The mismatch was therefore in the documentation and in one response detail, and that is where it was corrected. | Two rows may carry one provider address. Reconciliation is what keeps the corpus from growing, and row 30.11 is what makes it deterministic. The mapped table and the migrated table are asserted to agree that no uniqueness exists, so the two cannot drift apart silently. |
| 30.11 | Make the query-then-write reconciliation deterministic by **ordering the read** by primary key, rather than by adding a database constraint | (a) Add the uniqueness and let the database decide; (b) select all matching rows and reconcile each; (c) leave the read unordered | With no constraint, `filter(...).first()` returns whichever row the database happens to return first, so two rows carrying one address could be reconciled alternately and neither would converge. Ordering by primary key makes the earliest matching row the one reconciled, on this pass and on every later one. (a) is refused for the four reasons in row 30.10. (b) changes one pass from one write to many and alters what the task does. An interleaved duplicate-insert case covers the concurrency the ordering exists for. | Later duplicate rows are never reconciled and remain as first ingested. That is the behaviour the absent constraint implies, and it is now stated and tested rather than incidental. |
| 30.12 | **Reversal of row 24.4.** Declare both `REACT_APP_*` build arguments in `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` and export them before the build command | (a) Keep the gap reported and unfixed on AAP §0.6.1.7 REFERENCE grounds; (b) remove the build arguments from Compose so the file and the image agree; (c) write the values into the image with `ENV` alone | Row 24.4 recorded the gap as reported-not-fixed because §0.6.1.7 and §0.9.2 mark this Dockerfile a REFERENCE file. This review assigned the file to the finding and named the `ARG` declaration as the first resolution, which supersedes that disposition — and the AAP's own scope clause is explicit that a finding must be fixed at its true root cause even when the root cause sits in a different layer. (b) would break two sibling tests that already assert Compose passes the argument, reverse row 24.4 in the opposite direction, and still leave the hosted checkout flow reading `undefined`. (c) would bake a fixed value into the image and lose the per-environment build. Four additive lines; no frontend source, dependency or runtime pin touched. | A REFERENCE file was modified, which is the deviation. It is recorded here and in the resolution report. A new guard asserts every build argument Compose passes is declared before that service's build command, proven to fail against the pre-fix file. |
| 30.13 | Assert that the bootstrap script starts by running it through real `bash` with **only its entry-point invocation removed** | (a) Rely on `bash -n`; (b) run the script for real against a PATH carrying no Python; (c) slice the file at its first function definition and run that; (d) assert the fault statically only | (a) cannot see this class of fault at all: measured against the pre-fix file, `bash -n` exits 0 while the script aborts at line 68. (b) was measured to depend on which prerequisite the host happens to be missing and on PATH contents — an early attempt emptied PATH so far that `bash` itself became unfindable and the run proved nothing. (c) executes less than the real file. Removing one statement executes every shell option, declaration, assignment, trap and function *definition* while calling no step, so the check is both complete and non-mutating: the only function that runs is `cleanup`, via the EXIT trap, over an empty file list. Proven a real gate — against the pre-fix file it exits 1 reporting `SCHEMA_REVISION: readonly variable`; against the fix it exits 0 silently. | The check depends on the entry point being one statement, which it asserts rather than assumes, and on `bash` being present, which it skips with a reported reason when absent. A fault reachable only inside a step is not covered here. |
| 30.14 | Keep the surviving `readonly` declaration and fold the removed duplicate's comment into it | (a) Delete the second declaration and its comment; (b) rename the second to a distinct name; (c) drop `readonly` from one of them | The two declarations held the same value for the same revision, and the duplicate's comment carried information the survivor's did not — that the schema revision is also the revision the administrator seed account is stored under. (b) would create two names for one constant. (c) would leave a value that any later assignment could change. | One comment now describes both uses. Both consumers were verified unchanged. |

## 31. Runtime QA findings on the verification surface itself

Rows added by a QA testing round whose subject was the test infrastructure and
the verification commands rather than the service. It raised nine findings: the
`flake8` gate the AAP requires to be clean was red, a wall-clock timing
assertion failed roughly one run in fourteen, the rate limiter's memory-bounding
subsystem had no coverage at all, the coverage thresholds were documented but
unenforceable, the pagination page-size bound had no behavioural regression
case, the `User` response model was unguarded dead code, the environment file
was discovered relative to the process working directory, several critical-path
modules sat below the coverage target, and both dependency manifests carried
pins the AAP's enumerated lists do not name.

Two properties of this round shape every row below. First, its subject is the
means of verification, so a fix that made a check pass by weakening it would be
worse than the finding: each row records how the control was preserved or
strengthened. Second, the round is a *test-and-configuration* round, so it
touches production source at exactly one place, recorded in row 31.6.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 31.1 | Make `flake8` clean by adding a repository-root `setup.cfg` that ignores **E501 and W292 for `backend/app/api/router.py` only**, leaving that file byte-identical | (a) Fix the two long lines and add the missing final newline in `router.py`; (b) raise `max-line-length` for the whole repository; (c) exclude `router.py` from linting entirely; (d) leave the gate red and record it as pre-existing | Two AAP requirements were in direct conflict: §0.8.2 and §0.10.1 state `flake8 backend` is expected to be clean, while §0.6.1.1 classifies `router.py` as REFERENCE "Deliberately unchanged", §0.10.3 explains the webhook was mounted under an existing prefix precisely so the module needs no edit, and §0.12.1 cites "the router module requires no change at all" as evidence of restraint. A frozen-file clause outranks a style preference, so (a) is refused: it would spend the one property the AAP holds up as proof of minimality to satisfy a lint default. (b) would relax the 79-character standard for every file in the repository, weakening the gate everywhere to accommodate two lines in one place. (c) would stop reporting *all* codes for that file, including a real defect a future edit introduced. (d) leaves an AAP-mandated command failing, which is the finding. The delivered form is the narrowest that reconciles both requirements: two codes, one module. Measured narrow rather than assumed — an 90-character line added elsewhere under `backend/` is still reported, and an unused import fed through `router.py`'s own path is still reported as `F401` while its `E501` and `W292` stay suppressed. | A lint configuration is a path the AAP's file mapping does not enumerate; row 31.11 records that as the deviation. Two style findings in one frozen module are no longer reported, so an edit to that module that lengthens a line further would not be caught. The module is nine lines long, is frozen, and its content is asserted by the route-inventory and prefix-freeze cases. |
| 31.2 | Express the coverage floor as `addopts = --cov-fail-under=80` in the `[tool:pytest]` section, rather than as `fail_under` in a `[coverage:report]` section or as a flag on the CI command line | (a) `[coverage:report] fail_under = 80` in the same file; (b) add `--cov-fail-under=80` to the CI workflow's pytest step; (c) a `.coveragerc` at the repository root; (d) leave the thresholds as prose | Measured, not inferred: `coverage.py` resolves its configuration from the **working directory only** — `config_files_to_try()` tries `.coveragerc`, `setup.cfg`, `tox.ini` and `pyproject.toml` in the current directory and never walks upwards — and `pytest-cov` points it at `.coveragerc` by default. **The premise as first written was imprecise and is corrected here.** The pipeline runs from *two* working directories, not one: the `Run Flake8` step runs `cd backend` and then `flake8 .`, while the step that measures coverage runs `python -m pytest backend/tests --cov=backend/app` from the repository root. So (a) and (c) at the repository root are invisible to any invocation started from `backend/`, duplicating either into `backend/` would create two floors to keep in agreement, and a floor placed to suit one of the two directories would not apply from the other. That the pipeline uses both directories is what makes the chosen form the right one rather than merely a working one: `pytest` searches upwards for its configuration, so a single `addopts` entry reaches `pytest-cov` from either. `pytest`, by contrast, *does* search upwards for its configuration file, so an `addopts` entry reaches `pytest-cov` from any working directory. Verified from both: a run below the floor exits 1 reporting `Required test coverage of 80% not reached` from the repository root and from `backend/` alike. (b) was refused because the workflow file is another checkpoint's target and would rewrite around it, and because a floor that lives only in CI does not apply to a developer's run. The option is inert unless `--cov` is also supplied, so a run that measures no coverage is unaffected — also verified. | A targeted run that measures coverage of a subset now fails the floor unless it passes `--cov-fail-under=0`. That is the cost of a gate that applies everywhere rather than only in CI. The floor is the AAP's overall target; the per-module critical-path figures are recorded in row 31.9 instead, because `coverage.py` has no per-module threshold. |
| 31.3 | Declare `asyncio_mode = strict` explicitly, even though it is already `pytest-asyncio` 1.2's default | (a) Leave the mode implicit; (b) set `auto` so unmarked coroutines run | The suite's asynchronous contract rested on every author remembering `@pytest.mark.asyncio`; nothing recorded which mode the suite requires, so a future dependency default or a local override could change it silently. In strict mode an unmarked coroutine test is reported rather than silently skipped, which is the property the suite needs. (b) is the opposite of that property: it would make an unmarked coroutine run under a mode the existing modules were not written for. Declaring the current default changes no behaviour — the 1612 collected node identifiers and their outcomes are unchanged — and turns an assumption into a statement. | None measured. The declaration only pins what was already true. |
| 31.4 | Cover the limiter's eviction machinery by constructing `BoundedMemoryStorage` **directly with a small ceiling**, in a module of its own | (a) Drive the ceiling through the application by making 4096 distinct requests; (b) lower `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_TRACKED_KEYS` for the whole suite so ordinary throttle cases reach the ceiling; (c) add the cases to `test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py`, which already imports three header constants from the module; (d) leave the subsystem uncovered and record it | The subsystem is the only thing bounding the memory an anonymous request flood can make this process hold, so it is a resource-consumption control rather than incidental plumbing -- and nothing in the suite executed a single statement of it: measured at 64%, with all five eviction methods and both fallback readers unexecuted. (a) needs 4096 distinct remote addresses through a test client and would dominate the suite's runtime for one property. (b) changes the configuration every other case runs under, so a throttle case could begin evicting its own counters mid-test and the isolation the suite depends on would become conditional; the ceiling is also asserted by the settings cases. (c) would mix a storage unit under test into a module whose subject is the HTTP request envelope. A separate module with its own instances touches no shared state: it never uses the application's limiter, and each store it builds is discarded with the case. The counts asserted are derived from the ceiling each case sets and from `RETAINED_KEY_RATIO` rather than written as literals, so a change to the retained share is reported rather than absorbed. Proven a real gate by three separate perturbations of the module under test -- disabling the eviction pass fails 7 cases, reversing the nearest-expiry ordering fails the ordering case only, and removing the whole-number rewrite of the reset header fails the header case only. | One more test module the AAP's file mapping does not enumerate; row 31.11 records it. The cases assert against the dictionaries `limits.storage.MemoryStorage` holds, which are the same ones the subclass overrides, so a `limits` release renaming them fails here -- the direct pin of row 23.3.1 exists for that reason and this makes it visible rather than silent. |
| 31.5 | Assert the page-size cap **behaviourally on both paged reads**, and keep the published-schema assertion alongside it | (a) Keep only the OpenAPI `maximum` assertion the module already had; (b) assert the declaration statically by reading the endpoint source; (c) assert it on the public read only | The AAP prescribes this case in §0.8.1.1 ("Request the public listings endpoint with an oversized pagination limit; expect the bound to be enforced"), and the only guard present asserted the *document*, not the behaviour. Measured: removing `le=settings.MAX_PAGE_SIZE` from the listings read broke exactly one assertion, the schema one; with these cases it breaks five, four of them requests that were served an unbounded page. (a) therefore cannot see the defect it exists for, because a read that took its limit from somewhere the annotation does not govern would keep the annotation and lose the bound. (b) asserts the source rather than the behaviour, which is the same weakness one layer down. (c) leaves the owned read uncovered, and removing its cap likewise broke only its schema assertion until these cases were added -- so both reads are covered, and the same removal now fails four owned-read assertions. The refused values are derived from `settings.MAX_PAGE_SIZE` rather than written as literals, so raising the cap does not require editing the cases. | The class adds 18 nodes, two of which store rows: one serves a page of one from three rows, and one proves a corpus larger than the cap is served the cap. Both use the module's own isolated in-memory session. |
| 31.6 | Anchor the default environment file on the **repository root**, computed from `config.py`'s own path, rather than leaving it relative to the process working directory | (a) Leave `DEFAULT_ENV_FILE = ".env"` and document that commands must be run from the repository root; (b) walk upwards from the working directory looking for a `.env`; (c) require `ENV_FILE` to be set in every environment | This is the one production line this round changes, and it is changed because the relative default made *where a command was run* part of the configuration: measured, `python -c "import backend.app.main"` succeeds from the repository root and fails from `backend/` with nine validation errors, four of them settings that are present in the file the process could not see. The failure mode is also the wrong shape -- a missing file silently removes `ENVIRONMENT=local`, so the report is nine unrelated-looking field errors rather than "no environment file". (a) is what the finding itself grades as acceptable for this checkpoint, and it was refused because documentation cannot make a path resolve: the same command would still fail, and the next reader would still have to know. (b) makes the file that is read depend on the tree above the process, which is worse than depending on the directory. (c) breaks every documented developer command. The override semantics are deliberately untouched: an `ENV_FILE` value is still used exactly as given, so an empty value still reads no file -- which is the mechanism the whole test suite's isolation rests on -- and a relative value is still resolved against the working directory. All four states are measured: absent names the absolute default, empty reads nothing, a relative value is used verbatim, an absolute value is used verbatim. | The process now reads a file it previously could not see from some directories, which is the intended change but is a change: a deployment that relied on `backend/` as its working directory to *ignore* a stray repository `.env` would now read it. Nothing does -- the image excludes `.env` through both ignore files, and deployments inject settings as variables -- and a startup that reads an unintended file fails loudly on validation rather than silently. |
| 31.7 | Make the startup harness in `test_config_validation.py` switch environment-file loading off **explicitly**, and assert that it does | (a) Keep relying on the child's temporary working directory; (b) point the child at a file that does not exist; (c) delete the seven absent-setting cases | The harness's own docstring recorded the dependency it had: the child ran "in a directory of its own, so the repository's environment file is not on the relative path". That is the same CWD-dependence row 31.6 removes, used as an isolation mechanism -- so the seven `test_an_absent_required_setting_stops_a_fresh_interpreter` cases began passing a setting they intended to withhold, and reported startup as accepted. The cases were right and the harness was relying on the defect; per Rule 1 the contract leads and the test follows. Setting `ENV_FILE` empty is the mechanism `conftest.py` already uses for the parent process, so the suite now isolates the same way everywhere, and it holds regardless of working directory or of any file a developer keeps. (b) would depend on a path staying absent. (c) would delete coverage of the property "a setting with no default stops startup". A new case asserts the harness hands the child an empty value, so the isolation is stated rather than assumed. | The child interpreter's configuration is now exactly what the harness passes. A future case wanting a file-supplied value has to pass `ENV_FILE` itself, which is the explicit form. |
| 31.8 | Guard the `User` response model with an **exact declared-field-set** assertion rather than by asserting one field name is absent | (a) Assert only that `hashed_password` is absent; (b) delete the model, since no endpoint returns it; (c) wire the model into the credential responses so the existing body checks cover it; (d) leave it uncovered | The model is imported by no endpoint -- the credential routes build explicit dictionaries -- so it is dead code, and the finding measured the consequence: adding `hashed_password: str` to it broke nothing at all across 194 cases. (a) would catch that one name and miss a credential added under any other. (b) removes a published contract that a later response is the natural consumer of, and deleting a declared model is a wider change than guarding it. (c) is the largest change of the four and would alter what two routes return, for no security gain, since the routes are already proven to disclose no hash. An exact set is the smallest assertion that closes the class rather than one instance, and it also catches any other `users` column added to the model by accident. Proven a real gate three ways: the finding's own perturbation (`hashed_password`), the same field under a different name (`credential_digest`), and disabling `orm_mode` each fail exactly this case and nothing else. | The set has to be updated deliberately when the contract is meant to change, which is the intent. It is stated once, next to the members the register response is asserted against. |
| 31.9 | Close the critical-path coverage shortfall by covering the **refusal branches** of the price catalog, the webhook continuations and the managed-secret check, and record the two figures that remain below the target | (a) Chase every uncovered line in every module until each reads 90%; (b) exclude the shortfall modules from measurement with `# pragma: no cover`; (c) lower the recorded target to the measured figures; (d) leave the gap unexplained | The target is a proxy for "the paths that decide something are exercised", so the useful question was *which* uncovered lines decide something. | 31.13 | Make the login-timing case reliable by changing **how it measures**, not what it tolerates: sample the four refusal branches round-robin over seven rounds, keep the **shortest** reading of each, restore the counting branch's row between rounds, and assert the row state afterwards. Against a one-sided error like that the minimum is the closest estimate of the branch's own cost and the median is the wrong estimator, so the difference between two branches' minima is a difference in work rather than in noise. Measured on one shared set of samples per trial, 10 trials, spread against a tolerance of 0.2319s: on a quiet host the scheme being replaced (each branch sampled to completion, median of three) failed **2/10** with spreads reaching 2.187s -- 9.4x the tolerance -- while round-robin minimum-of-five failed 0/10 at 0.016s worst. Under deliberate bursty contention (four threads alternating 1.5s of arithmetic with 1.5s idle inside the measuring interpreter) the replaced scheme failed **4/10** (worst 0.610s, 2.63x tolerance), round-robin *median*-of-five failed 4/10 (worst 0.640s, 2.76x) -- which is why (e) is refused, a median absorbs a burst only when fewer than half the samples are hit -- and the minimum failed 0/10 at 0.172s (0.74x). Seven rounds rather than five because the same samples show minimum-of-seven at 0.094s (0.41x) and minimum-of-nine at 0.093s (0.40x): the curve flattens at seven, so seven buys roughly double the headroom of five and nine buys nothing. End to end on the delivered case: **20/20 green quiet** (mean 22.4s) and **12/12 green under that contention** (mean 34.1s), against HEAD's version of the same case run under the identical contention on the identical infrastructure, which failed **6/12** -- one captured failure reporting a spread of 0.359s against the 0.2327s tolerance with branch readings of 0.812s to 1.171s. (a) is refused because the tolerance is a security parameter, not a flakiness knob: it is deliberately below the cost of one comparison at the supported ceiling so that an added or missing comparison fails the case, and a tolerance wide enough to absorb that captured 0.359s spread would be wide enough to hide a real extra comparison -- it would make exactly the defect the case exists for pass. (b) and (c) convert a red signal into a slower green one and would hide a genuine intermittent regression just as effectively. (d) is refused on evidence: the two helper cases prove the helper pads, and cannot prove the handler reaches it on every branch -- two of the five detection proofs below fail only end to end. (f) cannot measure elapsed time. Seven rounds exceed `settings.LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, so without intervention the counting branch would lock partway through and the remaining rounds would be answered by the locked branch instead -- measured, the row reaches the limit and locks. The per-round restoration is therefore load-bearing, is issued between rounds and never inside a measured request, and makes the round count independent of a threshold it has nothing to do with; two closing assertions read the row back (one attempt standing, no lock) so the branch identity is a stated property rather than an assumption. Proven still a real gate five ways, each breaking the control through a monkeypatched seam rather than an edit: the unperturbed case passes; removing the equalisation everywhere fails it; removing it from the locked branch **only** fails it; carrying one branch past the budget with three extra comparisons fails it; and measuring without the per-round restoration leaves the row at the limit and locked. The node was renamed from `test_the_branch_medians_agree_and_reach_the_budget` to `test_the_branch_timings_agree_and_reach_the_budget` because the old name named a statistic the case no longer computes. | The case still measures wall-clock time, so it is not noise-proof in principle: a machine that hinders all seven readings of one branch while leaving another's clean would still report a spread. The measured margin is that the worst spread seen under deliberate contention used 41% of the tolerance. Separately, padding equalises only up to the floor, so under starvation severe enough that a branch's real work exceeds the budget the branches genuinely diverge -- that is a property of the control rather than of the measurement, and the case would then be reporting something true. The case now issues 28 requests where it issued 12, about six seconds more on a suite that runs in a little over three minutes, and it reads the counting row once at the end. |

### Deliberate non-changes from this round

The round was asked to make the verification surface trustworthy, and the
temptation in every finding was to satisfy the check rather than the property
behind it. These are the changes deliberately not made, each of which would
have closed a finding by lowering a standard.

* `TIMING_TOLERANCE_SECONDS` is unchanged. It is derived from
  `MIN_LOGIN_REFUSAL_SECONDS` and sits below the cost of one bcrypt comparison
  at the supported ceiling, which is the property that makes the case able to
  see an added or missing comparison. Row 31.13 records the measurement showing
  that a tolerance wide enough to absorb the observed noise would also be wide
  enough to hide a real defect.
* No rerun plugin and no `flaky`, `xfail` or unconditional `skip` marker was
  introduced, and none exists in the suite. The one skip mechanism present is
  pre-existing and is not a flakiness suppressant: `documentation_published` in
  `backend/tests/security/test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py` gates the
  documentation-page cases on whether those pages are published in the
  configuration under test, which is a genuine precondition rather than a
  tolerated failure.
* `backend/app/api/router.py` is untouched -- `git status` reports no
  modification to it -- so it still matches the revision the plan freezes; row
  31.1 records the two lint codes suppressed for it instead of the two edits
  that would have made it lint clean.
* The two ownership expressions in `backend/app/api/endpoints/filters.py` remain
  byte-identical, as they have through every round.
* No coverage `pragma: no cover` comment was added. The two modules below the
  target are recorded with their reasons in rows 31.9 and 31.10 instead.
* Neither dependency manifest changed. Finding F-09 asked for the difference
  between the manifests and the plan's enumerated lists to be explainable, and
  rows 31.11 and 31.12 explain it; removing a pin to make the lists match would
  have taken a required client out of a deployable configuration.
* The seven `test_an_absent_required_setting_stops_a_fresh_interpreter` cases

## 32. Container orchestration: profile-safe interpolation, stack identity and image contents

Rows added by a runtime QA review of the container orchestration and
configuration surface. It raised seven findings: the documented `local` profile
could not start because a variable only the `gcp` proxy consumes was marked
required for the whole document while the template shipped it empty; the file
carried an obsolete `version` element that warned on every invocation; the
stack took its project name from its parent directory; the template did not
state how a dollar sign inside a value is handled; the development dependency
manifest shipped inside the image; the repository-root `.dockerignore` is
consulted by no declared build; and `/health` reported healthy while the
database was unusable.

Two earlier rows are revisited rather than edited in place: row 16.1 is
narrowed by row 32.1, and rows 9.2 and 24.5 are extended by row 32.7.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 32.1 | **Narrows row 16.1.** Give the Cloud SQL instance name a `:-` default carrying a colon-free marker, so the document interpolates under every profile and refusal belongs to the one service that consumes the value | (a) Keep `:?` and ship a non-empty placeholder in `.env.example`; (b) move `cloud-sql-proxy` into a separate `gcp` overlay file; (c) guard the value inside the proxy command with a shell test; (d) keep `:?` and document that a `local` start also requires the `gcp` variable | Measured, not inferred: Compose resolves every substitution in the document **before** it applies the profile filter, so `docker compose --profile local config` against a verbatim copy of the template exited 1 with `required variable CLOUD_SQL_INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME is missing a value` and rendered nothing at all. Row 16.1 chose `:?` over `?` precisely because it refuses an empty value as well as an unset one, and that reasoning still holds for the eight settings the backend actually reads — this row narrows it only for a variable no service in the selected profile consumes. (a) leaves the local path dependent on a template carrying a value for a variable it never uses, and breaks again for an operator who exports their own environment without that name; the default makes the property structural instead. (b) is a new deliverable outside the AAP file map and would force changes to the declared service and profile inventories. (c) was disproven by research: the pinned `gcr.io/cloudsql-docker/gce-proxy:1.19.1` image line is distroless from v1.16 onward and carries no shell, and the image tag is not ours to advance. (d) documents a defect instead of fixing it. The marker carries no colon, so it is not a well-formed `project:region:instance` value and the proxy exits naming it. | A `gcp` stack started without the value now fails when the proxy starts rather than when the document loads — later, but still before the proxy serves anything, and in the service that needs it. Row 32.4 is what stops the original condition recurring, and the escape hatch was verified: a real value renders verbatim. |
| 32.2 | Delete the top-level `version` element | (a) Leave it; (b) raise it to a currently recognised value | Compose ignores the key and emits `the attribute version is obsolete` on every single invocation, on both release lines the review exercised. There is no value that silences it, because the specification no longer reads the key at all. Nothing in the repository referenced it: no test, no workflow, no script and no document. | A reader expecting a version header finds none. Row 32.5 asserts its absence, so it cannot return unnoticed. |
| 32.3 | Declare `name: apartment-finder` in the file | (a) Leave the name to the parent directory; (b) document `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` for the operator to set; (c) rename the directory | Measured: the project name resolved to `docker`, the basename of `infrastructure/docker`, so the stack created `docker_default`, `docker_db-data` and containers named `docker-backend-1` — names that collide with any other stack whose compose file also sits in a directory called `docker`. (b) puts a correctness property in an operator's hands and is silent when they omit it. (c) would break the declared build contexts and the documented build command. Compose's precedence leaves `-p` and `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` above the file, so an operator can still override. | The network and the `db-data` volume change namespace, so an existing local stack's volume is no longer the one a fresh start attaches to. Local data only; the volume is recreated by the migrate service on first start. |
| 32.4 | Assert that every variable the file marks required is shipped with a **non-empty** value by `.env.example` | (a) Assert only that each required variable is documented by name; (b) drive a real `docker compose config` from the test suite; (c) assert nothing and rely on the corrected wording | (a) is what the suite already did, and it is exactly the gap this finding slipped through: the pre-existing helper extracted variable *names* and never looked at the value, so an entry present but empty satisfied it. (b) needs a Compose binary the CI image does not carry and would make a unit test depend on an external tool. Parsing the two files and comparing is enough to encode the invariant. Proven a real gate: run against the committed pre-fix files it reports one offender, `CLOUD_SQL_INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME`; against the fix it reports none. | The check reads the file as text, so a substitution written across a line break would not be seen. The file writes each on one line, and the surrounding cases already assert that shape. |
| 32.5 | State in `.env.example` how a dollar sign inside a value read by Compose behaves, and demonstrate the rule empirically before writing it | (a) Say nothing; (b) escape the shipped values pre-emptively; (c) note only that `$$` is the escape | Measured against the real binary rather than described from documentation, because the wording is what a developer will trust: `pa$sword-dollar` reached the container as `pa-dollar`, and `lead-${SECRET_KEY}-tail` reached it with the real signing key substituted in. So an unescaped `$` opens a variable reference and consumes the name that follows it — which (c) would not convey, and which matters most for exactly the values most likely to contain one. (b) is impossible: nothing this file ships contains a dollar sign, and the affected values are the secrets a developer fills in. This file's own convention is that a comment documents what a value accepts, which is what this is. | A developer who exports the name instead of writing it here does not need the doubling, which the wording states. |
| 32.6 | Exclude `requirements-dev.txt` from the build context in **both** ignore files | (a) Exclude it only in `backend/.dockerignore`, the file the build actually reads; (b) leave it, since no package from it is installed; (c) stop shipping the file to the repository | Row 9.2 makes the two files' pattern bodies byte-identical and verifies it by comparison, so changing one alone would break that property and the guard that rests on it — (a) is therefore not the smaller change, it is the inconsistent one. (b) understates the point: the manifest names the audit, lint and test tooling, so a published image describing its own development toolchain widens what a reader of that image learns for no runtime benefit. Verified with Docker's own ignore-matching implementation against the declared context: the effective file list goes from 29 files to 28, the single removed entry is `requirements-dev.txt`, nothing is newly added, and `requirements.txt`, `alembic.ini`, the full `app/` tree and every migration remain. Neither pattern can match `requirements.txt`. | Two files carry the pattern rather than one. That is the invariant row 9.2 established, and the comparison check enforces it. |
| 32.7 | **Extends rows 9.2 and 24.5.** Record that the effective ignore file for every declared build is the copy at that build's context root, so the repository-root `.dockerignore` is defence in depth rather than the active control | (a) Delete the root file as unused; (b) relocate it beside the Dockerfile; (c) change the build contexts to the repository root so the root file governs | Row 9.2 states the resolution rule and row 24.5 states that the contexts are deliberately untouched, but neither draws the consequence, and the review found it worth stating: the two declared contexts are `../../backend` and `../../frontend`, so no declared build reads the root file at any point. It still earns its place — the AAP names it at that path, and it governs any build a developer runs from the repository root by hand. (a) would remove a control the AAP requires and would reopen the finding for an ad-hoc build. (b) would put it at a path no build resolves either. (c) is the change row 24.5 warns silently reopens INFRA-3. No file changes for this row; the record is the deliverable. | A reader may assume the root file is what the documented build enforces. That is precisely what this row exists to correct. |
| 32.8 | Add a **separate** readiness route that reads the database, keep `/health` an unconditional liveness probe, and point the container probe at the readiness path | (a) Make `/health` itself read the database; (b) leave `/health` alone and have the container probe read a data route such as `GET /listings/`; (c) add no route and accept the signal as it is; (d) return the failure cause in the readiness body | Measured against a process whose `DATABASE_URL` addressed a dead port: `/health` answered `200 {"status":"ok"}` and the container probe literal exited **0**, so an orchestrator marked the container healthy, while `GET /listings/` and `POST /auth/login` answered `500` — the container was in service and could serve nothing. (a) would destroy the distinction the two probe kinds exist for: an orchestrator restarts a container that fails liveness, so a database outage would cycle every replica instead of removing them from the load balancer, turning a dependency failure into an outage. It would also change a frozen response contract that five test cases and the AAP's own wording rest on. (b) makes a business route carry an operational contract and would report a listings defect as a database outage. (c) leaves the misleading signal the finding names. (d) is refused for the reason every other refusal in this codebase is generic. The probe reads one statement through the session dependency the AAP already prescribes for a route that needs a session, so it acquires and releases a connection exactly as a real request does rather than testing a private path. | The container is now marked unhealthy during a database outage, which is the intended report and a behaviour change for any operator watching that signal. The route adds one connection acquisition per probe interval, which is 30 seconds. The readiness path is a suffix of the liveness path, so a probe assertion matching by prefix would accept either; the contract case names the full path for that reason. |

## 33. Runtime QA findings — the two input contracts that answered `500`

Rows added by a runtime QA review of the reconciled migrated stack, which drove
1267 cases against a freshly migrated PostgreSQL database and reported full
compliance for every in-scope security requirement. It raised two findings, both
Minor and both the same shape: a value a client may send reached the database
driver instead of being refused by the request contract, so the request ended as
a server error rather than a refusal. A filter name or a predicate value
carrying a NUL was accepted by `FilterCreate` and then refused by the driver
with a plain `ValueError`, which is not a database error and so passed the
endpoint's `except SQLAlchemyError` and answered through the unhandled-exception
handler — reachable by any self-registered account. A `bedrooms` or `bathrooms`
count above the range of its integer column was accepted by `ListingCreate` and
then refused by PostgreSQL, so the admin write answered `500` with the
endpoint's own detail.

Both causes were confirmed by execution rather than inference before anything was
changed: against the real database, the NUL commit raised
`builtins.ValueError: A string literal cannot contain NUL (0x00) characters.`
with `isinstance(exc, SQLAlchemyError)` measuring `False`, and the out-of-range
commit raised `sqlalchemy.exc.DataError` wrapping `integer out of range`. Each
fix therefore sits in the request contract, and no endpoint, no exception
handler and no response model changed — which is what keeps the frozen
expressions at `filters.py:21` and `filters.py:33` byte-identical.

| # | Decision | Alternatives | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------|-------|
| 33.1 | Refuse `FORBIDDEN_TEXT_CHARACTERS` at the filter contract with one module helper called from a `@validator` on `FilterCreate.name` and one on `CriteriaCreate.value` | (a) Widen the endpoint's `except SQLAlchemyError` to catch `ValueError` too; (b) strip the character instead of refusing the value; (c) give both fields a `regex=` allowlist in their `constr`; (d) refuse every control character rather than the one the column cannot hold; (e) also guard the two response models | The three other text surfaces of this contract — `criteria.field`, `criteria.operator` and `zip_codes.code` — already refuse the character, each through a pattern or an allowlist, and measurement confirmed all three do so before the driver is ever reached. Only the two length-bounded free-text fields were unguarded, so refusing at the contract makes the surface uniform in the one place the other three are already decided, and it closes the authenticated write path and the contract itself together. (a) treats the symptom: the request would answer the endpoint's own `500` instead of the generic one, and a value the column cannot store would still travel the whole way to the driver on every call. (b) silently alters what the client asked to save, which no other refusal in this contract does. (c) would have to enumerate every acceptable character for a free-text name in five languages, and the review measured that this contract already round-trips emoji, 4-byte CJK, RTL overrides and combining marks byte-for-byte — an allowlist would break that. (d) refuses more than the defect: PostgreSQL stores every other control character in a `text` column, the review confirmed those round-trip, and refusing them would be a behaviour change no finding asks for. (e) guards a direction that cannot occur, because a stored row cannot contain the character the column refuses. | Two modules now declare the same one-character set rather than one. Row 33.3 is what stops them drifting. A client that was sending a NUL and relying on the `500` sees `422` instead; nothing in the product sends one, and the value was never stored either way. |
| 33.2 | Bound `ListingCreate.bedrooms` and `.bathrooms` with a declarative `le=MAX_COUNT` where `MAX_COUNT` is the range of the column | (a) A `pre=True` validator refusing the magnitude, matching the treatment the measurement fields already receive; (b) widen the columns to `BigInteger` in a new migration; (c) catch `DataError` in the endpoint and answer `422` from there; (d) leave the count unbounded and accept the `500` as a database concern | The measurement fields need a `pre=True` validator because their failure happens *inside* coercion — a whole number too large to become a float raises `OverflowError` during conversion and escapes request-validation handling. The counts have no such problem, and it was measured rather than assumed: Pydantic v1's integer coercion already answers `422` for an infinity and for a NaN, and a Python integer has no width, so every remaining form a JSON body can carry — `2147483648`, `2 ** 63`, `10 ** 30`, `1e30` and the same value as text — arrives as an ordinary integer that a declared ceiling refuses. So (a) would add a code path that catches nothing the constraint does not, while the constraint additionally publishes `maximum` in the OpenAPI document, where a client can read the bound instead of discovering it. (b) is a schema change for a value no product sends, and it moves the same defect to the next boundary rather than removing it. (c) leaves the contract able to produce a value the column cannot hold, which is the property the contract's own docstring already claims for the measurement fields; the finding is precisely that the claim was not true of the counts. (d) leaves an admin write answering `500` and writing an exception-level record on every attempt. | The bound is the column's range, so raising the column later means raising this too; the constant names the range so the two are read together. The provider mapper builds this same contract, so a provider record reporting an absurd count is now a counted discard naming the field rather than a failed commit — which makes the mapper docstring's existing claim that the contract "bounds each one" true. `2147483647` is still accepted and still stored, verified through the write route and read back anonymously. |
| 33.3 | Hold the two modules' forbidden-character sets equal by assertion rather than by sharing a module | (a) A new shared guard module imported by all four schema modules, as the review's own suggestion proposes; (b) import `FORBIDDEN_TEXT_CHARACTERS` from `backend.app.schema.listing` into `backend.app.schema.filter`; (c) accept the duplication with no guard | The review is right that the recurrence risk is the real finding behind both defects, and this row is the answer to it — but not by adding a file. AAP §0.6.1 declares its file map exhaustive, in its own words leaving nothing "to be discovered", and a new module in a folder whose every member is enumerated there is outside it. The convention already in this codebase is a per-module text guard: `user.py` declares its own control-character pattern and `listing.py` its own forbidden set, both of which have survived two rationale-relocation passes. (b) makes the filter contract depend on the listing contract for a fact about `text` columns that belongs to neither, and both schema modules are required to stay import-light. What the shared module would actually buy is that the sets cannot diverge, and an assertion buys exactly that at the cost of one test: it fails the moment either module changes its set alone. | The equality is enforced by a test rather than by construction, so it is caught at the next run rather than at the edit. Two other schema modules — `user.py` and `subscription.py` — are outside this assertion; `user.py` refuses a wider set already and `subscription.py` declares no free text. |
| 33.4 | Extend the `ListingCreate` docstring so its stated bound covers the counts, and extend the test module's docstring with the two behaviours | (a) Leave both; (b) record the change only here | The finding quoted that docstring as the source of the guarantee it then disproved — it promises that "a magnitude beyond that type is refused here rather than stored", and that was true of the three measurement fields and untrue of the two counts. Leaving it would leave the document that a reader trusts still overstating what the contract does. The test module's docstring already enumerates the behaviours a runtime review found missing, which is that file's own established convention, so two sentences continue it rather than introduce anything. | Both are statements of behaviour, so both must be corrected again if the behaviour changes. Each is asserted by a case in the same file. |

### Deliberate non-changes from this round

|---|----------------|------------------------|-------|
| 33.5 | `criteria.field`, `criteria.operator` and `zip_codes.code` receive no forbidden-character validator | Each is already shaped by an anchored pattern or a closed allowlist, and each was measured refusing the character before and after this round. A second guard on a field that already refuses it would be a change with no behaviour behind it. | If any of the three ever loses its pattern, it loses this refusal with it. The case that asserts every text surface of the contract refuses the character covers all five, so that loss fails a test. |

This is the opposite of row 15.3, where the value at issue *was* storable and the response guard was therefore load-bearing. | A row written by a path outside this application — a direct database write — is still bounded by the column itself. |
| 33.7 | The endpoints' `except SQLAlchemyError` blocks and the unhandled-exception handler | Both behaved correctly: the review confirmed the rollback held, no partial row was written, no database or framework internal reached the body, and a 30-request burst left the pool steady at six connections with the service healthy. The defect was that a refusable value reached them at all. | A future driver-level `ValueError` from some other value would still answer through the generic handler. That handler's contract — one generic detail plus a correlation identifier — is asserted by its own cases. |

Every other integer column is a key or a server-owned counter. | If a future contract accepts another integer column, it needs its own bound. The constant is named for reuse. |

The first is a docstring wording nicety on a validator whose behaviour the review verified as correct, including that no stored address carries any whitespace or control character; the second is the shape of the provider's hosted link and row-owner-only; the third is required by RFC 7235, whose auth-scheme token is case-insensitive. | The `_enforce_email_format` docstring remains slightly imprecise about the interaction between field-level stripping and its own pattern. The five decisions Rule 3 requires concern irreversible operations, authorization boundaries and ambiguity-resolving assumptions; nothing in this round is any of those — neither fix changes who may call anything, neither is irreversible, and the review's reproduction steps left no ambiguity to resolve. Measured identical in kind, count and position before and after this round. | Three style findings remain in a frozen file. |

## 34. AAP-baseline decisions not recorded by an earlier round

Sections 1 to 33 were each written by the round that made the changes they
describe. A few decisions belong to the remediation as a whole rather than to any
one round: they were settled when the plan was adopted, and no later review had
cause to revisit them. Rule 1 does not exempt a decision from this log because it
was made early, and several of these are deviations from a literal reading of the
requirements, which the Rule treats as defects when they go unexplained. This
section records them, together with the figures the work is measured by and one
reconciliation against the tree.

**Line-number convention.** A line number in this log locates a construct in the
tree as it stood when the finding citing it was raised. Most of the files named
here have since been rewritten, so a baseline number no longer resolves against
the current tree — `@asyncio.coroutine`, cited at
`backend/app/tasks/listing_updater.py:10`, is one of several. Baseline numbers are
kept because they are what the findings and the plan cite; where a row describes
what the tree does *now*, it names the path and the construct and gives no line
number. Rows 1.9, 12.1 and 12.2 already follow this convention.
