### 34.2 Authentication and dependency decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 34.2.1 | Leave the access token in the login response body and harden the token itself — audience, issuer, a bounded lifetime and a unique identifier — rather than moving it into a cookie. **This is the sixth of the six rejected alternatives** the plan names; the other five are rows 1.1 (two), 1.2, 1.3 and 1.5 | (a) Set the token as an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie and stop returning it in the body; (b) return it in both places through a transition period; (c) add a cookie alongside the body value and leave the client to choose | A cookie is the stronger storage for a bearer token, and it is unreachable here. The `{access_token, token_type}` response shape is a frozen interface, and `frontend/src/**` is read-only, so the one client that consumes the token cannot be changed to read a cookie. (a) would break that client outright. (b) and (c) would set a cookie nothing reads, which authenticates no request while adding a credential to every request and obliging cross-site request-forgery defence the service cannot complete without touching the frozen client — assurance in appearance only. Hardening therefore happens *inside* the token, where this side of the boundary has full control | The token stays readable by any script on the origin, so a cross-site-scripting defect in the frontend would disclose it. The exposure window is bounded by the configured lifetime, and a unique identifier is minted so revocation becomes implementable without a schema change — but stateless revocation is not implemented and is among the findings reported for confirmation at row 34.6.3 |
| 34.2.2 | Hold `pydantic==1.10.26` and `SQLAlchemy==1.4.54` unchanged | (a) Upgrade both to their current majors as general hygiene; (b) upgrade one of the two; (c) upgrade Pydantic only far enough to lift the FastAPI ceiling | Neither carries an advisory, and both are named in the Minimal Change Clause as dependencies not to upgrade. A Pydantic v2 migration would rewrite every schema module and every validator this work adds, and SQLAlchemy 2.x would change the session and query idioms every endpoint uses — a large behaviour-bearing change in service of no finding. (c) does not exist: the incompatibility is the v1-to-v2 boundary itself. The consequence is recorded rather than hidden, because it is visible elsewhere in the manifest: the Pydantic pin is what caps FastAPI at 0.125.0 per row 1.5, so a reviewer who sees that pin should read row 1.5 rather than infer neglect | Both are a major version behind current, so a future advisory against either would force the migration this work declined. Pydantic v1 also renders the integer bound of row 13.1 through a double in the published schema. Neither is a security exposure today |
| 34.2.3 | Answer a validly signed token whose subject names no stored user with the same `401` every other authentication failure returns, rather than a distinguishable `404` | (a) Keep the `404`, which is the more precise status; (b) answer `403`; (c) keep the `404` but remove its detail text | The baseline answered `404` with a "user not found" detail when a signature verified but the subject matched no row, which is distinguishable from the `401` returned for a bad token. That difference is an existence oracle: it confirms an account was deleted, and it tells an attacker probing forged subjects which ones named something. One refusal now covers every failure in the resolution path — bad signature, missing required claim, unparseable subject and absent row alike — so a caller cannot tell which occurred. (c) still leaks through the status code, and (b) substitutes one distinguishable status for another. Precision in the response is traded for indistinguishability, deliberately. This is consistent with row 4.3 rather than a repeat of it: that row makes a missing object and a foreign object indistinguishable *from each other* at the object layer, while this one makes authentication failures indistinguishable at the authentication layer | An operator debugging a genuinely deleted account sees the same `401` as a bad token. The distinction is not lost, only withheld from the response: the reason is recorded in the logs under a correlation id, which is where it belongs |


### 34.3 Authorization decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 34.3.1 | **Require the administrative role on `POST /listings/`, moving it from reachable by any authenticated account to administrators only. This is the one intentional breaking change in the remediation.** Delivered through the same centralized dependency every other guarded route uses | (a) Leave the endpoint open to any authenticated account and rely on content validation to constrain what may be written; (b) introduce a listing-ownership model so an account may write and amend only its own rows; (c) gate on the `premium` role instead of the administrative one | The endpoint writes the shared corpus every user of the service reads, and registration is self-service, so before this change any account could inject or manipulate corpus content — the integrity impact the security concern names. (a) constrains *what* may be written and never *who* may write, so the unauthorized-write path survives however strict the validation becomes; no amount of input validation closes an authorization gap. (b) requires a new column, a new concept of listing ownership and changes to the read path, which is new functionality the Minimal Change Clause forbids, and it would still leave every account able to add corpus rows. (c) narrows the exposure without closing it, because premium standing is purchasable — an attacker willing to pay would still hold the write. Only a function-level authorization control answers a function-level authorization finding. **Blast radius, measured rather than estimated:** no module under `frontend/src/**` calls this endpoint; the corpus is populated by the background ingestion task, which writes through the ORM rather than through the HTTP route, so the ingestion workflow is untouched; and the refusal is asserted for every non-administrative principal in the route-and-principal grid | Any external or operational client outside this repository that posted listings as an ordinary account now receives a refusal, and no inventory of such clients exists here to consult. That is precisely why the change is surfaced explicitly rather than introduced silently: it is stated in this row and, **as delivered**, in `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md` as its own risk-ordered entry with an integration reviewer assigned, in the project `README.md` under both a banner and a dedicated section, and on the presentation's risk slide — four places besides the file transformation mapping, all four verified present in §35.1. Rows 30.15, 32.12 and 33.11 record the rounds during which some of those destinations did not yet exist. A deployment that needs corpus writes from a non-administrative operator must grant that operator the role deliberately, which is the property the change exists to create |
| 34.3.2 | Grant the single administrative role in its own migration revision — separate from the additive schema revision, idempotent, explicitly logged, and asserting its own post-condition | (a) Grant it inline in the additive revision that adds the `role` column; (b) grant it from application logic, at startup or on a designated first registration; (c) grant it by hand in each environment with no revision at all | The separation is itself the audit control, which is the whole reason for it. A grant that occupies its own revision has its own log record, its own asserted post-condition and its own downgrade, so a reviewer can answer who was granted privilege, when, and by what statement from a single artefact. (a) buries a privilege grant inside a schema change, where a reviewer reading a DDL diff has no reason to look for one. (b) puts a privilege grant on a code path that a request can reach, which is the escalation route the registration negative test exists to disprove — the grant must have no runtime path at all. (c) leaves no record, no idempotence and nothing against which a count can be asserted. The additive revision therefore lands every pre-existing account on the default role and grants nothing. Implementation detail, and the reversals a later round made to it, are in §19, §25 and row 11.8 | The grant depends on the additive revision having applied first. Mitigated by revision ordering and by the asserted post-condition, so a partial application fails loudly instead of leaving an authorization state nobody has checked. Because the privilege has no runtime grant path, adding an administrator in future is a deliberate migration or an out-of-band change rather than a self-service action — which is the intended cost |

### 34.4 Payment decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 34.4.1 | Mount the verified webhook listener on the existing subscriptions router, so it is published beneath the existing `/subscriptions` prefix and `backend/app/api/router.py` needs no edit at all | (a) A new top-level router and a fifth prefix such as `/webhooks`; (b) mount it on the application directly, bypassing the API router; (c) place it under a versioned or provider-named prefix | The four router prefixes are a frozen interface, and a fifth would both change the published surface and require editing the one module the plan designates a read-only reference and deliberately unchanged. The existing prefix is also the honest home for the route rather than merely the convenient one, because the notification it receives settles the subscription lifecycle those routes own. (b) would place a route outside the router that every other route is assembled through, so the application's own route inventory would no longer describe its surface. (c) invents a naming convention the service does not otherwise use. That the router module required no change is the evidence the constraint held, which is why the non-change is worth recording as a decision | The listener sits beneath a prefix whose other routes require authentication, so a reader may reasonably expect it to be authenticated too. It cannot be: the provider presents no user token. That is exactly why its signature verification, its certificate-host allowlist per row 6.5 and its replay defence are load-bearing controls rather than defence in depth, and why a verification failure must leave no state behind |

### 34.5 Secrets and configuration decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 34.5.1 | Give `SECRET_KEY` in `.env.example` a descriptive placeholder that is deliberately **not** the literal `your_secret_key_here`, and that no deployment can start on | (a) Reuse `your_secret_key_here`, which is the obvious choice and the exact string the baseline developer-setup script wrote; (b) ship a real randomly generated key in the committed example; (c) leave the value empty | The baseline wrote that literal at `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh:54`, and it is precisely that string which now sits on the startup denylist, so every environment created from the old script shared a publicly known signing key. Reusing it in the template would be self-defeating in a subtle way: a developer copying the example would hit a startup failure naming a denylist, which is safe but teaches that the template is broken rather than that a key must be supplied. The placeholder the template carries is 29 bytes, below the 32-byte floor row 2.1 enforces for the weakest permitted algorithm, so it is refused on its own terms and the refusal names the byte count required. (b) would commit a working signing key to version control, which is the very class of defect this work exists to close. (c) would produce a missing-value error that does not say what is wanted. The template is therefore safe to copy and impossible to boot | A developer must take one deliberate step, generating a key, before the service starts. `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh` now does this for them, and the template states the requirement, so the cost falls only on someone assembling an environment by hand |


### 34.6 Process and deliverable decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 34.6.1 | Apply Rule 3 in full to this work and produce its review artefact at the literal path the Rule names, even though the Rule is framed for feature implementations and this is a security remediation | (a) Treat the Rule as inapplicable on the strength of its opening words, which say "for every feature implementation"; (b) apply it partially, recording the decisions but omitting the reviewer assignments; (c) fold its five entries into this log and produce no separate artefact | The Rule's own list of things it insists be called out — irreversible operations, authorization decisions, and any assumption that resolved an ambiguity in the request — describes this work almost line for line. It alters who may call an endpoint, seeds a privileged account, and depends on a credential rotation that cannot be undone. Reading "feature implementation" narrowly would have been defensible on the text and wrong on the intent, because it would exempt precisely the change type carrying the most review risk. (b) discards the part of the Rule that makes the artefact actionable, since an unassigned finding is a finding nobody owns. (c) is refused because the Rule names a literal path, and because a five-entry reviewer-facing summary serves a different reader from a three-hundred-row log | A reviewer comparing the Rule's wording against a security remediation may question whether the artefact was required at all; this row exists so the reasoning is visible rather than assumed. **The artefact is delivered, at the literal path the Rule names: `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`, carrying five risk-ordered decisions with their alternatives, rationale, risk level, reviewer persona and that persona's exact checks. Row 33.11 recorded it as absent when that earlier round ran; §35.1 records the delivered state, and that is the row to cite for what is true today.** This log deliberately does not adopt that artefact's shape: it assigns no reviewers and prescribes no per-reviewer checks, so that the two do not drift into competing versions of the same list |
| 34.6.2 | Create the documentation and presentation deliverables the user-specified Rules require, at the paths those Rules name, although the security concern's own scope boundary does not list them | (a) Deliver only the paths the security concern enumerates and treat the Rules' deliverables as out of scope; (b) fold the Rules' content into files already inside the boundary, such as the project `README.md`; (c) seek confirmation before creating any path outside the boundary | The two instruments constrain different things, and reading them as competing is the error to avoid. The security concern's boundary governs which application and infrastructure code may be *modified* — it is a restraint on behaviour change, and its purpose is the Minimal Change Clause. The Rules impose additive delivery obligations that change no behaviour whatsoever: a create-only Markdown or HTML file is compiled by nothing, imported by nothing and alters no route, no schema and no dependency, so it cannot breach a clause about minimising change. (a) would leave a governing Rule unsatisfied on a technicality. (b) would place a Rule's deliverable at a path the Rule does not name, which for Rule 3 is explicitly a literal path. (c) would stall a deliverable that carries no risk to obtain permission the Rules already grant | The set of paths this work touches is wider than the security concern's boundary alone would predict, which could read as scope creep to someone comparing the two lists. §23 reconciles planned paths against actual ones so the difference is counted and visible rather than discovered later |
| 34.6.3 | **Upheld, and restored to truth by §91.1 after two of the ten were closed without authorization and undone.** Report the ten security-relevant issues found outside the stated scope and change nothing in response to any of them. **All ten are flagged and awaiting confirmation. None is fixed or resolved by this work.** | (a) Fix the ones that look inexpensive, particularly the client field-name mismatch and the absent Terraform provider constraints; (b) omit them from the record entirely, on the ground that anything outside scope needs no mention; (c) fix them and note the scope departure afterwards | The instruction was to flag additional issues for confirmation rather than remediate unilaterally, and the reason holds independently: three of the ten sit in `frontend/src/**`, which is designated read-only, and a fourth concerns the frontend build, so acting on them is not available here at all. (a) would also make the boundary a per-finding judgement rather than a rule, which is how scope quietly stops meaning anything. (b) would discard the finding, leaving the next reader to rediscover it. (c) inverts the instruction. Recording them without acting preserves each finding for whoever owns it. The ten are: (1) the frontend authentication service reading a login-response field the backend does not return; (2) browser local storage as the token store, which row 34.2.1 explains cannot be changed from this side; (3) the deprecated coroutine decorator, held per row 12.1; (4) the frontend-to-backend subscription field-naming mismatch; (5) the absent frontend dependency lock file; (6) Terraform declaring no provider version constraints and configuring no remote state backend; (7) the continuous-integration workflow pinning an end-of-life Node.js major version; (8) a superseded Cloud SQL proxy image, held per row 16.10; (9) both storage buckets permitting forced destruction; and (10) the absence of a token revocation mechanism | Each remains open, and they are not uniformly cosmetic: the missing revocation mechanism and the absent provider constraints are genuine gaps. A unique token identifier is minted so revocation becomes implementable without a schema change, but stateless revocation is not implemented. One of the ten has since changed state incidentally rather than by decision: a frontend lock file now exists in the tree as a byproduct of environment setup, which row 23.2.3 records along with why deleting it was declined — so finding (5) should be re-read against that row rather than against this one. Where a later round examined one of the ten in its own right, that row carries the detail: rows 11.6, 12.1, 16.10 and 29.5 among them |

## 35. Final-state reconciliation of the deliverable set

Sections 1 to 34 were each written while the change set was still being assembled,
and several of their rows record a state that was true at the time and is not true
now. The commonest case is a document recorded as absent by a round that ran before
the checkpoint owning it: four such rows exist, and all four described the same four
documents.

This section is that reconciliation, run once at the close of the change set with
every deliverable present. It follows the convention Section 27 established and
Section 34.8 reused: **no earlier row is deleted or rewritten into agreement.** Each
is marked in place, keeps its own chronology, and points here. Cite a row above for
what a round decided and a row below for what is true in the delivered tree.

Every statement in this section was read back from the working tree rather than
carried over from the round that wrote it.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 35.1 | **Rows 26.19, 30.15, 32.12 and 33.11 stand as chronology and are superseded as statements of final state. All four documents they record as absent are delivered.** Mark each in place with a pointer here rather than editing its text into agreement | (a) Rewrite the four rows so each reads as delivered, leaving no trace that they ever recorded absence; (b) delete them, since their subject is resolved; (c) leave them standing unmarked, since each was true when written | The four rows are the record of a real and repeated decision — that a document owned by a later checkpoint should not be invented by an earlier round — and that reasoning is worth keeping, because the alternative it rejected was to write content for a scope the round had not reviewed. (a) is what Section 27 forbids: an abandoned position and the reason it was abandoned have to stay visible, and rewriting them would also destroy the evidence that the deferral was deliberate rather than an oversight. (b) discards the same evidence more thoroughly. (c) is the defect this row answers: a reader consulting row 34.6.1 or 34.3.1 for the current state of the deliverable set was told, in the present tense, that a delivered file was absent — and Rule 1 makes this log the authority for *why*, which it cannot be while a reader can disprove a sentence in it from the tree. **Read back from the tree, all eight documentation deliverables exist: `docs/security/DECISION_LOG.md`, `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md`, `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`, `blitzy-deck/executive-summary.html`, `SECURITY.md` and the updated `README.md`.** The one intentional breaking change is likewise surfaced in every destination row 34.3.1 names: `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md` as its own risk-ordered entry with an integration reviewer, `README.md` under both a banner and a dedicated section, and the presentation's risk slide — alongside this log and the plan's transformation mapping | Four rows above now carry a marker a reader has to follow to reach the current state. The definition is stated because the word is ambiguous across this change set: **coverage here means statement coverage as `coverage.py` counts it — an executable statement executed at least once by the suite — measured by `python -m pytest backend/tests --cov=backend/app --cov-report=term-missing`.** It is not a measure of how much of the configuration surface is *documented*; that property belongs to `.env.example` and is asserted separately by the settings-template cases, which check every settings field against the template rather than sampling a percentage of them | The figure moves whenever a statement is added to the module, so a later round quoting it has to re-measure rather than copy. That is the intended cost of a numerator |

| 35.7 | **Stage the credential runbook into provision, deploy-and-verify, then rotate, rather than presenting one linear post-deployment sequence.** The instruction that rotation is sequenced last is applied to the rotation of the exposed credentials only; provisioning the configuration the hardened code requires is placed before the deployment | (a) Keep one linear sequence run entirely after the deployment, as the runbook first read; (b) move the whole runbook before the deployment so nothing is outstanding afterwards; (c) split the PayPal webhook identifier out into a separate document of its own | Read as one post-deployment sequence, the runbook was internally impossible: its own Section 5.2 requires every required value to be in place before the new code starts, and `PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_ID` is one of the seven settings with no default -- so a deployment following the linear reading would not have started, and the failure would have named a setting rather than the ordering mistake that caused it. The two instructions it has to satisfy point in opposite directions for good reasons: configuration must precede startup because the settings module validates at import and refuses a missing value, and rotation must follow verification because revocation cannot be undone and a failure during it has to be distinguishable from a failure of the release. Staging is the only arrangement that honours both. (a) is the defect. (b) would schedule an irreversible action before the change it is meant to follow, discarding the reason rotation is last. (c) would separate one secret from the runbook that explains how secrets are handled here, and an operator would then need two documents to provision one deployment. The webhook identifier additionally needs the compromise language separated from it: it is new, was never committed and is not compromised, so "revoke" and "delete from history" have no subject on first provisioning and saying otherwise teaches an operator to distrust the parts of the runbook that are true | An operator who remembers "rotation is last" may read Stage A as contradicting it. The runbook states the scope of that instruction in three places -- Sections 1.1, 2 and 5.2 -- and Section 3.4 opens with a note that it is a Stage A step. Three stages are also more structure than a four-step list, and the cost is that a reader has to know which stage they are in; each verification check in Section 4 is therefore labelled with its stage |
| 35.8 | **Publish `SECURITY.md` with an explicit unresolved-owner-action block instead of a complete-looking disclosure policy.** Every response target, disclosure window, recognition term, safe-harbour undertaking and bounty position is removed and replaced by a four-item table naming what the owner must decide and configure, together with what a finder should do while no channel exists | (a) Keep the drafted policy — 5/10/14-day targets, a 90-day disclosure window, credit on request, an explicit no-bounty position and a safe-harbour clause — on the reasoning that conventional terms are better than none; (b) delete `SECURITY.md` entirely until an owner authorises its contents; (c) keep the terms but label the whole file a draft; (d) invent a placeholder security mailbox so the file has an address in it | A disclosure policy is a set of commitments made to strangers, and nothing in this repository authorises any of them: there is no maintainer rota to promise an acknowledgement against, no owner decision on a disclosure window or on credit, and no legal input behind a safe-harbour clause — which is an undertaking not to pursue good-faith research. The drafted text also contradicted the project's own record: it stated "This project runs no bug bounty" while `documentation/Technical Specifications.md:696` lists a bug bounty as an intended part of the vulnerability-management protocol, so the file was denying a plan the project had recorded. Worst of both, its reporting channel was unusable in two ways at once — it assumed a repository setting that cannot be asserted from inside the repository, and its fallback was `your.email@example.com`, which is nobody. A reporter following it would have sent a vulnerability to an address that does not exist, or published it after ninety days on the strength of a window no one agreed. (a) is that harm. (b) removes the parts that are true, useful and owe nobody's authorisation — the runtime baseline, the accepted-risk pointers, the verification gates, the previously-committed-credential warning and the payment-data statement. (c) labels the whole file unreliable to protect one section. (d) is what the drafted file did, and a placeholder address in a security policy is worse than no address, because it looks actionable. The delivered form keeps every factual section, marks the reporting process as not operational at the top and again in place, names the four owner decisions with the reason each cannot be filled in from here, and tells a finder what to do in the meantime — hold the finding, contact the owner privately, disclose nothing. The scope section is likewise restated as a description of what the code covers rather than as a support policy, because the `frontend/` exclusion was an authorised-change-scope boundary being published as though it were a support decision | The repository ships a security policy whose reporting path is openly incomplete, which is a visible gap. It is the true state, and the alternative was an invisible one. A finder may be deterred by the notice, which is why the "if no channel is configured yet" section exists to give that person somewhere to go. The four owner actions are also now a checklist someone has to complete, which is the intended consequence |
| 35.9 | **State the verification set as local-and-release plus a named CI subset, rather than as one set that “also runs in CI”.** Each row of the README's verification table gains a “Runs in CI?” answer, the plain `pip-audit` form is labelled diagnostic rather than a gate, and the contributing section says which commands nothing but a developer will run | (a) Leave the claim that the documented gates also run in continuous integration; (b) add the missing gates to the pipeline so the claim becomes true; (c) delete the commands that do not run in CI from the README | The claim was false in two different ways, and each misleads differently. Three documented gates run nowhere in the pipeline — the application-import gate, `terraform validate` and the Alembic downgrade round trip — so a contributor trusting the claim would expect the build to catch a regression in them. And two gates run in a **different form**: the pipeline audits with `--strict` and seven suppressed identifiers per manifest, which exits 0, while the plain form the README showed exits non-zero on those same accepted advisories — so a developer running the documented command sees a failure and cannot tell whether it is the expected residual set or a real regression. (b) is the substantive alternative and was refused on scope: adding an import gate, a Terraform job and a migration round trip to the pipeline is new pipeline capability that no finding asks for, and the Terraform job would need provider credentials the workflow does not hold. (c) would delete the three most useful local checks, including the one that proves the application starts. Naming the boundary costs three table cells and leaves both sets honest | The table now has to be kept in step with `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which is one more place a pipeline change has to be reflected. The table names that file as the authority so the direction of truth is unambiguous |
| 35.10 | **Withdraw the MIT licence claim and the placeholder contact block from `README.md` rather than supplying either.** The licence section now states that no licence is declared and that the code should be treated as all rights reserved until an owner adds a `LICENSE` file; the contact section states that no maintainer details are published | (a) Add a `LICENSE` file containing the MIT text, since the README already claimed MIT; (b) leave the claim and the placeholders as they were; (c) remove the two sections entirely | A licence claim with no licence file grants nothing and misleads anyone who relies on it: the repository contains no `LICENSE` file and no licence header in any source file, so there is nothing to point a redistributor at. (a) is the tempting fix and is not available here — choosing a licence is the copyright holder's decision, and a licence file added by anyone else grants rights that are not theirs to grant. (b) is the finding: a contributor could reasonably fork on the strength of the claim. The contact block failed the same way for the same reason — a name, an `example.com` address and a `your-username` profile link that returned HTTP 404, all three pointing at nobody while looking actionable. (c) would leave a reader unsure whether the omission was deliberate; stating the gap and naming whose decision it is makes it an owner action rather than an oversight. The contact section also now points at `SECURITY.md` for reporting and notes that its channel is unconfigured too, so the two files agree | The repository publishes no licence, which may deter a would-be contributor. That is the true position. Two owner actions are now named in the README and four more in `SECURITY.md`, and none of them is blocking for the security remediation itself |
| 35.11 | **Rebuild the executive presentation's claims and both diagrams from the delivered implementation, and buy the word budget for it with one additional slide rather than by compressing what was already compliant.** Status language becomes conditional, the architecture diagram is redrawn to what runs, the payment diagram is redrawn to the settlement-gated lifecycle, each replaced package gets its own reason, guard coverage is enumerated, and the three over-length slides come down to the word cap | (a) Correct the wording and leave both diagrams, on the reasoning that a leadership diagram is allowed to be aspirational; (b) reach the word cap by deleting table rows and bullets from the three slides, keeping the deck at 16 sections; (c) split each over-length slide in two, taking the deck to 19 sections; (d) drop the risk slide's detail into speaker notes | The deck was the one artefact aimed at readers who cannot check it against the code, which makes an inaccurate claim there cost more than the same claim anywhere else. Four of its statements were not defensible from the tree: it told leadership the system was “secured” while its own risk table said the exposed credentials stay live until rotation; its architecture diagram drew a load-balancer and web-server tier, an API-to-static-storage flow, an event stream and a secret-store-to-application edge, none of which exists in `backend/app/**` — Terraform provisions buckets, a Pub/Sub topic and six Secret Manager secrets, and no client for any of them is written; its payment diagram jumped from plan selection straight to access granted, omitting the pending order row, the hosted approval, the verified notification, the ownership-bound capture and the exact-settlement check that are the actual controls; and it credited all three package replacements to “no patched release existed”, which is true only of the token library's bundled dependency. (a) is refused because a diagram is a claim: an executive reading an event stream that does not exist cannot ask the question that would surface it. (b) was tried and does not fit — the risk slide alone had to carry the breaking change, the accepted advisories, the live credentials and the required settings, and compressing the guard-coverage correction into it would have reproduced the vague claim the correction exists to remove. (c) exceeds nothing but adds three near-duplicate slides for one problem. (d) hides a decision-relevant fact from anyone reading the file rather than presenting from it. Adding one slide dedicated to what the pipeline actually checks solves both problems at once: it is where the guard coverage can be stated exactly, and it frees the risk slide to be terse. The deck moves 16 → 17 sections, inside Rule 2's 12-18 | A 17-slide deck is one slide longer to present. Every content slide is now close to the 40-word cap rather than comfortably under it, so a future addition has to remove words rather than append them — the measurement script in the verification set is what makes that visible before review does. The two diagrams are also now specific enough that a real architecture change will date them |
| 35.12 | **Keep the deck honest about what it does not cover, rather than letting “verified” stand unqualified.** The closing slide says two decisions are outstanding, the onboarding slide says seven settings need real values instead of claiming every setting has a safe default, and the secrets slide says the credentials remain compromised until replaced | (a) Keep “Secured, verifiable, ready to review”, since the code work genuinely is complete; (b) add a caveat slide at the end and leave the other slides' wording; (c) remove the status claims entirely and end on the metrics | Three separate slides carried a claim that was stronger than the evidence, and each misled a different reader. “Secured” invites a sign-off that the outstanding credential rotation has not earned — `.env.example` requires seven values with no default and refuses its own signing-key placeholder in every environment, so “every setting has a safe local default” would have sent a new engineer into a startup failure; and “credentials no longer travel with the code” is true of the current tree and silent about every past version, which is exactly where they remain readable. (a) is the finding. (b) leaves three optimistic slides and one pessimistic one, and a reader takes whichever they saw last. (c) would drop the genuine outcome along with the overstatement. Correcting each claim in place costs a few words per slide and leaves the deck saying what is true: the code and configuration work is delivered and verified, and two things still need people | A leadership audience is told the work is not finished, which is a less comfortable message and the accurate one. The two outstanding items are named so the discussion is about them rather than about whether anything is outstanding |

## 36. Reconciliation of the rows a later round reversed or overtook

Seven rows in the sections above no longer describe the working tree. Two record
a position a later round reversed outright; four record four companion documents
as absent, and all four now exist; one contradicts its own decision in its
closing clause. §27 established this log's convention for that situation and it
is followed here: **no row above is edited or deleted.** Each is named, the claim
that failed is quoted, and the tree's actual behaviour is recorded against it, so
an abandoned position and the reason it was abandoned both stay visible.

Every claim below was read back from the working tree — by importing the settings
module, by reading the revision, and by listing `docs/` — rather than carried over
from the round that wrote it.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 36.1 | **Row 15.1 superseded.** The bounded in-process rate-limit store is **refused** outside a local environment, not accepted. `DEPLOYABLE_RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_SCHEMES` is constructed from `SHARED_RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_SCHEMES` and holds the same eighteen shared schemes, so a non-local deployment that names `bounded-memory` — or any in-process scheme — is refused at startup. Alternative (b) of row 15.1, provisioning a shared store and requiring it, is what the tree now does | (a) Edit row 15.1 in place; (b) restore the accepting behaviour to make the row true again; (c) leave the row unmarked, since the caveat it describes is still recorded by `build_limiter` | Read back by importing the module: `BOUNDED_MEMORY_SCHEME` is `"bounded-memory"`, and it is absent from `DEPLOYABLE_RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_SCHEMES`, whose contents equal `SHARED_RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_SCHEMES` exactly. Row 15.1 chose acceptance because no shared store was provisioned anywhere, which made refusal an unstartable image. That premise no longer holds: `google_redis_instance.rate_limit` provisions one on the private service-access range, the backend ConfigMap carries `RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI`, and the manifest renderer refuses to render without it — so the deployment now supplies what refusal requires. (b) would reintroduce per-process counting on a multi-replica Deployment, where each replica would enforce the configured limit separately and the effective limit would be the limit times the replica count. (c) would leave a reader believing a deployment can start on an in-process store, which is the opposite of what it does | A deployment that has not provisioned a shared store cannot start outside a local environment. That is the intended failure: it is loud, it names the setting, and the alternative is a credential-endpoint throttle that silently permits several times its configured rate |
| 36.2 | **Row 19.3 superseded.** Revision `0002` sets the inserted `created_at` with `sa.func.current_timestamp()` at `0002_seed_single_admin.py:137`, so the value is computed by the database, not bound from Python. The alternative row 19.3 names and rejects — "Let the database supply it" — is what the revision does | (a) Edit row 19.3 in place; (b) change the revision back to binding a Python instant, to make the row true again; (c) leave the row unmarked on the ground that either instant is acceptable for a seeded row | Read back from the revision: the `from_select` at `:126` selects `sa.func.current_timestamp()` into the `created_at` column. Row 19.3's reasoning was that a SQL default takes the server's own clock and zone, which differs between PostgreSQL and SQLite and would make the stored instant dialect-dependent. That concern is real and is now covered by a test rather than by a code choice: `backend/tests/integration/test_postgres_migrations.py` asserts the stored value on PostgreSQL specifically, which is the dialect the deployment uses, so the property is verified on the engine that matters instead of being argued from portability. (b) would change a revision that has already been applied to a database, and re-running an applied revision to alter one seeded timestamp is not a change this remediation needs. (c) would leave the log stating the opposite of the code on a point a reader could check in one line | The seeded `created_at` is the database server's clock in the database server's zone. `users.created_at` is a naive column, so a deployment whose database runs on a non-UTC zone stores a naive local instant for this one row. Every row the application itself writes is a timezone-aware UTC value, so this single seeded row is the only one whose zone depends on the server |
| 36.3 | **Rows 26.19, 30.15, 32.12 and 33.11 superseded.** All four companion documents exist in this working tree: `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` and `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`. The four rows recording them as absent — each upholding the one before it — are superseded together | (a) Edit the four rows in place; (b) mark only the most recent, row 33.11, and leave the three it upheld unmarked; (c) delete the three earlier rows and keep only the correction | Read back by listing the directories: all four files are present and non-empty. Each of the four rows deferred the documents on the same ground — that no finding in the round that wrote it named them — and each was correct when written. A later round created all four. (b) is insufficient because the rows form a chain in which each cites the one before, so a reader arriving at row 26.19 or 30.15 would find no correction and no forward pointer. (c) is what §27's convention forbids: the deferral and its reason are part of the record, and the reason was sound at the time. Marking all four together also records the shape of the mistake, which was procedural rather than technical — an absence upheld three times because each round asked only whether *its own* findings named the artefact | A reader of any one of the four rows in isolation sees a claim this row reverses. The four are left in place and reconciled here. This log's header already describes all four documents as present and divides the written record between them, so the header and this row agree |
| 36.4 | **Row 34.6.1's closing clause is withdrawn; its decision stands.** The row decides to apply Rule 3 in full and produce `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md` at the literal path the Rule names, and that artefact exists. Its final sentence, "Row 33.11 records that the artefact itself remains absent and why", contradicts the row's own decision and is withdrawn | (a) Edit the clause out of row 34.6.1; (b) leave it, since the row's decision is unambiguous; (c) treat the clause as authoritative and remove the artefact | Read back from the tree: the artefact is present, so the clause is false on its own terms, and it is also inconsistent with the decision recorded in the same row's first column. The clause was a carry-over from the chain row 35.3 reconciles: it cited row 33.11 as though the deferral still applied, in a row whose whole purpose was to end that deferral. What survives is the part of the clause that is still true and still useful — that this log deliberately does not adopt the artefact's shape, assigning no reviewers and prescribing no per-reviewer checks, so the two documents do not drift into competing versions of the same list. (b) would leave a row that argues against itself. (c) would delete a Rule 3 deliverable to satisfy a sentence | A reader of row 34.6.1's last sentence is sent to row 33.11, which row 35.3 supersedes. Both hops now end at a correction rather than at a false claim |

## 37. Deployment authority: network, secret delivery, workloads and release order

The rounds above hardened the application. None of them recorded the decisions
that make the hardened application *deployable*: which network the cluster and
the database share, how a Secret Manager value reaches a process, what creates
the workloads on a cluster that has none, how the deployment authenticates, and
what order a release applies things in. Those decisions were taken in this round
and are recorded here.

Two constraints bound every row below. The Python 3.9 pin is load-bearing at all
four of its sites and none is touched. The `--allow-unauthenticated` flag is not
reintroduced anywhere.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 37.1 | **The decision stands; the removal this row's risk column reports did not happen &mdash; see row 100.1.1.** `var.database_private_network` was left declared, and left with no default, so a deployment supplying nothing was refused over an input no resource reads; it now carries a default and says in its own description that it is retained rather than applied. One explicit VPC and one explicit subnetwork are the single network authority. `google_compute_network.primary` sets `auto_create_subnetworks = false`; `google_compute_subnetwork.primary` declares the node range and two named secondary ranges; the cluster names both the network and the subnetwork and references the secondary ranges by name; Cloud SQL takes `private_network = google_compute_network.primary.id` | (a) Keep the cluster on the implicit default network and keep taking the database network from a variable holding an arbitrary self-link; (b) declare the network but leave the subnetwork implicit; (c) place the database on its own network and peer the two | Before this round the cluster used the project's implicit default network while the database took a caller-supplied self-link, so nothing in the configuration required the two to be the same network and a plan could succeed with a database the cluster could not reach. (a) leaves that class of misconfiguration available. (b) reintroduces automatic subnet creation, which cannot carry the two named secondary ranges the cluster's `ip_allocation_policy` refers to. (c) adds a peering hop and a second address space for no reachability the single network does not already give. Naming the secondary ranges rather than letting them be allocated also makes pod and service addressing reviewable in the plan | The variable `database_private_network` was removed, so a deployment that was passing a self-link must stop. That is intentional: the removed variable is what allowed the two halves to disagree |
| 37.2 | Private service access is provisioned explicitly: `google_compute_global_address.private_service_access` reserves a `VPC_PEERING` range, `google_service_networking_connection.private_service_access` establishes the peering, `google_project_service.required` enables the seven APIs the configuration needs with `disable_on_destroy = false`, and the SQL instance carries a `depends_on` for the connection | (a) Rely on the peering already existing in the project; (b) enable the APIs out of band and document the prerequisite; (c) order the resources by implicit reference only | A Cloud SQL instance with `private_network` set cannot be created before the peering exists, and the peering cannot be created before the service-networking API is enabled. (a) and (b) are what the previous configuration assumed, which is why it carried a placeholder block listing prerequisites for a human to satisfy; that block is now deleted because the configuration performs the work. (c) is insufficient: nothing in the instance's arguments references the connection resource, so without an explicit `depends_on` the two can be attempted concurrently. `disable_on_destroy = false` is set so that destroying this configuration does not disable an API another workload in the project depends on | The first apply enables APIs and establishes a peering, which is slower than a plan against an already-prepared project. The reserved range is a durable allocation: destroying the configuration returns it, and a range in use by another peering will collide |
| 37.3 | Egress for the private nodes is a Cloud Router and a Cloud NAT gateway, configured `AUTO_ONLY` over `ALL_SUBNETWORKS_ALL_IP_RANGES` with error-only logging | (a) Give the nodes public addresses; (b) route the three third-party calls through a proxy; (c) leave egress absent | The nodes have no public address, and the application calls PayPal, Zillow and SendGrid, so without a NAT gateway those calls fail. (a) reverses the private-node decision, which is the control that keeps the nodes unreachable from the internet. (b) adds a component to operate and to secure for three outbound calls. Error-only logging is chosen because logging every translation on a busy egress path is volume without a corresponding signal | Every outbound call leaves through one gateway, so its address is the source the three providers see and any per-source limit applies to all replicas together |
| 37.4 | Cloud SQL is hardened in place: `ipv4_enabled = false` with the private network above, `ssl_mode = ENCRYPTED_ONLY`, automated backups with point-in-time recovery, and `deletion_protection = true` | (a) Keep the public address and restrict by authorized network; (b) require SSL without removing the public address; (c) leave deletion protection off so a teardown does not need a two-step | (a) and (b) both leave a database reachable from the internet, where an authorized-network list is the only thing between it and a scan; removing the public address removes the class. Backups and point-in-time recovery are the availability half of the same posture and cost a setting. (c) is convenient for a sandbox and is exactly the setting that lets a mistaken `terraform destroy` take the production datastore | `deletion_protection = true` means the instance cannot be destroyed until the flag is cleared, so tearing down a sandbox is deliberately a two-step operation |
| 37.5 | Secret values are written with the write-only argument pair — `secret_data_wo` with `secret_data_wo_version` — and each corresponding variable is declared `sensitive` **and** `ephemeral` | (a) Use `secret_data`, which persists the value in state; (b) create the secrets empty and add versions out of band; (c) read the values from a data source | With `secret_data`, the value is written to the state file and to any plan file, which turns state storage into a secret store. `ephemeral` makes the value available only during the run, so it can be consumed by a write-only argument and by nothing that would persist it. (b) leaves the configuration unable to describe what a deployment needs and makes a first apply incomplete. (c) requires the value to already be somewhere readable, which is the problem being solved. The `secret_version_generation` number is the handle for resending: increment it and the current values are written again; leave it and the stored versions are untouched. Verified by running a plan with real-looking values and searching the output for each: none appears | A value cannot be read back from state, so the deployment cannot tell an operator what is currently stored — only that a version exists. That is the intended trade |
| 37.6 | A Secret Manager value reaches a process through the Secret Manager CSI driver, mounted as a file and read by a shell prelude that exports it before `exec`-ing the application. **No `secretObjects` are declared, so no Kubernetes Secret object is created** | (a) Write the values into Kubernetes Secrets and mount those; (b) have the application call the Secret Manager API itself at startup; (c) inject the values as literal environment entries in the manifests | (a) is the common shape and is refused: a Kubernetes Secret is stored in the cluster datastore and is readable through the Kubernetes API by anything holding get on it, so it widens the set of principals that can read a credential. Omitting `secretObjects` keeps the value in the pod's own filesystem only. (b) would put a cloud SDK dependency and a network call into application startup and would require the application to know which backend it runs against. (c) puts credentials in a file in this repository, which is the finding the whole remediation exists to close. The prelude reads each file, fails loudly naming any that is missing or empty, and then replaces itself with the application process | The pod reads the secret version current at start, so a rotation reaches a pod on its next start rather than immediately; `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` sequences the restart. The CSI driver must be present on the cluster, which `secret_manager_config { enabled = true }` provides |
| 37.7 | The workload identity chain is declared on both sides and the runtime account holds **no project-level role**. The cluster sets `workload_pool`, the node pool sets `GKE_METADATA`, `google_service_account.backend_runtime` holds only per-secret `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` bindings — one per secret, granted on the secret rather than on the project — plus `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser`, and the Kubernetes service account carries the matching annotation | (a) Grant `secretAccessor` at the project level; (b) keep the nodes on the default compute service account; (c) grant the role on the project but restrict by condition | (a) and (c) both let the identity read secrets the backend does not consume, including any a future unrelated workload adds. A binding per secret makes the readable set exactly the six the backend reads, and adding a secret is then a deliberate edit. (b) is the previous state and gives every pod on the node the node's own broad identity. Node `oauth_scopes` includes `devstorage.read_only`, without which a node with explicit scopes cannot pull its own images | The two halves of the binding — the Terraform member and the Kubernetes annotation — must name the same namespace and account or the pod authenticates as nothing. Both are rendered from the same tokens, and the Terraform outputs carry the values the annotation must hold |
| 37.8 | Workloads are versioned Kubernetes manifests under `infrastructure/kubernetes/`, rendered by one script, `scripts/render_kubernetes_manifests.sh`, which both deployment paths call | (a) Declare the workloads as `kubernetes_*` Terraform resources; (b) adopt a templating tool such as Helm or Kustomize; (c) keep issuing imperative `kubectl` commands from the deployment script | Nothing in the repository created a Deployment or a Service, so neither deployment path could bootstrap a fresh cluster — both assumed the workloads already existed. (a) couples every application release to a Terraform apply and puts pod state into infrastructure state. (b) adds a build dependency for what is token substitution. (c) is the previous state and is how the two paths drifted apart. One renderer means the CD workflow and the deployment script cannot disagree with each other or with the manifests: it stops and names any token that is unset, and refuses to emit output that still carries a `${...}` placeholder | The renderer is a single point of failure for both paths, which is the property being bought. It is exercised by both paths and its refusals are asserted |
| 37.9 | A release applies three groups in a fixed order — prerequisites, then the migration Job run to completion, then the serving workloads — and the migration Job is a Job of its own carrying the release tag, running the same image and the same configuration as the backend | (a) Run the migration as an init container on the backend Deployment; (b) run it from the deployment host against the database directly; (c) copy the environment from a running Deployment, which is what the previous workflow did | The serving images change only in the third group, so new code never reads a schema the migration has not applied. (a) runs the migration once per replica per restart and blocks each pod's start on it. (b) requires the deployment host to reach a database on a private address, which a public runner cannot. (c) cannot work on a first deployment because there is no running Deployment to copy from, which is precisely the bootstrap gap. Naming the Job for the release tag keeps each release's migration record and makes a completed Job idempotent to re-apply | A failed migration stops the release before any serving image changes, leaving the previous version serving. The Job's logs are printed on failure by both paths |
| 37.10 | The CD workflow authenticates with workload identity federation, requests `id-token: write` with `contents: read`, declares a `concurrency` group, and gates deployment on the **whole** CI workflow via `uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml` | (a) Keep the long-lived service-account key in a repository secret; (b) list the individual CI jobs the deploy job depends on; (c) leave concurrency unset | (a) is a static credential with no expiry that anyone with repository-secret access can read. Federation issues a short-lived token per run and stores nothing. (b) is what the previous workflow did, and it silently omitted the unit suite and had no PostgreSQL job to omit — so a gate added to CI would not have been added to the deployment. Reusing the whole workflow makes that structural: a gate added to CI is added to CD with it. (c) allows two pushes to roll out concurrently and race on the same migration Job | Federation requires a pool and provider to be configured in the project, and the deploy job requires a runner that can reach a private control plane; both are prerequisites the workflow cannot create for itself |
| 37.11 | The private control plane is reached with `--region` and a runner label taken from `vars.DEPLOY_RUNNER_LABELS`, defaulting to `self-hosted` | (a) Keep `--zone`; (b) make the control-plane endpoint public; (c) add the runner's address to the authorized-network list | `--zone` cannot address a regional cluster at all, and a hosted public runner cannot reach a private endpoint whatever flag it uses. (b) is the straightforward fix and is refused because it undoes the control that keeps the control plane off the internet. (c) is not available for hosted runners, whose addresses are a large, changing published range. A runner inside the network is the only option that reaches the endpoint without weakening it | A deployment requires a self-hosted or VPC-connected runner. The default label makes that requirement explicit rather than implicit, and the workflow checks the control plane is reachable before it applies anything |
| 37.12 | Images are built with an explicit `-f` naming `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend` or `.frontend` and the matching build context, and the backend image is used for the serving Deployment and the migration Job alike | (a) Move or duplicate the Dockerfiles to the paths the previous commands assumed; (b) build the migration image separately | The previous commands named `./frontend` and `./backend` as build contexts containing Dockerfiles, and a repository-root context with no Dockerfile at all; none of those files exists, so both paths failed at the build. (a) would duplicate or relocate a file that `Dockerfile.frontend` is a read-only authority for. (b) would produce a second image that could differ from the one serving, which is the opposite of what a migration should run | The build context for each image is now explicit and must stay consistent with the Dockerfile's own `COPY` paths |
| 37.13 | The HTTP Cloud Function's source is real code committed at `infrastructure/functions/health/`, packaged by `data "archive_file"` and uploaded as a `google_storage_bucket_object` whose name carries the archive's `output_md5`; the deployment script's function step is skipped unless `DEPLOY_CLOUD_FUNCTION=true` | (a) Remove the function; (b) keep the archive reference and document the upload as a manual step; (c) have both Terraform and the script deploy it | The configuration referenced an archive object that nothing produced, so an apply could not succeed. The committed function is a genuine HTTP probe that reads no secret, no database and no network. Embedding the digest in the object name makes a source change a new object, so the function is redeployed when its code changes and not otherwise. (a) discards a resource the AAP lists. (b) leaves the same gap. (c) is two owners for one resource: Terraform owns the function, its source object and its invoker binding, so the script defers by default. `--runtime python39` and the absence of `--allow-unauthenticated` are both preserved in the script | Invocation stays limited to the principal the Terraform binding names. A deployment that opts the script in must keep its packaging consistent with Terraform's |
| 37.14 | Revision `0001` records the tables it created in a bookkeeping table, `alembic_0001_created_tables`, and its downgrade drops exactly those in foreign-key-safe order | (a) Split the revision so a true empty-database baseline creates the tables and `0001` only alters them; (b) always drop the six tables on downgrade; (c) accept the asymmetry | On an empty database the revision creates six tables and its downgrade left them behind, so upgrade and downgrade were not inverses. (a) is the textbook shape and would change the revision graph, which five test modules outside this round's scope assert on — `down_revision is None`, the linear head, and a `stamp 0001` step. (b) would drop tables the revision did not create on a database that already held them, which is data loss. Recording what was created keeps both paths correct with the graph untouched, and the bookkeeping table is created only when at least one table was created, so it does not appear on the legacy-baseline path. Offline `--sql` output is unchanged | The bookkeeping table is visible in the deployed schema between the two revisions. Its own downgrade drops it, and both paths are asserted end to end against PostgreSQL |
| 37.15 | CI gains a `postgres-integration` job running a health-checked `postgres:13` service, and the fixtures skip cleanly when no database is configured unless `POSTGRES_TEST_REQUIRED` is set, in which case they fail | (a) Point the whole suite at PostgreSQL; (b) keep SQLite only and rely on review; (c) make the PostgreSQL fixtures fail whenever no database is present | Every database fixture was SQLite while the deployment runs PostgreSQL 13, so no test exercised the dialect that ships — server defaults, `timestamptz`, `Numeric` scale and row locking all behave differently. (a) would make the whole suite need a database and would slow every run. (b) leaves the migration untested on its real engine. (c) would break a local run that has no database. The two-variable arrangement gives both: a developer's run skips, and CI sets `POSTGRES_TEST_REQUIRED` so a database that failed to start is reported rather than silently skipped | The job needs a service container. The suite's SQLite default is unchanged, so the eleven PostgreSQL cases are the only ones that need one |

## 38. Provisioning the seeded administrator's credential

Revision `0002` grants one address the administrative role and stores
`!locked-no-password-set`, which is not a hash any password produces — a
deliberate choice reconciled at row 27.1. The consequence is that the account
holds the role and cannot be signed in to, and until this round nothing in the
repository could give it a credential. `backend/app/core/admin_provisioning.py`
is that step. These are its decisions.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 38.1 | The credential is stored by a standalone operator module run as `python -m backend.app.core.admin_provisioning`, outside the application and outside any migration | (a) Add a third revision that hashes a configured password; (b) have the application create the credential at startup when it finds the sentinel; (c) expose an authenticated endpoint that sets it | (a) puts a credential-bearing value into the migration history, where it would be applied by whatever runs migrations and recorded in a revision file; row 27.1 kept the sentinel precisely to avoid a credential in a revision. (b) means every process start is a potential credential write, and a misconfigured environment would silently establish an administrator. (c) is a new authenticated route, which is product surface this remediation is not permitted to add, and it would need an already-authenticated administrator to call it — the situation being bootstrapped out of. A separate module invoked deliberately is the smallest thing that closes the gap, and it is the only writer of the value | The account cannot be signed in to until an operator runs the step. That is a visible, documented prerequisite rather than a silent one, and the deny-by-default authorization model treats an unreachable administrator as a safe state |
| 38.2 | The credential is read only from the `ADMIN_SEED_PASSWORD` environment variable. A non-empty `argv` is refused | (a) Accept it as a command-line argument; (b) accept either, preferring the argument; (c) prompt for it interactively | An argument appears in the shell history and in the process listing of every user on the host. (b) keeps that exposure available and makes the safer form optional. (c) cannot run in a Job. Refusing `argv` outright rather than ignoring it means an operator who reaches for the argument form is told, instead of having the value silently ignored while the run reads something else | An operator must set a variable, which is a slightly higher barrier than an argument. The refusal message names the variable |
| 38.3 | The credential is validated by constructing `UserCreate`, the registration request contract, and the check is applied whether the value came from the environment or from a caller argument | (a) Re-state the rules — length, byte ceiling, character classes — inside this module; (b) validate only on the environment path; (c) apply no policy, on the ground that an operator chose the value deliberately | (a) is a second copy of a policy that would drift from the first; constructing the real contract means the administrator is held to exactly what every account is held to, and a change to that policy applies here automatically. (b) was the first implementation and it was wrong: it let a caller bypass the policy entirely, which the module's own tests caught. (c) would let the single most privileged account in the system carry the weakest credential in it | The refusal text is a Pydantic validation message, which is shaped by the contract rather than written here. It is passed through the redactor before it is written, so a message that ever embedded the value would not print it |
| 38.4 | The module writes only to the address it holds as a constant, refuses a row that does not already hold the administrative role, and never assigns the role column | (a) Take the target address from configuration; (b) create the account when it is absent; (c) grant the role when the target lacks it | (a) would make the single most privileged account in the system configurable by whatever sets the environment, and the exactly-one post-condition would no longer be about a known address. (b) duplicates what revision `0002` does and would let this step establish an administrator on a database the revision never touched. (c) is the escalation path this module must not be: refusing the row means the step can only ever set a credential on an account the audited revision already promoted. A structural test asserts the module's source contains no assignment to the role column | An operator who runs the step before the migration gets a refusal naming the migration command, rather than a created account |
| 38.5 | A credential already in place is left alone and reported as `unchanged`; replacing one requires `ADMIN_CREDENTIAL_RESET=true` | (a) Always write the credential the variable currently holds; (b) always refuse when a credential is in place, and require a database edit to reset; (c) compare the supplied credential with the stored hash and write only when they differ | (a) means every repeat of the step — including one performed by an automated deployment — overwrites a working administrator credential with whatever the secret store currently holds, which is a silent lockout when the two have diverged. (b) leaves rotation with no supported path. (c) still writes on a legitimate no-op and cannot tell a deliberate rotation from a stale variable. The explicit flag makes replacement a stated intention, and the default makes the step safe to repeat, which is what lets a deployment path call it at all | While the flag is `true`, every run replaces the credential. `.env.example` and the rotation runbook both say to return it to `false` after a rotation window |
| 38.6 | The exactly-one-administrator post-condition is re-asserted before the caller commits, and a failure rolls the transaction back | (a) Trust the revision's own assertion; (b) check first and then write; (c) log a warning and commit anyway | The revision asserts the post-condition when it runs; anything could have changed the role column since. Asserting after the write and before the commit means a run cannot leave the authorization state in a shape the revision forbids. (b) would pass on a database that gained a second administrator during the run. (c) would store a credential on one of several administrators and report success. Verified end to end on PostgreSQL: with a second administrator present the run exits non-zero, the new credential does not verify, and the previous one still does | A database that already holds more than one administrator cannot be provisioned through this step until the extra rows are resolved. The refusal states the count and the expected address |
| 38.7 | The provisioning Job runs as its own Google and Kubernetes service account, reading its own three-secret `SecretProviderClass`, rather than as the backend's identity | (a) Reuse the backend identity and add `ADMIN_SEED_PASSWORD` to the six secrets it already reads; (b) reuse the backend identity and mount the extra secret only in the Job; (c) pass the credential as a literal in the Job manifest | (a) is the small change and is refused: it would let every serving pod read the administrator's password for the lifetime of the deployment, so a single compromised request handler would yield the most privileged credential in the system. (b) still grants the identity the accessor role, and the mount is not what enforces it — the IAM binding is. A separate identity makes the readable sets disjoint in both directions: the serving workload holds no grant on `ADMIN_SEED_PASSWORD`, and this identity holds none on the payment or email credentials. (c) puts a credential in this repository | One more service account, one more workload-identity binding and three more per-secret bindings to keep consistent. All are rendered from the same tokens and surfaced by Terraform outputs |
| 38.8 | The Job is in its own `admin-credential` renderer group, absent from `all`, and both deployment paths skip it unless explicitly asked — `PROVISION_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL=true` for the script, the repository variable of the same name for the workflow | (a) Include it in the release, after the migration; (b) leave it out of both paths and document only the manual command; (c) run it on a first deployment only, detected by absence | (a) makes a credential write part of every release, so the release depends on the secret store holding the right value at all times and a rotation becomes a side effect of deploying. (b) leaves the deployed path with no supported way to run it, which is the gap being closed. (c) requires the deployment to read the account's state to decide, which is the module's own job and not the pipeline's. Opt-in in both paths, with the same variable name, keeps the two consistent while keeping provisioning an operator act | An operator must set a variable to provision or rotate. Both paths print that they skipped and name the variable, so the step is discoverable rather than hidden |
| 38.9 | Records are emitted on a logger whose name is stated as a constant rather than taken from `__name__` | (a) Use `__name__`, as every other module does; (b) log to standard output directly | Under `python -m`, `__name__` is `__main__`, so `get_logger(__name__)` produced records under `backend.__main__` — a name that identifies the invocation rather than the module, and that differs between an imported run and the command an operator actually runs. Stating the name makes the audit trail for this operation searchable under one name. (b) would bypass the redacting filter, which is the mechanism keeping the credential out of the record | One module in the tree does not follow the `__name__` convention. A test asserts the name and that it contains no `__main__` |
| 38.10 | The audit record carries the outcome and the administrator count, and the address is redacted | (a) Register an exemption so the address is written in full; (b) omit the address field entirely | The shared redactor treats an email address as sensitive, in the message and in a context field alike, so the address is masked. An exemption would carve a hole in a redaction policy that applies to every record in the service, for a value that is a constant in this module and is stated in the README, the rotation runbook and the revision — so nothing is learned from having it in the record. What makes the run auditable is which outcome occurred and how many administrators existed afterwards, and both are recorded. (b) would lose the field's presence, which is what shows the redaction was applied | A reader of the log alone sees `[REDACTED]` where an address would be. The module targets exactly one address, so there is no ambiguity about which account a record concerns |
