## 39. Rationale relocated out of source and configuration comments (third pass)

Rule 1 forbids rationale in code comments. A review found eight sites across seven
files where a comment or docstring explained *why* an approach was chosen, or named
an alternative that was rejected, rather than confining itself to what the construct
is and does. The comments were reduced to mechanics, the enforced contract, the
operational instruction or the test's intent; the reasoning is recorded here.

Each change was verified to be documentation-only rather than inspected: for the six
Python files, the docstring-stripped abstract syntax tree is identical to the
previous revision's, and for the Compose file the parsed document is identical. The
same pass was applied to the material this round itself wrote.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 39.1 | `DEFAULT_ENV_FILE` is anchored on the repository root as an absolute path | A relative `".env"`, resolved by Pydantic against the working directory | A relative default resolves against the directory the process was started in, so the same documented command would read a different file — or no file at all — depending on where it was run, and the documented startup command is run from the repository root while the CI step runs from `backend/`. Anchoring on the module's own location makes both read the same file. A value supplied through `ENV_FILE` is deliberately still used as given, so a caller who wants a relative path keeps one | The anchor is computed by walking four directories up from the module, so moving `backend/app/core/config.py` changes it. `test_config_validation.py` asserts the resolved directory equals the repository root |
| 39.2 | Values a column cannot store are refused by the request contract, not by the database driver | Let the write reach the driver and fail there | A NUL in a text column, a non-finite or out-of-range value in a floating-point column, and a count above the integer maximum are all unstorable. Refused at the contract, each produces a validation error naming the field; allowed through to the driver, each produces a server fault on a request that was invalid on arrival. The refusal also names neither the character nor the value, so an invalid body is not echoed back | The bounds restate properties of the column types, so a column type change requires the contract to change with it. Both are asserted by `test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py` |
| 39.3 | `FORBIDDEN_TEXT_CHARACTERS` is held equal in `backend/app/schema/filter.py` and `backend/app/schema/listing.py` | Let each module declare its own set; import one from the other | Two contracts that refuse different characters would let a value rejected by one reach the database through the other. Importing one from the other would couple two schema modules that are otherwise independent. Equality is instead asserted mechanically, at `test_request_bounds_and_refusals.py:1340`, which is why the comment restating it was redundant and could simply be removed | The invariant lives in a test rather than in the type system. A third module declaring its own set would not be caught by that assertion |
| 39.4 | The Compose backend health check probes the readiness path, not the liveness path, and is written with `python` | Probe `/health`; use `curl` | The readiness path answers 503 while the database is unreachable, so a container whose database is unusable is not reported healthy — which is the condition a Compose health check exists to catch. `python:3.9-slim` carries no `curl`, so the probe is a `python` one-liner; `test_deployment_contract.py` asserts the executable and forbids `curl` | The probe depends on the readiness path continuing to answer 503 on an unreachable database, which `test_application_surface.py` asserts |
| 39.5 | `CLOUD_SQL_INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME` defaults to a marker containing no colon | Default to empty; omit the default and let the variable be required | The proxy requires a `project:region:instance` value. A marker with no colon cannot be mistaken for one, so the proxy exits naming it — a loud failure instead of a silent misconnection. An empty default would produce a less specific error, and making it required would block the `local` profile, which needs no proxy at all | The marker is a string that must stay malformed. The Compose file states the required value as an operational instruction |
| 39.6 | `HEALTH_BODY` and `READINESS_BODY` are declared in the test module rather than imported from `backend.app.main` | Import the application's own constants | Importing them would let the assertion compare the application with itself, so a change to the response body would change the expectation with it and pass. Declaring the expected body independently means a route that merely answers 200, or that answers a different body, fails | The two declarations must be updated deliberately if the contract changes. That is the intent |
| 39.7 | `/health` and `/health/ready` are excluded from the role matrix, and the framework's documentation routes are excluded by `include_in_schema` with their paths asserted by name | Add rows for the operational routes; filter the documentation routes silently | No role governs either operational route, so a matrix cell for them would assert nothing about authorization while inflating the expected cell count. Accounting for them separately keeps the matrix at exactly its expected size and still requires them to exist. Naming the documentation paths means the exclusion is asserted rather than incidental, so a route that stopped being excluded would be noticed | Two route sets are maintained outside the matrix. The matrix is compared against the application's own published routes, so a new route in neither place fails |
| 39.8 | `UserResponse`'s fields are asserted as an exact set, not as the absence of a hash field name | Assert only that no field is named `hashed_password` | An exact set fails when a credential is added under any name, and also when any other `users` column is added to the response model by accident. Checking one name only catches one name | The assertion must be updated when a field is deliberately added to the response contract, which is the point at which the addition should be considered |

---

## 40. Documentation accuracy corrections (second pass)

Three published statements no longer matched the delivered code. Section 20
established the convention these follow: a row records what the text said and
what it says now, because each changes a factual claim rather than a behaviour.
Each replacement below was checked against the code before it was written.

| # | Location | What the text said | What it says now |
|---|----------|--------------------|------------------|
| 40.1 | `.env.example` header, and `README.md` under "Environment configuration" | That an absent `ENV_FILE` makes the application read `.env` **from its working directory**, and that the settings class is "configured with `env_file = \".env\""`. Both describe a relative default. `backend/app/core/config.py` resolves `DEFAULT_ENV_FILE` to an absolute path under `REPOSITORY_ROOT`, so the claim was wrong in the one respect that matters operationally: it implied the file read depends on where the process started | All three resolution cases, stated explicitly and verified by exercising `_configured_env_file()`: absent reads `DEFAULT_ENV_FILE`, an absolute path to `.env` at the repository root; a value naming a path is used exactly as given, so a relative one resolves against the working directory; and a value present but empty reads no file at all. The README carries them as a three-row table and adds that a process environment variable takes precedence over the same name in the file. The rationale for anchoring absolutely is row 38.1, not the comment |
| 40.2 | `README.md`, after the verification gates | That after migration "**exactly one account holds the `admin` role and every other account holds `registered`**", and that the schema change is "reversible from the code" without qualification. The first half is true only at the instant after a legacy-baseline migration: revision `0002`'s promotion is `UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE email = :email AND role <> :role`, which touches exactly one row, so an account holding `premium` or `guest` keeps it. The second half was unqualified where the behaviour has two paths | The actual post-condition: exactly one account holds `admin` — the fixed target — and the revision **preserves** every other account's role rather than normalising it, with `0001`'s server default explaining why pre-existing rows land on `registered`. Reversibility is stated per path: on a database `0001` created the tables in, its downgrade drops exactly those; on one that already held them, it reverses only the columns it added. The verification table also names the PostgreSQL integration run, which is where both paths are proven |
| 40.3 | `SECURITY.md` "Reporting a Vulnerability", and `README.md` "Contact Information" | A placeholder maintainer address, `your.email@example.com`, published in both files as an alternative reporting channel — and in `SECURITY.md` explicitly labelled a placeholder to be replaced | **No email address at all.** GitHub private vulnerability reporting is now the only channel either file publishes: it is a real surface of this repository, it notifies whoever holds maintainer access, and it needs no address from either side. Both files state why no address is published — a placeholder contact is worse than none, because a reporter who uses it reaches nobody while believing a disclosure has been made — and both tell a deployment that wants an email channel to add a monitored role mailbox and test it before publishing it |

The alternative considered for 39.3, and rejected, was to substitute a different
address. Any address invented here would be as unreachable as the placeholder it
replaced, and labelling it a placeholder is what the finding objected to. The
alternative for 39.1 and 39.2 was to make the code match the documentation
instead; both were rejected because the code is correct in each case and the
documentation was describing an earlier revision of it.
## 41. The executive presentation: body-text budget and readiness claims

Rule 2 caps a content slide at four bullets and forty body words, and requires the
deck to communicate operational readiness. A review found three content slides over
the word budget and five places where the deck claimed a readiness the delivered
state does not yet support. Reducing a slide is a content decision with alternatives,
and so is choosing which words a corrected claim uses, so both are recorded here.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|-------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 41.1 | Operationalise the forty-word budget as an executable counter, and calibrate it against the review's own verdict before trusting it. Body text is the text of every `<li>` and non-label prose; it excludes headings, the eyebrow, `.scope` and `.audience`, icon-row labels, metric and KPI captions, the brand lockup, and Mermaid diagram source. **The clause that once included "every table cell" is superseded by row 96.5.1: a styled table is one of the non-text visuals Rule 2 requires, and counting a required visual's own contents against the body-text cap sets Rule 2's two clauses against each other. The delivered counter excludes table cells, and has since it was committed.** Bullets are counted from `<li>` start tags, and `<pre class="mermaid">` is exempt from the no-fenced-code check | (a) Count every word in the slide markup, which flagged all sixteen slides and so disagreed with the review; (b) count only `<li>` text, which flagged none and so also disagreed; (c) judge each slide by reading it | Rule 2 states the limit but not what counts toward it, and the two obvious readings both contradict the review. Calibration settles the ambiguity from evidence: the counter had to flag slides 7, 13 and 14 and nothing else. It now does, so the same instrument that reproduces the reviewer's finding on the original reports zero violations on the correction. Reading by eye cannot produce that guarantee | The derived rule is inferred from one verdict rather than published, so a future reviewer applying a stricter reading could disagree. The counter is not committed — it was validation scaffolding — so the rule survives only as this row and as the delivered slides that satisfy it |
| 41.2 | Reduce the three over-budget slides in place rather than moving the detail into reveal.js speaker notes | (a) Move the surplus text into `<aside class="notes">` on each slide; (b) add a linked appendix slide, which would push the deck toward the eighteen-slide ceiling; (c) split each over-budget slide into two | The Rule's suggested resolution offers speaker notes *or* linked documents, and the linked documents already exist: `docs/security/DECISION_LOG.md`, `TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `RESIDUAL_RISK.md` and `CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` carry every detail removed, and the deck's own onboarding slide already points a reader at that set. A notes aside would keep the text inside the same file the Rule caps, relocating the words without reducing what a slide asks a reader to absorb | Detail is now one click away rather than on the slide. A reader who never opens the linked set sees less than before, which is the intended trade for a slide that reads in one breath |
| 41.3 | On the roles slide, drop one bullet and compress the role table's second column to terse permission phrases, keeping all four rows | (a) Drop table rows to save words, for example by merging `premium` into `registered`; (b) keep the four bullets and delete the table; (c) replace the table with a diagram | The four roles *are* the model the slide exists to convey, so dropping a row would misstate the authorization design to satisfy a word count. The dropped bullet — that the four roles are the project's own documented design intent — is the least load-bearing sentence on the slide and is recorded at row 34.3 and in the traceability matrix. The table is also the slide's non-text visual, so deleting it would breach the no-text-only-slide requirement | Compressed cells such as "Plus entitlement" rely on the reader taking each row as cumulative over the row above. The column heading "Permitted" and the increasing order of the rows carry that, but it is terser than prose |
| 41.4 | On the supply-chain slide, drop the table's third column and one bullet, keeping every row including the `Overall` summary | (a) Drop the `Overall — 19 → 7 advisories` row, which is the single largest cell; (b) drop one of the three replaced components; (c) keep three columns and cut the bullets to zero | The `Overall` row states the headline outcome the slide exists for, and the three replaced components are the finding's own subject. The removed third column held the reason each replacement was necessary, which is exactly what Section 3 of this log and the residual-risk register set out at length — so it is the column whose loss costs the least | A reader now sees *that* three components were replaced and *what* replaced them, but not *why* each could not simply be upgraded. The remaining bullet states that no patched release existed, which carries the essential point |
| 41.5 | On the residual-risk slide, remove the bullet list entirely and let the existing callout plus the four-row risk table carry the slide | (a) Keep one or two bullets and shrink the table to two rows; (b) keep four bullets and delete the table | The slide's purpose is the risk-to-control pairing, which only the table expresses; a two-row table would drop two live risks, including the exposed credentials that are still unrotated. The callout already states the headline in eight words, so bullets would restate it. Zero bullets is within "at most four" | A slide with no bullet list reads differently from its neighbours. The callout and the table's emphasised first row preserve the visual hierarchy, and the slide retains a rendered icon as its non-text visual |
| 41.6 | State the deployment prerequisites on the title, credentials, risk, onboarding and closing slides, rather than describing the remediation as secured and ready | (a) Leave the claims and rely on the review documents to correct them; (b) add a single caveat slide, leaving the other five claims as they stood | An executive reads the title and closing slides and may read nothing else, so a caveat on a middle slide does not reach the audience the overstatement misleads. The five corrected places are the five that made the claim. The specific corrections: the title now names steps still required before a deployment; the credentials heading says rotation is pending and a bullet states the values remain in past revisions until rotated; the risk table names the third-party placeholders and that startup refuses them outside local; the onboarding slide states that marked placeholders need real values; and the closing slide says verified and documented rather than secured, with the breaking change and the deployment prerequisites awaiting sign-off | The deck is now less flattering about the same work. That is the point of the correction, but it means the summary reads as qualified where a reader may have expected completion |
| 41.7 | Express the onboarding slide's configuration claim as "ten marked placeholders" rather than naming a count of third-party values | (a) "seven third-party values need real ones", which was written first and is wrong twice over; (b) "five third-party keys", which is accurate but silent on the signing key, the database password and the administrator credential; (c) drop the number and say "replace every marked placeholder" | `.env.example` carries forty-nine assignments, of which ten hold a `CHANGE_ME` or `REPLACE` marker: five third-party integration keys and five locally-generated secret assignments. "Seven" came from confusing this with the seven accepted residual advisories, and "third-party" excluded half the values a reader must supply. Ten marked placeholders is grep-provable against the committed file, which is the property an accuracy claim needs. The numberless phrasing was rejected because the rest of the deck quantifies and a reader can check a number | The count is tied to the current `.env.example`. Adding or removing a marked placeholder without revisiting this slide would make it wrong again, which is the same failure this row corrects |

Row 40.7 corrects a claim introduced by the fix for the very finding it belongs to.
It is recorded rather than quietly amended because the finding is about accuracy, and
a log that omitted the error would misrepresent how the corrected text was reached.
The general lesson, applied to the whole deck before this section was written: when a
finding is about accuracy, every quantitative claim in the artifact is in scope, not
only the lines the finding cites. The other eight counts the deck makes were each
re-derived from the delivered code — the advisory totals from `pip-audit` against
`backend/requirements.txt`, the scan total from `bandit -r backend/app -ll`, and the
access-control total from the test module's own `ROUTE_MATRIX`, `PRINCIPALS` and
`MATRIX_CASES` tables — and all eight hold.

## 42. Final reconciliation, and the infrastructure and release-path round

This section is written last and it **supersedes** every earlier row that describes
which of this remediation's documents exist and which findings remain open. Where an
earlier row and this section disagree about the state of the tree, this section is
correct and the earlier row is a record of what was true when it was written. That is
the convention §27 established, and the reason for it is that an abandoned claim and
the reason it was abandoned both have to stay visible.

It also records the decisions of the round that closed the infrastructure, release
path, guard, register and credential-response findings.

### 42.1 Artefact presence, and the current unresolved inventory

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.1.1 | **Rows 26.19, 29.11, 30.15, 32.12 and 33.11 are withdrawn.** Each says that some combination of `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` and `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md` "remains absent". **All four are present in this tree, together with `SECURITY.md` and `blitzy-deck/executive-summary.html`.** The header of this log, which describes four documents as carrying the written record, therefore now describes the tree accurately | (a) Edit the five rows in place so no trace of the withdrawn claim survives; (b) leave them standing on the ground that each was true when written; (c) add a one-line note beside each row | (a) is what §27's convention forbids. (b) leaves five verifiably false statements in the document Rule 1 makes the authority for *why*, and a reader who disproves one of them from a directory listing has no reason to trust the rest. (c) scatters the correction across five places, so a reader who finds one has no way of knowing there are four more. A single superseding section is the form that answers the question once, and it is the form §27 already uses | A reader of any of the five rows in isolation sees a claim this section withdraws. The rows are left in place and marked here rather than rewritten, which is deliberate: the sequence of positions those rows record — deferring an artefact because no finding named it, then delivering it when one did — is itself part of the account |
| 42.1.2 | **The "ten findings outside the stated scope" of row 34.6.3 is restated as an itemised inventory rather than a count.** One of the ten has closed by a change of state rather than by decision, and four operator-owned items have been added by this round, so a bare number is now the least accurate way to publish it. Every document that carried the figure now points here instead of republishing it: `SECURITY.md`, `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`, `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, and the summary cell of §34.1 | (a) Update the number in row 34.6.3 and in `SECURITY.md` to whatever it now is; (b) leave the number and add a caveat; (c) drop the inventory from `SECURITY.md` and keep it only here | (a) reproduces the defect this row exists to fix: a count in two documents drifts the moment either changes, and it already had — row 34.6.3's own risks cell had to caveat that finding (5) no longer described the tree. (b) publishes a number the same paragraph disowns. (c) removes the disclosure from the document a reporter actually reads. Naming the items, in one place, with the other documents pointing at it, is the form that cannot drift: a reader compares an item against the tree, not a total against a total | The inventory is longer than a number and will be skimmed. Mitigated by ordering it so the items awaiting a decision come before the items awaiting an operator |

### 42.2 Infrastructure decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.2.1 | **Superseded in part by row 94.4.1 — the reconciliation stands, the three names do not.** `cloud_function_source_archive_object` was deleted with the fixed-name source object, and the script now reads `CLOUD_FUNCTION_SOURCE_OBJECT` with `CLOUD_FUNCTION_SOURCE_MD5` instead of a single `CLOUD_FUNCTION_SOURCE_ARCHIVE`, because the surviving object is named after its content digest and a name alone cannot establish that the bytes are the reviewed ones; the function's name and entry point became constants in the script that match the configuration. **Reconcile the Cloud Function's identity across Terraform and the deployment script**, by introducing `cloud_function_name`, `cloud_function_source_archive_object` and `cloud_function_entry_point` and requiring the same values in `scripts/deploy.sh` as `CLOUD_FUNCTION_NAME`, `CLOUD_FUNCTION_SOURCE_ARCHIVE` and `CLOUD_FUNCTION_ENTRY_POINT`. **This is a deliberate departure from an earlier instruction** that named the `function-test` / `function-name` divergence as flagged-for-confirmation only and told the Terraform work not to reconcile it | (a) Hold the earlier instruction and leave the two names apart; (b) rename the Terraform resource to the script's name; (c) stop deploying the function from the script and let Terraform own it entirely | The divergence stopped being a cosmetic inconsistency once the invoker restriction was added: Terraform held a policy on `function-test` while the script published `function-name`, so **the control governed a function nobody invoked and the invoked function had no control**. A review finding subsequently required the reconciliation, and a finding that names a specific defect outranks a general per-file instruction not to touch it. (b) would rename a resource address `outputs.tf` resolves against. (c) would remove `--runtime python39` from the script, which is one of the four sites the runtime pin is documented at — so it would fix one finding by breaking a documented invariant. Driving both tools from one variable achieves the reconciliation without either cost | The variable defaults to `function-test`, the historical name, so no existing function is replaced — which also means the deployed name stays unhelpful until an operator sets it. An operator who supplies a different `CLOUD_FUNCTION_NAME` to the script than to Terraform recreates the divergence; the effective-policy read-back in the script is what catches the consequence |
| 42.2.2 | **Set the function's invoker policy authoritatively** with `data.google_iam_policy` plus `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_policy`, replacing the additive `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_member` | (a) Keep the additive member resource; (b) keep it and add a second resource that removes the public principals; (c) manage the policy outside Terraform | An additive binding adds one member and says nothing about the members already there, so a function that had ever been deployed with unauthenticated invocation kept an `allUsers` binding that the member resource left untouched — the restriction looked applied and was not. An authoritative policy replaces the whole policy, so the public binding is removed **without this configuration having to name a public principal at all**, which keeps the strings `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` out of the file. (b) would require naming them. (c) puts a security control outside the tool that is reviewed | An authoritative policy also removes any binding an operator added out of band, including one added for a legitimate second caller. That is the intended behaviour of a policy resource and the reason `cloud_function_invoker_member` exists, but it will surprise someone. `scripts/deploy.sh` reads the effective policy back after publishing, so a divergence is reported rather than assumed away |
| 42.2.3 | **The Terraform half of this row stands; the boundary it stopped at was later moved, and its refusal of alternative (c) no longer holds &mdash; see rows 82.3, 82.4 as amended by 92.8, and 92.12.** A later round added the Kubernetes manifests to this repository and delivered the mount here, so the reasoning below — that no manifests exist and adding them would invent a topology — describes the tree as it was, not as it is; §42.1 items 11 and 12, which this row's risk column cites, are marked closed for the same reason. **Authorize secret delivery in Terraform and stop at the repository boundary**: enable Workload Identity and the managed Secret Manager add-on on the cluster, put the node pool on the GKE metadata server, create one dedicated workload identity, grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` **per secret**, bind `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` for the named Kubernetes service account, and publish the annotation a manifest must carry | (a) Grant the accessor role at the project level; (b) grant it to the node service account; (c) add Kubernetes manifests to this repository so the mount is delivered here too; (d) inject the values at deployment time from the pipeline | Six per-secret grants mean the identity reads those six versions and nothing else in the project, which (a) would not achieve and (b) would additionally hand every workload on the node the same access. (c) is the one that looks like completeness and is not: this repository contains no Kubernetes manifests at all, so adding them would mean inventing a deployment topology the rest of the change set does not describe, and the review's finding asks for a delivery model to be selected and its access proved, not for a deployment to be authored. (d) puts secret values through the pipeline, which OWASP's preference order places below runtime retrieval. The startup validator already refuses to run when `SECRET_BACKEND` names the managed backend and any of the six is absent from the process environment, so the proof the review asks for is enforced at the consuming end | The mount itself is outside this repository, so an operator can hold every grant and still start a pod with no secrets — and the failure mode is a refused startup naming the missing settings, which is the intended shape. Recorded as unresolved items 11 and 12 in §42.1 rather than presented as delivered, and the presentation and readme say the same |
| 42.2.4 | **Grant the node identity `roles/container.defaultNodeServiceAccount` and create the nodes with the `cloud-platform` access scope**, moving the scopes into `gke_node_oauth_scopes` | (a) Keep the two narrow scopes and add only the base role; (b) add the base role and the `devstorage.read_only` scope; (c) leave both as they were | Access scopes and IAM roles are two independent gates and a node needs to clear both: with only the logging and monitoring scopes, a node holding `roles/artifactregistry.reader` still cannot pull a private image, because the scope caps what any credential on the instance may request. (a) therefore leaves the pull broken. (b) is a legitimate narrower choice and is admitted by the variable's validation, which requires one of the two scopes rather than mandating `cloud-platform`; the default is the scope GKE documents for node pools, with the IAM roles doing the bounding. (c) leaves the base role ungranted, which the variable's allowlist previously made impossible to add at all | `cloud-platform` is a broad scope, and a reader who looks only at scopes will read it as over-permissive. The bounding is in the role allowlist, which admits six node-pool roles and rejects `roles/editor` and `roles/owner`, and both halves are asserted by `backend/tests/security/test_terraform_contract.py` |
| 42.2.5 | **Enforce the control-plane allowlist on the private endpoint and stop exempting Google's public ranges**, with `private_endpoint_enforcement_enabled = true` and `gcp_public_cidrs_access_enabled = false` | (a) Leave the allowlist as it was and correct the comment instead; (b) enable enforcement and leave the public-range exemption at its default | The file's comment claimed the listed CIDRs were the only blocks that could reach the control plane, and without enforcement that was not what the configuration did. (a) would resolve the contradiction by weakening the claim rather than the exposure, which is the wrong direction when the claim is the one a reviewer relies on. (b) leaves a documented set of Google-owned ranges able to reach the endpoint, which is exactly the kind of exception nobody remembers is there | An empty `gke_master_authorized_networks` list now authorizes nothing outside the cluster's own VPC, so an operator who leaves it empty and expects to reach the control plane from a workstation will find they cannot. That is the intended posture, and it is stated in the prerequisites block of `main.tf` and in the connectivity check the deployment workflow runs before it migrates |
| 42.2.6 | **The private-services-access half stands; the cross-variable validation this row describes is WITHDRAWN &mdash; superseded by row 82.8 and recorded as withdrawn at row 100.1.4.** No equality check between `gke_network` and `database_private_network` exists: this configuration creates the VPC and both the cluster and the database attach to the created resource, which is stronger than validating that two supplied inputs look alike. **Tie the cluster and the database to one VPC by variable validation, and provision private services access**: `gke_network` must equal `database_private_network`, `gke_subnetwork` must sit in the same project and in `var.region`, and a reserved global address plus a service-networking connection are created with the instance ordered after them | (a) Document the shared-VPC requirement in a comment and trust the operator; (b) create the VPC and subnetwork here; (c) accept the two networks independently and add a runtime check | A configuration that accepts a cluster on one VPC and a database on another creates a deployment where the pods cannot reach the database, and it accepts it silently — the failure appears much later as a connection timeout. Cross-variable validation refuses the combination before any resource is planned, which is the earliest point it can be caught. (b) would put network creation in a file whose scope is the resources the findings name. (c) detects the problem after the infrastructure exists. Private services access is the documented prerequisite for a private Cloud SQL address, so provisioning it here is what makes `ipv4_enabled = false` reachable rather than aspirational | The equality check makes `gke_network` redundant with `database_private_network` for any valid input, which a reader may see as duplication. It is deliberate: the two variables document two consumers, and the validation is what makes the invariant checkable and testable rather than conventional. The reserved range defaults to a `/16`, which is Google's recommendation and larger than a small deployment needs |
| 42.2.7 | **Replace the `HUMAN ASSISTANCE NEEDED` block in `main.tf` with an explicit prerequisites list and an open-risks list** | (a) Delete the block outright; (b) leave it; (c) move its content into the readme | The block asked a reader to work out what still needed configuring, which is the opposite of what a reviewed infrastructure file should do. (a) loses real information — six of its concerns are genuine prerequisites this configuration depends on and does not create. (c) separates the requirement from the file that has it. Naming the prerequisites and the open risks in place answers the reader at the point of the question, and the two lists say **what** is expected and **what** is left, never why, which is what Rule 1 requires of a code comment | The lists will go stale if a prerequisite is later created here. A contract test asserts the block is present and names the private-services API and the SecretProviderClass, so its removal is caught, though its accuracy is not |

### 42.3 Release-path decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.3.1 | **Run the Alembic upgrade in an isolated one-shot pod on the new image, before `kubectl set image`**, in `scripts/deploy.sh` | (a) Keep the order and accept the window; (b) run the migration from an existing pod before the rollout; (c) let the deployment workflow be the only path that migrates correctly | The script rolled the new image out, waited for it to be ready, and only then applied the migrations — so the new code served traffic against a schema it expected columns to exist in. (a) accepts a window in which a request can read a column that is not there. (b) runs the new revisions from the **old** image, which has no knowledge of them. (c) leaves a script in the repository that does the wrong thing, and a script is what someone reaches for when the pipeline is unavailable. The one-shot pod carries the Deployment's own environment, identity, pull secrets and volumes, so it reaches the same database with the same configuration as the workload | The overrides are assembled with `jq`, which the script now requires on `PATH` alongside `docker`, `gcloud` and `kubectl`. A missing tool is reported by name before anything is built |
| 42.3.2 | **Deploy the function from the same Cloud Storage archive Terraform declares, addressed as `gs://<bucket>/<object>`, and confirm the object exists first** | (a) Create a `functions/` directory in this repository and deploy from it; (b) keep `--source=./functions` and create the directory later; (c) drop the function deployment from the script | `--source=./functions` named a directory that does not exist, and under the script's strict shell that ended every deployment at that line. (a) means authoring a Cloud Function whose source this change set does not otherwise describe, which is new functionality. (b) is the defect restated. (c) removes the `--runtime python39` pin site. A Cloud Storage source is a form `gcloud functions deploy` accepts and is the same artifact Terraform builds from, so the two tools stop being able to disagree about what is deployed | The archive has to be uploaded before either tool runs; it is prerequisite 4 in `main.tf`. The script's `gcloud storage objects describe` check turns a missing archive into a named failure rather than a partial deployment |
| 42.3.3 | **Gate deployment on the whole of `ci.yml` by making it a callable workflow**, replacing the duplicated three-step `verify` job | (a) Keep `verify` and add the missing gates to it; (b) trigger deployment from a `workflow_run` on CI's completion; (c) leave the subset | (a) duplicates every gate, and two copies of a gate drift — the copy in the deployment workflow had already lost the lint step, the full unit suite and any integration check. (b) works but decouples the two: a `workflow_run` deployment reports separately from the run that qualified it, and the association is only visible by timestamp. A called workflow puts the gates and the deployment in one run graph, so `needs: ci` is a fact about that run rather than a fact about a previous one | The frontend job inside the called workflow tolerates its own failure, so a frontend regression does not block deployment. That is the same tolerance §42.3.5 records, and it is stated in the readme rather than left to be discovered |
| 42.3.4 | **Run the deployment job on a runner named by `vars.GKE_DEPLOY_RUNNER`, defaulting to the self-hosted pool, and fetch credentials with `--region` and `--internal-ip`** | (a) Keep the GitHub-hosted runner and add the runner's egress addresses to the authorized networks; (b) make the control-plane endpoint public again; (c) reach the cluster through a bastion invoked over SSH | The control plane is private, and a GitHub-hosted runner is neither on the VPC nor at a stable address, so `get-credentials` could not reach it — and it asked for a zonal path to a regional cluster besides. (a) is not available: GitHub-hosted runners have no stable egress range to authorize, and authorizing a broad range would undo §42.2.5. (b) reverses a finding to make a pipeline work. (c) adds a hop and a second credential to manage. A runner on the network is the arrangement the private endpoint presumes | The pipeline now depends on infrastructure that is not provisioned by this repository, and it fails with a named message when that infrastructure is absent — the connectivity step reports that the private endpoint did not answer and what would make it answer. The `GKE_CLUSTER_ZONE` secret is renamed `GKE_CLUSTER_REGION`, so an existing deployment must add the new name |
| 42.3.5 | **Delete the `npm run lint` step, split the pipeline into three jobs, and let the frontend job tolerate its own failure while nothing depends on it** | (a) Replace `npm run lint` with another frontend command; (b) remove the frontend job entirely; (c) let the frontend job fail the workflow, as it did | `frontend/package.json` declares `start`, `build`, `test` and `eject` and no `lint`, so the step failed on every run and **every gate after it never executed** — the dependency audit, the static analysis, the guards and the whole test suite were unreachable in practice. (a) has no candidate: the immutable source does not compile, so `build` and `test` fail too. (b) hides a real defect by deleting the evidence. (c) is where the pipeline already was, and it is what made the backend gates unreachable. Separating the jobs makes the backend gates run unconditionally and leaves the frontend state visible under a job whose name says what it is | A tolerated failure is a failure someone stops looking at. Mitigated by the job's name — "known blocker, gates nothing" — by a step that states the condition in its log, by a contract test asserting no other job depends on it, and by the readme saying it plainly rather than describing the pipeline as green |
| 42.3.6 | **Implement the integration gate against the backend only**: a PostgreSQL service container, `alembic upgrade head`, a SQL assertion that exactly one administrator exists, then live probes of health, readiness, the public listing read, registration, login, and the refusals a non-administrator must receive | (a) Leave the step as an empty `run` with its placeholder comment; (b) stand up frontend and backend together and drive a browser; (c) call the integration gate satisfied by the unit suite | The step was an empty `run` that always succeeded, which is worse than absent because the pipeline reported an integration gate it did not have. (b) cannot work while the client does not compile, and tying a genuine gate to a known-broken component would make it useless on its first run. (c) confuses two things: the unit suite runs against an in-process client and a SQLite database, and the integration gate is the only place the real interpreter, the real driver, PostgreSQL, the real migrations and the real middleware stack are exercised together. The probes chosen are the frozen contracts and the one intentional breaking change, so the gate fails if either moves | The gate covers the API and not the browser path, and its name should not be read as covering more than it does. Its assertions are enumerated in `backend/tests/security/test_release_contract.py`, so what it checks is itself checked |
| 42.3.7 | **The Dockerfile half of this row stands; its build-argument claims are CORRECTED &mdash; see rows 92.5 and 92.6.** When this row was written the workflow read one of the two values from the secrets context while the manifests were rendered from the variable context, and `scripts/deploy.sh` passed no build argument at all &mdash; so "the workflow requires both and fails by name when either is unset" and "the two values come from repository variables" were not yet true of either path. Both are true now. The original text follows. Name both Dockerfiles explicitly in every build and pass the two frontend build arguments | (a) Add a `Dockerfile` to each build context; (b) move the Dockerfiles into their contexts; (c) build from the repository root | `docker build ./frontend` and `docker build ./backend` require a `Dockerfile` in the context, and neither context has one — the definitions live in `infrastructure/docker/`, as the Compose file already reflects with its own `dockerfile:` keys. (a) and (b) would duplicate or move a file two other consumers already address by path. (c) would change the context and break the `COPY` paths. Naming the file with `-f` is what the Compose definition already does, so the three consumers now agree. The frontend image declares two `ARG`s and inlines them into the bundle; a build that omits them produces a bundle pointing nowhere, so the workflow requires both and fails by name when either is unset | The two values come from repository variables rather than secrets, which is correct because both reach the browser. An operator who has not set them gets a named failure in the first job step |

### 42.4 Guard and residual-register decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.4.1 | **Add a syntax-tree reachability assertion over `backend/app` and keep the textual grep as a pre-filter** | (a) Keep the grep alone and describe it more modestly; (b) replace the grep with the semantic check; (c) adopt an external policy-as-code scanner | The grep matches text, so an import alias, a module attribute, a dynamic import, a renamed request parameter or a different bracket style all pass it while making an accepted advisory reachable — and the register described it as failing whenever reachability returned, which overstated what it does. (a) leaves the acceptance resting on a check that a rename defeats. (b) loses a fast check that needs nothing to import cleanly. (c) adds a dependency and a second configuration language for eight patterns. Two layers, each described for what it is, is what the register can honestly claim | The semantic check is code, so it can itself be wrong. Six of its cases exercise the detection against sources that use each evasion, so the detection is demonstrated rather than assumed, and a future evasion it does not model is a gap it will not report |
| 42.4.2 | **Narrow the textual guard from `backend/` to `backend/app/`** | (a) Keep the wider scope and write the guarded literals evasively in the new test module; (b) keep the wider scope and accept that the guard fails; (c) exclude `backend/tests` with a grep flag | The guard's subject is code a request can reach, and `backend/tests` is not in the runtime image — `backend/requirements.txt` is what the image installs. A test module that names a construct in order to assert its absence is not a use of it, so under the wider scope the guard reported a problem that did not exist. (a) would mean writing string concatenation to hide literals from a grep, which is the sort of cleverness that outlives its reason. (b) is a red build with no signal. (c) is the same narrowing expressed less clearly. The new scope also matches the static-analysis gate, which has always been `bandit -r backend/app` | A guarded construct introduced under `backend/tests` is no longer reported. That is intended, and the semantic assertion covers `backend/app` for the same set, so the reachable tree is covered by both layers |
| 42.4.3 | **Register the seven development-only advisories in `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`** as well as in the development manifest's header | (a) Narrow the workflow comments to point at the manifest header instead; (b) leave them documented only in the manifest; (c) fold them into the register's seven and publish one figure of fourteen | The workflow comments said every suppressed identifier was registered in the register, and four of the fourteen were not — so the comment was wrong about four of them however defensible the split was. (a) fixes the sentence and leaves an auditor reading two documents to reconstruct one list. (c) would merge a runtime advisory and a scanner-tree advisory into one number, which is the distinction the register exists to keep. Registering both sets in one file, counted separately, is what makes the fourteen suppressions checkable from one place — and a test now asserts every suppressed identifier appears there | Two counts now live in one document and could be conflated by a hurried reader. Each section states its scope in its first sentence, and the two are separated by the manifest they belong to rather than by severity |

### 42.5 Credential-response decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.5.1 | **Add the listing-provider API key to the rotation runbook as a fifth credential, with a deletion step that searches the log estate rather than the repository's history** | (a) Keep the runbook scoped to the credentials committed as literals; (b) add the key with the same four steps as the committed credentials; (c) note it in the register instead of the runbook | The runbook declared an exhaustive scope and omitted a credential the service had put into request URLs and then printed to standard output, so a potentially exposed value had no revoke, rotate, delete or audit procedure at all. (a) mistakes the store for the exposure: a key written into a URL and printed to a log is disclosed as effectively as one written into a committed file. (b) would prescribe a history rewrite for a value that was never in history and omit the stores that actually hold it. (c) puts an operator procedure in a document about dependency advisories. Its step 3 is therefore a search of container logs, the aggregation service and its indexes, proxy access logs, build logs and developer machines, and its step 4 reads the provider's own usage logs — because ingestion has a predictable shape, an unexplained burst or an unfamiliar source address is legible as an incident | The log estate is not enumerable from this repository, so the runbook lists the classes of store rather than the stores themselves, and an operator with a store not on the list has to recognise it. The verification section asks for the date the last record leaves the estate, and says that a future date means the rotation is complete while the exposure is not — which is the distinction most likely to be quietly skipped |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.6.1 | The Cloud SQL proxy **image tag** `1.19.1`, while adding `-ip_address_types=PRIVATE` to its command | (a) Move to the current proxy image in the same edit; (b) leave the command alone too | The finding is that the proxy connects over the public address against an instance that has none, and one flag closes it. The image currency is a separate item, reported per row 16.10 and awaiting confirmation, and the review's own resolution text prefers migrating it under an approved follow-up. Doing both in one edit would put a confirmed fix and an unconfirmed upgrade in the same change | The superseded image remains, and the v1 proxy's flag spelling is what the added argument uses; a future image migration has to revisit that argument |
| 42.6.2 | `force_destroy = true` on both storage buckets, and the absent provider version constraint and remote state backend | (a) Fix all three while the file is open | All three are reported and awaiting confirmation, and this round's mandate is the findings named against it. They are now stated in the "Open risks" block of `main.tf`, so a reader of the configuration meets them where they apply rather than only in this log | Three known gaps persist in a file this round otherwise hardened, which reads as inconsistency to anyone who does not check the inventory in §42.1 |
| 42.6.3 | `node-version: '14'` in the pipeline, and every file under `frontend/` | (a) Advance the Node version while the workflow is open; (b) repair the client | The Node version is reported item 6 and the frontend is read-only for this work. Advancing Node would additionally change the behaviour of the one job this round deliberately leaves failing, making its state harder rather than easier to read | The pipeline installs an end-of-life toolchain in a job that is expected to fail. The job's name and its first step both say so |
