Verified unchanged after this round: `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` and `scripts/deploy.sh`. `.github/workflows/cd.yml` no longer sets up Python at all, because the job that did was the duplicated `verify` job §42.3.3 removed — so the pin sites are the four the requirements name, with no fifth copy to drift | Seven advisories remain accepted. Contract tests assert the pin in the pipeline and in the script, and that neither names a newer interpreter |


### 42.7 Disclosure-channel and public-prose decisions

These belong with §42.2 to §42.5 as decisions of this round rather than with §42.6's
non-changes; they are placed last only so that the numbering of the rows above is left
undisturbed.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.7.1 | **Publish no contact address at all, in either `SECURITY.md` or `README.md`, and state the operator prerequisite instead of an address** | (a) Invent a plausible address such as `security@` on a domain this project does not control; (b) keep `your.email@example.com` with a stronger warning beside it; (c) point the fallback channel at GitHub issues; (d) delete the reporting section until a mailbox exists | (a) publishes an address that resolves to someone else, and a vulnerability report sent there is a disclosure to a third party. (b) is what stood: the address was already labelled a placeholder in both files, and it was still the only fallback the policy offered — a label does not stop a reporter using the one address on the page. (c) instructs a reporter to disclose publicly, which is the exact outcome the policy's first line forbids. (d) removes the disclosure route a researcher looks for, and with it the statement of what to do instead. Naming the absence, and naming the two steps that end it, is the only option that neither misdirects a report nor hides that no channel exists | A researcher who reads only the channel headings sees two channels and may not read the warning that neither is live. Mitigated by putting the warning **above** both channels as the first thing in the section, and by a test asserting each channel carries its own operator prerequisite |
| 42.7.2 | **Withdraw the published response-time table to a labelled proposal rather than delete it or keep it in force** | (a) Keep the commitments as published; (b) delete the table; (c) soften the numbers | (a) commits to acknowledging within five business days when nothing receives the report and nobody is accountable for reading it — an undertaking to a researcher that the repository cannot honour. (b) loses the operator's target and leaves the next person to invent one. (c) is the same defect at a different number: the problem is not the value, it is that no channel exists to measure it against. Keeping the table, and labelling the column "not yet in force", preserves the intent as something an operator switches on | A reader skimming the table sees numbers and takes them for commitments. Mitigated by the column heading itself carrying "not yet in force", so the qualification cannot be separated from the figures, and by a test asserting both the heading and the withdrawal sentence |
| 42.7.3 | **Describe the pipeline as delivered — three jobs, one of them tolerated and gating nothing — and mark each verification command "Enforced" or "Local only"** | (a) State the blockers as the review's guidance offered, without changing the description of the gates; (b) claim the gates run, as before, now that the pipeline is fixed; (c) drop the verification table | The workflows were repaired in this round, so (a) would describe a blocker that no longer exists. (b) is nearly true and therefore the more dangerous error: the gates do now run, but `terraform validate`, the container build and the migration downgrades are **not** gated, and a contributor who reads "those same gates run in CI" will not run locally the only checks those three ever get. (c) removes the reader's ability to reproduce any of it. Marking each row is what makes the distinction the review asked for legible per command rather than as a caveat | The table now carries a third column a reader must consult. Mitigated by stating the distinction in a sentence above it, and by a test asserting both markers are present |
| 42.7.4 | **State in `README.md` and `SECURITY.md` that frontend integration is non-operational and separately scoped, and enumerate the client defects without fixing any of them** | (a) Say nothing, as before; (b) relax a backend contract so the client works — the login response field, the missing header, the PayPal product shape; (c) fix the client | (a) is what the review found: a README promising that a React frontend consumes the API, beside a client that cannot. (b) inverts the entire remediation, weakening a hardened contract to accommodate a broken caller, and is refused. (c) requires editing `frontend/src/**`, which is read-only for this work — the constraint rows 34.2.1 and 35.6.3 both rest on. Naming the defects precisely, attributing them to a predating condition, and stating that repair belongs to an authorized frontend change is the only treatment that neither conceals the limitation nor breaches the scope | A reader may take "non-operational" as a defect introduced here. Mitigated by stating in both documents that the defects predate this work, and by recording them as items 1, 4 and 14 of the inventory above |


### 42.8 Executive-deck decisions

Eight review findings landed on `blitzy-deck/executive-summary.html`: two shared with the
prose artefacts (the CI-enforcement and frontend-operability claims), four specific to the
deck (the dependency rationale, the completion claims, the content-length cap and the
contrast failures), and two accessibility items. Several of the fixes had to satisfy a
review finding and a literal Rule 2 requirement at the same time, and those are the rows
worth recording: where the two pulled in different directions, the choice is not obvious
and a competent engineer could have resolved it the other way.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 42.8.1 | **Raise title-slide contrast with a navy scrim behind the text, leaving Rule 2's hero gradient byte-identical** | (a) Alter the gradient's light end so white text clears 4.5:1 against it; (b) move the text off the light end of the gradient; (c) darken the title text to navy | Rule 2 specifies the hero gradient literally, including its three colour stops and their positions, so (a) edits a value the rule fixes. (b) holds at 1920×1080 and stops holding at every viewport where the gradient angle puts a different band behind the text, which is precisely the fragility finding N6 raised. (c) discards the white-on-gradient identity the rule describes. A scrim is the only option that changes neither the gradient nor the text colour: it is a separate layer between them. Measured worst case across the gradient's lightest stop is white 6.13:1 and mint 4.93:1, both above the 4.5:1 threshold M19 cites | A scrim darkens the hero's appearance relative to the rule's intent. Mitigated by holding it at 0.55 falling to 0.30 alpha, the lowest values that clear the threshold — an earlier 0.15 light end measured mint at 3.97:1 and was rejected on that measurement — and by a test asserting both the scrim and the unmodified gradient |
| 42.8.2 | **Publish the seven open operator items on a slide of their own, taking the deck to seventeen sections** | (a) Fold the open items into the existing risk slide; (b) carry them only in speaker notes; (c) report the count without itemising | M17 requires the open critical and major items be reported explicitly. (a) cannot hold: the risk slide was already the worst offender against the 40-word cap at 193 words, and adding four items to it would breach M18 to satisfy M17. (b) hides from the audience what the review asked be shown to them, since notes are not projected. (c) is what the metric card does, and a count without owners does not tell a reviewer what to action. Rule 2 permits twelve to eighteen sections, so a seventeenth is inside the range rather than a deviation from it | Seventeen sections is one above Rule 2's stated target of sixteen. Accepted because the range, not the target, is the constraint, and because the alternative was a rule breach rather than a preference |
| 42.8.3 | **Draw the provisioned-but-unwired components as unconnected dashed nodes rather than deleting them from the architecture diagram** | (a) Delete the managed secret storage, event stream, object storage and React client nodes entirely; (b) keep the arrows and annotate them as pending; (c) keep the diagram as it was | M17 requires removing data-flow arrows that do not exist, and M15 requires stating that the client is non-operational. (a) removes the arrows but also removes the reader's ability to see that the secret storage was provisioned and that the platform resources exist unused, which understates what was delivered and hides what an operator still owns. (b) leaves the false flow on the slide with a caption contradicting it, and a viewer reads the arrow. (c) is the finding. Drawing the node without an arrow is literally true in both directions: the component exists, the flow does not. Each label carries its own state, and the client's reads "not operational, separately scoped" | A dashed unconnected box may read as a diagram error rather than a deliberate statement. Mitigated by an on-slide note that solid lines are flows that exist today, by each node's label naming its own state, by the accessible description explaining the convention, and by a test asserting the three flows the review named are absent |
| 42.8.4 | **Keep `--blitzy-text-muted: #999999` declared while removing every text use of it** | (a) Change the token's value to a darker grey; (b) delete the token; (c) keep the muted text and argue the affected text is large | Rule 2 reproduces the custom-property block literally, so (a) and (b) both edit a mandated declaration. M19 forbids the colour on normal text, measuring it at 2.85:1 on white. The distinction that resolves both is that the rule fixes the token, not its usages: the value stays declared exactly as specified and is now used only for diagram line colours and strokes, which are not text and are not subject to the 4.5:1 threshold. Text that carried it moved to `--blitzy-text` at 12.63:1 or the primary dark at 13.60:1. (c) is false — the affected labels are 0.8em body text | A future editor may reintroduce the token on text, believing its presence sanctions the use. Mitigated by a test that strips CSS comments and then fails if the literal value appears in any text-colour declaration |
| 42.8.5 | **Give the closing lockup explicit margin spacing rather than a line-height** | (a) Set `line-height: 1.2` on the brand word; (b) leave the inherited spacing as it was | Rendered-pixel measurement, not inspection, decided this. The two lines were structurally touching, with zero empty background rows between them. (a) was tried and measured **worse** — it reduced clearance from 5.408 to 1.512 CSS pixels, because 1.2 times the 18.56px size is smaller than the display face's own ascent plus descent and the negative half-leading pulls the lines together. That failure mode depends entirely on the font's metrics, so it would change under any substitution. An 8px margin is independent of the face and measured six empty pixel rows at deck scale, nineteen device rows at triple density. (b) leaves the finding | None material. The margin is additive spacing on a single element |
| 42.8.6 | **Carry the removed detail in speaker notes, and make each table's caption screen-reader-only** | (a) Delete the detail the word cap displaced; (b) move it into a companion document; (c) make the captions visible | M18's own guidance offers notes or a companion document, and the detail is the substantiation a reviewer asks for when a slide is challenged — (a) loses it. (b) separates it from the claim it supports. Notes travel with the slide and are not projected, so they cost nothing against the cap. For the captions, N5 requires them and (c) would spend the constrained word budget on text that sighted readers already get from the surrounding heading; the screen-reader-only treatment gives assistive technology the caption without competing for the budget. The word counts were nevertheless taken **with** the captions included, the strictest reading, and the worst content slide still measures 39 | A caption that is never visible cannot be proof-read on the rendered slide. Mitigated by asserting caption presence per table in a test rather than relying on visual review |
| 42.8.7 | **Restate the dependency rationale as three different reasons rather than one** | (a) Keep the single "no patched release" line; (b) drop the Why column | M16 found the deck asserting that all three replaced packages had no patched release, which is true of none of them as stated: the token library's own two vulnerabilities were fixed by its maintainers, and what cannot be fixed is a cryptography component it requires. (a) is the finding. (b) removes the reason a non-technical reader most needs, since "we replaced three packages" without a why reads as churn. Each cell now carries that package's actual reason — a component nobody will fix, an unmaintained wrapper that had stopped working, an archived kit that cannot verify notifications — matching the plan's rationale rather than a generalisation of it | Three distinct reasons are harder to hold than one. Mitigated by a speaker note that states the correction explicitly, so a presenter who learned the earlier version is corrected rather than left to contradict the slide |

---

## 43. Deployment topology, dialect fidelity and the verification gate

This section records the decisions of the round that answered a review of the
deployment surface and of the verification surface itself. The round's subject was
not a new control but the question of whether the controls already delivered are
*operable* and *proven*: a private control plane addressed from a runner with no
route to it, a schema and a set of concurrency controls exercised only on a dialect
that implements neither row locks nor deferred unique indexes, a set of test
assertions that could not fail if the property they name regressed, and a
verification gate that could not complete on a clean checkout.

Three properties hold across every row below, and are stated once here rather than
repeated. **The runtime pin is untouched** at all five sites; row 1.9 carries the
constructs and `test_the_runtime_pin_is_still_carried_at_every_site` asserts them.
**No frozen interface moved**: `backend/app/api/router.py` and the two ownership
predicates in `backend/app/api/endpoints/filters.py` are byte-identical, the login
response shape is unchanged, and all eight route paths and four prefixes stand.
**Every row was proven by perturbation**, not by inspection: the control was broken
through an edit or a monkeypatched seam, the named assertion was confirmed to fail,
and the file was restored and its digest compared. Where a row says "proven", that
is what it means.

### 43.1 Reaching a private control plane

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 43.1.1 | Keep the control plane private — `enable_private_nodes` and `enable_private_endpoint` both stay `true` — and move the two cluster-touching deployment jobs onto a VPC-resident self-hosted runner named by the repository variable `GKE_DEPLOY_RUNNER_LABEL` | (a) Make the endpoint public and rely on the authorized-network list alone; (b) address the cluster through Connect Gateway with fleet membership; (c) put a bastion or proxy in the path; (d) leave the workflow on a hosted runner and accept that it cannot connect | The finding was that a private endpoint was being addressed from `ubuntu-latest`, which has no route to it — so the pipeline could not deploy at all, and the first alternative that suggests itself is to open the endpoint. That is refused: AAP §0.5.1.5 mandates a private control plane, and (a) would spend the control to fix the client. (b) and (c) both work, and both add infrastructure this repository does not declare — a fleet membership and a workload-identity binding, or a bastion host and its own access policy — which is a larger change than moving the client. (d) is the finding. Moving the client is the smallest change that keeps the control: the runner sits inside a network the authorized-network list can name, which is exactly the arrangement the private endpoint is designed for. | The pipeline now depends on a self-hosted runner being registered and labelled; without it the deployment cannot run. That failure is made explicit rather than left to a connection timeout — see row 35.1.2. |
| 43.1.2 | Add an `ubuntu-latest` `preflight` job that **refuses** an unset `GKE_DEPLOY_RUNNER_LABEL` and refuses any of twelve named GitHub-hosted runner images | (a) Let the deployment job fail on its first `kubectl` call; (b) document the requirement in the README only | A `runs-on` naming a label no runner carries leaves a job queued rather than failed, and a label pointing at a hosted image produces a connection timeout deep inside the deployment — after the images have been built and pushed. Both failure modes are slow and neither says what is wrong. The preflight states the requirement as a check, before anything is built. The twelve images are named so that a variable set to one of them is refused by name rather than diagnosed later. | The list of hosted images is a denylist and cannot be exhaustive; a new image name would pass it. It is a convenience check ahead of the real control, which is that the runner must be able to reach the endpoint at all. |
| 43.1.3 | Make `gke_master_authorized_networks` a **required** variable with three validations — non-empty, syntactically valid CIDR, and RFC 1918 private ranges only | (a) Keep `default = []`; (b) require it without validating the values; (c) default it to a documented placeholder range | With `default = []` a plan applies cleanly and produces a control plane no client may reach, which is the same unusable outcome as the finding, reached from the other direction. Making it required forces the operator to name the network the runner is in. The private-range validation is the part that carries security weight: a public CIDR in that list would re-expose the endpoint the private setting exists to close, and it would do so while every declaration still read `enable_private_endpoint = true`. (c) would ship a range nobody intended to authorize. | A `terraform plan` now fails until the variable is supplied. That is the intent: the value cannot be guessed, and a wrong guess is a security decision. |

### 43.2 Deployment mechanics

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 43.2.1 | Give the node pool the single `cloud-platform` access scope and keep least privilege in the IAM role list, adding `roles/storage.objectViewer` beside `roles/artifactregistry.reader` | (a) Enumerate narrow scopes covering the registry; (b) keep the two logging and monitoring scopes and rely on IAM alone | The pool carried `logging.write` and `monitoring` only, so a node could not pull the private image the deployment pushes — the cluster would run nothing. Access scopes are a legacy ceiling applied *before* IAM, so the documented arrangement is a broad scope with narrow IAM, not narrow scopes with narrow IAM: (a) reintroduces a second place where a permission can be missing, and every permission then has to be granted twice. The two roles cover both shapes a `gcr.io` reference can resolve to — Artifact Registry for a redirected host, and a Container Registry bucket for a legacy one — so the pull works either way. | The scope is broad. Least privilege now rests entirely on the dedicated service account's role list, which is where it is visible and reviewable; the scope no longer masks a missing role by denying it twice. |
| 43.2.2 | Address the cluster by **one** location value used by both Terraform and the workflow, with the `--region` credential flag | (a) `--location`, which accepts a region and a zone alike; (b) make the cluster zonal and keep `--zone` | Terraform creates a **regional** cluster (`location = var.region`) while the workflow fetched credentials with `--zone`, so the two disagreed about the shape of the thing they were addressing. One value now addresses the resource from both sides. (a) tolerates either shape and was the position first taken here; the delivered workflow names `--region`, which is what a regional cluster is addressed by and which cannot silently accept a zone. (b) would downgrade the cluster's availability to fix a flag. | A reader familiar with `--zone` or with the earlier `--location` position has to know that `--region` is what is delivered. `test_the_cluster_is_addressed_by_one_location_value` states the contract, and `test_the_regional_cluster_is_addressed_by_region` asserts the flag. |
| 43.2.3 | Build each image with `-f infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.<component>` and the context that definition copies from | (a) Add a `Dockerfile` at `frontend/` and `backend/`; (b) move the definitions to the component directories | `docker build ./backend` looks for `backend/Dockerfile`, which does not exist — the authoritative definitions live under `infrastructure/docker/`, and the Compose file already builds them with `-f` and the component context. (a) creates a second definition to keep in agreement with the first. (b) relocates files the AAP maps at their current paths. Naming the definition explicitly makes the workflow, the deployment script and Compose all build the same artifact from the same file. | The `-f` and the context must stay consistent, since the backend definition copies `requirements.txt` from the context root. `test_each_image_is_built_from_the_definition_that_declares_it` asserts both. |
| 43.2.4 | Gate the deployment on a **completed successful run of the CI workflow** through `workflow_run`, and delete the deployment workflow's own partial verification job | (a) Duplicate CI's full gate inside the deployment workflow; (b) keep the partial job and add the missing checks to it; (c) leave the partial gate as it was | The deployment ran behind a job that checked a dependency audit, a static analysis and one test directory — not the linter, not the full suite, not coverage, not the compensating-control guards, not the integration cases. Any of those could fail and a deployment would still proceed. (a) and (b) both create a second copy of the gate, and two copies of a gate drift: the reason this finding exists is that one copy already had. Triggering on the other workflow's conclusion means there is exactly one gate, and `workflow_run` reports `success` only when every job of that run succeeded. The deployment checks out `workflow_run.head_sha` and tags its images with it, so what is deployed is the revision that was verified rather than whatever the branch has since become. | A `workflow_run` trigger only fires for workflow files on the default branch, so the gate cannot be exercised from a feature branch. `test_the_deployment_workflow_is_gated_on_this_workflow` ties the awaited name to CI's declared `name` so the two cannot be renamed apart. |
| 43.2.5 | Run the schema migration as a **one-shot pod built from the new image, before any rollout**, and exit non-zero on its failure without changing what is serving | (a) Migrate after the rollout, as the script did; (b) migrate from an init container on the Deployment; (c) migrate from the runner against the database directly | Migrating after the rollout serves new code against an old schema for the duration — the window in which the authorization dependency reads a column that does not yet exist. (b) runs the migration once per replica and couples it to the rollout it is meant to precede. (c) needs a database route from the runner and a second copy of the credentials. A one-shot pod from the new image runs exactly the revisions that image carries, once, and its exit status is the gate: the script reports that nothing was rolled out and stops. The additive design with server defaults is what makes migrating first safe — the old code tolerates the new columns. | The migration pod is bounded (900 seconds) and its logs are collected; a migration that hangs stops the deployment rather than proceeding. That is the intended trade. |
| 43.2.6 | Keep the Cloud Function step, gated on `FUNCTION_SOURCE_DIR` being supplied and the directory existing, and require `FUNCTION_NAME`, `FUNCTION_ENTRY_POINT` and `FUNCTION_REGION` | (a) Delete the step, since the repository contains no function source; (b) hard-require the inputs unconditionally | The step deployed a placeholder name from a `./functions` directory that does not exist, so it could only ever fail. Deleting it is tempting and is refused for two reasons: it removes the fourth runtime pin site, which is load-bearing and cited by two review documents, and it removes the `--no-allow-unauthenticated` that closes INFRA-4. (b) would make the script unrunnable in this repository, since the source genuinely is absent. Gating on the source directory lets the script run here and deploy the function wherever the source exists, and the required-input checks stop a partial invocation. | The step is inert in this repository, so its behaviour is asserted statically rather than executed. `test_no_deployment_publishes_the_function_to_everyone` covers the flag across the script, the workflow and the module. |
| 43.2.7 | Write `--no-allow-unauthenticated` explicitly rather than omitting `--allow-unauthenticated` | Omit the flag and rely on the platform default | An absent flag is indistinguishable from an oversight, and a reader cannot tell whether the public invocation was closed deliberately or simply forgotten. The explicit negative form states the decision. It also gives the assertion something to find: the forbidden flag is a suffix of the permitted one, so the check strips the permitted spelling before searching, and the presence of the negative form is asserted separately. | The two spellings differ by a prefix, so a careless edit could turn one into the other. That is precisely what the assertion is for. |
| 43.2.8 | Surface the undeclared `@paypal/react-paypal-js` dependency as a **named precondition check** in the deployment workflow, and report it rather than fix it | (a) Add the dependency to `frontend/package.json`; (b) say nothing and let the image build fail | The package is imported by `frontend/src/index.tsx` and `frontend/src/services/paypal.ts` and is declared nowhere, so the frontend bundle cannot build. Fixing it means editing `frontend/package.json`, which AAP §0.9.2 places out of scope — and it would also require regenerating the lockfile, a second out-of-scope change. (b) leaves a build failure whose cause is a stack trace from a bundler. The preflight compares every scoped import under `frontend/src` against the manifest and names what is missing, so the failure is legible and attributable. | The check reports a problem it is not permitted to fix, which is the correct outcome for an out-of-scope finding but is unusual in a pipeline. It is recorded among the flagged findings in row 34.6.3. |

### 43.3 Proving the controls on the dialect that runs them

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 43.3.1 | Isolate each production-dialect case in a **database of its own** (`blitzy_case_<hex>`, created and dropped by fixture), rather than in a schema of its own | (a) A schema per case with `search_path` set through the connection URL; (b) one shared database with truncation between cases; (c) a transaction rolled back per case | (a) was built first and measured to fail: `backend/app/db/database.py` supplies its own libpq `options` string for every PostgreSQL URL, and libpq `options` passed through `connect_args` **replaces** any `options` a URL carries — so `?options=-csearch_path%3D<schema>` was silently discarded. Because the Alembic subprocess opens its connection through the application's own engine, the revisions resolved unqualified names in the default schema, and fourteen cases failed with `NoSuchTableError` and an empty table set. The alternative was to change `database.py` to merge rather than replace, which is a production change made for a test's benefit. (b) cannot test a migration, whose subject is the schema itself. (c) cannot test one either, and cannot test lock contention between two connections. A database per case is the only level of isolation that lets a real Alembic run and two real connections coexist. | The role must hold `CREATEDB`; the fixture asserts `rolcreatedb OR rolsuper` and skips with a clear reason otherwise. Each case pays a database creation, and databases are dropped `WITH (FORCE)` so a leaked connection cannot leave one behind. |
| 43.3.2 | Observe lock contention through `pg_stat_activity` on a connection set to **AUTOCOMMIT** | Poll the view on an ordinary connection | The observer saw nothing at all until this was changed, and the reason is a property of the server rather than a bug in the query: PostgreSQL holds the statistics views stable for the duration of a transaction, so an observer inside one sees a snapshot taken before the contention began and polls it forever. AUTOCOMMIT gives each poll its own transaction and therefore its own snapshot. Measured directly before adoption: the query then reports the waiting backend with `wait_event_type = 'Lock'`, `wait_event = 'transactionid'` and the `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` text, and the counter reaches 2. | The reason is not obvious from reading the fixture, so it is stated in the fixture's docstring as a fact about the server. The polling loop is bounded at 30 seconds, so a contention that never appears fails rather than hangs. |
| 43.3.3 | Compare every added column against an **expected shape** — exact type compiled for PostgreSQL, precision and scale, nullability, and normalised server default — rather than against a set of column names | (a) Keep the name-and-constraint reflection; (b) compare types as their generic `str()` | Name-level reflection cannot see the differences that matter on a real dialect: a `NUMERIC(10, 2)` reduced to `NUMERIC`, a server default dropped, a timezone qualifier lost. Measured while building it: `str()` of a reflected type **strips the qualifier**, reporting `TIMESTAMP` where the column is `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, so (b) would silently accept the loss of the qualifier that every entitlement comparison depends on. Compiling against `postgresql.dialect()` reports it. Defaults are normalised before comparison because PostgreSQL renders them with a cast — `'registered'::character varying`, `now()`, `'NULL::numeric'` — which is a rendering difference rather than a difference in the default. | The expected shapes are a second statement of the model's declarations, so an intended change must be made in both places. That is the point: it is asserted for ten columns and proven a real gate by changing one server default from `USD` to `EUR`, which failed exactly that column's case. |
| 43.3.4 | Let the **real unique index** decide the outcome of a repeated webhook delivery, and keep the scripted barrier alongside it, relabelled | (a) Replace the scripted barrier with the real-index cases; (b) keep only the scripted barrier | The scripted barrier raised the integrity error itself, so it proved that the handler answers a duplicate correctly and proved nothing about whether a duplicate is *detected* — on SQLite there is no deferred index to detect it with. The real-index cases hold only the first delivery and never script the waiter's fate: the second blocks on the index, and what it receives comes from the database. (b) is the finding. (a) would discard a deterministic case that runs everywhere for one that needs a server, and the two answer different questions. Both are kept and the barrier's docstring now says which question it answers — that the outcome "is decided here rather than by a database". | Two mechanisms cover one property, which is redundancy rather than duplication: removing the `UniqueConstraint` fails the real-index cases and leaves the barrier green, which is exactly the discrimination the pair exists to provide. |
| 43.3.5 | Assert the row lock by exercising the **production helper** and capturing the statement it issues, and add a separate case proving the counting path reaches that helper | (a) Keep the test's own reconstruction of the query; (b) assert the source text of `_lock_row` | The test built its own `with_for_update()` query and compiled it, so it asserted that SQLAlchemy can emit `FOR UPDATE` — which is true whatever the application does. Removing the lock from production code left it green. Capturing the statement the helper itself issues closes that gap, and the second case closes the one it leaves: a helper can be correct and unreached. (b) asserts text rather than behaviour. | The capture is a monkeypatch on `Query.with_for_update`, which couples the case to that method's name. Proven a real gate: removing `.with_for_update()` from the endpoint fails both the statement case and the PostgreSQL contention case. |
| 43.3.6 | Make the production-dialect cases **opt-in by marker**, skipped when no server is named and **failed** when `REQUIRE_POSTGRES_TESTS` is set | (a) Require a server unconditionally; (b) skip silently in every environment | (a) makes the suite unrunnable for a developer without a server, which pushes people towards not running it. (b) is how a dialect gate quietly stops existing: a runner that loses its database reports a passing job over seventeen skips. The two-variable form gives both properties — green and honest locally, mandatory in CI. Both directions are measured: without the URL, 9 passed and 14 skipped at exit 0; with the requirement set and no URL, 14 errors at exit 1. | Two environment variables to keep set in CI. `test_the_gate_refuses_to_skip_the_dialect_cases` asserts the requirement is `1` in the workflow, so the honest mode cannot be turned off by editing one line unnoticed. |
| 43.3.7 | Bound every subprocess and every wait the suite performs, with a different bound for each according to what it waits on | A single shared timeout constant | An unbounded `subprocess.run` around an Alembic invocation hangs a suite rather than failing it, and the same is true of a lock-contention poll and of an engine connecting to a port nothing listens on. The bounds differ because the waits differ: 300 seconds for two Alembic revisions, 180 for a fresh interpreter importing the application, 30 for lock contention on a local server, 30 for the statistics poll, and 2 for a connection to a closed port on loopback. One shared value would be either too small for the migration or too large to be a useful bound on the connection. Each expiry reports the captured output rather than only the timeout. | Five constants rather than one. Each is named for what it bounds and stated next to it. |
| 43.3.8 | Prove that schema creation stays out of application startup with a **fresh interpreter that makes the creation raise** | (a) Scan the source for `create_all`; (b) trust that the removal stays removed | The schema was previously created at import time and migrations now own it, and nothing failed if that returned — the most consequential kind of gap, because the reintroduction would look like a convenience. (a) is kept as the cheap half but sees only the literal call: an import-time creation reached through an alias or a helper would pass it. The subprocess replaces `Base.metadata.create_all` with a stand-in that raises, then imports the application, enters its lifespan through a client and serves a liveness request — so the whole startup path is covered rather than the import alone. Proven a real gate: reintroducing the call failed both cases. | The subprocess needs the trusted-host base URL to be served, which is a detail of the harness rather than of the property. Bounded at 180 seconds. |

### 43.4 Making the assertions able to fail

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 43.4.1 | Suppress the exception message on the unhandled-error log record — `exception_message=None` — so the record carries the failure's class, module, route, method and correlation identifier and no message text | (a) Broaden the redactor to catch address-shaped values; (b) keep the message and assert only that the email sentinel is absent; (c) keep the message and drop the assertion | This began as a test gap and turned out to be a live disclosure. The log-record cases injected two sentinels and asserted neither absent; writing the assertion showed that the redactor removes the email address and **does not** remove the street address, which was reaching every 500-error record through `exception_fields`' redacted message. So the finding's suggested fix could not pass until the leak was closed. (a) is refused: address shapes cannot be matched without heuristics, and the redactor's declared scope is keys, tokens, secrets and passwords rather than arbitrary personal data. (b) and (c) would leave an arbitrary-content channel open in the one handler that catches exceptions from every route. The chosen form follows a pattern the codebase had already established for exactly this reason — the ingestion failure path passes `exception_message=None` with the note that no message text is carried — so this makes the two consistent rather than inventing a rule. The traceback is still emitted at `DEBUG`, which production levels suppress, so local diagnosis is unaffected. | A 500 is now diagnosed by correlation identifier and exception class rather than by message. Blast radius checked before the change: three references to `exception_message` exist, and none asserts it on this path. The database-error call sites keep their messages, and bound values cannot reach them because the engine hides parameters. |
| 43.4.2 | Assert the frozen response contracts as **required members plus forbidden sensitive members**, and keep exact equality for the health body and the error envelope | (a) Keep exact set and list equality everywhere; (b) drop to required members everywhere | The AAP permits adding a field to the login response and forbids removing one, so exact equality asserts the opposite of the contract: it fails a permitted addition. But a bare membership check would pass a credential added under a new name, so the forbidden set is the other half. Proven in three directions: an added `expires_in` is now tolerated where the old assertion would have failed; an added `hashed_password` fails; a removed `token_type` fails. (b) is refused for the health body and the 500 envelope, where minimality is itself the control — the envelope carrying exactly a detail and a request identifier is what proves nothing else leaks — so those keep exact equality deliberately. | The forbidden list is a denylist and cannot be exhaustive. It is scanned recursively at any depth, and the required-member half is what carries the contract. |
| 43.4.3 | Regression-protect the cross-origin policy at **two layers**: the keywords the middleware was installed with, and real preflight negotiation through the assembled application | (a) Assert the module constants; (b) assert only preflight responses | Nothing failed if the explicit method and header lists became wildcards again, which with credentialed responses is the misconfiguration that was fixed in the first place. (a) reads the constants but not what was installed, so a wildcard passed directly to the middleware would pass. Reading `app.user_middleware` reads the configuration that is actually in effect. But configuration alone cannot show that it is enforced, so the second layer negotiates a real allowed preflight, an unlisted origin, an unlisted method and an unlisted header. Proven three ways: wildcard methods and headers fail four cases, a wildcard origin alongside credentials fails five, and removing the middleware fails the class. | The header assertions test membership rather than equality, because the framework adds the CORS-safelisted request headers to its own reply. That is a property of the framework and is stated where it is relied on. |
| 43.4.4 | Execute the setup script's environment step in an **isolated repository root**, and drive **both** of its key-generation branches | (a) Assert the script's text; (b) run the whole script; (c) drive only the branch this host takes | The script generates the signing key that replaces the placeholder at the heart of the Critical finding, and nothing executed that path — so its output was never checked for strength, for uniqueness or for reaching the file. (a) reads the code that generates a value without ever seeing a value. (b) would install dependencies, create a database and migrate. Overriding `REPO_ROOT` after the bootstrap — the variable is deliberately not `readonly` — and calling the one function runs the generation and the write and nothing else. (c) would leave the interpreter fallback untested on a host that has `openssl`, so `command` is overridden in the test driver to report it absent, which forces the other branch deterministically without depending on `PATH`. Thresholds are imported from the configuration module rather than restated, so the case cannot disagree with the validator. | The driver overrides a shell builtin, which is test scaffolding rather than a change to the script. Proven a real gate: a fixed key containing `CHANGE_ME` that the script's own length and variety checks accept fails the placeholder and uniqueness cases, and silently dropping one template entry fails the write-through case. |
| 43.4.5 | Assert the image's build-context exclusions as **effective**, by implementing the context's own ignore-matching rules, over both contexts the backend image is built from | (a) Run `docker build` and inspect the result; (b) assert the ignore file contains the expected patterns; (c) use `fnmatch` directly | The definition copies its whole context, so an ignore file is the only thing between a developer's environment file and a published image — and nothing asserted that any pattern actually matches anything. (a) is unavailable: there is no container engine on the verification host. (b) asserts the presence of text, which is what the finding already had at the source level. (c) is wrong in a way that would produce false confidence: `fnmatch`'s `*` crosses a path separator, so a pattern would appear to match paths the real matcher does not. The implemented matcher works segment by segment, treats `**` as spanning any number of segments including none, and tests every ancestor so a directory pattern removes its subtree. Both contexts are covered because the image is genuinely built from both — Compose and the deployment script use the component directory, and a root-context build is governed by the root file — and a pattern set protecting one and not the other protects nothing in practice. | The matcher is a reimplementation and could diverge from the engine's behaviour. It is exercised in both directions: sixteen paths that must be excluded and five the image needs that must not be, so a rule widened until it broke the build fails too. Proven a gate by removing the environment-file patterns from one context, which failed that context's cases and left the other's green. |
| 43.4.6 | Split each wall-clock timing case into a **counted primary gate** and a `timing`-marked confidence measurement | (a) Widen the tolerances; (b) delete the wall-clock cases; (c) mark them flaky or rerun them; (d) leave them as the only gate | A wall-clock assertion cannot be made independent of the machine taking it, and this was not theoretical: one of these cases **failed during this round's own regression run** under the load of the rest of the suite. (a) is refused for the reason row 31.13 gives — the tolerance is a security parameter, and widening it far enough to absorb contention would hide a real extra comparison. (b) discards a measurement that covers the property end to end. (c) converts a red signal into a slower green one. The counted form measures what the branches *do* rather than how long they take: one credential check, two hash comparisons, one budget equalisation per refusal, and a single distinct refusal triple across all four branches. That is deterministic on any machine, and it catches the original defect — reintroducing the unknown-address short-circuit fails exactly the unknown branch, in eighteen seconds, with no clock read. The four cases that genuinely read a clock now carry the marker; one case that carried it but reads no clock was moved out, so the marker names exactly the measurements it describes. | Two mechanisms per property. The marker is registered with the note that deselecting it loses no coverage of the control, so `-m "not timing"` is a supported way to run the suite on a noisy host. |
| 43.4.7 | Establish the rate limiter's storage as reachable by **operating** it — a health probe, an increment read back twice, a release — rather than by finding the object in place | (a) Keep the object check; (b) rename the case to the property it proved | The case was named "the configured storage is reachable" and asserted that an attribute was not `None`, which is true of a storage that cannot be reached at all. Measured: with the backend's `check()` forced to `False` and its `incr` raising, the original assertion still passed. (b) is honest and was the finding's own alternative, but it leaves reachability unasserted — and outside `ENVIRONMENT=local` the validator refuses an in-process store, so reachability is a deployment property worth gating. The probe key is namespaced and released in a `finally`, so operating it leaves the shared counters as they were found. | The cases touch the process-wide limiter. They release what they take and the autouse fixture clears counters around every case, so nothing carries between them. |

### 43.5 A verification gate that can complete

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 43.5.1 | Remove the frontend lint step and the frontend test step, keeping `npm ci` | (a) Add a `lint` script to `frontend/package.json`; (b) add frontend tests; (c) leave both steps and accept a red pipeline | `npm run lint` names a script the manifest does not declare, and the test step runs a suite that has no test files — so both failed on a clean checkout, and because they sat ahead of every backend gate, **none of the backend gates was reachable**. (a) and (b) both require editing `frontend/` paths that AAP §0.9.2 places out of scope, and (b) would mean authoring a frontend test suite. (c) is the finding, and its real cost is not the red mark but the eight checks that never ran behind it. `npm ci` is kept because lockfile integrity is genuinely checkable and it succeeds. This is a scope decision rather than a preference, and it is recorded as one. | The frontend is now installed but not linted or tested by this pipeline. That gap is a consequence of the read-only boundary, not of this decision, and `test_the_workflow_invokes_no_npm_script_that_is_not_declared` reads the manifest as the authority so a step calling an undeclared script cannot return. |
| 43.5.2 | Move the pipeline's Node major to one the committed lockfile supports, leaving the frontend image's own base untouched | Change both together | The workflow pinned a major several years past end of life while the committed lockfile is `lockfileVersion` 3 and declares `engines.node >= 18`, so the two disagreed about what could install. The image definition is out of scope, so the two now differ deliberately; the assertion reads the floor from the lockfile rather than restating it, so the pipeline's major is checked against the authority. | Pipeline and image build the bundle on different majors. Recorded here as a known divergence rather than left to be discovered. |
| 43.5.3 | Provision PostgreSQL 13 as a pipeline service and run the marked cases against it, with the requirement variable set | (a) Run the suite on SQLite only; (b) provision the latest PostgreSQL | (a) is the finding: the migrations, the row lock and the unique index were never exercised on a dialect that implements them. The major is pinned to match what the Compose stack and the Terraform instance both declare, so a behaviour that differs between majors surfaces here rather than after a deployment; (b) would test a version nothing runs. The service's superuser satisfies the fixtures' `CREATEDB` requirement, which was verified by running all seventeen marked cases against a superuser connection before the workflow was written. | One more service in the job. It is health-checked before the steps that need it, and the requirement variable means an unreachable server fails rather than skips. |
| 43.5.4 | Add a secret and ignore-policy gate that decides by **value** rather than by path | (a) Exclude documentation paths from the scan; (b) scan only files outside `.env.example`; (c) rely on the ignore rules alone | The credentials this repository committed cannot be un-leaked by a code change — that is an operational rotation, sequenced last — so what a pipeline can enforce is non-recurrence. Path-based exclusion is the obvious approach and it hollows the gate out precisely where it matters: `.env.example` is the file most likely to receive a real password by accident, and the workflow files are where a real credential is most likely to be pasted. Deciding by value keeps both inside the scan — a connection string whose password is a documented placeholder is documentation, and one whose password is anything else is a credential. This was not theoretical while building it: the gate flagged this work's **own** new pipeline service credential, and rather than excluding the workflow directory the service password was made self-declaring. (c) checks that a secret cannot be added and not that one is already present. | The placeholder markers are a convention the gate depends on; a real password happening to contain one would pass. Test fixtures are excluded from the connection-string scan, because a synthetic address is what they are for. Proven both ways: a planted credential and a weakened ignore rule each fail it. |
| 43.5.5 | Audit each manifest in its **own step**, with each comment naming only its own register | Suppress all fourteen identifiers in one step | One step suppressing fourteen identifiers under a comment naming the residual-risk register sends a reader to a document that records seven of them, and the other seven appear to be undocumented. Two steps make the arithmetic legible: seven runtime identifiers documented in the register, seven development identifiers documented in the manifest that declares them, disjoint sets. The assertion asserts each step names its own authority **and not the other's** — a distinction added after the first version of it passed a perturbation that pointed the development step at the runtime register. | Two steps to keep in agreement with two registers. The cross-checks assert every identifier appears both in the step that suppresses it and in the register that documents it, and that the accepted section of the runtime register names exactly the runtime seven. |
| 43.5.6 | Replace the placeholder integration step with real gates, adding the import check, the migration reversal and the administrator count to the pipeline | (a) Leave the placeholder; (b) delete the step | The step was a comment asking a person to write commands, which succeeds without running anything — so the pipeline reported a passing integration gate it did not have, and three of the project's stated success criteria were enforced nowhere. (b) removes the report without adding the checks. What replaced it are exactly those criteria: the application imports, both revisions apply and reverse and re-apply, and exactly one account holds the administrative role afterwards with every other on the default. Each is asserted in the pipeline and each has a case asserting the pipeline still carries it. | The migration steps need the settings a deployment needs, so the job supplies them as environment values with an empty `ENV_FILE`. That was verified by running the same environment against a scratch database before the workflow was written. |
| 43.5.7 | Gate the line numbers that review documents quote for the runtime pin | (a) Refresh them by hand; (b) remove the line numbers and cite constructs only | The pin-site citations in the review artefacts had drifted, which is worse than an absent citation: it sends a reviewer performing a mandated check to the wrong line. (a) is what this round did, and by itself it only resets a clock that had already run down once. (b) is the convention the decision log and the traceability matrix follow for claims about the current tree, and it is applied to those two documents here — but a reviewer being told to verify a pin benefits from the exact line to open, so the review artefact keeps its numbers and they are asserted instead: each citation is parsed, the file opened and the numbered line checked for the construct. Proven a gate immediately — it failed on a stale citation the moment it was written, and again when one was reintroduced. | The assertion couples two documents to line numbers in five files, so an intended move requires updating the citation. That is the intent; the alternative is a citation nobody notices has gone stale. |

### 43.6 Deliberate non-changes from this round

The round touched the deployment surface, the test surface and the pipeline, and it
would have been easy to widen. It did not, and the restraints are recorded so that
their absence is not read as an oversight.

| # | Non-change | Why it was left alone |
|---|-----------|----------------------|
| 43.6.1 | `backend/app/db/database.py` still replaces rather than merges the libpq `options` it supplies | Merging would have made schema-level test isolation possible, and it is a production change whose only beneficiary is a test. Row 35.3.1 chose database-level isolation instead, which needs nothing from production code. |
| 43.6.2 | `@asyncio.coroutine` remains in the ingestion task | Valid on the pinned interpreter, not security-relevant, and removing it would breach the Minimal Change Clause. It is reported as forward-compatibility debt and is the decisive evidence that the pin is a property of the code. |
| 43.6.3 | The linter still runs from `backend/` rather than from the repository root | That invocation exercises the second of `setup.cfg`'s two `per-file-ignores` patterns, so both documented working directories are covered. Row 31.2's rationale cited this step imprecisely and the row is corrected rather than the step changed. |
| 43.6.4 | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` keeps its own Node base | Out of scope per AAP §0.9.2. The resulting divergence from the pipeline's major is recorded in row 35.5.2. |
| 43.6.5 | No new test module was created for the pipeline and container assertions | They were added to `backend/tests/security/test_deployment_contract.py`, whose subject is already the deployment declarations, so the unplanned-path count in section 23.2 is unchanged by this round. |
| 43.6.6 | The scripted webhook barrier was kept rather than replaced | Row 35.3.4. It answers a different question from the real-index cases and runs where they cannot. |
| 43.6.7 | Exact response-key equality was kept for the health body and the error envelope | Row 35.4.2. Minimality is the control at those two places, so relaxing them would remove a check rather than correct one. |

## 44. What the executive summary is allowed to claim

This section records the decisions of the round that answered a review of the
executive presentation and of the status language the project publishes. Two
defects drove it. The presentation exceeded Rule 2's body-text limit on eight of
its ten content slides, the worst carrying nearly five times the permitted count —
so the artefact governed by a rule about executive readability was the least
readable thing delivered. And the status it reported was an overstatement: it said
twenty findings were closed and titled its closing slide "Secured", while that same
slide said credential rotation was still outstanding. The presentation contradicted
itself on the only question its audience was being asked to decide.

Two properties hold across every row. **No content was deleted without a home**:
every fact removed from a slide is carried by a companion document that the slide or
the deck points to, and the rows below name which. **Every row was proven by
perturbation**: the limit or the claim was reintroduced, the named assertion was
confirmed to fail, and the file was restored and its digest compared. Nine
perturbations, nine caught.

### 44.1 Meeting the body-text limit without losing the substance

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 44.1.1 | Cut every content slide to the limit by **compressing to the executive register** — short noun phrases in table cells and bullets — rather than by splitting slides | (a) Split the dense slides into two each; (b) raise the limit; (c) move prose into diagram source, which the limit does not count | (a) would have pushed the deck from sixteen sections toward or past Rule 2's eighteen-section ceiling, trading one breach for another. (b) is not available: the limit is the rule. (c) would satisfy the counter while defeating its purpose — text hidden in a diagram is still text on the slide, and gaming a measure is not meeting it. Compression is what the rule actually asks for: the audience is non-technical leadership, and a forty-word cap is a readability instruction, not an arithmetic obstacle. | Terse cells carry less nuance than the sentences they replace. Each slide keeps a pointer to where the nuance lives, and row 36.1.4 records the two facts that left the deck entirely. |
| 44.1.2 | Reduce slide 14 from a four-row risk table with sentence-length cells to a **three-row table plus the existing callout**, and add a `slide-foot` pointing at `docs/security` | (a) Keep four rows with shorter cells; (b) drop the callout and keep the table intact | At 196 words this was the worst slide in the deck, and the reason was duplication: its first table row restated the breaking change the callout directly above it already announced. Removing the row removed a repetition rather than a risk — the breaking change is still on the slide, in the callout, where it reads more prominently. (b) would have kept the duplication and dropped the clearer of the two presentations. The footer names the directory holding the rotation runbook and the residual-risk register, so the detail is one hop away rather than absent. | The footnote abuts the table with tight leading, confirmed in the browser as legible, non-overlapping and inside the frame. It is a spacing observation, not a clipped element. |
| 44.1.3 | Drop the four bullets from slide 7 to three and let the **role table carry the model** | Keep four bullets and shorten the table | The table is both the slide's visual and its content, and three of the four bullets restated what its rows already said. What the table cannot say — that the role is read from the account record rather than from the browser, that anything unrecognised is denied, and that the single administrator is granted separately — is exactly what the three surviving bullets say. Those three are the security properties; the enumeration of roles is the table's job. | None identified. The four roles and their permissions are unchanged on the slide. |
| 44.1.4 | Accept that **two metrics leave the presentation**: the static-analysis count and the sixty-eight-entry change map | (a) Keep them and cut a cluster slide instead; (b) add a sixth metric card | Slide 2's card grid is five columns wide by the theme's own definition, so five cards is the shape available, and M-02 required two of them to carry the verified-versus-outstanding split that the deck previously did not report at all. Choosing between metrics was therefore forced, and accuracy about what is verified outranks a scan count for this audience. Neither fact is lost: the change-map total is reconciled in `TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` §2.8 and the static-analysis gate is a pipeline step with its own assertion. (b) would have broken the grid. | A reader of the deck alone no longer sees those two figures. Both are in the documents the deck's onboarding slide points to. |

### 44.2 Reporting a status that matches the evidence

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 44.2.1 | Report **fifteen proven by test and five carrying an operational step** on the title slide, in the metric grid and on the closing slide, instead of twenty closed | (a) Say twenty addressed and leave the split to the companion documents; (b) report twenty closed and footnote the exception | The deck said all twenty were closed while its own closing slide said rotation was outstanding, so the artefact was already internally inconsistent — the overstatement was not load-bearing, it was contradicted three slides later. (a) is closer to honest but still lets a reader conclude the work is finished, and the deck is read by people who will not open the matrix. (b) buries the part that requires a decision. The split is the actual outcome and is small enough to state in the headline. | A less triumphant headline. That is the correct impression: five findings genuinely need an operational step. |
| 44.2.2 | Retitle the closing slide **"Hardened and verifiable, not yet finished"** in place of "Secured, verifiable, ready to review" | (a) Keep the title; (b) "Secured, pending rotation" | "Secured" is a completion claim, and the slide carrying it also asked for a rotation that has not happened — the two could not both be true. (b) keeps the word whose meaning is the problem. The replacement says what is true: the controls are in place and asserted, and an operational step remains. | None identified. The slide's three bullets already said this; the heading now agrees with them. |
| 44.2.3 | Correct the traceability matrix's own prose from "**Six** findings are PARTIAL" to fifteen PASS and five PARTIAL, and name the five | (a) Change the table to match the prose; (b) leave it | The tallied rows are unambiguous — fifteen PASS, five PARTIAL, and the five classes the prose then lists correspond one-to-one to the five PARTIAL rows, so the table and the reasoning agreed and only the numeral was wrong. (a) would have invented a sixth partial finding to protect a typo. This is the failure mode the section exists to prevent, found inside the section itself: a summary sentence a reader would trust over the evidence beneath it. | The deck's headline numbers are now derived from this document, so the two must stay in agreement. Row 36.3.2 makes that a gate rather than a convention. |

### 44.3 Making the limits and the claim able to fail

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 44.3.1 | Assert Rule 2 **in the test suite**, not in a throwaway script — section count, per-slide body words, bullets, a non-text visual on every slide, permitted slide types, no emoji, Lucide-only iconography, exact dependency pins, no local asset, and deferred diagram re-run | (a) Measure once by hand at review time; (b) check only the word count that was breached | The presentation had drifted past a numeric limit with nothing watching, which is what an unasserted rule invites. (b) would leave the other nine constraints in the same position the word count was in. The assertions read the file the way the rule reads it — the heading excluded from the body count because the rule caps body text, and diagram source excluded because it renders as a picture — so the gate measures the property rather than a proxy for it. | Ten assertions couple the suite to one presentation file. That is the point: the file is a Rule 2 deliverable, and every edit to it is now measured. |
| 44.3.2 | Assert that the matrix's **prose tally matches its own rows**, and that the deck's status language matches the same tally | Fix the numeral and move on | Fixing the numeral leaves the next one to be found by a reader. The assertion parses both stated numbers out of the prose and compares each against the rows it summarises, so neither can be edited without the other. The same case asserts the deck names the outstanding operational step and carries no all-closed claim. | The assertion depends on the prose keeping a recognisable "N are PASS / N are PARTIAL" form. That form is the one a reader needs anyway. |

### 44.4 Deliberate non-changes from this round

| # | Non-change | Why it was left alone |
|---|-----------|----------------------|
| 44.4.1 | The theme, its custom properties and all ten component classes are untouched | The breach was body text, not styling. Every class the compressed slides use — `kpi-grid`, `icon-row`, `data-table`, `callout`, `slide-foot` — was already defined in the inline theme, so no new styling was authored. `slide-foot` was defined and previously unused; row 36.1.2 uses it as defined. |
| 44.4.2 | Sixteen sections, and the title, divider, content and closing types | Within Rule 2's twelve-to-eighteen bound before and after. Row 36.1.1 rejected splitting slides partly to keep it that way. |
| 44.4.3 | Both diagrams keep their full source | Diagram content is excluded from the body count because it renders as a picture, so neither diagram was under pressure. Compressing them would have cost clarity for no gain, and the browser confirmed both render as vector with every node and edge label present. |
| 44.4.4 | The inline theme still does not import the canonical stylesheet Rule 2 cites | The cited path does not exist in this repository. Recorded when the deck was written and unchanged here; the rule reproduces every value needed to author the theme inline. |
| 44.4.5 | The title slide's `.scope` was tightened rather than left over the limit, though the limit binds content slides only | Rule 2 caps content slides, and the reviewer's finding named only content slides. Adding the verified-versus-outstanding split pushed the title slide to forty-four words, and leaving it there would have invited an argument about whether the cap reaches it. Tightening to thirty-nine costs nothing and removes the question. |

## 79. Rationale relocated out of comments (third pass), and the decisions behind this round's changes

A third re-review found rationale still embedded in `setup.cfg`, in two schema modules, in
the payment service and in comments this round had itself introduced. The boundary applied
is the one §54.17 set and §65 tightened: a comment may state what the code does and what it
refuses; it may not name or compare an alternative approach, and it may not use a purpose
connective to assert that a behaviour is *the reason for* a construct. Every clause removed
is recorded below, so nothing is lost by its removal.

### 79.1 Rationale removed from comments

| # | Location | Reasoning removed from the comment |
|---|----------|-----------------------------------|
| 79.1.1 | `setup.cfg` — whole file | Every setting's justification was written in place. The file now states what each setting does and points here. The reasoning: one copy at the repository root serves both documented invocation directories *because* flake8 and pytest each search upwards while coverage.py does not, which is why the coverage floor sits under `[tool:pytest]` rather than in a `[coverage:report]` section; the per-file ignore is scoped to two path spellings *because* flake8 resolves a pattern against the invocation directory, so whichever of the two is in use the other matches nothing; strict asynchronous mode is declared *rather than* inherited so an unmarked coroutine is reported instead of silently skipped. |
| 79.1.2 | `backend/app/schema/filter.py` — `FORBIDDEN_TEXT_CHARACTERS` | A NUL is refused by the request contract *instead of by the driver*, so the refusal is a validation error naming the field rather than a driver error naming the statement. |
| 79.1.3 | `backend/app/schema/listing.py` — `FORBIDDEN_TEXT_CHARACTERS`, `ListingCreate`, `Listing`, `_require_finite_measurement`, `_check_listing_url` | Four clauses: the NUL refusal, as in 35.1.2; a magnitude beyond the column's type is refused *rather than stored*, and the count bound exists *for the same reason*; the measurement validator runs pre-conversion so an oversized whole number is refused *instead of raising* during conversion, where the error would name the driver rather than the field; and the host is read from the parsed URL *rather than from the raw text*, so an address carrying an allowlisted name outside its host does not match. |
| 79.1.4 | `backend/app/schema/subscription.py` — `SubscriptionCreated` | An order carrying no allowlisted approval target is refused *rather than returned*, so this response type cannot exist without one. |
| 79.1.5 | `backend/app/services/paypal_service.py` — `open_http_client`, `_approval_host_suffixes`, `_read_bounded`, `_api_error`, `PROVIDER_ORDER_FIELD` | The shared client is yielded only to a call on the loop that opened it *because* a connection pool belongs to the loop that created it; the approval suffixes are derived from validated configuration *rather than from a literal* so one allowlist governs both the certificate host and the approval target; the bounded read abandons an oversized body mid-transfer *instead of assembling it in memory and measuring afterwards*, which is the defect finding F22 named; and the provider order is recorded beside the request identifier so a provider case can be matched to a local request *without correlating on time*. |
| 79.1.6 | `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py` — module docstring, `_normalised_address`, `client_address` | The peer address is the innermost proxy *rather than the caller*, so counting against it puts every caller in one bucket and one abusive caller exhausts the limit for all of them; reading the chain without bounding it has the opposite failure, since the caller writes the header and takes a fresh counter per request; an entry that is not an IP address is refused so a value shaped to look like a hostname or a counter key cannot become one; and a truncated chain narrows the identity *rather than widening it*. |
| 79.1.7 | `backend/app/main.py` — `UNMATCHABLE_ROUTE_ERRORS`, `_matched_endpoint` | An unexpected failure propagates so the caller fails closed *rather than continuing with an unmatched route and the governance that route carries*. |
| 79.1.8 | `backend/app/services/email_service.py` — `ACCEPTED_STATUS`, `send_email` | Another 2xx is reported as a failure *rather than as a delivery* because reaching one means the request was answered by something other than the Mail Send endpoint — a redirect target, a proxy, or an error page returning 200 — so treating it as success would report a message as sent that the provider never queued. |
| 79.1.9 | `backend/app/services/zillow_service.py` — `REQUEST_ID_HEADER` | Sending the identifier makes a provider-side record joinable to the local one *rather than by matching timestamps*, which is a guess. |
| 79.1.10 | `backend/app/db/database.py` — `_pool_args` | A connection closed underneath the pool is replaced *rather than handed to a request handler*; and the pool arguments are withheld from a SQLite URL because that pool refuses `pool_timeout` outright and acts on neither `pool_recycle` nor `pool_pre_ping`, so returning them for every backend would stop both the local stack and the test suite. |
| 79.1.11 | `backend/app/api/endpoints/subscriptions.py` — `_REVOKED_STATUSES` | `REVOKING_EVENTS` is the map's keys so a notification added to the map is recognised by the route *without a second edit*, which is what stopped the two from drifting apart. |
| 79.1.12 | `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | Three clauses: `BACKEND_ENVIRONMENT` is required *rather than defaulted* because naming the five values it governs without also naming the environment leaves every one of them unenforced; the integration workflow is made callable so the deployment workflow gates on the complete gate set *rather than on a job of its own*; and that gate set is called *rather than duplicated*. |

### 79.2 Decisions behind this round's changes

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 79.2.1 | Derive `REVOKING_EVENTS` from `_REVOKED_STATUSES` and add `PAYMENT.CAPTURE.DECLINED` and `CHECKOUT.PAYMENT-APPROVAL.REVERSED` to that map | (a) Add the two notification names to the existing hand-maintained tuple and to the status map separately; (b) recognise the two but map them to the refunded status; (c) leave both unrecognised, on the reasoning that the provider also sends a capture notification for the same event | The two lists had already drifted: the tuple and the map each named four events and the map's keys were the authority, so a notification could be recognised with no outcome or given an outcome without being recognised. Deriving one from the other removes the class of defect rather than the instance. Both events report a settlement the provider withdrew before any money moved, so `cancelled` describes them and `refunded` would assert a refund that never happened. (c) is what the tree did, and it left an account holding an entitlement the provider had withdrawn | A notification added to the map is now live immediately, with no separate step to forget — and equally no separate step at which to notice. The parametrized lifecycle test covers every key of the map, so an addition is exercised by that test the moment it is made |
| 79.2.2 | Prefer the client's verb-named method in the non-streaming fallback of `_read_bounded`, before falling back to `request` | (a) Always call `request(method, url, ...)` in the fallback; (b) require every client to expose `stream` and give the payment suite a streaming double; (c) keep the buffered calls and measure afterwards, as the tree did | (a) was implemented first and broke five test doubles that define only `post(self, path, **kwargs)`. (b) would rewrite doubles across a 3,700-line suite for no security gain, and the doubles exist to assert what the service *sends*, which a streaming double makes harder to read. Preferring the verb method issues the same call the previous implementation issued, so the fallback is behaviour-compatible with the tree it replaces while the streaming path carries the new bound | A client exposing a verb method whose signature differs from `(url, **kwargs)` would break. Every client the service uses is either `httpx.AsyncClient` or a double in this repository, and both satisfy that shape |
| 79.2.3 | Default `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` to `0`, so the forwarded chain is not read unless a deployment says how many proxies it operates | (a) Default to `1`, since the deployment this repository provisions sits behind a load balancer; (b) read the rightmost entry whenever the header is present; (c) trust the leftmost entry, which is the convention some proxies document | (b) and (c) both let a caller influence its own counter key, which is worse than the defect being fixed: (c) lets a caller mint a fresh key per request and stop the limit applying at all. (a) would silently change behaviour for anyone running the service directly, where the header is caller-supplied — the same hole as (b). Zero preserves exactly today's behaviour, so the change is opt-in and a deployment states its own topology | A deployment that does not set the value keeps counting every caller behind its proxy under one key. That is the pre-existing behaviour rather than a regression, and it is called out in `.env.example` and in the README's deployment notes with both failure directions named |
| 79.2.4 | Refuse every SendGrid status other than `202`, and record the refusal | (a) Keep accepting the 2xx range; (b) accept `2xx` but record anything other than `202`; (c) raise rather than returning `False` | The Mail Send endpoint reports one status for a queued message. Any other success status means the request was answered by something else, so (a) reports a message as sent that the provider never queued. (b) keeps that outcome while adding noise. (c) would change the function's contract, which callers treat as a boolean and which the notification path depends on not raising | A provider change that introduced a second success status would be read as a failure. The status is asserted against a named module constant and the refusal is recorded with both the received and the expected status, so such a change is visible in the first record rather than after a silent non-delivery |
| 79.2.5 | Bound the database engine with `connect_timeout`, `pool_timeout`, `pool_recycle` and `pool_pre_ping`, all from validated settings, and apply them to a PostgreSQL URL only | (a) Hard-code the four values; (b) apply them to every backend; (c) add only `pool_pre_ping`, on the reasoning that a stale connection is the observed failure | (b) does not work: the pool a SQLite URL resolves to refuses `pool_timeout` with a `TypeError`, which would stop the local stack and the whole test suite. (a) leaves an operator unable to tune a bound their own network dictates. (c) leaves the two waits unbounded, and an unbounded wait on a database is the finding. The values are settings with bounded ranges so a misconfiguration is refused at startup | A `connect_timeout` set too low refuses requests during a slow but recoverable network event. The accepted range is 1 to 300 seconds and the default of 10 is the same order as the outbound HTTP timeout the service already applies |
