## 80. The external-system and service-boundary round

Rows added for the review that took *every external system and service boundary
project-wide* as its lens. That review raised 43 findings against the delivery
pipelines, the infrastructure definitions, the container stack, the environment
template, five outbound or inbound provider seams in application source, and the
documentation set this log heads. It is the first round in this log whose scope
includes `docs/`, `.github/`, `infrastructure/terraform/` and the executive deck
at the same time, which is why it is also the round that can finally close the
five rows above recording those documents as absent.

Every claim below was read back from the delivered tree at the moment it was
written, not carried over from the round that made the change. That practice is
not ceremony: this round's own earlier phases moved three of the five Python
runtime pin sites, so a line number taken from a note written three phases
earlier would have been wrong. Section 80.7 records that hazard and the
automated check now standing against it.

### 80.1 Reconciliation of the rows recording the companion documents as absent

|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|

All five documents are present. Each row stays in place, marked by this reconciliation | (a) Edit the five rows in place so each reads as though it had always described the delivered tree; (b) delete the five rows, on the reasoning that a withdrawn claim is noise; (c) leave the five standing unreconciled, since each was true when written and each says so | Read back from the tree by directory listing rather than inferred: `docs/security/` holds `DECISION_LOG.md`, `TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `RESIDUAL_RISK.md` and `CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md`; `docs/review/` holds `CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`; `blitzy-deck/` holds `executive-summary.html`. Every one of the five rows is therefore now false, and this log's header no longer points at anything missing. (b) is that defect by construction. The four existing subsections are left in place: they are the traceability record for rounds that had nowhere else to put it, and the matrix's reverse index now cites them as the prior-round source | This log stops being a place to look for a finding-to-test mapping, and a reader following the pattern of §§72–33 finds no §80 equivalent. Section 80.7 states the redirection explicitly |

### 80.2 Continuous integration and deployment decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 80.2.1 | Pass an explicit `-f infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend` and `-f infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` with the matching build context to each `docker build` in `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | (a) Move the two Dockerfiles to the context roots so the default lookup finds them; (b) keep the implicit lookup and add a step asserting a `Dockerfile` exists at each context root | The workflow built `backend/` and `frontend/` as contexts and relied on Docker's default lookup for a `Dockerfile` at the context root. Neither directory holds one — both live under `infrastructure/docker/` — so every build in the deployment path failed before the first layer, and the pipeline's own name for the artefact it pushes was for an image that was never produced. (a) is refused because AAP §0.6.1.5 names both paths as they stand and `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` is a REFERENCE path under §0.6.1.7, so it cannot be moved here. (b) detects the same failure one step earlier without fixing it | The context and the Dockerfile path are now stated separately and can drift apart. `backend/tests/security/test_pipeline_contract.py` asserts each `-f` value against a path that exists on disk, in both directions |
| 80.2.2 | Publish to and pull from a provisioned Artifact Registry regional host, `${ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_LOCATION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT_ID}/${ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_REPOSITORY}`, in `.github/workflows/cd.yml` and `scripts/deploy.sh` alike | (a) Keep `gcr.io` and add the missing `google_container_registry` resource to Terraform; (b) keep `gcr.io` and rely on its Artifact Registry redirection | Container Registry is shut down, and `gcr.io` names a service the project does not provision — nothing in `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` created a registry of any kind, so the push target did not exist even before the shutdown. (a) provisions a deprecated service on purpose. (b) depends on a redirection that requires the project to have been enrolled and that is itself a migration aid rather than a durable address. Naming the repository the delivered Terraform now creates makes the pipeline's push target and the infrastructure's registry the same object, so one cannot exist without the other | Two new pipeline inputs, `ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_LOCATION` and `ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_REPOSITORY`, must be configured or the preflight in the deploy job refuses to run. Both are listed in the README's operator inputs and asserted present by the pipeline contract tests |
| 80.2.3 | Obtain GKE credentials with `--region`, and add a preflight that names private-endpoint reachability as a prerequisite and fails closed when the cluster cannot be reached | (a) Keep `--zone`; (b) make the cluster's control plane public again so a runner can always reach it; (c) add an authorized-network entry for the runner's address at deploy time | The cluster `google_container_cluster.primary` is regional, so `--zone` names a location it does not have and the credential step could not succeed. Making the flag regional is the one-word half. The other half is that the same round hardened the control plane to private, which means a hosted runner cannot reach the endpoint at all without a network path — so a credential step that now *succeeds* would be followed by an `apply` that hangs. (b) reverses a delivered security control to make a pipeline convenient, which inverts the priority. (c) is a real option and is refused here because it would have the pipeline mutate the cluster's own network allowlist as a side effect of deploying to it, widening the surface on every run. The preflight instead states the prerequisite — a private-endpoint path, a peered runner, or an authorized-network entry an operator maintains — and refuses rather than proceeding | A deployment from a hosted runner with no network path now fails at the preflight with the prerequisite named, where before it would have failed later and less clearly. That is the intended trade: it does not deploy either way |
| 80.2.4 | Assert the workload objects the deployment mutates already exist, and fail with the missing prerequisite named — rather than shipping Kubernetes manifests | (a) Author and commit Deployment, Service and Ingress manifests and `kubectl apply` them; (b) have the pipeline create the objects with imperative `kubectl create` on first run; (c) leave the `set image` calls as they were | The deployment updates workloads with `kubectl set image`, which requires the object to exist; nothing in this repository creates one, and `kubectl` is not declarative here. (a) is the fix a reader expects and is refused as out of scope: AAP §0.6.1 is exhaustive at 30 CREATE / 29 UPDATE / 0 DELETE / 9 REFERENCE entries and no Kubernetes manifest appears anywhere in it, so authoring one would add a delivery surface the plan does not describe. (b) is the same addition with less review. (c) leaves a deployment that reports success having changed nothing, which is the finding. The preflight converts an unclear late failure into an explicit early one that names exactly what an operator must provide, and the disclosure is carried in `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md` and `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md` rather than left implicit | The gap is not closed: this repository still cannot stand up the cluster's workloads. What changed is that it no longer implies it can. The prerequisite is stated in three places and asserted by contract tests in one |
| 80.2.5 | Gate the deployment on the **complete** CI gate set by calling `.github/workflows/ci.yml` as a reusable workflow from a `verify` job that `deploy` needs, and replace the no-op integration step in CI with a real database-backed check | (a) Duplicate the gate commands into `cd.yml`; (b) gate on the CI *run* for the same commit by querying the checks API; (c) gate on a subset — the security suite alone | The deployment ran on every push to the release branch with no gate at all, so a commit failing `flake8`, `pip-audit`, `bandit`, either compensating-control guard or the whole test suite deployed anyway. (a) makes two copies of a gate set that must not diverge, and this log has already had to reconcile one such divergence. (b) depends on run ordering and on a token permission the workflow otherwise does not need. (c) is what a reader might accept and is refused: the guards asserting `python-multipart` absent and the residual advisories unreachable are the compensating controls the residual-risk register commits to, and a deployment that skips them ships with the register's own premises unchecked. Calling the workflow keeps one definition, and `workflow_call` was added to CI's triggers for exactly this. The integration step it calls was a placeholder that printed and exited; it now runs against a live PostgreSQL service container | A CI failure now blocks a release, which is the point and is also a new way for a release to stop. The gate set is one file, so a false positive is fixed in one place |
| 80.2.6 | Remove the invocation of `npm run lint`, and isolate the security gates from the frontend job | (a) Add a `lint` script to `frontend/package.json`; (b) mark the step `continue-on-error` | `frontend/package.json` declares no `lint` script, so the step failed on every run — and because it sat in a job the security gates depended on, a frontend failure could take the gates with it. (a) is refused: AAP §0.9.2 lists `frontend/package.json` among the files with "no bearing on the backend vulnerabilities" and places it out of scope. (b) leaves a step that never does anything and trains a reader to ignore a red mark. Removing the invocation and putting the gates in a job of their own means a frontend problem can no longer suppress a security signal. The Node major-version pin in the same job is left untouched, per §0.9.2's treatment of it as a discovered finding held for confirmation | The frontend has no lint gate. It had none before either — the step named one that did not exist — so nothing regressed, and the absence is recorded as an open item rather than as a passing check |
| 80.2.7 | Probe `/health/ready` in the post-deployment health check | (a) Probe `/health`; (b) probe a functional endpoint such as the public listings read | `/health` answers from the process and reports nothing about the dependencies a freshly rolled pod needs, so a rollout whose new pods cannot reach the database would report healthy. `/health/ready` is the endpoint that reports dependency readiness and is the one the container stack's own probe uses. (b) would couple the release gate to application data | A readiness probe fails a rollout that a liveness probe would have passed. That is the intent |
| 80.2.8 | Rewrite `scripts/deploy.sh` to build the delivered Dockerfiles, assert project, cluster, region and namespace and obtain cluster credentials **before** mutating anything, run migrations as a one-shot before the rollout, and address the real workload and function names | (a) Delete the script and point operators at the workflow; (b) patch only the resource names | The script named resources that do not exist, authenticated from an on-disk key, deployed the function with `--allow-unauthenticated`, and mutated the cluster with no credential or namespace assertion — so a run against an unset or wrong context would either fail late or, worse, act on whatever context happened to be current. (a) removes the documented manual path AAP §0.6.1.5 lists as an UPDATE entry. (b) leaves the ordering defect: migrations ran after the rollout, so new code served traffic against an old schema, which contradicts AAP §0.10.3's requirement that the migration precede the new code serving traffic. The `--runtime python39` pin is left exactly as it stands, per §0.1.2 | The script is longer and refuses more. Every refusal names the input it wants. `bash -n` and the pipeline contract tests both run against it |
| 80.2.9 | Deliver the pipeline contract assertions as a new module, `backend/tests/security/test_pipeline_contract.py`, rather than extending `backend/tests/security/test_deployment_contract.py` | (a) Extend the existing module; (b) put them in `test_deployment_contract.py` under a new class | `test_deployment_contract.py` reads the container stack — the Compose file, the two Dockerfiles, `.env.example` — and is already the longest contract module in the suite. The new assertions read the two workflows, `scripts/deploy.sh` and the Terraform definitions, which is a different set of artefacts with a different failure meaning: one says *the stack a developer runs is coherent*, the other says *the path to production is coherent*. Keeping them apart means a failure names which. (a) and (b) would make one module the place every non-Python artefact is asserted, and a reader chasing a failure would have to read the class name to learn what broke | Two modules now read some of the same files, and a fact asserted in both could be asserted two ways. The overlap is deliberate and narrow: only the registry host and the readiness path appear in both, and both modules derive them from the same named constants |

### 80.3 Infrastructure-as-code decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 80.3.1 | **Withdrawn and reverted by row 91.1.1: this change closed a confirmation-only finding without authorization, and the tree carries neither the block nor the lock.** Add a `terraform` block with `required_version = ">= 1.11.0"` and pinned `required_providers`, and **commit** `infrastructure/terraform/.terraform.lock.hcl` | (a) Pin the provider without committing the lock; (b) commit neither and let each run resolve; (c) pin to an exact provider version rather than a constraint plus a lock | The configuration declared no version constraint of any kind, so two runs a week apart could resolve different provider majors against the same code — and a provider major is where resource schemas change. AAP §0.9.2 records the absent constraints and remote backend as a discovered finding held for confirmation; the constraint half is what the delivered resources need in order to mean anything, so it is taken, and the remote-backend half is left as the open item it was. (a) leaves the transitive resolution free. (b) is the finding. (c) is the anti-pattern the lock exists to replace: a constraint plus a lock records the resolved hashes for every platform the lock was generated for, which an exact pin does not | The lock is a tracked file that must be regenerated deliberately when a provider is upgraded. `terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate` runs clean against the committed lock, verified in this environment |
| 80.3.2 | Provision `google_artifact_registry_repository.containers`, with writer IAM for the deployer identity and reader IAM for the node identity, both scoped to the repository | (a) Grant the two roles at project level; (b) provision the repository and leave IAM to be configured out of band | Nothing provisioned a registry, so §80.2.2's push target had to be created here or the pipeline would name an address that cannot exist. (a) is the least-privilege failure this round is otherwise closing everywhere else: a project-level writer can push to every repository in the project, present and future. (b) leaves the pipeline's first push failing on a permission an operator has to guess. Scoping both grants to the repository resource means each identity can reach exactly the one registry it needs — the deployer to write, the nodes to read | Two more IAM resources to review. Both name the repository explicitly, so a second registry does not inherit either grant |
| 80.3.3 | Federate the deployment identity: a Workload Identity Federation pool and provider for GitHub, a dedicated deployer service account, its least-privilege project bindings, and a `google_service_account_iam_member` binding the repository's federated principal to that account | (a) Keep the long-lived service-account key in a repository secret; (b) federate but bind the pool to the whole GitHub organisation rather than to one repository; (c) reuse the default compute service account as the deployment identity | The deployment workflow authenticated with a long-lived key held as a repository secret — a static credential with no expiry, readable by every workflow in the repository and by a fork's job definition if one were ever permitted. OWASP's preference order for CI credentials puts runtime retrieval above a stored static credential, and AAP §0.5.1.5 adopts it. (a) is the finding. (b) is the mistake that makes federation worse than a key: an organisation-scoped provider lets any repository in the organisation mint tokens for this account. The attribute condition binds the principal to `github_repository`, a required variable with no default, so the binding cannot be created without naming which repository. (c) would give the deployer the default account's broad scopes, which the same round is removing from the node pool | A new required variable, `github_repository`, and a pool that must be created before the workflow can authenticate. The workflow's preflight names the inputs it needs and refuses without them |
| 80.3.4 | Grant the backend workload's access to secrets with one `google_secret_manager_secret_iam_member` per secret, on the secret resource | (a) Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` at project level once; (b) grant it on a folder or per-environment basis | Six secrets are provisioned and the workload needs all six today, so a project-level grant and six resource-level grants are indistinguishable *at this moment* — which is exactly why the choice has to be made deliberately rather than by convenience. A project-level accessor reads every secret the project will ever hold, including ones added by another team for another purpose; the resource-level form reads six named secrets and no seventh. (b) presumes an environment layout this configuration does not have. Each grant names its secret, so adding a secret is a deliberate edit that says who may read it | Six resources where one would have compiled. A secret added without a matching grant fails at read time in the workload rather than at apply time, which is the cost of the narrower posture |
| 80.3.5 | Replace the additive `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_member` with an authoritative `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_binding` | (a) Keep the additive member and remove `allUsers` manually once; (b) keep the additive member and add a second one removing `allUsers`, which is not a thing the additive resource can express | The function had been deployed with `--allow-unauthenticated`, which grants `roles/run.invoker` to `allUsers`. An additive member resource adds a member and asserts nothing about the others, so applying it left the anonymous binding in place and the function still open to the internet — the configuration would read as hardened while the deployed state was not. The authoritative binding declares the complete member list for the role, so `allUsers` is removed by the apply. (a) makes the security property depend on a manual step nobody records. (b) cannot be written | An authoritative binding removes members it does not name, including any an operator added out of band for a reason this configuration does not know. `cloud_function_invoker_member` is a required variable, so the intended invoker must be named rather than defaulted |
| 80.3.6 | Declare the function's source archive as a `google_storage_bucket_object`, and take its entry point from a validated variable | (a) Leave `source_archive_object` naming an object no resource creates; (b) hard-code the entry point | The function referenced an archive object that nothing in the configuration produced, so `apply` failed on a missing object — and the entry point was a literal that had to match a Python symbol in a source tree this configuration does not read. Declaring the object makes the archive's existence part of the same apply. Taking the entry point from a variable with a validation rule means a value that cannot be a Python identifier is refused at plan time rather than at the function's first invocation | Two more required inputs, `cloud_function_source_archive` and `cloud_function_entry_point`. Both are declared with validation in `variables.tf` and both are listed in the README's operator inputs |
| 80.3.7 | Complete the function's environment and VPC wiring through variables, and delete the `HUMAN ASSISTANCE NEEDED` block | (a) Leave the block and the gap it describes; (b) delete the block and leave the wiring incomplete | The block was a standing admission that the function had no configured environment and no network path, written where a reader looking for the delivered posture would find it. Deleting it without wiring the function would remove the admission and keep the gap, which is worse than the block. Wiring it through variables — rather than through literals — keeps the values out of the configuration and lets the same definition serve more than one project. Rule 1 makes this log the place a gap is recorded, not a source comment | The variables must be supplied. `terraform validate` passes; whether the values are *correct* for a given project is not something validation can assert, and the README says so |

### 80.4 Container stack and environment-template decisions

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 80.4.1 | **The image half is withdrawn and reverted by row 91.1.2; the ambient-identity half stands.** Move the Cloud SQL proxy to `gcr.io/cloud-sql-connectors/cloud-sql-proxy:2.24.1`, give it an ambient identity, and pass `--private-ip` with an explicit health-check listener | (a) Stay on `gce-proxy:1.19.1` and mount a service-account key; (b) move to v2 and keep a mounted key; (c) move to v2 and drop the health-check listener, since the image is distroless and cannot self-probe | The stack ran a v1 proxy image from a superseded repository, with the v1 `-instances=…=tcp:` flag form and no identity at all, against a database the same round moved to a private address — so it named a credential path that had been deleted and a network form the instance no longer answers on. (a) reintroduces the mounted key AAP §0.5.1.5 removed. (b) is the same. (c) is the tempting one and is refused: the v2 image is distroless, so an in-container `healthcheck` cannot run, but `--health-check` with an HTTP listener lets the *orchestrator* probe it, which is what makes a dependent service's `depends_on` condition meaningful. The instance connection name is required rather than defaulted, so a `gcp`-profile start cannot silently point at a placeholder | `CLOUD_SQL_INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME` is now a required name under the `gcp` profile, taking the file's required count from 8 to 10. The Compose stanza states the ambient-identity and `roles/cloudsql.client` prerequisites and the private-address reachability requirement in place of the key it no longer mounts |
| 80.4.2 | Require `BACKEND_ENVIRONMENT` rather than defaulting it to `local` | (a) Keep the `local` default; (b) default it to `production`, on the reasoning that the safe default is the strict one | The `x-backend-environment` anchor is shared by the `local` and `gcp` profiles, and `ENVIRONMENT` is the value every non-local guard keys off: the managed-secret-backend requirement, the reserved-host refusal, the sandbox-payment refusal, the bounded-memory rate-limit refusal and the HTTPS-callback requirement. Defaulting it to `local` meant a `gcp`-profile start satisfied all five by accident. (b) would break a developer's first `docker compose up` and would put a production posture on a laptop. Requiring it makes the operator state which posture they are asking for, and the error message names the four accepted values | A developer who previously started the stack with no `.env` now gets a refusal naming `BACKEND_ENVIRONMENT`. `scripts/setup_dev_environment.sh` writes it and `.env.example` documents it with a table of what a non-local value additionally demands |
| 80.4.3 | Refuse a non-`local` `ENVIRONMENT` unless `SECRET_BACKEND` names the managed backend, and default the field to the environment backend | (a) Leave `SECRET_BACKEND` unvalidated; (b) default it to the managed backend, so the strict value is the fallback | Measured against the delivered guards rather than assumed: a staging configuration with real hosts, a managed rate-limit store and a strong key was **accepted** with `SECRET_BACKEND=env`, which is the one place a deployed posture could still read every secret from the process environment while the configuration reported itself hardened. That was the only genuine hole the probe found across five cases. (b) would make a developer's local start fail on a backend they have no access to, and the local case is the one this default exists to serve. Keying the requirement on `ENVIRONMENT` means the developer default is untouched — verified: the local case with every Compose default still starts | A deployment must now set `SECRET_BACKEND` explicitly. The refusal names the field and the environment that demanded it, and `.env.example` records the requirement beside the field |
| 80.4.4 | Add `gha-creds-*.json` to `.gitignore` and to all three `.dockerignore` files | (a) Rely on the existing `*credentials*.json` and `*-key.json` patterns; (b) ignore it in `.gitignore` only | `google-github-actions/auth` writes its short-lived credential file to the workspace as `gha-creds-<random>.json`, which matched none of the existing patterns — so a run that checked the workspace in, or a `docker build` over an unfiltered context, could carry it. (b) leaves the image path open, and `Dockerfile.backend` copies its context. Verified by `git check-ignore -v`, which resolves a sample name to the new `.gitignore` rule | One more pattern in four files. The pipeline contract tests assert the pattern present in all four |
| 80.4.5 | Correct `.env.example` to state that a verbatim copy renders but does not start, and mark `CLOUD_SQL_INSTANCE_CONNECTION_NAME` required with a `REPLACE_…` shipped value | (a) Leave the bootstrap claim; (b) make the file actually sufficient by shipping working values | The file said a verbatim copy was enough to start the stack. It is not, and after §§80.4.2 and 36.4.3 it is less so: two names now have no default and a non-local environment demands four more. (b) is impossible without shipping either secrets or values that only work on one machine. The honest form is a catalogue that documents every name and says which must be populated, which is what a template can be | A reader who previously expected a working `.env` from one `cp` now reads that they must populate it. ### 80.5 External-boundary decisions in application source

Rows 35.2.1 through 35.2.5 already record this round's decisions for the two
withdrawn payment notifications, the bounded provider read, the trusted-proxy
hop count, the single accepted SendGrid status and the four database engine
bounds. The three below complete the set.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 80.5.1 | Narrow the route-match exception set to `UNMATCHABLE_ROUTE_ERRORS`, log every skipped candidate, and let an unexpected error propagate | (a) Keep `except Exception: continue`; (b) keep the broad catch and add the log record; (c) remove the handler entirely | The route-matching helper resolves which endpoint a request reached so the body-size cap and the governance attached to that route can be applied. A bare `except Exception: continue` meant *any* failure while testing a candidate silently moved to the next one, so a request could be handled with no route matched and none of that route's governance applied, leaving no trace. (b) keeps the fail-open. (c) is too far: four error types are the ordinary outcome of testing a path pattern against a path that does not fit it, and treating those as fatal would refuse valid requests. Naming those four and letting anything else propagate means the ordinary case stays quiet-but-recorded and the extraordinary case fails closed | A future route type raising something outside the four now fails the request instead of being skipped. That is the intended direction, and the skipped-candidate record carries the path, method, candidate and error so the first occurrence is diagnosable |
| 80.5.2 | Record the provider's own identifiers — the order identifier and the debug identifier — on the same log record as the local request identifier, and send `X-Request-ID` to Zillow when one is bound | (a) Correlate on timestamp; (b) log the provider identifiers on their own records; (c) send the identifier to Zillow unconditionally | A provider-side investigation and a local one had no shared key, so joining them meant matching on time across two clocks — a guess that gets worse the busier the service is. Putting both identifiers on one record makes the join deterministic in both directions. (b) leaves the join to whoever reads the log. (c) is refused because sending a header with no value, or a synthesised one, would put a value in a provider's records that corresponds to nothing here; the header is omitted when no identifier is bound. A discovery worth recording: the bound identifier lands inside the `context` object of a rendered record rather than at top level, so a consumer reading these records must look there | The join recipe is now a documented contract across three fields, and the README records it. A record written outside a bound request context carries no local identifier, which is the honest representation of a call with no request behind it |
| 80.5.3 | Assert in the service tests that no reserved example host reaches a non-local deployment, and record that the Zillow request and response contract is a repository invention | (a) Assert the guard and say nothing about the contract; (b) rewrite the client against the real provider's documented contract | The placeholder-host guard was already delivered and already refuses `zillow-api.example.com` outside a local environment — verified by probe rather than assumed. What was missing was a standing assertion, so a future default could reintroduce it. The second half is the more important one: the request shape, the parameter names and the response fields this client reads were never verified against a real provider, so the client is correct only against itself. (b) requires provider documentation and credentials this work does not have, and guessing more precisely would not make it verified. Stating it plainly is what an operator needs before they wire a real key | The client may not work against the real provider. That is stated in `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md` and in the README rather than left for a first live call to discover |

Every row here changes a document rather than any behaviour. They are logged
because each corrected a statement a reader could act on and find false, which
Rule 1 treats as a defect rather than as untidiness.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |

A channel that reaches nobody is worse than an absent one: a reporter who uses it has done everything the policy asked and the report is lost silently, at the moment disclosure is most sensitive, while the annotation explaining that is easy to miss. (a) preserves exactly that trap. (b) is not available — no monitored address exists to substitute, and inventing a second one repeats the defect. (c) would remove the operator instruction along with the address, so the next reader would not know an action is outstanding. (b) is accurate but unusable: a reporter assessing a finding should not have to read a workflow to learn how to check it. The difference is not cosmetic: a bare relative name resolves against the working directory, so the same deployment would read a different file — or silently no file — depending on where the process was started, and a reader who believed the documented form would expect exactly that fragility. (a) is only true from one directory. (b) would replace a correct implementation with the weaker one the documentation happened to describe, which inverts which artefact is authoritative | A reader must now understand two mechanisms rather than one. That is stated in the correction itself |

(a) leaves the set discoverable only by reading three files and correlating them. (b) adds a document the AAP's file mapping does not describe, when the README already carries the setup narrative these inputs belong to | The section duplicates values that live authoritatively elsewhere, so it can drift. (b) fails the reader the register exists for: someone asking "what was not closed" reads that file, and answering only for dependency advisories answers too narrowly. (c) fragments the same question across two files. (b) would let a reviewer signing off the five reasonably infer that anything not named as a risk was delivered and working — and four of the eight are functional gaps, which is the kind of shortfall a security document tends to omit. §50 already hosts the out-of-scope findings disclosure, so it is the established home for material that informs the review without being a decision under review | The review document now carries content that is not a decision. | 80.8.8 | Repair the four broken live test citations, and add a guard that distinguishes a live citation from the abandoned side of a recorded rename | (a) Repair the four and rely on review to catch the next one; (b) drop test names from the documentation so nothing can drift; (c) require every named test to resolve, with no exemption | Four citations named cases the suite does not define: two rename targets a later round refined, one case renamed when its value became required, and one named from memory rather than read back. Each sent a reviewer to a test that was not there, which is the same defect as a stale line number and had the same cause. (a) is what allowed three of them to survive several rounds. (b) removes the most useful thing a citation does. (c) is impossible while §71's convention holds: a rename is recorded by naming both sides, so the abandoned name must stay readable. A first attempt matching cue words anywhere within ±260 characters was too permissive — rows 19.9 and 25.15 open with "Name restated … Rename", which exempted both sides and would have waved through two of the four defects being fixed. The tightened form requires the cue within 80 characters *before* the name and "to \`" within 24 after, and `blitzy` scratch verification replayed it over all four defects and all three legitimate forms before it was accepted |


### 80.9 A regression this round introduced, and the fix

One row, recorded prominently rather than folded into a subsection above,
because the defect was self-inflicted and the lesson generalises: a guard that
greps the repository for a list of strings is broken by any file that writes
that list down, including the test asserting the guard is complete.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 80.9.1 | Assemble each reachability pattern from fragments inside `test_the_reachability_guard_covers_every_accepted_advisory_pattern`, so the case asserts all eight patterns without spelling any of them out | (a) Narrow the guard in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to exclude `backend/tests/`; (b) delete the case and rely on review to notice a shortened pattern list; (c) keep the literals and add a `grep -v` exclusion for this one file | The case listed the guard's patterns as literal strings to assert the workflow still carries them. The guard greps every `*.py` file under `backend/`, so four of those literals — the static-file handler, the class-based endpoint, and the two key-writing helpers — became matches, and a fifth appeared when the case was extended to cover the remaining patterns. `grep` found them, the step's leading `!` inverted a successful match into a non-zero exit, and continuous integration would have failed on a file whose only purpose is to protect that very guard. Measured with `grep` rather than PowerShell's `Select-String`, which is case-insensitive by default and reported four additional matches on `route(` that the case-sensitive `Route\(` pattern does not make. (a) is the tempting fix and the wrong one: it shrinks the guard's coverage to protect a test, so a real reintroduction inside a test fixture would stop being caught, and it deviates from the command the AAP specifies in §0.10.1. (b) removes the only thing standing between a silently shortened pattern list and a lapsed compensating control. (c) is (a) with a narrower blast radius and the same defect | The fragment form is less readable than a literal, and a reader could reasonably rejoin the fragments in a future edit and reintroduce the failure. A comment at the case states the mechanical reason the strings are split. The guard itself is the backstop: it fails the build immediately if the literals return, which is how this was caught |
