## 81. Performance and resource findings: bounded work, declared workloads, and one withdrawn position

Rows added by a static review of the whole delivered tree for performance and
resource behaviour. It ran no request and executed no test, and asked instead
whether the delivered code and configuration *guarantee* bounded work. It raised
fourteen findings: one Critical, eleven Major and two Minor. They fall into six
behavioural groups and one documentation group, and that last group is why this
section is not only about resources — the finding it carries is a defect against
Rule 1 in this very file.

The review's finding numbers are per-review, so the rows below cite behaviour.
For the reader who holds that review in hand, the mapping is: an authorization
dependency that blocked the event loop and unindexed predicates beneath it
(P-01, P-02); an ingestion pass that read every stored postal code into one
provider request and then issued one query per returned record (P-03); three
in-process lifecycles with no finite bound — the database engine, the log
listener's shutdown, and the provider response reader (P-04, P-05, P-06); a
rate-limit store the application requires and nothing provisioned (P-07); a
delivery pipeline that built from contexts holding no Dockerfile, addressed a
regional private cluster by zone from a public runner, ran a migration pod with
no resource envelope and no deadline, mutated workloads no file declared, and
wrapped unbounded remote calls in finite-looking loops (P-08 to P-12);
verification executed twice per push (P-13); and row 15.1 of this log, which
recorded a position the tree had since reversed without marking it (P-14).

Two properties of this round are worth stating before the rows, because they
bound what follows. **No security control changed.** Every fix is about how much
work is admitted, how long it may run, or where a declaration lives; no refusal
was relaxed, no role boundary moved, no claim stopped being required, and no
credential handling changed. And **no dependency was added, removed or moved** —
the manifests are byte-identical to the round before, so nothing in this section
alters the audited dependency set or the seven accepted advisories.

### Work off the event loop, and the predicates beneath it

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.1 | Make the role dependency `require_role` returns a **synchronous** function, so the framework dispatches it to a worker thread | (a) Keep it `async def` and wrap the lookup in `run_in_threadpool`; (b) keep it `async def` and wrap the lookup in `asyncio.to_thread`, as row 1.10 does for the provider fetch; (c) convert the entitlement read to an asynchronous driver | The inner `dependency` was the only `async def` in `backend/app/core/authorization.py`, and it called `effective_role`, which issues a synchronous ORM read of the subscription rows. Every guarded route therefore blocked the loop for the duration of that query — including the two routes that are themselves `async def`. A synchronous dependency is offloaded by the framework itself, so one keyword removes the block with no wrapper, no second code path and no change to the session's strictly sequential use. (a) and (b) leave the coroutine in place and add a construct at every call site the loop then awaits, which is the same outcome reached less directly; row 1.10 uses `to_thread` because that call site *is* a coroutine the ingestion task owns, and this one need not be. (c) is an asynchronous SQLAlchemy migration across every endpoint, which no finding asks for and which SQLAlchemy 1.4 under the frozen pin does not make cheap. Deny-by-default, the three refusal decisions, the audit records and the returned row are unchanged | A synchronous dependency occupies a worker thread for the length of its query, so the thread pool rather than the loop is now the contended resource; the query is bounded by row 35.10's statement timeout and the indexes of row 35.2. The first test written for this was **not** a gate — it compared the lookup's thread against `threading.main_thread()`, and the framework's test client drives the loop on a portal thread, so it passed against the defect. It was rewritten to capture the loop thread from a coroutine dependency declared ahead of the guard and to require the lookup threads to be disjoint from it, and only then did reverting the fix fail it |
| 81.2 | Declare six **non-unique** indexes whose columns are read from the predicates that exist, in the ORM metadata **and** in a migration revision | (a) Index each foreign-key column alone; (b) index only the entitlement read the review named; (c) declare them in the ORM alone and let the schema follow at some later point; (d) add a covering index per query with included columns | PostgreSQL does not index a foreign-key column on declaration, so every child read and every composite predicate in this schema was a sequential scan. The shapes are therefore taken from the statements: `filters(user_id, id)` for the owner's page, `zip_codes(filter_id)` and `criteria(filter_id)` for the children of a page, `subscriptions(user_id, status, end_date)` for the entitlement decision, `subscriptions(user_id, plan_id, status)` for the duplicate-plan check, and `listings(zillow_url)` for the ingestion reconciliation read. (a) would index less than the composite predicates use and would leave the entitlement read scanning. (b) leaves the other four. (c) leaves the deployed database without the index the code depends on, which is the class of drift migrations exist to prevent. (d) is tuning beyond the finding. Declaring in both places is what lets one test assert that the revision and the ORM describe the same set, so neither can gain an index the other does not | Six indexes are six write-time costs on tables the ingestion pass writes. The `listings` entry is deliberately non-unique and adds **no** uniqueness, which upholds rows 28.1 and 30.10: two rows may still carry one provider address, and row 30.11's earliest-row ordering is what keeps reconciliation deterministic. Measured on PostgreSQL 13 rather than asserted: `pg_indexes` reports exactly the six, all non-unique, and the only unique index on `listings` remains its primary key |
| 81.3 | Deliver them as a **new** revision `0003`, additive and independently reversible, rather than amending revision `0001` | (a) Add the indexes to `0001`, which is where the tables are created; (b) create them from application code at startup; (c) create them by hand per environment | `0001` and `0002` are applied revisions: any database that has run them will never run them again, so an amendment to `0001` reaches a fresh database and never an existing one — the drift is silent and permanent. A third revision reaches every database exactly once. It follows the conventions the existing two set: a docstring stating the contract, presence guards that make re-application a no-op, an offline `--sql` branch that emits the statements unconditionally, and a downgrade that drops only the six names it created. (b) puts DDL on a request-serving path and reintroduces the import-time schema creation this work removed. (c) leaves no record and nothing to assert against | The reversal count changed: three revisions now reverse rather than two, which row 35.39 corrects in the two documents that state it. Reversibility was measured on PostgreSQL 13 — `upgrade head` gives six indexes, `downgrade -1` gives none, `upgrade head` gives six again, with the administrator count and the added columns untouched throughout |
| 81.4 | **Narrow** the migration gate's "this revision creates no table" assertion rather than drop it | (a) Delete the assertion, since an index on `listings` makes its literal form unsatisfiable; (b) exclude `0003` from the gate; (c) rename the tables in the assertion | The assertion read `"listings" not in emitted`, which was a proxy for the property it meant: that a schema revision creates and drops no table. An index statement names its table, so the proxy broke while the property held. It was re-aimed at the property — `"CREATE TABLE listings"` must not appear in the emitted upgrade and `"DROP TABLE listings"` not in the reversal — and an ordering assertion was added so the index drop precedes the webhook-table drop. (a) and (b) both remove coverage to accommodate a change the coverage was not written about, which is what row 30.6 refuses in the same situation | The assertion is now specific to the statement rather than the table name, so a revision that dropped a *column* of `listings` would not fail it. The revision cases assert the column set separately |

### The ingestion pass

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.5 | Bound the postal-code read **in the statement** — `order_by(code).limit(INGESTION_MAX_ZIP_CODES)` — and emit one record per pass when the cap is reached | (a) Read everything and slice the list in Python; (b) count first and refuse the pass above a threshold; (c) leave it unbounded and bound only the provider request | The read was `distinct().all()` across every saved filter's codes, so one pass materialised the whole corpus of tracked codes regardless of size. (a) transfers every row before discarding most of them, which is the resource cost the finding names. (b) turns a large corpus into no ingestion at all. (c) leaves the read unbounded, and it is the read that grows with the product. Ordering makes the retained set deterministic rather than whatever the database returns first, and the cap record names the setting, the ceiling and the count, so an operator can tell a truncated pass from a complete one | A corpus above the ceiling is ingested for its first *N* codes in code order and never for the rest; the ceiling is configuration, and each pass that reaches it says so exactly once, so the condition is visible on every pass rather than only the first. `INGESTION_MAX_ZIP_CODES` defaults to 1000 against a validated ceiling of 100000 |
| 81.6 | Send the provider **one request per chunk** of at most `INGESTION_ZIP_CODE_CHUNK` codes, and refuse an oversized chunk **at the service boundary before a request is assembled** | (a) Chunk in the task and trust every caller to respect the size; (b) enforce the size inside the provider client by truncating the list; (c) keep one request and bound only the response | The task is not the only possible caller of `fetch_listings`, so the size is enforced where the request is built as well as where it is split — the refusal is recorded with the count and the cap, and no request leaves. (b) would silently drop codes a caller asked about, which is worse than refusing. (c) was already true and insufficient: the response was bounded by `MAX_PROVIDER_LISTINGS` and its streamed body cap, and the *request* was what grew without limit | Two places now know the chunk size, and both read it from the same setting rather than a literal. A caller passing more than the cap gets no listings and one refusal record; the task never does, because it chunks first |
| 81.7 | Replace the per-record identity query with **one batched read per chunk** that keeps the earliest row per address | (a) Keep one `first()` per record and rely on the new index; (b) read every candidate row and reconcile each; (c) hold a process-level cache of identities across passes | The pass issued one query and one savepoint per returned record, so a full provider response cost up to a thousand round trips. One `IN` read per chunk, ordered by primary key and keeping the first row per value, reproduces exactly what the per-record `first()` returned — which matters because row 30.11 made that earliest-row rule the reconciliation contract, and an index alone would have made a thousand queries fast rather than making them one. (b) changes what the task does. (c) makes correctness depend on process lifetime. Savepoint-per-record failure isolation, ownership scoping and redaction are unchanged | The batched read holds one chunk's candidate rows in memory; the chunk size bounds it. A row inserted by another process between the read and the write is handled as before, by the savepoint around the individual write |
| 81.8 | Have the record writer **return the row it wrote** instead of a boolean | (a) Re-query inside the loop when an address repeats within a chunk; (b) de-duplicate the chunk's records before writing; (c) accept a second row for a repeated address | The batched read is taken once per chunk, so a chunk containing the same address twice would not see the row its own first record created. Returning the row lets the second record refresh it, which is what the per-record query did. (a) reintroduces the query the change removes. (b) discards a later record that may carry newer values, where the previous behaviour kept them. (c) would grow the corpus on repetition | The writer's signature changed from `bool` to `Optional[Listing]`; no test and no other module called it directly. A repeated address within one chunk stores one row carrying the later values, which a case asserts explicitly |
| 81.9 | Express both bounds as **validated settings with ceilings**, and derive every expected count in the tests from them | (a) Module constants; (b) literals at the call sites; (c) one setting for both | A deployment tunes ingestion volume without a code change, and a validator refuses a zero, a negative or an absurd value at startup rather than at the first pass. Deriving the test expectations from the settings means a changed default cannot leave a stale literal asserting the old one | Two more settings to carry through the three places a setting must appear — the test baseline, the Compose backend environment and `.env.example`. Both have code defaults, so both are declared with the defaulting operator in Compose, which is what the deployment-contract case requires |

### Bounded in-process lifecycles: the engine, the log listener and the provider reader

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.10 | Give the engine **three** bounds — a connect timeout, a server-side statement timeout and a socket-level `tcp_user_timeout` — rather than the connect timeout the finding asked for | (a) A connect timeout alone; (b) connect and statement timeouts only; (c) a pool timeout instead; (d) a timeout wrapper around the readiness handler | The engine passed only `-c timezone=utc`, and libpq waits indefinitely when no connect timeout is given, so the readiness handler could block a worker thread past the point where the container probe had abandoned its request. The third bound is not decoration and was the one measured decision here: `statement_timeout` cancels on the **server**, and a cancellation cannot reach a client whose packets are no longer acknowledged, so it does not bound a caller already holding a pooled connection to a host that has stopped answering. `tcp_user_timeout` does. It was verified against the deployment's own driver before being adopted — psycopg2 2.9.12 on libpq 18.0.3 accepts the parameter, and the session reports `statement_timeout` as `3s` and `timezone` as `UTC`. (c) bounds waiting for a connection from the pool, not waiting on the connection. (d) bounds one handler and leaves every other query unbounded | A platform without the socket option ignores it; the deployment runtime is Linux. Three settings must agree, and their relationship is a ladder rather than three independent numbers, which row 35.11 records. A long legitimate statement is now cancelled at the ceiling — no statement in this service approaches it |
| 81.11 | Order the bounds as a documented ladder — statement 3s < socket 4s < probe 5s — and render the session options from a **template function** rather than a constant string | (a) Independent defaults with no stated relationship; (b) derive each from the probe timeout at import; (c) keep the constant and interpolate at the call site | The ladder is the property that makes the container probe meaningful: the innermost bound must expire first, or the probe abandons its request while the query is still running and the operator learns nothing. Stating it in `.env.example` and in the Compose environment puts it where someone changing one number will see the other two. A function that renders the options from the configured value keeps one source for the string and lets a case assert the rendering rather than a literal. (b) couples application configuration to a container health-check value the application cannot read. (c) leaves the interpolation duplicated at each use | Three numbers must stay ordered, and nothing enforces the ordering at startup beyond the individual ceilings; a case asserts every bound is below the probe timeout, so the ladder fails a test rather than a deployment |
| 81.12 | Leave the readiness handler **synchronous** | (a) Make it `async def` and await an asynchronous probe; (b) run the probe in a background task and answer from a cached result | It is synchronous today, so the framework already runs it on a worker thread, and with row 35.10's three bounds every wait it can make is finite. (a) would put a blocking driver call back on the loop, which is the defect of row 35.1 in a different place. (b) answers readiness from a stale observation, which is what readiness must not do | The handler occupies a worker thread while the database is unreachable, for at most the socket bound. Its docstring states that, and a case asserts the handler is not a coroutine |
| 81.13 | Replace the standard listener's `stop()` with a **bounded** sentinel enqueue and a **bounded** join | (a) Keep `stop()` and accept its behaviour; (b) drain the queue first and then call `stop()`; (c) make the queue unbounded so the sentinel always fits; (d) abandon the listener thread without stopping it | Read from the pinned interpreter's own source rather than assumed: `QueueListener.stop()` enqueues its sentinel with a bare `put_nowait`, which **raises** on a full queue, and then joins its thread with **no timeout**. On a bounded 4096-slot queue under load, interpreter exit could therefore raise or hang, and this runs from an `atexit` hook. A bounded `put` with a deadline and a `join` with a timeout make the exit path finite: at most the drain budget, plus one second, plus two. (b) is what the code already did and is not sufficient, because a producer can refill the queue between the drain and the sentinel. (c) removes the queue's own memory bound to fix a shutdown path. (d) loses records the listener still holds | Interpreter exit can now take up to eight seconds in the worst case, where it was previously either fast or indefinite. A queue that will not drain leaves records unwritten, which is reported rather than silent — row 35.14 is that half |
| 81.14 | **Retain** the listener reference when a stop does not complete, and publish the failures through a read-only register | (a) Clear the reference first, as the code did; (b) clear it on failure and log; (c) raise from the stop | Clearing the reference before stopping meant a listener that would not stop was left running with nothing holding it — invisible, unstoppable and still consuming its thread. Keeping the reference until the thread has genuinely exited means a caller can try again and a case can observe the state. The three reasons are named constants — the queue did not drain, the sentinel was refused, the thread did not exit — deduplicated in a register a caller reads as a tuple, so the failure is observable without the module exposing anything mutable. (b) records the failure and still loses the handle. (c) raises from an `atexit` hook, which is the behaviour being removed | The register grows to at most three entries and is cleared when the listener is rebuilt. A caller that ignores it sees no difference; the previous behaviour swallowed the outcome entirely, and two cases now fail if it is swallowed again |
| 81.15 | **Stream** every provider response: refuse an oversized declared length before reading anything, cap the accumulated bytes, then decode | (a) Keep buffering and measure after, as the code did; (b) refuse on the declared length alone; (c) lower the byte ceiling; (d) put the cap in a transport wrapper | All three provider helpers awaited a buffered call and only then measured the body against the ceiling, so the memory was already committed before the refusal — across a twenty-connection pool. The listing provider in this same codebase already streams with a declared-length refusal and an accumulating cap, so this is that established shape applied to the second provider rather than a new one. (b) trusts a header the sender controls, and an under-declared body would still be read whole. (c) changes a documented contract without closing the path. (d) is a construct between the client and every call for a property two functions can hold | The stream is stopped as soon as the accumulation exceeds the ceiling, so a refused response is read up to at most the ceiling plus one chunk rather than exactly the ceiling. The token-refresh path closes its stream without reading the body at all. A case drives a genuinely unbounded asynchronous body through a real client and asserts the producer never finishes |
| 81.16 | Make the measured body a **required argument** of the decoder and of the error classifier | (a) Let the decoder re-read the response; (b) pass it optionally, defaulting to a re-read; (c) return the decoded object from the reader | A second read of a streamed response is either impossible or unbounded, so the decoder must be given the bytes that were measured; making the argument required means no call site can silently fall back. Threading the same bytes into the failure classifier is what lets an error response keep its issue code without a second read — the property row 30.5's allowlist depends on. (a) and (b) both leave a path where an unbounded read is reachable | The three helpers must write the read and the decode as one expression each, because a standing case asserts the decoder is called with the response and that the buffered accessor appears nowhere in them. One consequence was caught by the existing suite rather than by review: naming the local body `body` shadowed the request payload parameter of the order call, so a token refresh re-sent an empty order — the local is `response_body` throughout for that reason |
| 81.17 | Update the eleven provider test doubles to the **streaming** contract, and add a class of cases driving a real client | (a) Give the doubles a buffered shim so they satisfy both shapes; (b) keep the doubles and assert only the source text; (c) replace the doubles with a real client everywhere | A double that answers a buffered call cannot exercise a streamed reader, so leaving them would have left every existing size-cap assertion passing against a code path no test entered. The doubles now expose the chunked reader, the declared length, how many bytes were streamed and whether a decode happened, so each existing assertion becomes stronger rather than merely still passing. The real-client class exists because a stand-in cannot prove a bound against the library's own behaviour: two facts only a real client shows are that an asynchronous generator is required for a streamed body, and that a buffered response pre-populates its content so the buffered accessor still succeeds — which is why one perturbation passed until a genuinely streamed failure case was added. (c) would put a transport double in every payment case for no gain | Eleven doubles across three modules now share one contract; each is asserted through the same shared provider guard, so a double that drifts fails there. A fourth module needed no change at all, because it already drove a real client over a mock transport |

### The store the rate limiter shares its counters through

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.18 | Provision a **managed store** and a **seventh** managed secret for its address, and do **not** assemble that address inside the infrastructure configuration | (a) Compose the address in Terraform from the instance's generated authentication string; (b) publish the authentication string as an output and let the operator combine it; (c) provision the store and leave the address entirely to the operator with no secret | The application refuses an in-process store outside a local run and requires a shared store's address, and nothing anywhere provisioned one — the finding is a provisioning gap, not a code defect, and the application side needed no change. The store is declared on the same private network as the database, with private service access, authentication enabled and server-authenticated transit encryption, and its working set is evicted by least recent use, because a rate-limit key is one caller address for one route in one window. The address is delivered exactly as the other six secrets are: a write-only secret version fed by an ephemeral input. (a) is refused for a specific reason rather than style: a write-only argument must receive an ephemeral value, and the generated authentication string is a state-persisted attribute, so composing the address there would write the credential into state. (b) publishes a credential through an output. (c) leaves the deployment with no delivery path for a value it cannot start without | The operator assembles the address once, from the published host and port plus the instance's authentication string, and supplies it as an ephemeral input — a manual step, recorded in §81.52. The published output carries host and port only, and a case asserts the authentication string is published by no output |
| 81.19 | Declare the store as a Compose service on **both** profiles, with no published port, no volume, and eviction by least recent use | (a) Declare it on the deployable profile only; (b) publish its port for local inspection; (c) give it a volume so counters survive a restart; (d) leave Compose alone and treat the store as a cloud concern | A stack whose environment names anything other than `local` needs a store to address, and either profile can be configured that way — selecting the `local` profile says which services run, not what `ENVIRONMENT` is set to. Declaring the service on both means a store is present whichever profile is selected, while the shipped defaults remain the local pair, so nothing changes for a developer who changes nothing. No port is published, so the store is reachable only from the stack's own network and needs no password there. No volume, because the counters are rebuilt by the traffic that follows a restart; persisting them would write a durable record of caller addresses for no benefit. (b) exposes an unauthenticated store on the host. (c) is that durable record | One more service in the stack, which the service inventory, the profile map and the probe map in the deployment-contract cases all now encode; adding a service is a deliberate edit in those three places. The backend waits for the store to report healthy, so a store that will not start holds the backend rather than letting it start and refuse |
| 81.20 | Have the deployment publish the address **through a file**, and refuse an in-process scheme in the pipeline itself | (a) Read the secret into an environment variable and pass it with a literal flag; (b) let each pod's own startup validation refuse a bad address; (c) template the address into the workload declaration | A value passed as a command-line literal is visible in a process listing and in any command echo; read to a file under a restrictive mask in a temporary directory removed by a trap, it reaches neither. The scheme check exists because the failure mode without it is diffuse: a misconfigured secret would otherwise fail every pod's startup validation individually, after a rollout has begun, where the same condition detected in the pipeline ends one step with one message. (c) puts an address in a versioned file, which row 35.23 refuses for images and refuses here for the same reason | The pipeline now fails for a class of misconfiguration it previously passed on. The refusal names the three in-process schemes explicitly, and a case asserts no workflow carries a shared-scheme address of its own |
| 81.21 | Validate the address input by **scheme allowlist** and refuse placeholder and loopback hosts | (a) Accept any non-empty string and rely on the application; (b) deny-list the three in-process schemes; (c) validate only that the value is not empty | The allowlist admits exactly the schemes the application accepts, which structurally excludes the in-process ones rather than enumerating them as refusals — the same allowlist-over-blocklist principle RFC 8725 sets for the `alg` parameter and this work applies to the accepted signing algorithms. A placeholder or loopback host would provision a deployment that starts and then counts against a store nothing else can reach. The scheme sets are imported from the application's own settings module in the tests rather than restated, so the application stays the authority for what is shared | The regular expression is a second statement of the accepted scheme set, in a language that cannot import the first. The imported-set assertion is what stops the two drifting |

### The deployment contract

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.22 | Create `infrastructure/k8s/` as the **single** workload inventory both delivery paths apply | (a) Keep mutating workloads assumed to exist, and document the assumption; (b) declare the workloads in Terraform through the Kubernetes provider; (c) let each delivery path carry its own declarations | Nothing in the repository declared a Deployment, a Service, an autoscaler, a probe or a resource envelope, so the delivered system had no statement of what it runs — two delivery paths mutated two different sets of assumed objects, and neither could be reviewed against anything. One versioned inventory makes the workload shape reviewable, and it is what lets a case assert that both paths apply the same objects. (b) would put workload declarations behind a provider this configuration does not use and behind state this work deliberately keeps free of secrets. (c) is the divergence being removed. The manifests declare shape and reference managed configuration by name; they invent no environment-specific value | Eight paths the plan's file mapping does not enumerate, recorded as an update to §23.2 by row 35.38. The declarations are asserted statically: no Kubernetes cluster and no container runtime exists on the verification host, so nothing here was applied — a boundary this section states rather than implies |
| 81.23 | Have each container name a **logical image**, and substitute that exact string at release | (a) Mutate the running deployment's image with an imperative command, as both paths did; (b) put a workflow expression in the manifest; (c) adopt a templating or overlay tool; (d) commit one registry reference and rewrite it in place | An imperative image change alters one field of whatever the cluster happens to hold and leaves every other property undeclared, which is how a cluster ends up with no relationship to any file. Substituting a fixed logical string means the same declarations apply everywhere, no manifest names a registry, a project or a tag, and the applied object is the declared object with one field resolved. (b) makes the manifests unusable outside the workflow that renders them. (c) adds a tool to the delivery path for one substitution. (d) leaves a stale reference in the file whenever the rewrite is skipped | The substitution is a text replacement, so the logical names must remain exactly as written; a case asserts each manifest names one of them and that no manifest names a registry, a project, a tag or a workflow expression. Both paths perform the same two substitutions |
| 81.24 | Express the migration as a **Job** carrying a wall-clock deadline, no retries and a retention window, kept in a subdirectory, and drive it delete-confirm-apply-wait | (a) Keep reconstructing a pod specification from the running deployment; (b) run the migration as an init container on the API; (c) apply the job alongside the workloads; (d) keep polling for completion | The previous step derived a pod from the deployment and dropped its resource envelope entirely, giving the schema change the lowest scheduling class and no deadline at all — a migration that hung held the release open indefinitely. A declared Job carries the same resource envelope and security context as the API, a deadline, an attempt limit of none and a retention window, and the release waits on its completion condition under a bounded wait. It lives in a subdirectory because a completed Job's pod template is immutable, so a non-recursive apply of the workloads must not reach it; the previous job is deleted, its absence is **confirmed**, and only then is the new one applied. (b) runs the schema change once per replica. (c) fails the apply on the immutable template. (d) is the unbounded polling of row 35.27 | A release now fails if a migration exceeds its deadline, where previously it waited. Deleting and confirming before applying costs one extra bounded call and removes the case where a stale job's result is read as this release's |
| 81.25 | Build each image with an explicit Dockerfile path and its own context | (a) Move each Dockerfile into the directory used as its context; (b) build from the repository root; (c) keep the contexts and add a symbolic link | This is the Critical finding, and it is not subtle: both delivery paths ran a build against directories that contain no Dockerfile, so neither path could ever have produced an image. Naming the file explicitly keeps each Dockerfile where the plan's file mapping puts it while giving each build the context its own instructions require. (a) moves a path the mapping enumerates. (b) sends the whole tree to the daemon and breaks both files' relative copies. (c) adds a filesystem indirection to avoid a flag | Two build invocations must keep the file and the context paired; a case asserts each image is built from the file that defines it and that both paths exist, and that no build without an explicit file remains in either path |
| 81.26 | Address the cluster by **one canonical regional location** and reach it from a **VPC-connected deployer** over its private endpoint | (a) Keep the zone value and make the cluster zonal; (b) keep the public runner and enable a public endpoint with an authorised network; (c) carry both a zone and a region and choose at run time | The cluster Terraform declares is regional and its endpoint is private, and the pipeline addressed it by zone from a hosted public runner — a combination that cannot connect, and whose failure mode without a private endpoint would be worse than a failure. One location value replaces the zone one, the region flag replaces the zone flag, the credential step requests the internal address, and the deploying job runs on a labelled self-hosted runner. (a) would rebuild the cluster to match a pipeline variable. (b) reopens a control plane this work made private, which is finding INFRA-1's own remediation. (c) keeps two sources for one fact | Two operational prerequisites a human must satisfy, both recorded in §81.52: a repository secret carrying the region in place of the zone one, and a runner with network access to the private control plane. The pipeline now fails at the credential step rather than at an endpoint the cluster does not expose |
| 81.27 | Bound **every** remote call, and probe **readiness** rather than liveness after a release | (a) Keep the retry loops, which already looked finite; (b) bound the loops by attempt count alone; (c) impose an overall step timeout in the workflow | A loop with a fixed number of attempts around a call that never returns runs forever, which is precisely what the pipeline had: finite-looking loops wrapping unbounded remote calls. Each call now carries its own request deadline and each transfer a connect and a maximum time, and the post-release probe is bounded by a wall-clock deadline rather than an attempt count. It reads the readiness route, because the liveness route answers as soon as the process serves and would report a release healthy while its database was unreachable. (c) bounds the step and leaves the operator without the failing call | The deadlines are constants in one place per path; a case joins continuation lines into logical commands, strips comments, and requires the flags on each invocation, so a bound written in a comment or an error message does not satisfy it — which is how two of this round's assertions were found to be false gates, per row 35.30 |
| 81.28 | Export the liveness route's path from the application beside the readiness one, and read both from there | (a) Write the paths as literals in the manifests and the cases; (b) read them from the application's route table at test time; (c) declare them in configuration | The manifests and the pipeline both need the two paths, and the application is the only place that knows them. Exporting the liveness path alongside the readiness path that was already exported gives one authority, and the probe cases import both rather than restating them, so renaming a route fails a test instead of silently leaving a probe pointing at nothing. (b) is indirect for a constant. (c) makes a route path a deployment variable | One more exported name. A case asserts the probe paths equal the exported values, and renaming either exported name fails three cases |
| 81.29 | **Realign** the standalone deployment script with the canonical inventory rather than retire it, and guard its function step on the source it deploys | (a) Delete the script and leave the workflow as the only path; (b) leave the script and document that it is unsupported; (c) reduce it to a wrapper that invokes the workflow | The script built a context with no Dockerfile, deployed a function source the repository does not contain, targeted a workload nothing declares, and executed a schema change inside a serving pod. Every one of those is a defect against the same inventory the workflow now applies, so aligning it removes four defects and leaves one documented path for an operator without the pipeline. The function step is guarded on the source directory existing, which removes the deploy-an-absent-source defect while keeping the frozen runtime flag in the file byte-identical. (a) removes an operator's only manual path and the plan enumerates the script. (b) leaves a script that cannot work. (c) is not available: the workflow requires a runner inside the network | Two paths must stay in step, which the cases assert by requiring both to build the same images and apply the same inventory. Executing a schema change inside a serving pod is gone entirely |
| 81.30 | Rewrite two of this round's own assertions to read **parsed invocations** rather than file text | (a) Leave them, since both passed; (b) narrow them to a substring unlikely to appear in prose | Both passed against a deliberately broken pipeline, which makes them worse than absent: the private-endpoint flag and the readiness path each also appear in a comment and in a failure message, so reading the file text was satisfied while the flag was not on the command. They now read the commands with comments stripped, and only then did each perturbation fail as it must. This is the same class of defect as the thread-identity case in row 35.1, and it is recorded for the same reason — an assertion that cannot fail is a false report of coverage | Both assertions are now coupled to the command parser rather than to the file, so a change in how the pipeline expresses a command must keep the parser's assumptions true; the parser is one helper, asserted by its own case |

### Verification arranged once

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.31 | **Partition** the backend suite between two steps — the security subtree, then everything else — with coverage appended across both | (a) Drop the whole-suite step and keep the security one; (b) drop the security step and keep the whole-suite one; (c) keep both and accept the cost; (d) run the whole suite and select the security subtree by marker | Integration ran the whole suite and then ran the security subtree again: measured by collection, that subtree is 1640 of the 1913 cases, so 86% of the suite executed twice per push. Partitioning keeps both gates named and reported separately while executing each case once. The order is security-first so the coverage data has something to append to, and the second invocation is the one that enforces the coverage floor, so the floor is applied to the whole measurement rather than to half of it. Verified by execution rather than by reading: collection gives 1913 whole, 1640 security, 273 remainder — an exact partition, nothing overlapping and nothing dropped — and running the two commands in sequence reports the floor met at 91.27% and writes the report the workflow uploads. (a) and (b) each lose a gate. (d) makes the split depend on marking every case | The two steps must stay complementary: one names the subtree, the other excludes it. A case asserts exactly that, and asserts the appending and the floor are on the second step only. A gate inventory asserted exactly-once across both workflows is what stops either step being lost, per row 35.35 |
| 81.32 | **Remove** the integration step whose script was comment-only | (a) Implement an integration suite behind it; (b) leave it as a marker of intent; (c) replace it with a skip | A step that runs no command reports success and verifies nothing, which is indistinguishable in a green pipeline from a gate that passed. Its stated intent — drive the assembled application end to end — is what the delivered suite already does: it drives the assembled application through the framework's test client against a real database and a real provider transport. (a) would build a second harness for coverage that exists. (b) is the defect. Removing it also removed the last unresolved-assistance marker from either workflow, which a case now holds at zero | If a genuine end-to-end suite is added later it needs a step of its own. A case asserts neither workflow carries a step whose script runs no command, so a placeholder cannot return quietly |
| 81.33 | Delete the deployment's duplicate verification job and trigger the deployment on **CI's completion**, gated on its conclusion | (a) Keep the job and accept the duplication; (b) keep the job but narrow it to a subset; (c) keep the push trigger and add a status check | The deployment re-installed both dependency manifests and re-ran both dependency audits, the static analyser and the whole security suite for the same commit CI had just checked — a second environment build and, at the suite's current size, 1640 more cases per push. Consuming CI's result is what "run each gate once" means when two workflows exist: the deployment now starts only when CI completes on the release branch and proceeds only when its conclusion is success. (b) leaves duplication and makes it arbitrary. (c) leaves the deployment starting before its gates have run | The deployment depends on CI's name, which a case reads from CI's own declaration rather than restating. A cancelled or failed CI run reaches the workflow and stops at the condition, which is visible rather than silent |
| 81.34 | Release the commit **CI verified**, carried explicitly, rather than the branch head | (a) Keep the default commit reference the event provides; (b) re-resolve the branch head at deploy time | This is the correctness detail the change turns on, and it is easy to miss: under a completion trigger the default commit reference is the *default branch head*, not the commit whose run finished. Left alone, the pipeline would have built, tagged and released a commit CI had never checked. The triggering run's head commit is carried in one workflow variable, the checkout pins that reference, and every image tag, the migration image, both substitutions and the running-image confirmation read it — eight references in total, none of them the default any longer. The concurrency group is keyed on the triggering run's branch for the same reason | One variable now governs what is released; a case asserts the default reference appears nowhere and that both image tags read the variable. A push whose CI run is superseded before deployment releases the commit that was verified, which is the intended behaviour |
| 81.35 | Hold an **exact-once** inventory of the verification gates across both workflows | (a) Assert each gate merely appears; (b) assert the step counts; (c) leave the arrangement to review | The failure this round fixed and the failure it must not cause are the same shape seen from two sides: a gate that runs twice wastes a pipeline, and a gate that runs zero times loses a guarantee. An inventory compared for exactly one occurrence catches both. It names both dependency audits, the static analyser, both halves of the backend suite, the frontend suite, both linters and both compensating-control guards | The inventory is a list of command fragments, so rewording a command means updating it; that edit is the point at which someone confirms the gate still runs |

### The withdrawn position, and the documents that state a figure

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 81.36 | **Row 15.1 is superseded in full, and row 2.5 is named as the controlling decision.** Row 15.1 is marked in place, and the rows that restore and provision the shared store are cited from it | (a) Edit row 15.1 so it reads as the current position, leaving no trace of the withdrawn one; (b) delete row 15.1; (c) leave it standing on the ground that a reader will find the later rows; (d) change the application to match row 15.1 and readmit the bounded in-process store | Row 15.1 accepted a bounded in-process rate-limit store outside a local run. `backend/app/core/config.py` refuses it, rows 23.3.1, 27.7, 30.18 and 31.12 all reason from the refusal, and no row recorded the reversal — so this log carried two incompatible positions and a reader could act on the withdrawn one. That is a defect against Rule 1 in the file Rule 1 makes authoritative, which is why it is the one finding of this round that is not about resources. Row 15.1's own reasoning is what dates it: it rejected provisioning a shared store as "infrastructure work an order of magnitude wider than the defect", and rows 35.18 to 35.21 are that work, delivered. (a) is what §27's convention exists to forbid — an abandoned position and the reason it was abandoned must stay visible. (b) destroys the record. (c) is the finding. (d) would remove a control to make a documentation sentence true, inverting the priority between them | A reader of row 15.1 in isolation now reads a withdrawal notice before the withdrawn text, which is the pattern rows 27.8 and 34.8.1 established. The row's caveat about per-process counting remains accurate for a local run, where the bounded store is still what the application admits and what the shipped defaults name |

The three situational references are gone entirely, which is the more durable half of this row. Behavioural contrasts were deliberately left in place throughout, per §10.17's second recorded consequence — a docstring that says a helper returns the row it wrote, or that a step ends rather than continuing, documents what the code does |

(b) would rewrite a table earlier rows cite by number. (a) was refused once §23.1 was actually re-measured against the tree, because its figures no longer describe it. **Measured now, against baseline `a26f7fb` plus the working tree and the untracked set:** all **59** planned paths of AAP §0.6.1.1–§0.6.1.6 are delivered and **0** remain pending, where §23.1 recorded 47 delivered and 12 pending; **33** unplanned paths are touched, where §23.2 lists 11 and row 31.11 takes the count to 13; and the total changed-path figure a downstream document must use is therefore **92**, not the 70 of §23.1 or the 72 of row 31.11. Of the 33, this round adds 10; 13 are the ones §23.2 and row 31.11 record; and the remaining 10 were delivered by rounds between them — the four migration and revision test modules, the two setup-script modules, the deployment-contract module, the shared test-value module, the frontend ignore file, and the frontend image definition row 30.12 argues. Each of those ten is argued in the round that added it; none was added to §23.2's inventory, which is why the count there and the count in the tree had diverged | Three places now carry a count of unenumerated paths — §23.2, row 31.11 and this row — and this row is the current one. §23.1's table is marked with a pointer here so a reader who arrives at it first is not left quoting 70.
