## 82. The deployment surface: private networking, managed secret delivery, release gating and the decommissioned managed runtime

Rows added by the review round whose subject was the deployment surface —
`infrastructure/terraform/**`, both GitHub Actions workflows, `scripts/deploy.sh`,
the ignore files and the environment template — together with the documentation
that describes them. That round raised twenty-nine findings, and it is the first
round in this log whose subject is how the service is deployed rather than what the
service does. Sections 1 to 34 are silent on every decision below, which is why
Rule 1 required this section: a decision that was never recorded is, for the Rule's
purposes, a decision that was never explained.

Four properties shape the rows.

**The findings interlock rather than accumulate.** Twelve of the twenty-nine were
symptoms of four root causes: the configuration provisioned secrets with no path to
the workload, provisioned a cluster with no network, described a workload the
repository never defined, and named a hosting runtime the provider had already
decommissioned. Fixing each root cause closed several findings at once, which is
why some rows below answer three or four findings between them.

**One finding was a blocker rather than a defect.** No Kubernetes workload
definition existed anywhere in the repository, yet both delivery paths addressed
`deployment/backend` and `deployment/frontend` as though they did. Nothing about
secret delivery, migration ordering or readiness gating could be made true until
those definitions existed, so §82.3 precedes every row that depends on it.

**Every command in these rows was executed here before it was written down.** The
deployment surface has almost no automated coverage — one test module reads the
environment template and nothing else in the suite touches Terraform, either
workflow or either script — so verification had to come from running things. Where
a row claims a command exits zero, the command was run in this working tree.
Running rather than reasoning caught four defects in this round's own first drafts,
recorded in §82.15, §82.16, §82.20 and §82.22.

**Two rows exist to withdraw claims made earlier in this log.** They are in
§82.27, following the convention §27 established.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 82.1 | **Delete the managed-runtime Cloud Function and its invoker binding outright, rather than migrate the runtime or leave the resource in place.** The configuration now provisions no managed-runtime function at all | (a) Advance the function's runtime to a supported Python and keep the resource; (b) keep the resource on `python39` and record the decommission as a known issue; (c) keep the resource but comment it out; (d) replace it with a second-generation function or a Cloud Run service on a supported runtime | Three independent facts made deletion the only honest option, and each was read from the tree rather than assumed. First, **the runtime is decommissioned**: Google retired the Python 3.9 managed-functions runtime on 5 April 2026, and after a retirement date that provider will not create or update a function on the runtime and may disable existing ones — so the resource could not be applied at all, which makes it a broken claim rather than a working deployment. Second, **the runtime cannot be advanced here**: the Python 3.9 pin is a hard AAP constraint and `listing_updater.py` uses `@asyncio.coroutine`, removed in 3.11, so (a) is unavailable on the terms this work is bound by. Third, **there was nothing to deploy**: the resource named a source archive `function-source.zip` that does not exist in this repository, an entry point `hello_world` that no module defines, and a display name "My function", and no `functions/` directory exists — so even on a supported runtime the resource described no software. (b) leaves a configuration that cannot be applied, which is the finding. (c) leaves the same claim in a form no linter checks. (d) is a platform migration into a product this work has no authorization to introduce, and it would still need the source that does not exist. Deleting the resource makes the configuration describe only what it can actually create, and the workload it purported to run is re-expressed by §82.2 on a platform where the 3.9 pin is preserved rather than fought | The configuration no longer provisions any function, so a deployment that genuinely depended on one loses it. Nothing here did: the resource had no source. A binding already granted on a function that exists in a live project is **not** revoked by removing the resource from this configuration, which is a separate and real risk — §82.19 adds the explicit reconciliation step that revokes it, because Terraform's silence about a resource is not the same as its absence. Three variable names (`cloud_function_name_ingest`, `_process`, `_analyze`) now describe nothing this configuration provisions; §82.26 records why they are kept anyway |
| 82.2 | **Re-express the periodic ingestion workload as a Kubernetes CronJob running on the same backend image**, whose base image pins CPython 3.9 | (a) Schedule the ingestion inside the API process with an `asyncio` task at startup; (b) leave the workload unscheduled, since nothing scheduled it before either; (c) run it as a second container in the backend Pod; (d) introduce a workflow-orchestration product | Measured first: `run_listing_updater()` is referenced by no scheduler — `main.py`'s lifespan creates no task — so the periodic ingestion the deleted function was supposed to provide **did not run anywhere**, while `update_listings()` exists, is covered by `test_tasks.py`, and was executed end to end in this working tree for this decision (exit 0, one structured pass logged). (a) couples a batch workload to request-serving capacity, so an ingestion pass competes with user requests and a scaled deployment runs the pass once per replica. (b) leaves a documented capability absent and would make the deletion in §82.1 a net loss of function. (c) has the same multiplication problem as (a) plus a lifecycle mismatch — a batch job that ends would restart forever in a Deployment. (d) is new infrastructure for one hourly command. A CronJob is the platform's own primitive for exactly this, runs on the image already built and tested, and `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` means a slow pass cannot overlap the next. Crucially, the workload keeps the pinned interpreter: the schedule moves, the runtime does not | The schedule is now a manifest value rather than a provider-managed trigger, so changing it is a deployment rather than a console edit. The CronJob reads the same managed secrets as the API, so it holds the same credentials — which is why §82.5 grants them per secret to one identity rather than broadly. An ingestion pass that fails leaves the corpus stale and is visible only in logs; the pass logs a structured summary on every run, which is the signal to alert on |
| 82.3 | **Version the Kubernetes workload, service, configuration and secret-delivery definitions in this repository, under `infrastructure/k8s/`, and apply them from both delivery paths** | (a) Manage the workloads with Terraform's Kubernetes provider; (b) keep addressing objects created out of band and confine the pipelines to `kubectl set image`; (c) generate the manifests inside the pipeline from a template held in the workflow file; (d) adopt a packaging tool such as Helm or Kustomize | Both delivery paths addressed `deployment/backend` and `deployment/frontend`, and nothing in the repository created either — so the entire deployment sequence rested on objects that had to already exist, and no reviewer could tell what they contained. That is the finding, and it is unfixable without the definitions. (a) would put workload lifecycle behind the same apply that owns the cluster and the database, so a rolling image change would compete with infrastructure state and a failed apply could touch both; it also needs cluster credentials at plan time. (b) is the status quo: it leaves the cluster's actual contents undescribed, which is precisely what allowed a migration step to read a live Deployment's environment and copy it. (c) hides the definitions inside a workflow file, where they cannot be validated, diffed or applied by an operator. (d) adds a templating dependency and a release-management model for eleven objects, when the only variability is a small set of values §82.6 handles. Plain manifests plus one substitution pass are the least machinery that makes the cluster's contents reviewable, and they are validated: every manifest parses, and `kubectl create --dry-run=client` accepts all seven built-in-kind files | Eleven objects are now this repository's responsibility to keep correct, and a manifest that drifts from the cluster is a silent divergence — mitigated by both paths applying the manifests before changing anything, so an apply is the only way an image moves. The `SecretProviderClass` is a custom resource, so its schema cannot be validated client-side without the cluster; it is checked structurally instead, against the settings class. Hardening choices (non-root, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, resource limits) are now stated in files rather than inherited from whatever created the objects, which is the intent but does mean a change to them is a repository change |
| 82.4 | **The CSI-driver decision in this row stands; its delivery mechanism is WITHDRAWN &mdash; see row 92.8.** The six values are mounted as files by the driver and exported by a shell prelude before the process starts; **no `secretObjects` is declared and no Kubernetes Secret is synchronised**, so no credential is written into the cluster datastore. §37.6 records the mechanism and §88.2 records the last workload moving onto it. The withdrawn text follows as chronology: Deliver the six managed secrets through the provider's Secret Manager CSI driver into a synced Kubernetes Secret, consumed by `envFrom` reference only, and set `SECRET_BACKEND` so the application validates the delivery itself | (a) Fetch the secrets in the pipeline and write them into the manifests or a Kubernetes Secret; (b) add a Secret Manager client to the application and read them at startup; (c) mount them as files and change the settings loader to read files; (d) keep them as plain Kubernetes Secrets managed by hand | The configuration provisioned six secrets and connected them to nothing — no accessor binding, no workload identity, no injection mechanism — so the secrets existed and the workload could not read them. Measured constraint that decides the shape: `config.py`'s `_check_value_source` refuses startup unless all six arrive **from the process environment** when `SECRET_BACKEND` names the managed backend, and no Secret Manager client exists anywhere in `backend/app`. Delivery therefore has to be platform-side and has to land as environment variables. (a) puts plaintext secret values through the pipeline's own memory and filesystem, which is the exposure the workflow finding is about, and any diagnostic that prints a manifest then prints a secret. (b) is application code this work is not authorized to add, and it would move a network dependency into startup. (c) contradicts the validator the application already ships. (d) is unmanaged state with no provenance. The CSI path never materialises a value in the repository or the pipeline: the driver reads the secret with the Pod's own identity and writes it into a Secret the container consumes by name. Setting `SECRET_BACKEND` to the managed backend is what makes the application refuse to start if the delivery silently failed, so the control is self-checking rather than assumed | The delivery depends on the cluster add-on, the workload identity binding and the manifests all being correct together, and a failure surfaces as a Pod that will not start rather than as a clear message about secrets — the trade accepted deliberately, because the alternative is a Pod that starts on the wrong values. The synced Secret exists in the cluster's own storage, so cluster-level read access is equivalent to secret access; that is a property of every Kubernetes secret consumption model and is why the accessor grants in §82.5 are per-secret and the namespace holds nothing else |
| 82.5 | **Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on each of the six secrets individually to one dedicated runtime identity**, and bind that identity to one Kubernetes service account | (a) Grant the role once at the project level; (b) reuse the node service account; (c) grant it to the default compute identity, as the baseline effectively did; (d) grant a broader Secret Manager role such as admin or viewer at the project | A project-level grant is the difference between "this workload may read these six values" and "this workload may read every secret this project will ever hold", and the second is unbounded in time — a secret added next year is covered by a grant written today. Six explicit bindings state the whole set the workload can reach, and adding a seventh secret is then a visible change. (b) would give every workload on the node the API's secrets, including any future workload. (c) is the least-privilege finding itself. (d) grants write or metadata access nothing needs. The binding to the Kubernetes service account is the other half: without it the identity is unreachable from the Pod, and with it only that one namespace and name can assume it | Six bindings to maintain rather than one, and a secret added without a binding fails at Pod start — loud rather than silent, which is the correct failure direction. The bindings are generated from the same list the manifests consume, so the two cannot disagree about which secrets exist |
| 82.6 | **Carry deployment-specific values as double-underscore substitution tokens in the manifests, substitute them at deploy time, and refuse to continue if any token survives** | (a) Commit real values for a reference environment; (b) commit empty values and rely on the operator to fill them; (c) hold the values in a Kubernetes ConfigMap created out of band; (d) use a templating tool's value files | The manifests must be committed, and fourteen of the values in them cannot be: measured from `config.py`, outside the local environment the settings validator **refuses** a rate-limit store that is not shared between processes, and eight further fields are refused if they carry a placeholder marker or a reserved example domain, while both payer-redirect addresses must be HTTPS. So there is no committable value that is both safe and startable — (a) and (b) are not available on the application's own terms rather than by preference. (c) moves the same values out of review, which is what §82.3 exists to stop. (d) adds tooling for a `sed` pass. The token style is double underscores rather than angle brackets because `<` and `>` are themselves placeholder markers the validator refuses, so a leftover angle-bracket token would produce a confusing validation error instead of a clear rendering error. The survival guard is the load-bearing part: an unsubstituted token would otherwise reach the cluster as a literal string and the Pod would fail validation on a value nobody set. Verified three ways — a missing input is reported by name and exits non-zero, a complete render leaves zero tokens, and a deliberately unsubstitutable token is reported with its file and line and refuses to continue | Fourteen values must be supplied per environment, and the failure for a missing one is a refusal to render rather than a partial deployment. Two prose comments in the manifests originally contained a literal example token and tripped the guard during verification; both were reworded, which is a reminder that the guard is strict by design and that documentation inside a rendered file has to respect it |
| 82.7 | **Put the rendering pass and its survival guard in one script that both the workflow and the deployment script call.** The substance of this decision stands; the name it was written with, `scripts/render_manifests.sh`, is **WITHDRAWN &mdash; see rows 88.3 and 92.9.** The surviving implementation is `scripts/render_kubernetes_manifests.sh` | (a) Inline the same `sed` pipeline in both callers; (b) render only in the workflow and have the script apply raw manifests; (c) write the renderer in Python | The workflow and the script are two delivery paths to the same cluster, and the fourteen-value list plus the guard is exactly the logic that must not differ between them: if one path forgets a token the other substitutes, the two produce different objects from the same repository. One implementation makes drift impossible rather than unlikely. (a) duplicates fourteen names in two languages of quoting. (b) would leave the operator path unable to deploy at all. (c) adds an interpreter dependency to a deployment host for string substitution. The script is a path the AAP's mapping does not name, which §82.28 records | One more shell script to keep correct, and a bug in it breaks both paths at once — which is the same property that makes it valuable, and is why it is verified independently rather than only through its callers |
| 82.8 | **Create one shared VPC, subnetwork and secondary ranges in this configuration, and attach both the cluster and the database to it**, with private services access and a Cloud NAT for egress | (a) Accept an operator-supplied network through a variable, as the baseline's `database_private_network` did; (b) use the project's default network; (c) create two networks and peer them; (d) leave the database on a public address with authorized networks | The cluster and the database were not attached to any explicit common network: the cluster's IP allocation was an empty block, so the provider chose ranges, and the database's private network came from a variable with no default — so whether the two could reach each other at all depended on inputs this configuration did not describe. Private services access was absent entirely, which is the prerequisite for a private database address, and nothing provided egress for nodes with no public address, so a private cluster could not pull an image or reach an external provider. (a) leaves the most important property of the topology outside the configuration and unvalidated. (b) is a network with automatic subnets in every region and no range control, which is what secondary-range planning exists to avoid. (c) is two networks and a peering to solve a problem one network does not have. (d) is the exposure being closed. Named secondary ranges are used rather than provider-chosen ones so the pod and service CIDRs are stated and reviewable | The configuration now owns network topology, so a change to a CIDR is a change to a resource other resources depend on, and range sizing is a decision made once and awkward to revise later. The Cloud NAT gives every node outbound reachability, which is deliberate — images and the listing provider must be reachable — but is broader than a per-destination allowance; it is logged for errors so a surprising destination is visible. The database's dependency on the peering is declared explicitly, because without it an apply can order the instance before the connection and fail |
| 82.9 | **Keep the control plane private and deploy from a runner inside the VPC**, with the runner label configurable and a preflight that fails with an actionable message | (a) Widen the control plane's authorized networks to admit the hosted runner; (b) make the control plane public; (c) run the deployment from a bastion via an interactive session; (d) use the provider's connect gateway | The cluster is regional and private-endpoint-only while the pipeline used a public hosted runner and a zonal credential command — two independent reasons the deployment could not work, and the identity fix that had been applied addressed neither: federated identity grants authority, not a network path. (a) would require admitting GitHub's published egress ranges, which are large, shared with every other customer of that platform and subject to change without notice — it converts a private control plane into a semi-public one for the convenience of one caller. (b) discards the control the finding is about. (c) is not automatable. (d) is a plausible alternative and is not adopted here because it introduces another provider surface and its own IAM model for a property an in-VPC runner already has; it is named so that a reviewer sees it was considered. Making the label configurable means an environment with a differently-labelled runner needs no code change, and the preflight turns an unreachable endpoint into one clear message rather than a timeout inside `kubectl` | The deployment now depends on infrastructure this repository does not provision: a self-hosted runner inside the VPC. That is a real operational prerequisite and it is stated in the workflow, in the script and in the README rather than assumed. A project without such a runner cannot deploy from CI at all until one exists — which is the honest position, since the alternative was a pipeline that appeared to work and could not |
| 82.10 | **Provision a regional Artifact Registry repository and address every image through it**, retiring `gcr.io` entirely | (a) Keep `gcr.io` and rely on the provider's automatic redirection; (b) codify the legacy registry as a resource and document the migration; (c) use a different registry | The pipelines pushed to `gcr.io` while no registry resource existed anywhere in the configuration, so the destination was unprovisioned and unmanaged. Writes to the legacy Container Registry ended in March 2025, so (a) depends on a redirection whose behaviour differs by project according to whether a migration has been performed — a deployment property that cannot be read from this repository. (b) codifies a deprecated product. (c) adds a credential and a network dependency for no benefit. A provisioned regional repository makes the destination explicit, and the node identity's pull permission is granted **on that repository** rather than at the project, per §82.11 | Existing image references elsewhere in an operator's tooling break, since the host name changes. Nothing in this repository still names the legacy host — verified, zero occurrences — and the region becomes part of every image reference, so a multi-region deployment needs a decision this configuration does not make for it |
| 82.11 | **Grant the node identity the provider's minimum node role, and grant image pull on the registry repository rather than at the project** | (a) Keep the baseline's role set and add `roles/artifactregistry.reader` at the project; (b) use the default compute service account; (c) grant `roles/editor`, which many examples do | The node identity lacked the role the provider now requires for nodes and its OAuth scopes could not pull from a private registry, so nodes would fail to register or fail to pull — a correctness defect and a least-privilege defect in the same place. The scope set is now a validated variable that must contain a pull-capable scope, so a deployment cannot silently configure nodes that cannot start their own images. Repository-scoped pull is strictly narrower than the project-level grant in (a): it permits reading one repository rather than every repository the project will ever hold. (b) is the finding. (c) is a project-wide administrative grant on every node | The role and scope sets are now asserted by validation, so an operator wanting a different set must widen the allow-list deliberately — intended, and it does mean a legitimate unusual scope needs an edit here. A second repository would need a second binding |
| 82.12 | **Replace the signing-key repeat-run validation, which was a silent no-op, and add the missing sequential-run rule — both without regular-expression backreferences** | (a) Add the sequential-run rule and leave the existing repeat-run regex in place; (b) drop structural validation from the configuration layer and rely on the application's; (c) compute the checks in a `locals` block or an external data source | The finding was that the configuration accepted signing keys the application rejects. Building a parity harness to prove the gap closed found a second, unreported defect: `!can(regex("(.)\\1{3,}", var.secret_key))` never rejected anything, because Terraform's regular-expression engine has no backreferences, so the expression raised an error that `can()` converted to `false` and the negation made `true` for **every** input including `aaaa`. It had never worked. (a) would leave that in place and close only the reported half. (b) would remove a defence-in-depth check whose whole purpose is to fail before a weak key is written to a secret. (c) cannot be used: a variable validation block may reference only the variable it validates. Both rules are therefore expressed with window comparisons over substrings — distinct-character counting for repeats, and containment tests against inlined printable-ASCII alphabets for sequences — which use no construct newer than the rest of the file. **Parity proven by measurement, not by reading:** 24 keys were put through the real validation and through the application's own validator; every verdict matched, and no key is accepted by the configuration that the application refuses | The sequence alphabet is printable ASCII, so a sequential run built from non-ASCII code points is caught by the application and not by the configuration. The direction of that gap is the safe one — the configuration is never more permissive in a way that matters, because the application still refuses the key at startup — and it is stated rather than left to be discovered. The rules are more code in a variable block than a regular expression would be, which is the cost of an engine without backreferences |
| 82.13 | **Gate deployment on the whole CI workflow for the exact commit, using a `workflow_run` trigger and that run's head revision for both checkout and image tag** | (a) Add the missing gates to the deployment workflow so it reproduces CI; (b) keep the push trigger and add a `needs` on more of its own jobs; (c) require a branch protection rule and trust it; (d) trigger on a release tag instead | Deployment depended on three security steps of its own and not on CI at all, so a commit could deploy having failed the frontend checks, the full backend suite, the reachability guards and the integration gate. (a) duplicates every gate in a second file, and two copies of a gate is one gate plus a maintenance obligation to keep them identical. (b) does not reach the other workflow's result. (c) is a repository setting this repository cannot assert, so the pipeline would still be trusting something invisible to a reviewer. (d) changes the release model. The `workflow_run` form consumes CI's own conclusion, and pinning both the checkout and the image tag to that run's head revision is what makes the gate mean something: without it a push landing while CI ran would deploy code CI never saw. The security job is retained as defence in depth rather than as the gate | The trigger is now indirect, so a deployment is one step further from the push that caused it and the run's provenance must be read from the triggering run. A workflow file change only takes effect on the default branch, which is the platform's rule for this trigger and is worth knowing before relying on a change in a branch |
| 82.14 | **Split CI into four independent jobs — backend, frontend, integration and infrastructure — with no dependency between them** | (a) Keep one job and fix the failing step in place; (b) keep one job and move the frontend steps to the end; (c) make the security steps a job the frontend job depends on | The concrete harm in the lint finding was ordering, not just the missing script: one job ran the frontend checks before the dependency audit, the static analysis, the reachability guards and the security suite, so a frontend failure prevented every security gate from running and the build reported one failure while hiding whether the others would have passed. (a) fixes today's failing step and leaves the ordering hazard for the next one. (b) reorders the same fragility. (c) inverts the dependency the wrong way. Independent jobs mean each gate's result is always known, and the workflow conclusion — which §82.13's gate consumes — is success only if all four succeed | Four jobs each set up their own environment, so total compute rises and the pinned interpreter and Node versions are declared in more than one place. The pins were preserved exactly, and a mismatch between them would now be a divergence to catch in review |
| 82.15 | **Lint the frontend with the ESLint already installed by its toolchain, excluding the one source file no parser accepts**, and pass `--passWithNoTests` to the test step | (a) Add a `lint` script to `frontend/package.json`; (b) use the TypeScript compiler's no-emit mode as the gate; (c) drop the lint step; (d) lint without the exclusion and accept a red gate | The workflow invoked `npm run lint` and no such script is declared — and the manifest declaring it is a read-only reference here, so (a) is unavailable. (b) was measured and rejected on evidence: no-emit compilation exits 2 with eighteen parse errors, **all** in one file that contains JSX under a `.ts` extension, which is a read-only frontend defect reported rather than fixed. (c) removes a gate. (d) is a gate that always fails, which is indistinguishable from no gate. The delivered command was executed verbatim in this tree and exits 0 while remaining a real gate: an error-level violation or a parse failure in any of the other twenty-two source files fails it. The test step needed the same treatment for the same class of reason — the workspace contains no test files at all, so the coverage command exited 1 on "no tests found" and would have failed the job by itself; the flag makes an empty suite pass while still writing the coverage artefact the upload step expects | One source file is not linted, and a genuine defect introduced into it would not be caught. The exclusion is stated at the step, the underlying defect is recorded among the findings reported for confirmation, and it is one file out of twenty-three. A suite that passes with no tests is a weaker signal than one that passes with tests; that is a property of the read-only frontend rather than of this gate |
| 82.16 | **Make the integration gate real: a database service, both migration revisions applied and reversed, the startup import, and a live server answering liveness, readiness, registration, sign-in and the public read** | (a) Remove the step, since a gate that always passes is worse than none; (b) assert the migration round trip only; (c) run the existing suite a second time and call it integration | The step contained comments and no commands, so it always succeeded and reported a gate that did not exist — and the project README claimed those gates ran in CI. (a) is honest and gives up the coverage the plan asks for. (b) covers the schema and not the surface. (c) measures nothing new. The delivered job runs against a real database service with no environment file, so every setting arrives from the process environment and the run cannot pass by reading a developer's file. **Executed here in full**, against a database created and dropped for the purpose so the shared one was never at risk: both revisions apply, reverse independently and reapply; exactly one administrative account exists; the entrypoint imports; and the running server answers liveness, then readiness — which reports unavailable while the database is unusable, so it proves the migrated schema is reachable — then registration, sign-in with the frozen response shape, and the unauthenticated public read. Two defects in the first draft were found by running it: registration answers 200 rather than the 201 assumed, because the route declares no status code; and a fixed test address made the step fail on any re-run against a retained database, so it now mints a unique address per run | The job is the slowest in CI and needs a service container. It exercises real HTTP and a real database, so a genuine infrastructure flake fails a build — accepted, because the alternative was a step that could not fail at all |
| 82.17 | **Run the schema migration as a one-shot Job built from the new image, before any change to a serving deployment**, and abort with the serving deployments untouched if it does not complete | (a) Keep the baseline order and migrate inside an already-updated pod; (b) run the migration as an init container on the Deployment; (c) migrate from the pipeline runner over a database connection | The baseline updated the serving image and waited for the rollout, then ran the migration inside the new pod — so new code served requests against the old schema for the duration, which is the window every migration ordering rule exists to eliminate. (b) runs the migration once per replica and on every restart, so a slow migration multiplies and a crash loop retries a schema change. (c) requires database reachability from the runner and runs the migration from an image other than the one being deployed, so the code and the schema change can disagree. A Job from the exact new image is the only form where what migrates and what will serve are the same artefact. **Proven by position rather than by reading:** in the script the Job is applied and its completion recorded before the serving apply and rollout wait; in the workflow the Job precedes the serving apply likewise | A failed migration leaves the Job object and its logs behind for diagnosis and the previous version still serving, which is the intended outcome but does mean an operator must clear the Job before retrying — both paths delete a same-named prior Job first, so a retry is not blocked. A migration that succeeds and a rollout that then fails leaves a schema ahead of the serving code, which the additive-with-defaults design of both revisions is what makes safe |
| 82.18 | **Decide deployment success on the readiness endpoint, retaining liveness for the probe the platform runs** | (a) Keep gating on liveness only; (b) gate on the rollout status alone; (c) add a synthetic transaction against a business route | Liveness answers whether the process is up; it does not answer whether the database is usable, so a deployment whose credentials or network path were wrong passed the gate and reported success. (a) is the finding. (b) is weaker still: a rollout completes when pods pass their probes, and the liveness probe is what they pass. (c) would write data on every deployment. Readiness is the endpoint that already exists for this question and reports unavailable while the database cannot be reached, so gating on it makes the pipeline's success claim equal to the property an operator cares about | A transient database interruption at exactly the moment of the gate fails a deployment that would have recovered. The gate retries before failing, and the failure message states that the deployment is running but its database is not usable, so the diagnosis is immediate rather than inferred |
| 82.19 | **Reconcile public invoker bindings explicitly, revoking both anonymous principals from any legacy function that still exists** | (a) Rely on having removed the unauthenticated flag from the deployment command; (b) rely on having deleted the resource from the configuration; (c) manage the complete invoker policy authoritatively in the configuration; (d) do nothing, since the function no longer exists here | This is the row that separates a configuration change from a revocation, and conflating the two is the error. Removing the flag stops *granting* the binding again; removing the resource stops *describing* it — neither revokes a binding a previous apply or deploy already made, and a non-authoritative member resource by construction leaves other members in place. So (a), (b) and (d) all leave a live public invoker binding on a function that may still exist in the project, which is the finding. (c) would be the right shape if the function were still managed here, and it is not, per §82.1 — an authoritative policy resource for a resource this configuration does not create is not something it can own. The delivered form is an explicit, idempotent reconciliation in the deployment path: look for the legacy function, and when it exists revoke the invoker role from both anonymous principals and report each revocation. Absence is not an error; presence is reported with the instruction to delete it once its bindings have been reviewed | The step names a legacy function whose name is a default that a deployment can override, so a differently-named legacy function would be missed — stated at the step. It is a revocation performed by a deployment, which is unusual and deliberate: the alternative is a manual step that may never happen. Once the legacy function is deleted the step becomes a no-op and can be removed |
| 82.20 | **Diagnose a failed deployment with a Job's status, a narrow pod listing, recent events and container logs — never a full pod description** | (a) Keep the pod description, which is the most informative single command; (b) keep it and redact its output; (c) print nothing and rely on cluster access | A pod description prints the container's entire environment section, so on a migration failure it printed the values the workload holds — and the same workflow had been copying environment definitions from a live deployment onto an ad-hoc pod, so those values could include secrets. (a) is the exposure. (b) is a filter over an output format that is not a contract, so a future format change silently defeats it. (c) makes a failed deployment undiagnosable from the pipeline. The delivered set answers the questions a failure raises — did the Job complete, which pod, in what phase, for what reason, what happened recently, and what did the process say — and none of the four outputs carries an environment section. Verified: the description command appears nowhere, and neither does the expression that copied the environment | Slightly less information on a genuine failure, and an operator with cluster access can still describe the pod deliberately. A future diagnostic added carelessly could reintroduce the exposure, which is why a standing CI check asserts that no workload declares an inline environment entry at all |
| 82.21 | **Send an explicit `Host: localhost` header from every health probe, in the manifests and in both delivery paths** | (a) Add a health-path exemption to the host-validation middleware; (b) add the pod's address range to the allowed hosts; (c) probe through the service name only | Measured from the source: the trusted-host middleware validates the header on **every** request with no exemption for health paths, so the platform's own probe — which addresses the pod by its address — would be refused and the pod would never become ready. (a) changes production security behaviour to accommodate a probe, and a health path exempt from host validation is a small unauthenticated hole in exactly the control being added. (b) cannot be written: pod addresses are assigned from a range and are not known when the configuration is written. (c) does not apply to the platform's own probe. Setting the header on the probe is the narrowest fix and leaves the middleware unmodified. The same reasoning applies to a port-forwarded probe from a deployment path, which presents a loopback address the allowed-host list does not name | The probe header must stay in agreement with the allowed-host list, which is asserted by the standing manifest check rather than left to review. A future middleware change that stopped accepting the value would fail readiness rather than fail open |
| 82.22 | **Validate the operator-supplied version string and fold it deterministically into the Kubernetes name alphabet** before using it in an object name | (a) Use the version verbatim, as an image tag does; (b) use a fixed Job name and delete the previous Job each time; (c) derive the name from a hash of the version | The version is used as both an image tag and part of a Job name, and the two alphabets differ — a tag may carry upper case and a name may not, so a perfectly valid tag produces an invalid object name and the deployment fails at the apply with a message about a name rather than about the version. (a) is that failure. (b) loses the correspondence between a Job and the release it migrated, which is the first thing wanted when diagnosing. (c) produces a name nobody can read back to a release. The fold was **executed across eight inputs** rather than reasoned about: a plain version, one with upper case and a hyphen, one with dots and an underscore, and an all-alphabetic one all produce valid names, while a value containing a slash, one beginning with a hyphen, and an empty value are refused with a clear message | Two versions differing only in case fold to the same Job name; both paths delete a same-named prior Job first, so this is a collision that resolves rather than one that blocks. A rejected version is rejected before anything is built, which is the intended direction |
| 82.23 | **Add the generated federated-credential pattern to all four ignore files, not the two the finding named** | (a) Add it to the two files the finding cites; (b) broaden the existing credential pattern to match both spellings; (c) rely on the credential file being written outside the tree | The authentication action writes its credential into the workspace as `gha-creds-*.json`, and the existing pattern matches `*credentials*.json` — which does not match `creds`, verified by asking Git directly before and after. (a) is literal compliance and leaves two ignore files that both state their pattern set is identical to the root's now disagreeing with it, and leaves the pattern absent from the two contexts the documented image builds actually use. (b) would widen a pattern to catch a specific known filename, which is less precise about what is being excluded and why. (c) is not true of this action. The delivered form adds the pattern to the repository ignore file and to all three image ignore files, and the parity the backend file claims still holds — 172 patterns each, identical | Four files carry the pattern rather than one, so a future credential filename must be added in four places. The parity claim is now something to keep true, and it is checked by comparing the two pattern sets rather than trusted |
| 82.24 | **Correct the environment template's start claim by separating rendering from starting**, rather than by weakening the template or changing the value | (a) Delete the sentence; (b) ship a signing key that does start, so the sentence becomes true; (c) leave it and treat it as approximate | The template claimed a verbatim copy "renders and starts", and the second half is false: the signing-key placeholder it ships is refused in every environment including local, so both the API and the migration service exit on it — which the template's own header and the rotation runbook already stated correctly, so the file contradicted itself. (a) removes a useful statement, because the rendering half is true and worth knowing: every name the orchestration marks required is present, so substitution does not fail. (b) is refused by an existing decision — a committed working signing key is the class of defect this work exists to close. (c) leaves a reader to discover by failure what the file could have told them. The corrected passage states both facts, names the one value that must be replaced, and points at the script that generates one. Verified: the shipped value is refused by the application's own validator, the stale wording is gone, the template still documents every settings field, and the contract suite still passes | None identified. The passage is longer than the sentence it replaces, which is the cost of being accurate about two different outcomes |
| 82.25 | **Keep the ingestion task's deprecated coroutine decorator, and re-verify it under the new execution path** | (a) Replace it with `async def` as forward-compatibility hygiene; (b) replace it and pin the interpreter harder to compensate | An earlier row already held this construct on the ground that it is valid on the pinned interpreter and is among the findings reported for confirmation rather than fixed. This round gave it a new reason to be re-examined rather than a new reason to change: the workload now runs from a scheduled Job that invokes it directly, so its callability under the pinned interpreter stopped being incidental. It was therefore **executed** — the exact command the Job runs, in this tree, exiting 0 — rather than assumed. (a) is out of scope and would edit a file for a reason no finding raises. (b) does not follow from anything | The construct will fail on Python 3.11 or later, which is a forward-compatibility debt this round does not discharge and which the residual-risk register carries. It is also, usefully, one of the reasons the pin is not merely a preference |
| 82.26 | **Keep the ten unused cosmetic Terraform variable names, including the three that now name a resource this configuration no longer provisions** | (a) Delete all ten; (b) delete only the three that name the removed function; (c) rename the three to describe the replacement workload | The plan states in terms that pre-existing unused variables are deliberately left alone as cosmetic, and every one of the ten carries a default, so none forces an operator to supply anything and none affects an apply. (a) is a change no finding asks for, in a file where the round already makes substantial changes — the wider the incidental diff, the harder the substantive changes are to review. (b) is the same objection at smaller scale, and it is the one option with a real argument in its favour, which is why this row exists: three names surviving their resource is untidy. It is untidy and inert, and recording it is the cheaper remedy than editing. (c) would invent names for a workload the manifests already name properly | Three variable names describe nothing. A reader may look for the function they name and not find it; this row and §82.1 are where that reader should land. If a later round is given licence to tidy, deleting the three is the change to make |

### Deliberate non-changes from this round

The round's subject was a deployment surface that had almost no automated
coverage, so nearly every finding could have been closed by making a claim
narrower rather than by making the deployment work. These are the changes
deliberately not made.

* **The interpreter pin was not advanced**, at any surviving site. §82.1 removes
  two sites by removing the resources that declared them; the two version
  declarations and the one code-level constraint that remain are unchanged, and
  §82.27 enumerates them.
* **The frontend was not edited.** `frontend/package.json` is a read-only
  reference, so the lint gate was solved inside the workflow per §82.15 rather
  than by adding the script that would have been the obvious fix. The JSX-in-a-`.ts`
  defect the exclusion works around is reported, not repaired.
* **`infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` was not edited by this round.** It
  carries a change made by an earlier round, which §82.27 records and withdraws a
  claim about; this round only corrected the documents that described it wrongly.
* **`backend/app/api/router.py` remains untouched**, as it has through every round,
  and no application source was modified at all: this round changed infrastructure,
  pipelines, scripts, ignore files, the environment template and documentation.
* **The trusted-host middleware was not given a health-path exemption.** §82.21
  records the probe-side fix chosen instead, because an exempt health path is a
  hole in the control being added.
* **No gate was weakened to make it pass.** The lint step is a real gate over
  twenty-two files rather than a no-op; the integration job runs real commands
  against a real database; the readiness gate can fail; and the signing-key
  parity harness was used to find a defect rather than to confirm an assumption.
* **The credential rotation was not performed.** It is operational, irreversible
  and sequenced last by design; `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` owns it.
* **No provider version constraint and no remote state backend were added.** Both
  are among the findings reported for confirmation at row 34.6.3 and neither is in
  this round's scope, even though the round makes large changes to the same files.
  This statement describes the tree as delivered, in both halves. *The clause that
  once followed it &mdash; that a provider constraint and a tracked lock were added
  later and authorized at row 94.8.3 &mdash; is withdrawn by row 96.1.1:* row
  80.3.1 added them, row 91.1.1 reverted them, and row 94.8.3 is itself withdrawn.
  Neither the constraint nor the remote state backend has been configured.

### 82.27 Reconciliations this round owes to earlier rows

Two rows above became false as a consequence of work done since they were
written, and one figure they carry is quoted by other documents. §27's convention
applies: neither row is deleted, both are marked in place, and the current
position is stated here.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 82.27.1 | **Superseded in its count by row 91.2.1: a later round reinstated the two declarations this row records as deleted, behind an authorization gate, so the tree carries four declarations and one code constraint again.** Row 1.9's substance stands and its site list is withdrawn. The pin is held wherever it is declared, as that row says. Its enumeration of five sites no longer describes the tree: the sites are now `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend` (`FROM python:3.9-slim`), `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (`python-version: '3.9'`) and the code-level constraint in `backend/app/tasks/listing_updater.py` (`@asyncio.coroutine`) — **two version declarations and one code constraint** | (a) Edit row 1.9 in place and leave no trace of the five-site list; (b) leave the list standing, since the pin itself is genuinely unchanged; (c) restore the two removed declarations so the list becomes true again | Read back from the tree: the managed-runtime declaration at `main.tf` and the deployment command's runtime flag at `deploy.sh` are both gone, because §82.1 deleted the resource and the command that targeted a decommissioned runtime. So two of the five sites do not exist to be pinned. (a) is what §27's convention forbids: the count *five* has been quoted by §34.1 and by three sibling documents, and a reader arriving with that figure needs to find out here where it went rather than to find it silently absent. (b) leaves a list a reader can disprove in thirty seconds. (c) would restore a resource that cannot be applied in order to make a documentation sentence true, which inverts the priority. **The direction of the change matters and is easy to misread:** the pin was not relaxed anywhere. Two places that declared it stopped existing, and the constraint the pin protects — code that a newer interpreter would break — is unchanged and was executed under the pinned interpreter for §82.25 | Every document quoting *five* is wrong until it is corrected, which is why this row names them: `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `README.md` and the presentation each state the count and each is corrected in this change set. A reader who sees three where they expected five may read it as the pin having been loosened; the paragraph above exists to prevent that reading |
| 82.27.2 | **Row 27.8's alternative (c) is no longer refused: the change it declined was subsequently made.** `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` declares both `REACT_APP_*` build arguments and exports them before the build command, so the values do reach the bundle. The file is a modified path, not an unmodified reference | (a) Leave row 27.8 as written, since it was accurate when written; (b) revert the change so the row becomes true again; (c) delete the row | Read back from the tree: the file carries two `ARG` declarations and an `ENV` export ahead of its build command, added by the round whose commit message names the developer bootstrap. Row 27.8 refused that change as out of scope on the ground that the plan classifies the file as a read-only reference — a correct reading of the plan at the time, and superseded by what was actually delivered. This matters beyond one row, because two sibling documents inherited the claim: the traceability matrix listed the file among nine paths "read to constrain the design and never modified" and recorded it as "confirmed unmodified; absent from the changed set", which is disprovable from a diff. Both statements are corrected in this change set. (b) would revert a change that closes the gap row 27.8 itself described as unclosed. (c) would hide that the position changed. **This round does not modify the file**; it corrects the records that described it | The plan designates the file read-only and it has been modified, so this is a scope departure by an earlier round that this row records rather than resolves. The change is narrow and additive — two build arguments and an export, no base image or command change — and it makes the file agree with the orchestration that passes those arguments. §82.28 counts it among the paths delivered beyond the plan, which is the honest classification: it is neither a planned change nor an untouched reference |

### 82.28 The rebuilt planned-versus-actual inventory

This subsection supersedes §23.1 and the closing figures of row 31.11. It is the
authority for every path count in this change set, and the reason it exists is the
one row 31.11 gave: a round that adds paths without rebuilding the reconciliation
makes the reconciliation wrong. Both earlier measurements were taken mid-project
and neither describes the delivered tree.

Measured with `git diff --name-status <baseline> HEAD` against baseline revision
`a26f7fb`, plus the untracked additions this round contributes, and compared path
by path against the 59 implementation and deliverable paths the plan enumerates at
§0.6.1.1 to §0.6.1.6.

| Quantity | Count |
|---|---|
| Paths changed | **91** |
| — added | **61** |
| — modified | **30** |
| — deleted | **0** |
| Paths the plan enumerates as changes (§0.6.1.1–§0.6.1.6) | **59** |
| — planned and delivered | **59** |
| — planned and still pending | **0** |
| Paths delivered beyond the plan | **32** |
| Reference-mode paths the plan enumerates (§0.6.1.7, plus the router module) | **10** |
| — still unmodified, as planned | **9** |
| — modified beyond the plan | **1** (`infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend`; see §82.27.2) |

`59 + 32 = 91`, and `61 + 30 + 0 = 91`. The plan's headline of **68** entries is a
different quantity: 59 planned changes plus the 9 counted reference paths, which
are read rather than written. **68 is not a count of changed files and must not be
quoted as one** — that distinction is the one statement §23.1 made which still
holds.

**This table's delivered figures are superseded, and its reference count with them.**
Rounds after it delivered further paths, and the scope revert of §91.1 removed one, so
the delivered figure is **124** — 94 added and 30 modified — of which **64** are beyond
the plan. Row 91.4.1 records the decision that
`docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` §2.10 is the single place that total is
published, and this table stands as the measurement its own round took. The row above
counting **10** reference-mode paths is superseded by row 91.4.2: the plan states
**nine**, and `backend/app/api/router.py` is contextual evidence counted in none of
them.

**The 32 paths delivered beyond the plan**, grouped by why they exist. Reverting
them was considered as a whole and refused. They partition as: **3** load-bearing at
build or run time, **9** required by a delivery path, **1** required by a build,
**1** a scope departure by an earlier round, and **18** holding passing coverage or
tooling configuration whose removal would lower assurance to satisfy a count —
`3 + 9 + 1 + 1 + 18 = 32`.

| Group | Count | Paths | Why they exist | Cost of keeping them |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Image ignore files | 2 | `backend/.dockerignore`, `frontend/.dockerignore` | Row 23.2.1. The plan names only the repository-root file, and the documented builds use `backend/` and `frontend/` as contexts, where Docker reads the ignore file from the context root. Honouring only the literal path would leave the image-content finding open for the documented builds | Three files to keep in agreement. The backend file claims parity with the root and that claim is verified by comparing pattern sets; the frontend file states its own narrower scope and claims none |
| Bounded rate-limit storage | 1 | `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py` | Row 23.2.2.
