## 83. The verification surface itself: audit records, pipelines, secret delivery and the deliverables

This round answers a review of thirty-two findings across the whole delivered
surface rather than one module: eleven critical, eleven major and ten minor. Its
subject is unusual for this log, because most of the findings concern the
machinery that proves the remediation rather than the remediation itself -- what a
migration writes into a build log, what a pipeline actually executes, whether a
provisioned secret is reachable by anything, and whether the documents this log
sits beside describe the tree they ship with. Four of its rows therefore revisit
earlier rows rather than only adding to them — three supersede and one upholds —
under the convention section 27 established: the earlier text stays, and is
marked.

### 83.1 Audit records, redaction and telemetry

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.1 | Redact before truncating in the exception-field builder, not after | (a) Truncate first and redact the shortened text, which is the cheaper order; (b) skip redaction for values below the truncation length; (c) raise the truncation length so the question does not arise | Truncation splits a value at a fixed offset. A credential that straddles that offset survives as two fragments, and neither fragment matches the pattern the redactor looks for, so redaction applied afterwards finds nothing and the leading fragment is written verbatim. The order is the control. (a) is exactly the defect the finding reported. (b) inverts the reasoning -- a short value is the easiest to match, not the safest to skip. (c) reduces the probability without removing the case, and a longer record is a worse record | Redacting the full text before shortening it costs a pass over a longer string on a path that only runs when an exception is already being recorded. Measured as immaterial against the cost of the exception itself |
| 83.2 | Give the queue handlers a counted, sanitised emit-failure fallback and treat a plain stream handler as foreign | (a) Leave the standard library's `handleError`, which writes the failing record and its traceback to standard error; (b) swallow an emit failure silently; (c) re-raise it | The standard fallback writes the *unredacted* record to a stream nothing governs, so a handler that fails while writing a redacted line publishes the unredacted one instead -- the redaction is bypassed precisely when something has already gone wrong. (b) loses the signal entirely, which is what makes a degraded sink invisible. (c) turns a logging failure into an application failure. A counted, sanitised fallback keeps the failure observable without publishing the payload, and the count is what the readiness route and the monitoring in section 35.3 read | A caller cannot see the failing record's content when a sink degrades, only that one degraded and how many times. That is the intended trade: the count answers "is something wrong", and answering "with what payload" is what leaked |
| 83.3 | Report a degraded audit or logging sink as one log record carrying a stable signal, and alert on it in the infrastructure, rather than adding a field to the readiness response | (a) Add the counters to the readiness body; (b) expose a separate authenticated diagnostics route; (c) leave the counters readable only in process | The readiness body is read by an unauthenticated caller -- that is what a probe is -- so a count of failed audit writes there tells anyone who can reach the service how well its auditing is working. The signal belongs where the rest of the audit trail is. The record is then counted by a log-based metric and alerted at a threshold of zero, because the signal is only emitted once a record has already been lost and there is no volume at which losing audit records is acceptable. (a) also breaks a test that fixes the body's keys, and that test is correct. (b) is a new route, which the Minimal Change Clause forbids for something a log record already carries. (c) leaves the counters unreachable by any operator | The signal is only as useful as log retention, so the same change sets retention on the bucket the records land in. An alert policy with no notification channel records incidents and notifies nobody; the channel list is an operator input, documented as one, and defaults to empty rather than to a fabricated address |
| 83.4 | Make the log level a validated setting, and refuse `DEBUG` outside a local environment | (a) Leave the level fixed at its code default, as the baseline did; (b) accept any level in any environment; (c) accept `DEBUG` anywhere but strip tracebacks at that level | The level was unreachable by configuration, so an operator could not raise verbosity to diagnose an incident. Making it configurable reopens a question the exception builder had settled, though: `log_exception` writes a traceback at `DEBUG`, and a traceback carries statement text and module paths. Refusing `DEBUG` outside `local` is what keeps both properties -- the level is operable, and the one level that publishes a traceback is confined to a developer's own machine. (c) would make `DEBUG` mean something different in different environments, which is worse than refusing it | An operator cannot raise a staging or production deployment to `DEBUG` without changing the environment name, which is deliberate. `INFO` and the reason codes carry the diagnosis instead, which is what section 35.2's counted signal and the stable decision codes exist for |
| 83.5 | Correlate with a W3C trace context minted per request, propagated on outbound calls, and returned on the response | (a) Keep the existing request identifier alone; (b) adopt a bespoke header; (c) add a tracing SDK | A single request identifier correlates records inside one process and nothing across a boundary. `traceparent` is the standard already understood by every collector, costs one header, and needs no dependency -- (c) would add a runtime library and an exporter for a correlation problem two identifiers solve. (b) would be a private convention nothing else reads. An inbound `traceparent` is adopted when well formed and minted otherwise, and a fresh span is bound per request, so a caller cannot pin two requests to one span | Returning `traceparent` on the response adds a per-request header, which broke three login-uniformity tests that compare every non-volatile header between two refusals. The header was added to the volatile set with the reason recorded there: any future per-request response header must join it, or those tests will fail for a correct change |

### 83.2 What a migration and a pipeline are allowed to publish

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.6 | Record the administrator by a stable non-reversible reference -- the leading twelve hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 digest of the address -- in the grant revision, in its error messages, and in every line the setup script prints. Keep the address itself as the value both compare against | (a) Keep recording the address, which is the most useful thing to read; (b) omit any identifier, recording only counts; (c) record a random per-run identifier | The grant revision's records land in a build log through `kubectl logs`, and the setup script's output lands in a developer's terminal and scrollback, so an address written there is published wherever those go. (a) is the finding. (b) makes a record unusable for correlation: two runs cannot be read against each other, and a post-condition failure cannot say which account it was about. (c) correlates nothing across runs, which is the property that matters. A digest prefix is the same in every environment and on every run, is not reversible to the address, and is short enough to read -- and because the revision and the script derive it from the same address, one output can be read against the other. A comparison is not a disclosure, so the address stays where it is compared | Twelve hexadecimal digits of a digest over a low-entropy input is not a secret: anyone who guesses the address can confirm it. The reference is a correlation handle, not a confidentiality control, and it is only ever written beside an already-published role name. What it removes is the *unconditional* publication of an address to every reader of a build log |
| 83.7 | Republish the migration container's output in the deployment workflow, rather than removing the step | (a) Drop `kubectl logs` so nothing is republished; (b) filter its output in the workflow with a pattern match; (c) write the output to an artefact instead of the log | Republishing is safe *because of* the changes made first: the migration environment installs the governed redacting configuration, removes every foreign handler, and the grant revision no longer records an address -- so the container's output is governed JSON before the workflow ever reads it. Removing the step would discard the only view an operator has of a failed upgrade, to solve a problem already solved upstream. (b) puts the redaction decision in a shell pattern, duplicating a control that already exists in one place and will drift from it. (c) hides the output behind an extra download for no gain | The safety of the step is a property of the logging configuration rather than of the step itself, so a future change that reintroduces an ungoverned handler in the migration environment would make this step leak again. That coupling is stated here and asserted by the migration tests, which read the governed stream directly |
| 83.8 | Report a failed migration pod with named `jsonpath` reads over an allowlist of fields, never with a pod description | (a) Keep `kubectl describe pod`, which is the conventional diagnostic; (b) describe the pod and redact the output; (c) report nothing beyond the phase | A description renders every container's environment, including values injected from secrets, into the build log of whatever ran it -- and a failed migration is exactly when someone reads that log closely. The fields that actually say why a run ended are few and nameable: the phase, each container's termination reason and exit code, and the pod conditions. Reading those individually is both narrower and more legible than a description. (b) redacts a format that changes between provider versions, which is a control that silently stops working. (c) leaves an operator with "Failed" and nothing else | A cause outside the allowlist -- an unusual scheduling failure, say -- is not reported and needs a manual look. Accepted: the manual look is a deliberate act by a person, while a description publishes to everyone who can read the log |
| 83.9 | Give the migration pod its own specification, its own service account and exactly one secret, written in the workflow rather than copied from the serving Deployment | (a) Keep copying the Deployment's environment, identity, volumes and mounts, which guarantees the pod can reach whatever the application can; (b) copy it and remove the entries not needed; (c) run the migration inside a serving pod with `kubectl exec` | The migration environment resolves one setting and reads no other, which is what makes a one-secret pod possible -- and copying the serving environment hands a schema-upgrade job the signing key and every provider credential for no reason. (a) is the finding. (b) makes the pod's entitlement a subtraction from a list that lives in another object, so a value added to the Deployment silently appears in the migration pod too. (c) is worse still: it runs the upgrade inside a process that holds every secret. Writing the specification here means the pod's entitlement is visible in the file that creates it, and the identity is granted read access to one secret in section 35.3 | The pod no longer inherits image-pull secrets, so a cluster pulling from a registry that needs one requires that to be added deliberately. The `SecretProviderClass` volume must also be mounted for the synchronised secret to exist, which the specification does -- a grant of one secret with a class mounting six would fail at run time, so both halves are asserted together |
| 83.10 | Report an operator's own identity by the same non-reversible reference rather than echoing the account | (a) Echo the active account, which is genuinely useful when several are configured; (b) print nothing; (c) print only the account's domain | A deployment script's output is a build log or a shared terminal. The purpose the echo served -- confirming which credentials a deployment ran under -- is served exactly as well by a stable reference, because the question is "was it the same identity as last time", not "what is the address". (b) removes the confirmation. (c) is a partial disclosure that still identifies a small organisation | An operator reading the line cannot tell *which* account it was without computing the digest themselves. The digest is a one-line command and the trade is the same as row 35.6's |

### 83.3 Secret delivery, and the enablers that make a grant mean something

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.11 | Grant read access one secret at a time to two dedicated identities, and enable the two cluster features without which those grants deliver nothing | (a) Grant a project-wide secret role, which is one binding instead of seven; (b) reuse the node pool's identity; (c) create the identities and the grants and stop there | Six secrets existed with no reader and no delivery path, so the provisioning was inert. (a) makes every secret created in future readable by whatever holds the role, which is the opposite of the property a per-secret grant creates: a secret added later is unreadable until it is granted deliberately. (b) would mean any pod that can reach the node's metadata endpoint holds every application credential. (c) is the subtler error and the one worth recording: a `workloadIdentityUser` binding with no workload identity pool, and a `SecretProviderClass` with no Secret Manager add-on, are resources that look complete and deliver nothing -- the same shape as the finding being fixed. The pool, the add-on and `GKE_METADATA` on the nodes are therefore part of the fix rather than an aside | Workload identity changes how a pod obtains credentials, so a workload relying on the node's identity would stop working. Nothing in this repository does. The Kubernetes service account names are inputs with defaults, and the migration one is asserted equal to the name the deployment workflow runs the pod as, so the two descriptions cannot drift apart silently |
| 83.12 | Declare the delivery as two `SecretProviderClass` documents -- all six secrets for the serving workload, one for the migration job -- in a version-controlled manifest the deployment renders and applies | (a) One class carrying all six, mounted by both workloads; (b) create the Kubernetes secret imperatively in the pipeline from values held as pipeline secrets; (c) leave delivery to be configured by hand against the cluster | Two classes is what makes the migration identity's single-secret grant enforceable: one class carrying six would require the migration identity to be able to read six. (b) puts every secret through the pipeline, which is the delivery mechanism this work exists to remove, and pipeline secrets are the tier OWASP places *below* a managed store. (c) leaves the last step of the path undocumented, which is how the gap being fixed arose. The manifest names versions to mount and carries no payload, and the only substitution the pipeline makes is the project identifier | A mount is a property of the workload rather than of the provider class, and the migration pod mounts its own. **The rest of this column is WITHDRAWN &mdash; see rows 82.4 as amended by 92.8, and 92.12:** the backend Deployment *is* in this repository, at `infrastructure/kubernetes/40-backend.yaml`, and it mounts the class itself, so its mount is not an operator step; and no synchronised Kubernetes secret materialises at all, because neither provider class declares `secretObjects`. The identity emails remain published as outputs so the annotation can be confirmed without reading the state file |
| 83.13 | Remove the provisioned event stream rather than wire it up | (a) Wire a publisher and a subscriber to it; (b) leave it provisioned, since it costs little; (c) leave it and document that nothing uses it | Nothing in the repository publishes to the topic, subscribes to it, or is triggered by it, and no requirement calls for an event stream. (a) is new functionality. (b) leaves a resource with an access policy of its own, reachable by whatever holds a project role, that no reader of the code can account for -- an unattended surface is a liability whatever it costs. (c) documents the anomaly instead of removing it. Its output is removed with it, because publishing the name of a resource nothing uses invites a consumer | If an event stream is wanted later it must be provisioned again, deliberately, alongside the publisher and subscriber that need it. The two topic-name variables predate this change and were already read by nothing; they are left declared, and recorded as such, because removing a declared input changes the configuration's interface for no security gain |
| 83.14 | Implement the two actionable items of the deferral block and delete it, refusing to carry a secret in the function's environment | (a) Leave the block, since two of its three items are open-ended; (b) delete the block without implementing anything; (c) implement the items and leave the block as a note | A block that tells a reader configuration "may need customization" is indistinguishable from configuration that was never finished, and it sat in the file that provisions the infrastructure. The two actionable items -- the function's environment and its egress -- are now operator inputs with validation. The environment map's validation refuses a name that reads as a credential, because a function's environment is rendered by the deployment API and by the console, so a secret there is readable by anyone holding view access. (b) would hide the omission rather than close it. (c) keeps the ambiguity the row exists to remove | The two open-ended items -- adjusting the cluster to requirements, adding whatever else a use case needs -- are not carried forward anywhere, because neither states a requirement that can be met or verified. Removing them loses nothing an implementer could have acted on |

### 83.4 Pipelines that are evidence rather than output

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.15 | Delete the integration workflow's frontend steps -- the lint step, the unit-test step, the coverage upload and the dependency install that fed them -- rather than raise the Node version so the install works | (a) Raise `node-version` from the end-of-life major so `npm ci` can read the lockfile, and keep the steps; (b) keep the steps and mark them non-blocking; (c) keep `npm ci` alone as a resolution check | None of the frontend steps could produce evidence: `frontend/package.json` declares no `lint` script, and `frontend/src` holds no test file, so two steps invoked things that do not exist. The install could not run either -- the committed lockfile is version 3, which the end-of-life major's bundled package manager cannot install -- and the coverage upload pointed at a directory nothing produces. That makes (a) tempting, and it is the option this round declined: the end-of-life Node pin is one of the ten findings the plan reports for confirmation rather than fixes at row 34.6.3, so changing its value here would resolve a flagged finding unilaterally. Deleting the steps removes the pin site instead of choosing a new value for it, which satisfies the executability finding by strict subtraction and leaves the flagged finding untouched. (b) keeps a green step that checks nothing, which is worse than no step. (c) keeps the one command that cannot run | The workflow no longer touches the frontend at all, so a frontend regression is caught by nothing in this pipeline. The frontend source is read-only in this work and outside the AAP's in-scope list, so there was nothing for such a gate to protect; if the frontend re-enters scope, the gate has to be built with a Node version, a lint configuration and at least one test, which is a deliberate piece of work rather than four steps that happen to be present |
| 83.16 | Replace the empty integration step with a gate that starts the application against a real PostgreSQL service, applies both revisions forward, reverses them and reapplies them, then exercises the running service over HTTP | (a) Leave the deferral comment; (b) assert the migrations against the suite's SQLite engine, which the unit tests already use; (c) start the application and probe only liveness | An empty step reports success without checking anything, which is the least honest state a pipeline can be in. The gate's value is precisely what the unit suite cannot cover: the revisions run against the engine the deployed database runs, so the reversibility the plan claims is observed on PostgreSQL rather than asserted on SQLite, and the service is exercised through its own HTTP surface. (c) misses the case that matters -- a process that answers liveness while unable to reach its database is a failed rollout that looks healthy. The signing key is minted inside the step and written nowhere, so the workflow file carries no key of its own | The gate adds a database service and a few minutes to every run. It also has real preconditions: placeholder provider values are accepted only under a local environment name, which is why the step sets one. Verified end to end against PostgreSQL 13 before being committed, rather than written and hoped for |
| 83.17 | Make the deployment workflow's gate job run the same checks the integration workflow runs, and gate the rollout on all of them | (a) Leave the gate at the security subset it carried; (b) trigger the integration workflow and wait for it; (c) trust that the commit already passed on the branch | A release was being cut from a revision that had cleared a subset of the checks an ordinary push clears, which means the pipeline's own guarantee did not extend to the thing it deployed. (c) is the assumption that makes that gap invisible -- nothing enforced it. (b) is the tidier design and is a workflow-orchestration change larger than the finding, with its own failure modes. Repeating the gate set is duplication, and it is duplication a test detects: the step names of both jobs are asserted to cover the same set, so the two cannot drift | The two workflows list their gates separately, so a gate added to one must be added to the other. That is exactly what the parity assertion reports, and it fails loudly rather than leaving the deployment gate quietly narrower |
| 83.18 | Pin every action to the commit its release tag pointed at, recording the release in a trailing comment | (a) Keep the moving major tags, which receive fixes automatically; (b) pin to full version tags rather than commits; (c) vendor the actions | A tag is a mutable reference its publisher can move onto other code, and an action runs with access to the job that uses it -- including its credentials. (b) is better than a moving major and still mutable. (c) is disproportionate. Every commit was resolved from the upstream repository at pin time, and every tag involved was lightweight, so the object each pointed at is the commit itself. The trailing comment is what lets a reader, and a dependency updater, see which release a hash is | A pinned action does not receive a fix until the pin is raised, so the pins need maintenance and a stale pin is an unpatched dependency. The recorded release is what makes raising one reviewable |
| 83.19 | Quote every parameter expansion in every workflow command and both scripts | (a) Fix only the expansions a reviewer named; (b) adopt a shell linter in the pipeline | An unquoted expansion carrying a space becomes two words and one carrying a glob becomes a file list, which in a deployment command is a silent misdeployment rather than an error. (a) leaves the class open. (b) is a reasonable addition and a larger one; the property is instead asserted directly by a scanner in the test suite that walks each command with a quoting-context stack, because nested quoting inside a command substitution defeats the naive count. That scanner reports zero on the developer setup script, which was already correct -- the control proving it is not vacuously passing | The scanner understands the shell constructs these files use rather than the whole language, so an exotic construct could be misread. Every construct present is covered, and a false positive would be a failing test rather than a silent gap |
| 83.20 | Gate the rollout on readiness as well as liveness, in the workflow and in the deployment script | (a) Keep the liveness probe alone; (b) add readiness only to the workflow; (c) rely on the rollout status the orchestrator reports | Liveness says a process is answering; readiness says the dependencies it needs are reachable. A rollout that answers liveness while unable to reach its database is a failed rollout that reports success, and (c) does not close that -- a ready replica count describes what the orchestrator scheduled, not what the application can do. The script previously performed no HTTP probe at all, so (b) would leave the operator path weaker than the automated one for no reason | Both paths now need a route to the service, which the script obtains with a port forward. A deployment where that is unavailable has to probe by another means; the alternative is not knowing whether the release works |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.21 | **Restored to truth by row 91.1.1, which undid the constraint row 80.3.1 had added after this row was written.** Add no provider version constraint and no remote state backend to the Terraform configuration, although this round adds resources that depend on a recent provider | (a) Add `required_providers` with a version constraint; (b) add both a constraint and a backend | Both are named in row 34.6.3 as findings reported for confirmation rather than fixed, and reporting a finding then fixing it in the same body of work makes the boundary a per-finding judgement. The dependence is recorded instead: the resources added this round were validated against the provider the tree resolves today, and the version is named in this row so a future reader knows what they were validated against | A future initialisation could resolve a provider that rejects one of the added arguments, and the failure would surface as a validation error rather than as a security defect. The finding remains open and is where the fix belongs |
| 83.22 | Leave the address in `administrator_summary`'s captured output, and leave both `"1\|address"` comparisons in the setup script | (a) Have the embedded interpreter emit the reference instead, so the address never crosses a process boundary; (b) compare on the count alone | The value is captured by a command substitution and compared; it is never written to a terminal or a log, so it is not the disclosure the finding concerns. (a) would add a digest computation inside the comparison path for no change in what is published. (b) would stop the check from confirming *which* account holds the role, which is the assertion worth making | A shell tracing mode would render the captured value. That is true of every command substitution in the script and is not specific to this one |
| 83.23 | Leave the Content Security Policy on the presentation at `connect-src 'none'`, accepting two console messages that appear only with developer tools open | (a) Widen `connect-src` to the delivery network so the messages disappear; (b) self-host the assets without source-map references; (c) omit the policy | With developer tools attached, the browser fetches the source-map side-files the delivery network's assets name, and the policy blocks them. The fetches are the debugger's, not the page's -- the file contains no request-issuing call of any kind -- and nothing rendered depends on them. (a) would permit the page to *send* data to the delivery network, which is what the directive exists to prevent, in exchange for quieting a message. (b) is a larger change to a deliverable that is required to be a single self-contained file. Verified in a real browser: every asset passed its integrity check, both diagrams drew, every icon rendered, all eighteen sections were reachable, and no integrity check failed | A reviewer who opens developer tools sees two messages mentioning the policy and may read them as a fault. The expectation is stated in a comment beside the policy itself, which is where such a reader will look |
| 83.24 | Keep the reserved-domain security alias rather than inventing a plausible mailbox | (a) Use a real-looking address at a domain this project does not control; (b) omit the email channel and offer only the private reporting channel; (c) name an individual | An address that looks deliverable but is not silently discards reports, which is worse than an address that is obviously inert. A reserved domain resolves nowhere by design, so the inertness is visible and pointing the alias at a monitored mailbox is a deployment step rather than an editing step. (c) is what the finding reported, and it breaks whenever the individual changes. (b) is defensible -- the private channel is the preferred one and needs no address -- but leaves a reporter without a fallback when that channel is unavailable | The email channel does not work until an operator delivers the alias. It is recorded as a deployment step in the review document, and the policy states plainly that the private channel is the only one that currently reaches anyone |
| 83.25 | **Rows 30.16, 32.11, 33.12 upheld.** The three pre-existing `flake8` findings in `backend/app/api/router.py` | (a) Correct them, which edits a file the AAP freezes; (b) suppress them with per-file ignores that would hide a new finding in the same file | Pre-existing in a file the AAP freezes, recorded as rows 12.6, 15.7, 26.18, 30.16, 32.11 and 33.12. Measured identical in kind, count and position before and after this round | Three style findings remain in a frozen file |

### 83.7 What a document may instruct an operator to do

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 83.29 | Send a generated secret straight into the store or file that will hold it, and never render it on a terminal | (a) Keep printing the value and add a warning to clear the terminal afterwards; (b) print it into a clipboard utility; (c) have the setup script own every generation so that no document shows a command at all | A value rendered on a terminal is retained by shell history, by terminal scrollback and by any session recording, and no rotation reaches any of those — so printing a replacement manufactures a fresh copy of exactly the exposure the rotation exists to remove, on the operator's own machine. (a) depends on the operator remembering, which is the assumption every one of these findings rests on. (b) is platform-specific and still exposes the value to any process that can read the clipboard. (c) is right for local bootstrap and is what the setup script already does, but the runbook has to serve an operator rotating a production value, where the destination is the managed store rather than a file. Two forms are delivered, and neither renders the value: a pipe into `gcloud secrets versions add --data-file=-`, and `( umask 077; printf … >> .env )`, which additionally creates the file unreadable to other accounts on the machine | The pipe form gives no confirmation of what was stored, so an operator cannot eyeball the value — which is the intent, and section 4 of the runbook reads the value back from the store rather than from a terminal. Five commands across three documents now share one shape; a sixth introduced in a document the scanner does not cover would not automatically follow it |
| 83.30 | Document history eradication as a procedure, and name the five places a force-push does not reach | (a) Name the tool and leave the operator to its documentation; (b) describe the rewrite only, since pushed refs are what a reviewer sees; (c) omit the step and rely on rotation alone | Step 3 of the sequence previously stated what to achieve without stating how, and the failure mode is a rewrite that *looks* complete: heads and tags rewritten while the value survives in the provider's hidden pull-request refs, in forks, in mirrors and backups, in continuous-integration caches, artefacts and images, and in every clone taken before the rewrite. Naming those categories, and making a re-clone mandatory rather than advisory, is the difference between a procedure and an aspiration. (c) is not available: rotation de-authorises the credential but the committed value stays readable, and removal is required alongside revocation | The procedure is destructive and rewrites shared history. It is therefore stated with its preconditions and sequenced strictly after revocation, so that a rewrite performed early cannot leave a live credential inside an existing clone |
| 83.31 | Return the misplaced subsection to the section it belongs to, rather than renumbering it to match where it sat | (a) Renumber it to `24.6`, a one-character change; (b) leave it and add a pointer from section 21 | The block measures the scope of the second rationale pass and refers to section 21.22 by number, while section 24 concerns the compose runtime environment and has no bearing on it. Renumbering would make the heading agree with its location and disagree with its content, and would strand the cross-reference's context. The move is length-neutral and leaves both sections ending on their own material. The generalisation matters more than either instance: the check written for this class walks every heading in this log rather than the one heading the review named, and it is what found this second occurrence | None to the tree. A reader following an external reference to "the last subsection of section 24" would now find it under section 21 |
| 83.32 | Pin the presentation's three taggable remote assets with subresource integrity, declare the diagram module's hash in an import map, and constrain every origin with a Content Security Policy — retaining two documented residuals rather than vendoring | (a) Vendor all four assets into the repository, which pins them on every browser; (b) pin only the two scripts, since a stylesheet executes nothing; (c) leave the assets as they were and rely on the delivery network's own integrity | Each asset is code that runs with full access to the page, and a delivery network is a third party that can serve different bytes to different requests, so (c) is the state the finding names. (a) would pin everything, at the cost of committing roughly 540 KB of minified third-party code — including a 25 KB module and a 356 KB icon bundle — into a security remediation change set, where every reviewer would then have to take it on trust; the hashes declared inline are reviewable in a way vendored bytes are not. (b) leaves a stylesheet able to load fonts and images and to reposition anything on the page. The two residuals are stated in the document itself beside the tags: the typeface stylesheet is negotiated per browser so no hash describes it, and import-map integrity is a recent addition that an older browser ignores. Both fall back to origin restriction, which the policy supplies, and `connect-src 'none'` means an asset compromised past its hash still cannot send anything anywhere | Two console messages appear when developer tools are open, for the source-map side-files the policy blocks — row 35.23 records why the policy is not widened to quiet them. A version bump to any pinned asset requires its hash to be recomputed, and a stale hash fails closed: the asset is refused and the slide it serves stops rendering, which is loud rather than silent |

---

## 84. Release automation, infrastructure and audit governance

This section records the decisions made in response to the release-readiness
review of the deployment script, the two workflows, the Terraform configuration,
the developer bootstrap script and the written record. Each subsection covers one
grouping of that work.

### 84.1 Audit governance: registering the development advisory set

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.1.1 | **Carry two registers in `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`** &mdash; a *Runtime register* for the seven advisories in `backend/requirements.txt` and a *Development register* for the seven in `backend/requirements-dev.txt` &mdash; and reduce the development manifest's header to package and pin metadata that points at it | (a) Leave the development set documented in the manifest header, as it was; (b) merge both sets into one undifferentiated register of fourteen; (c) drop the development suppressions and let the audit fail | The audit gate suppressed fourteen identifiers while the register covered seven and explicitly said the development set was "deliberately excluded from every count", so seven advisories were suppressed in continuous integration with **no entry in any authoritative artifact** &mdash; a second accepted set that a reader of the register, `SECURITY.md` or the executive deck could not see. (a) is the finding: it leaves an accepted-risk argument, with its control evidence and its rationale, living inside a dependency manifest, which Rule 1 reserves for the decision log and the register. (b) would apply one control argument to two populations that differ by an order of magnitude &mdash; a runtime package is installed where requests are served and needs a per-defect argument, a development package is absent from the image and its control *is* that absence &mdash; so a merged register would overstate one half and understate the other. (c) is addressed by row 35.1.2 | A reader who quotes "seven" without naming a manifest is now ambiguous where before they were merely incomplete. Mitigated by stating the manifest beside every figure in the register, `SECURITY.md`, `README.md` and the deck, and by §34.1 recording **14** with its split as the single origin for the quantity |
| 84.1.2 | **Keep the seven development suppressions** rather than removing them by moving to tooling versions that carry no advisory | (a) Raise `pytest` to 9.0.3 and the scanner stack to its fixed releases; (b) drop `pip-audit` and lose the dependency gate; (c) stop pinning the development manifest so resolution floats to fixed releases | Every one of the seven fix versions was offered to pip under CPython 3.9.25 with `--dry-run --no-deps` and **every one was refused**, because each declares `Requires-Python >=3.10`. (a) is therefore not available without advancing the interpreter, which row 1.9 forecloses at all five pin sites. (b) would remove the control that detects a vulnerable runtime dependency, trading a development-only advisory for a runtime blind spot. (c) would make the verification environment unreproducible, which is the same class of gap as the missing manifest recorded as INFRA-5, and would still resolve to 3.9-compatible releases | The development tooling stays on versions with known advisories. Accepted because none of the five packages is declared in the runtime manifest, so none reaches the deployed image or any request; the controls are stated per advisory in the Development register |
| 84.1.3 | **Publish the total as fourteen while keeping the two registers distinct**, and state the manifest alongside every advisory figure in the register, `SECURITY.md`, `README.md` and the executive deck | (a) Advertise only the runtime seven, as the artifacts did; (b) advertise only the total of fourteen; (c) publish the union of distinct identifiers without a per-manifest breakdown | (a) is what the review found: leadership and security artifacts advertised seven while the pipeline suppressed fourteen, so the pipeline and the documents disagreed. (b) inflates the apparent exposure of the deployed service sevenfold, because it counts tooling that no deployed process installs. The pair of figures with the split is the only form that is true from both directions, which is why the register's total-suppression accounting states both and why the two sets are recorded as disjoint | Two figures are more to keep in agreement than one. Mitigated by §34.1 holding the quantity once and by a contract test asserting the register and both workflows agree, so a change to one without the other fails the build |
| 84.1.4 | **Supersede row 31.12's pointer at "the development manifest's own accepted-advisory register."** The substance of that row stands &mdash; `redis` and `PyYAML` are still explained there &mdash; but the destination it names no longer exists | (a) Rewrite row 31.12 in place; (b) leave the pointer and let a reader follow it to a header that no longer holds the content | The row's own closing sentence anticipated this move, recording that the register "is the document that should carry the development register alongside the runtime one". Now that it does, the pointer resolves to the register rather than to the manifest. (a) would erase the fact that the content moved, which is precisely what §27 established this log records rather than hides. (b) leaves a dangling reference, which the review treats as a documentation defect in its own right | A reader of row 31.12 in isolation follows a superseded pointer. Mitigated by this row and by the manifest header itself naming the register, so either path arrives at the same place |
| 84.1.5 | **Assert the suppression sets from the tests rather than trusting the comment beside them** | (a) Rely on the workflow comment naming the register; (b) check the sets by review at release time | The condition the review found was a comment claiming every suppressed identifier was registered while seven were not, so a comment is demonstrably capable of drifting from the lists beside it. `backend/tests/security/test_release_automation_contract.py` now asserts that each audit invocation suppresses exactly the registered set, that each set appears in the register, and that both workflows agree with each other &mdash; so adding a suppression without registering it, or registering one without suppressing it, fails the build. (b) detects the drift only after it has shipped | The tests encode the identifier lists in a third place. Accepted deliberately: three sources that must agree and are compared automatically is stronger than two that agree only by inspection |

### 84.2 Release automation: reaching the cluster, and what is published

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.2.1 | **Reach the private control plane over the authorized DNS endpoint**, adding `control_plane_endpoints_config { dns_endpoint_config { allow_external_traffic = … } }` while `enable_private_endpoint` stays `true`, and passing `--dns-endpoint` on both release paths | (a) Make the control plane public; (b) add the runner's egress to the authorized-networks list; (c) run the release from a VPC-connected self-hosted runner or through a bastion | The release workflow ran on a public GitHub runner against a cluster whose endpoint is private, so it could never have reached the control plane at all &mdash; the failure was total rather than intermittent. (a) trades a release path for a permanently public administrative surface. (b) is not durable: GitHub-hosted runner egress is a large, changing range, so the list would either be ineffective or effectively public. (c) is a legitimate answer and is deliberately kept available rather than foreclosed &mdash; `var.gke_dns_endpoint_external_traffic` set to `false` selects it. The DNS endpoint is authorized by the IAM permission `container.clusters.connect` rather than by source address, needs no bastion or peering, and is non-destructive on an existing cluster | Access now depends on an IAM permission rather than on network position, so the binding for the deploying principal is the control that matters and must be reviewed as such. The endpoint requires a recent `gcloud`; the workflow pins the SDK setup action rather than assuming the runner image |
| 84.2.2 | **Write cluster credentials into a kubeconfig private to the run** (`KUBECONFIG_FILE="$(mktemp)"`, exported, removed by the `EXIT` trap), and assert the resulting context and namespace before anything mutates | (a) Use the invoking user's default kubeconfig, as the script did; (b) set the context explicitly with `kubectl config use-context` | The script previously ran `gcloud config set project` and then `kubectl` with no credential acquisition at all, so it applied to whatever context happened to be active on the machine &mdash; a confused deputy that could roll a release into an unrelated cluster while reporting success. (a) is that defect. (b) still shares mutable global state with everything else on the host, and a concurrent process can change it between the set and the use | A release now fails on a host where `mktemp` or the temporary directory is unavailable. Accepted: failing to start is the correct outcome when the credential cannot be isolated |
| 84.2.3 | **Refuse a reused image tag, roll out by digest, and verify the running `imageID`** | (a) Roll out by tag, as the script did; (b) rely on `immutable_tags` in the registry alone; (c) use `kubectl rollout restart` after pushing over the tag | `kubectl set image` with an unchanged tag is a no-op that exits 0, so a release could report success having changed nothing. (a) is that defect. (b) is a genuine and stronger control and is *also* adopted (row 35.4.2), but it protects the registry rather than the rollout: a tag that was never pushed twice can still be re-applied to a Deployment with no effect. (c) restarts pods without proving which image they came up on. Reading each pod's `containerStatuses[].imageID` back through the Deployment's own selector is the only check that establishes what is actually running | Three controls now guard one property, which is deliberate: the registry refuses the push, the script refuses the tag, and the verification refuses the outcome. A digest-pinned Deployment is harder to read at a glance than a tagged one |
| 84.2.4 | **Apply the migrations before the rollout, in a bounded one-shot pod built from the newly published image** that inherits only the backend Deployment's `serviceAccountName`, `env`, `envFrom`, `volumes` and `imagePullSecrets` | (a) Keep the original order, exec'ing into `pods.items[0]` after the rollout; (b) use a Kubernetes `Job`; (c) add an init container to the Deployment; (d) run Alembic from the runner against the database directly | (a) is two defects at once: new code serves traffic against an unmigrated schema for the length of the rollout, and `items[0]` is whichever pod the API listed first &mdash; possibly an old one, possibly none. (b) is the idiomatic vehicle but this repository ships no manifests, so a Job would have to be authored and owned somewhere that does not exist. (c) runs the migration once per replica and blocks every pod on it. (d) requires the runner to reach the database, which the private-network configuration deliberately prevents. A one-shot pod inheriting the Deployment's own identity uses exactly the credentials and settings the application uses, so a migration that succeeds proves the application's own delivery path works | The pod is not owned by a controller, so a node failure mid-migration surfaces as a failed release rather than a retry. That is the intended behaviour: the release stops and nothing rolls forward |
| 84.2.5 | **Make the migration pod name unique per run attempt** (`backend-migrate-<sha:12>-<run_id>-<run_attempt>`) and wait for the absence of any prior pod on a bounded deadline before creating it | (a) Keep the deterministic per-commit name; (b) let `kubectl run` generate a suffix; (c) delete with `--wait=true` and no deadline | (a) means a re-run of the same commit &mdash; the ordinary response to a transient failure &mdash; collides with the terminated pod from the first attempt and fails `AlreadyExists`, so the retry cannot work. (b) makes the pod unlocatable for the cleanup trap and for an operator reading logs. (c) can hang indefinitely, which converts one stuck pod into a stuck release with no diagnosis. The chosen form is DNS-safe, ~41 characters, and identifies the attempt it belongs to | A name encoding the attempt is longer and less memorable. The absence wait adds up to 300 seconds to a release that follows a hard-killed attempt |
| 84.2.6 | **Never cancel a release in flight** (`concurrency.cancel-in-progress: false`) | (a) Cancel superseded runs, the common default for cost; (b) omit `concurrency` entirely | This workflow publishes images, applies schema revisions and rolls two Deployments forward. Cancelling between any two of those leaves the cluster part-way through: a migrated schema with old code, or one Deployment forward and one back. (a) optimises runner minutes at the cost of a half-applied release. (b) permits two releases to interleave, which is worse than either | A queued release waits for the one ahead of it. Accepted deliberately: a release is not a build |
| 84.2.7 | **Probe `/health/ready` through a port-forward after the rollout**, rather than the liveness route or an external address | (a) Probe `/health`; (b) probe the public ingress address; (c) trust `kubectl rollout status` alone | `/health` answers 200 while the database is unreachable; `/health/ready` answers 503, which is precisely the failure a release can introduce by rolling forward against a database it cannot reach. (b) depends on ingress, DNS and certificates that are outside this repository and would report their failures as release failures. (c) reports that pods became ready by their configured probe, which is not the same as the application answering. A port-forward reaches the Service the release just changed, with no external dependency | The forward is a transient local process that must be torn down; the step is bounded and cleans up. A cluster with no reachable Service fails the step, which is the intended signal |
| 84.2.8 | **Require `jq` and `timeout` as prerequisites** and check every prerequisite before doing anything | (a) Parse JSON with `grep`/`sed`; (b) implement the deadlines in pure bash with `SECONDS` loops; (c) check tools lazily as each is first used | The script reads digests and pod image identifiers out of API responses, and hand-rolled JSON parsing is the classic source of a release that silently matches the wrong field. Deadlines exist so a hung `docker push` or `gcloud` call cannot stall a release indefinitely. (c) means a release can fail half-way through because a tool needed at step 6 was never present | Two more prerequisites on a release host, both stated in `usage()` and checked with a clear message. `timeout` is absent on stock macOS, so a release from a developer laptop needs coreutils |
| 84.2.9 | **Pair the two federated-identity actions and keep them together** &mdash; the authentication action obtains the short-lived credential and the SDK setup action consumes it, with `id-token: write` granted at the job rather than the workflow | (a) Keep the long-lived service-account key in a repository secret; (b) grant `id-token: write` workflow-wide; (c) use only the SDK action and authenticate inside a step | (a) is the finding: a static key that never expires, is copied into every fork's secret UI expectation, and cannot be scoped per run. (b) widens the token grant to jobs that have no business exchanging it, including the verification job. (c) means the credential is materialised in shell rather than by an action that scopes and cleans it up. The two actions must both be present and in that order, which is easy to break by deleting one, so it is recorded here as a pairing rather than as two independent choices | Workload Identity Federation must be configured in the Google Cloud project before the first release; the README records the two secrets it needs. A misconfigured provider fails at authentication with a message about the provider rather than about the release |
| 84.2.10 | **Keep the verification job separate from, and a precondition of, the deploy job** (`needs: verify`), running the dependency audit, the static analyser and the security suite there | (a) Fold the gates into the deploy job's early steps; (b) rely on the CI workflow having run on the same commit | (a) means a release that fails its own gates has already authenticated to Google Cloud and configured a registry helper before it stops. Separation keeps every credential-bearing step downstream of every gate. (b) is not sound: the CI workflow runs on pull requests and pushes, but nothing guarantees it completed for the exact commit being released, and a required-check configuration lives outside this repository | The two jobs each install dependencies, so a release pays that cost twice. Accepted for the ordering property |
| 84.2.11 | **Pin each action to its current major** (`checkout@v7`, `setup-python@v6` and the corresponding majors for authentication and SDK setup) rather than to a full version or a commit digest | (a) Pin to an exact patch version; (b) pin to a commit SHA, the strictest supply-chain form; (c) leave the previous, deprecated majors in place | The workflow carried majors whose runner support is deprecated, which is a build that will stop working rather than a security control. (b) is the strongest option and was rejected as disproportionate here: it pins to a digest with no automated updater configured in this repository, so the pins would rot and the next reviewer would face stale actions with no way to tell an intentional pin from a forgotten one. (a) has the same problem in a milder form. Majors receive security fixes without a manual bump | A compromised action release inside a trusted major would be consumed automatically. Recorded here as the accepted residual of this choice, with (b) named as the upgrade path if the repository ever adopts an updater |

### 84.3 Paths delivered beyond the plan, reconciled

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.3.1 | **Record thirteen further unplanned paths, taking the delivered-beyond-plan set from the eleven of §23.2 to twenty-four**, and index all twenty-four in `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` §2.9 and §4.1. They are `setup.cfg`; `frontend/.dockerignore`; `backend/tests/support.py`; and the modules `test_migration_gate.py`, `test_migration_revisions.py`, `test_revision_contracts.py`, `test_admin_seed_migration.py`, `test_rate_limit_store.py`, `test_deployment_contract.py`, `test_setup_script.py`, `test_setup_script_bootstrap.py`, `test_release_automation_contract.py` and `test_operator_documentation.py` | (a) Leave §23.2 at eleven and let the matrix keep deferring to it; (b) delete the paths not enumerated by the plan; (c) fold them into §23.2 in place, as though that round had recorded them | (a) is the finding: the matrix asserted bidirectional coverage with no gaps while real delivered paths appeared in neither of its indexes, so the assertion could be disproved by listing the changed files. (b) would delete the verification configuration that makes the documented commands reproducible, the ignore file that closes INFRA-3 for the frontend build context, and passing coverage of both migration revisions, the rate-limit bound and the release automation &mdash; lowering assurance to satisfy a count. (c) would misattribute this round's paths to an earlier one and destroy the record of when each appeared, which §27 established this log does not do. Each path's own justification: `setup.cfg` makes `flake8`, `pytest` and `coverage` behave identically from the repository root and from `backend/`, the two directories the documented commands and the CI workflow use; `frontend/.dockerignore` covers a build context the root file does not reach; `backend/tests/support.py` holds shared values and imports nothing from `backend.app`, so importing it constructs no application; the ten modules each cover a unit that no planned module executes | The delivered-beyond-plan set is now more than twice what §23.2 recorded, which a reader may read as scope drift. Nineteen of the twenty-four are test modules and one is a lint configuration, so the runtime surface beyond the plan is two files: `rate_limit.py` and the two ignore files. The plan's 68 is unchanged and remains the figure other documents quote |

### 84.4 Infrastructure the release paths depend on

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.4.1 | **Provision an Artifact Registry Docker repository and publish to `<region>-docker.pkg.dev`**, retiring `gcr.io` from both release paths | (a) Keep `gcr.io` paths; (b) create a `gcr.io` redirect repository in Artifact Registry and keep the old paths working; (c) use a third-party registry | Container Registry was shut down for writes, so (a) is a release that cannot push. (b) works but preserves a legacy path shape that no longer matches where the images live, and it still requires the Artifact Registry resource this repository did not have &mdash; so it is the same amount of provisioning for a less honest result. (c) adds a credential and a trust boundary for no benefit inside one cloud project | Existing references to `gcr.io` anywhere outside this repository break. The README records the new path shape, and a test asserts the string `gcr.io` appears in neither release path |
| 84.4.2 | **Set `immutable_tags = true` on the repository** | (a) Leave tags mutable and rely on the script's reuse check; (b) enforce immutability by convention | The script's check reads the registry before pushing, which is a check with a window: two releases could pass it concurrently. The registry refusing the second push closes that window at the source, and it applies to a push from anywhere, not only from the script. (b) is not a control | A tag genuinely published in error cannot be overwritten; it must be superseded by a new tag. That is the intended cost |
| 84.4.3 | **Scope the registry IAM to the repository**, with a writer binding for the release principals and a reader binding for the node service account | (a) Grant the roles at project level; (b) reuse the node service account for pushing | (a) grants write access to every repository the project will ever have, including ones created later for unrelated purposes. (b) collapses the publish and pull identities, so a compromised node could push images. Separate, repository-scoped bindings keep both blast radii small | Adding a second repository later needs its own bindings. Deliberate |
| 84.4.4 | **Grant `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` per secret per principal**, expanded with `setproduct` over the six secrets and a required, validated principal list, and publish the resulting pairs as an output | (a) Grant the role at project level; (b) grant it on each secret to a single hard-coded service account; (c) leave delivery to whatever the cluster is configured with, as before | Six secrets and their versions existed with **no accessor binding at all**, so the delivery path was undefined and the workload's access, if any, came from somewhere outside this configuration. (a) grants access to every secret in the project including ones added later. (b) hard-codes an identity that differs per environment. The chosen form is read-only, so a compromised workload can neither add a version nor change a binding; the list rejects `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` and must be non-empty, so a plan cannot apply with delivery left unspecified; and the published pairs make a secret with no accessor visible in `terraform output` rather than discoverable at runtime | `terraform apply` now requires a principal list that had no previous equivalent, so an existing workspace must supply it. The README records it as required |
| 84.4.5 | **Gate the Cloud Function and its invoker binding with `count`** rather than deleting the resource or advancing the runtime | (a) Advance the runtime to a supported version; (b) delete the resource; (c) leave it and let `apply` fail; (d) fail the whole release when the function step is reached | The runtime is past its published decommission date, so create and update are refused &mdash; and the runtime pin is a hard constraint of this work that must not be advanced, which forecloses (a). The review that raised it says the same: do not silently weaken the pin. (b) destroys a deployed function as a side effect of a documentation-accuracy fix. (c) makes every unrelated `apply` fail on a resource nobody asked to change. (d) blocks the image and schema work, which is unaffected. The gate defaults to off, so the resource leaves the plan and the script's step reports itself blocked with the decommission, the pin, and the two decisions available to an owner | The function is not managed until an owner sets the flag, and an existing deployed function drifts from configuration in the meantime. That is the visible form of an escalation, and it is stated in the resource's own comment, in the variable's description, in the script's output and in the README |
| 84.4.6 | **Express the function's name, region, entry point and source object as variables whose defaults are exactly the values the script freezes** | (a) Leave the literals in both files; (b) have the script read them from `terraform output` | The two files named different functions from different sources, so Terraform's invoker binding governed a resource the script never deployed &mdash; the restriction protected nothing. (a) leaves two literals to drift again. (b) couples the script to a Terraform state it may not be able to read, and to a workspace selection. Shared defaults plus a test asserting the four values agree across the two files gives one contract that fails a build when it diverges | The agreement is enforced by a test rather than by construction. Named as such so a future change knows what to keep |
| 84.4.7 | **Publish the cluster's name and its regional location as outputs, and describe the location as a region rather than a zone** | (a) Leave the pipeline's own variables as the only record; (b) publish a combined `location` string | The workflow addressed a regional cluster with `--zone`, which cannot resolve. Publishing the authoritative values from the configuration that creates the cluster gives the pipeline something to be checked against, and naming the kind in the description is what stops the same substitution recurring | Outputs are only as useful as the consumer that reads them; the workflow still takes the region from a repository variable, validated against a region-shaped pattern so a zone is refused with the pattern quoted |

### 84.5 The developer bootstrap contract

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.5.1 | **Require a named database administrator (`SETUP_DB_ADMIN_USER`) and preflight it before any side effect**, skipping the check when an existing environment file already names a configured `DATABASE_URL` | (a) Keep connecting as whoever invoked the script; (b) prompt for the administrator interactively; (c) preflight unconditionally | The script created a role and a database with `psql`/`createdb` carrying no connection options, so it silently used the invoking account's ambient identity &mdash; and it did so *after* building a virtual environment, installing two manifests and writing an environment file, so a privilege failure arrived only once the machine had been changed. (a) is that defect. (b) cannot work in an unattended run. (c) would demand an administrator from someone re-running the script purely to refresh dependencies. The preflight and the step consult the *same* helper to decide whether a mutation will happen, so they cannot disagree | Anyone creating the database must now supply an administrator name and its authentication. Stated in `usage()` and in the README, and the refusal names both the variable and the privileges required |
| 84.5.2 | **Pass `--no-password` on every administrative `psql` invocation** | Allow the interactive prompt | An unusable credential should fail with a message, not block an automated run forever on an invisible prompt. A hung setup script is indistinguishable from a slow one | An operator relying on interactive entry must use `PGPASSWORD` or `.pgpass` instead. The refusal says so |
| 84.5.3 | **Replace `createdb` with `psql_admin --command "CREATE DATABASE … OWNER …"`, and drop `createdb` from the required-tool list** | (a) Give `createdb` the same connection options; (b) keep it in the tool list for safety | (a) is workable but leaves two tools to keep in agreement about identity, host and port. One wrapper is the only place a connection is made, which is what makes the identity auditable. Keeping a tool in the prerequisite list that the script never invokes would fail setup on a machine that is in fact able to run it | A reader familiar with `createdb` finds a `CREATE DATABASE` statement instead. The tool list now matches what is actually called, asserted by a test |
| 84.5.4 | **Refuse a database password containing `$`, `\`, `"`, `'` or a backtick, rather than escaping it** &mdash; and offer to generate one when the prompt is answered empty | (a) Escape the value for each consumer; (b) accept anything and document the hazard | The same password is written three times: literally as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, and percent-encoded inside two connection URLs. Compose interpolates `$` in the literal form, and the two URLs need percent-encoding, so (a) means three transformations that must all stay correct as the file evolves &mdash; and the original defect was exactly one of them being absent. Refusing an alphabet that needs no transformation removes the class of bug rather than handling it. Generation on an empty prompt means the safe path is also the easy path | A user's preferred password may be refused. The refusal names the accepted set, and pressing Enter produces a conforming one |
| 84.5.5 | **Verify the written file by parsing it and requiring all three entries to agree, rather than by trusting one parser** | (a) Read it back with `dotenv_values`; (b) compare only the literal entry | (a) was the first implementation and it **silently passed a file whose `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` contained a bare `$`**, because `python-dotenv` does not interpolate the `$NAME` form that Compose does. A check that models one consumer certifies a file the other consumer misreads. The delivered check requires all three entries present, requires no raw value to contain any character a reader transforms, requires the literal to match exactly, and requires each URL's password segment to percent-decode to it &mdash; then and only then is the file moved into place | The check is stricter than any single consumer requires. That is the point, and the code comment was corrected to say what the check does rather than which parser it imitates |

### 84.6 Operator documentation

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.6.1 | **Guard the environment-file copy with an explicit existence test that reports what it did**, and name the setup script as the preferred path | (a) `cp -n`; (b) `cp -i`; (c) keep the unguarded copy | The documented `cp .env.example .env` overwrites a file holding real secrets and exits 0. (a) refuses correctly but *silently* and also exits 0, so a reader cannot tell whether their file was replaced &mdash; the failure mode is the same confusion in the other direction. (b) prompts, which is wrong for a documented setup step that may run unattended. An explicit test can say "leaving it untouched" on stderr, which is the information the reader needs | Four lines of documentation where there was one. Both branches are executed by a test, so the guidance cannot rot |
| 84.6.2 | **Generate the signing key into the file, never through the terminal** &mdash; rewriting the existing `SECRET_KEY` line in place under a restrictive umask &mdash; and confirm the result by its length | (a) Print it and have the reader paste it, as documented; (b) append a second `SECRET_KEY` line; (c) write it to a separate file and reference that | (a) puts a live signing key into scrollback, shell history, CI logs and any transcript, which is the same class of exposure this remediation exists to close. (b) leaves two assignments of one name in a dotenv file, where which one wins depends on the reader &mdash; an ambiguity in the one setting whose value must be unambiguous. (c) adds a second file to protect and a second path to configure. Rewriting the line in place keeps one assignment, one file and one mode. Confirming by length proves the write happened without displaying the value | The block is a here-document rather than a one-liner, so it is longer to read. A test executes it and asserts empty stdout, empty stderr, exactly one changed line, and that the generated value appears in no output |
| 84.6.3 | **End the documented reversibility check at `alembic upgrade head` with `alembic current`, and mark it as being for a disposable database** | (a) Keep the two downgrades as the final step; (b) remove the reversibility check; (c) keep it but add only a warning | (a) leaves the schema with the `role` column and the administrator seed removed, and every command in the sequence exits 0 while doing it, so a reader following the documentation to verify their setup destroys their authorization data. (b) discards proof of a property the migration design depends on. (c) relies on the reader noticing a warning about a command they have already run. A sequence that ends where it started is safe to follow as written, and the warning becomes a statement of cost rather than a plea | The sequence is five commands rather than three. The disposable-database requirement is stated in the row itself, not only in the surrounding note |
| 84.6.4 | **Restate the five runtime-pin sites in `SECURITY.md` while naming `RESIDUAL_RISK.md` as the single maintained inventory** | (a) Correct the count to five and leave two independent inventories; (b) delete the table and link to the register; (c) leave the count at four | (c) is the finding, and it understated a hard constraint by omitting the one site that is a language construct rather than a version declaration &mdash; the site that makes the pin self-enforcing. (b) is tidier but a disclosure policy that cannot state its own supported runtime without a second document is less useful to a reporter, who is the audience. (a) is the risk of two inventories drifting, which is why the restatement says in the file that it must not diverge and a test asserts both documents name the same five sites | Two places list the sites. The test makes divergence a build failure rather than a discovery |
| 84.6.5 | **Split the rotation runbook's two kinds of work explicitly**, rather than softening the language that called every credential compromised | (a) Change "every credential" to "most credentials"; (b) move the webhook identifier out of the runbook entirely; (c) leave it | The runbook opened by instructing the reader not to reason about whether the values leaked, while its fourth entry is new configuration that was never committed. (a) leaves the reader to work out which is which at each step. (b) removes the one place an operator is told the identifier must exist before webhook verification can work, and it must be created in the same change window. Marking the distinction at the heading, the scope table, the four-step preamble, the section itself and the verification step means a reader arriving at any of those points knows which kind of work they are doing | The runbook is longer and carries a distinction on several pages. Accepted: the alternative is an operator hunting a breach that never happened, or skipping a provisioning step because it looked like incident response |

### 84.7 Reconciliation of rows that no longer describe the working tree

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.7.1 | **Row 12.5 is withdrawn.** It recorded the unquoted expansions in `scripts/deploy.sh` as a deliberate non-change on the ground that no finding named the script. A finding now does, the script has been rewritten, and normalized ShellCheck reports **zero findings of any kind** where it previously reported seven `SC2086`. The row is left in place and marked by this reconciliation | (a) Delete row 12.5; (b) edit it in place to say the opposite; (c) leave it, since it was accurate when written | (a) and (b) erase the record that the position changed and why, which is the whole value of a decision log across rounds. (c) leaves a reader who finds row 12.5 believing unquoted expansions are still present and accepted &mdash; a claim they can disprove from the tree, which is the condition this log exists to avoid. §27 established this supersession pattern for exactly this situation | A reader of row 12.5 in isolation sees a withdrawn position. It is marked, and the review that changed the ground is named |
| 84.7.2 | **§23.2's title figure of eleven no longer describes the delivered set**, which is twenty-four. §23.2 stands as the record of what that round found; row 35.3.1 carries the thirteen further paths and the matrix indexes all twenty-four | (a) Renumber §23.2 to twenty-four; (b) leave the figure and let the matrix disagree with it | (a) attributes this round's paths to an earlier one. (b) is a number in one artifact contradicting a number in another, which is the defect class §34.1 exists to prevent | Two figures for one quantity, distinguished by round. §34.1 records where each is established |
