### 84.10 The executive presentation, and the truthfulness of a readiness claim

Appended after Section 84.9 rather than before it: the non-changes above are
the record of that round, and renumbering them would move row identifiers
other artifacts already cite.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 84.10.1 | Distinguish **remediated in code** from **operationally verified** throughout the deck, and state once, plainly, that no part of the work has been deployed | (a) Soften the existing claims with hedging words such as "largely" or "substantially"; (b) add a single disclaimer footnote to the title slide; (c) leave the claims and rely on the reader knowing a release had not happened | A hedged claim is still a claim about a running system, and a footnote is the part of a slide a reader skips. The deck is read by people who read nothing else, so the distinction has to sit in the sentences that carry the message: the title scope line, the metric label, and the closing headline. (c) was how the defect arose | A reader may take "not yet released" as a sign the work is unfinished rather than unshipped. Mitigated by the closing slide asking for review and naming exactly what remains |
| 84.10.2 | Draw secret delivery as a **dashed, separately-classed link** with the state written into the node label, rather than as a solid link into the workloads | (a) Remove the secret-storage node from the diagram until injection is wired; (b) keep the solid link and explain the gap in prose beneath the diagram; (c) mark the whole node as hardened as before | A viewer reads the drawing before any prose, so the state has to be carried by the drawing. (a) would hide a component Terraform genuinely provisions, understating the work in the opposite direction. (b) leaves the diagram itself asserting something untrue. (c) is the defect | A dashed line is a convention a reader may not know. Mitigated by the node label carrying "read access granted" and "injection pending" as words, and by the slide's lede stating what the dash means |
| 84.10.3 | State the **two refusal regimes separately**: the signing-key placeholder is refused in every environment, and the remaining secret placeholders are refused anywhere but a local run | (a) Say the shipped template's placeholders are refused, without qualification; (b) say only that the signing key is refused; (c) restate the original claim that every setting carries a safe local default | (a) was the first correction drafted, and it is wrong in the opposite direction: it would tell a reader a local start is impossible, which it is not once a key is generated. (b) omits that the other placeholders block every non-local environment. (c) is the defect. The validator distinguishes the two cases, so the deck does too | A two-clause sentence is longer than a one-clause one. Accepted: the cell is a table cell rather than a bullet, so no Rule 2 word budget applies, and the browser pass measured the slide still clearing its frame by 239 pixels |
| 84.10.4 | Give the four release gates a **slide of their own**, rather than adding rows to the risk table | (a) Extend the existing risk table with four more rows; (b) list them in the closing slide's bullets; (c) leave them in the project readme only | The gates are the reason nothing has shipped, so they warrant the same weight as the risk table rather than being appended to it. (a) would have pushed one slide past its bullet and word budget and past its frame. (b) is capped at three bullets. (c) leaves the deck's own audience unaware | Seventeen slides rather than sixteen. Within Rule 2's twelve-to-eighteen bound, and asserted as such |
| 84.10.5 | Assert the dashed edge against the **authored `-.->` source and the `classDef` dash pattern**, not against the class name the renderer emits | (a) Assert the emitted `edge-pattern-dashed` class; (b) assert the computed `stroke-dasharray` through a browser; (c) assert nothing about the dash and rely on the label wording | The renderer classifies `-.->` as *dotted* and emits `edge-pattern-dotted`, so (a) would fail against a correctly rendered deck. (b) needs a browser in the test path, which the suite does not have. Asserting the source and the style declaration pins what the author controls, and a browser pass confirms what the renderer does with it | A future renderer could change how it draws `-.->` without the source changing. Recorded: the browser pass measured both edges dashed and all fourteen others solid, and that measurement is the thing to repeat if the renderer pin moves |
| 84.10.6 | Make the database-administrator refusal case run in a **scratch repository**, so the presence of an environment file in the checkout cannot decide its outcome | (a) Delete the environment file from the checkout so the case passes; (b) assert whichever branch the ambient checkout happens to take; (c) require the case to run only when no environment file exists | The script resolves paths from its own location, and it correctly asks for no administrator when it has nothing to create &mdash; so in a checkout that has been set up, the case ran the entire setup, installed dependencies as a side effect, and asserted nothing. (a) treats a working checkout as the anomaly, when a checkout that has run the bootstrap is the normal state. (b) is a test that cannot fail. (c) hides the branch rather than covering it | A copied script is a copy, so a path the script resolves outside its own root would behave differently. None does: the copy reaches the check needing nothing but the tools on `PATH`, and the case asserts no virtual environment was created |
| 84.10.7 | Cover the **other branch as well**: a configured environment file means the administrator check is skipped, and says why | (a) Cover only the refusal; (b) treat the skip as an implementation detail | Demanding a privileged account for work the script will not do is the defect least privilege exists to prevent, and it was previously unasserted &mdash; it was the branch silently taken whenever the case ran in a set-up checkout. Naming it makes both halves of the decision intentional | None identified. The case asserts the announcement rather than the absence of a database object, so it needs no database |

## 85. Final reconciliation, and the decisions of the delivery round

This section is the authority for every current-state figure in this change set. It exists
because a review found that the inventory in §23 had gone stale, that three rows still
described four delivered documents as absent, and that later decisions were citing §23.1
as authority for numbers that no longer held. Rather than edit those rows in place, which
§27's convention forbids, each is marked superseded and the reconciled figures are given
here once. Anything in an earlier section that disagrees with §85.1, §85.2 or §85.3 is
wrong, and this section is what a downstream document quotes.

### 85.1 The final inventory

Measured with `git diff --name-only a26f7fb HEAD` plus the working tree and the untracked
set, excluding only the throwaway `blitzy_adhoc_*` verification harnesses, which are never
committed:

| Quantity | Count |
|---|---|
| Paths the AAP plans (§0.6.1.1–§0.6.1.6) | **59** |
| Paths actually changed so far | **58** |
| — of those, planned and delivered | **47** |
| — of those, unplanned | **11** |
| Planned paths still pending | **12** |

The AAP's own headline of **68** entries is 59 planned changes plus the 9 REFERENCE
paths of §0.6.1.7. The two numbers are not interchangeable, and a traceability matrix must
not present 68 as a count of changed files — a position the matrix holds.

This subsection also claimed that all 9 REFERENCE paths remain unmodified. **That claim is
withdrawn by row 36.1.2:** eight are unmodified and one,
`infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend`, was modified by row 30.12's four additive
lines. The nine are now verified per path rather than as a group.

Landing all 12 pending planned paths with the 11 unplanned ones in place gives **70**
changed paths, not 59. **That projection is superseded:** the delivered figure is **86**,
measured in `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` §2.10. **That figure is itself
superseded: row 91.4 carries the delivered count measured after the scope revert of
row 91.1, and §2.10 of the matrix is where it is published.**

## 86. The delivery surface: health probes, pipelines, deployment and governance accuracy

Rows added by a QA review of the delivery surface — the workflows, the
deployment script, the Terraform root module, the readiness probe and the
governance documents themselves. It raised fifteen findings, eleven Major and
four Minor, and this is the first round whose scope is the delivery path rather
than the application's request handling. Two properties of the round shape every
row below.

First, **this round owns what earlier rounds deferred.** Row 30.17 placed
`.github/workflows/**`, `infrastructure/terraform/**` and `scripts/deploy.sh`
in "another checkpoint's scope". That checkpoint is this one, and §86.9 withdraws
the deferral rather than leaving it to be read as still current.

Second, **eight of the fifteen findings were defects in things that had never
been executed.** A workflow step that names a script that does not exist, a
Dockerfile flag omitted where the context has no default `Dockerfile`, a cluster
addressed by zone when Terraform declares it regional — none of these fails a
compiler, a linter or a test, because nothing in this repository read a workflow
file at all. That absence is itself the finding behind the finding, and rows
35.6.1 to 35.6.3 are the answer to it: three of this round's fixes are test
modules that make the delivery surface something the suite checks rather than
something a reviewer has to read. Every fix in this round was verified by
executing the defect first and the fix second, and the fixes to files that
cannot be executed here were verified by mutation testing, described in row
35.6.2.

### 86.1 The readiness probe (M6)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.1.1 | Bound `GET /health/ready` rather than remove it or make it internal | (a) Remove the route, which the finding offers as its first option; (b) require a token or a network boundary, which it offers as its second; (c) leave it and accept the cost; (d) answer from a background poller instead of the request path | Removal was priced before it was declined, and it is expensive in a way the finding could not see: the Compose backend health check probes this path, six cases in `test_application_surface.py` and one in `test_deployment_contract.py` assert it, the README documents it, and row 32.8's evidence — that `/health` answered 200 throughout a database outage while `GET /listings/` and `POST /auth/login` answered 500 — is the reason a readiness probe exists at all. Decisively, finding M10 in the same review *prescribes probing this route* after a rollout, so removing it would resolve one finding by breaking another. (b) fails for the same reason: a rollout probe runs before any credential exists, and a Kubernetes kubelet presents none. (d) trades a bounded read for a permanent timer and a staleness window no caller can reason about. What the finding actually objects to is unbounded work reachable anonymously, so the work is bounded — three ways, each independently — and the surface is left where two other findings and four artefacts expect it | Readiness now has three settings that did not exist, and each must be carried in `config.py`, `.env.example`, the Compose backend anchor and `TEST_SETTINGS` or a symmetric-difference gate in `conftest.py` fails. That gate is what makes the cost visible rather than latent |
| 86.1.2 | Apply the probe's timeout **transaction-locally**, with `SELECT set_config('statement_timeout', :milliseconds, true)` and the same for `lock_timeout` | (a) Set `statement_timeout` as a connection option in `_connect_args`, so every session carries it; (b) set it on the engine URL; (c) `SET LOCAL statement_timeout = :milliseconds`; (d) impose no statement timeout and rely on the connect timeout alone | (a) and (b) are the obvious placements and both are wrong here for one measured reason: `backend/migrations/env.py` imports and runs against the **application engine**, so a globally applied statement timeout would bound Alembic DDL. A migration that adds a column to a large table would then fail on a timeout meant for a health probe — a fix creating a worse defect than the one it closes. (c) was written first and does not work: `SET` takes a literal, not a bound parameter, so the value cannot be parameterised and would have to be interpolated into SQL. `set_config(..., true)` is the parameterised, transaction-scoped equivalent and takes the value as a bind. (d) leaves a stalled-but-connected database holding the probe open indefinitely, which is the finding | The bound is PostgreSQL-specific, so `READINESS_BOUND_DIALECTS` names the dialects it applies to and other dialects get the connect timeout and the cache alone. Verified against the real database: inside the probe transaction `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` both read `2s`, and after rollback `statement_timeout` reads `0` — so the bound provably does not leak to the next user of the connection |
| 86.1.3 | Reuse one outcome for `READINESS_CACHE_SECONDS` and admit **one** caller at a time to the underlying read, using two separate locks | (a) One lock covering both the cached state and the database read; (b) no single-flight admission, so a cold cache lets every concurrent caller read; (c) no cache, and rely on the rate limit alone | A single lock was the first design and it was wrong: holding the state lock across the database read means a slow read blocks every reader of the *cache*, so a stalled database converts a cheap cached answer into a queue — reintroducing the exhaustion the row is meant to prevent. Splitting them gives a short critical section over the cache tuple and a separate single-flight lock held only for the read. (b) leaves a thundering herd on every cache expiry, which is the finding at a lower frequency. (c) would still let sixty callers a minute each open a session | Two locks is more machinery than one, and the ordering between them matters. A case asserts a burst costs exactly one database read, so a regression that reverses the ordering or drops the single-flight is caught by behaviour rather than by review |
| 86.1.4 | Rate limit the route at `RATE_LIMIT_READINESS`, folded into the existing rate-limit expression validator | (a) A dedicated validator for the new setting; (b) no rate limit, since the cache already bounds database work | The route was the only rate-limitable endpoint without a limit, and adding the field to the existing validator's list means its expression is validated by the same code as every other limit rather than by a second copy of that logic. (b) misreads what the cache does: the cache bounds *database* work, not request work, and an unlimited anonymous route still consumes a worker per call | A kubelet probing more often than sixty times a minute would receive 429. The default is well above any normal probe interval and the value is configuration, not code |
| 86.1.5 | Rewrite the RBAC matrix's readiness case to assert the bounded contract instead of asserting that every principal receives 200 | (a) Leave the case and add new ones elsewhere; (b) delete the case | The finding named this test as part of the defect, and it was right to: a case asserting that anonymous callers always receive 200 *entrenches* the unbounded surface, so leaving it would mean the suite actively defending the thing being fixed. The rewritten case sends `RATE_LIMIT_READINESS + 1` probes per principal and requires the first sixty to answer 200, the sixty-first to answer 429, and the whole burst to cost exactly one database read — so it now asserts the bound rather than the absence of one. (b) would lose the coverage that readiness is reachable by every principal, which is still a requirement | The case is slower than the one it replaces, because it issues sixty-one requests per principal. It is the only place the rate limit and the cache are asserted together, which is worth the cost |

### 86.2 Credential hygiene (m4, ignore-rule half)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.2.1 | Add both `gha-creds-*.json` and `**/gha-creds-*.json` to **four** ignore files, not the two the finding names | (a) Add them to `.gitignore` and the root `.dockerignore` only, as the finding's line references imply; (b) add the exact pattern alone, without the recursive form; (c) disable credential-file creation in the action instead | The finding cites `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore`, but the root `.dockerignore` does not govern the frontend build context — that context has its own file — and `backend/.dockerignore` opens by asserting pattern identity with the root, so omitting it would make that assertion false. Covering the two the finding names and leaving two build contexts uncovered would close the citation and not the hole. (b) leaves a credential written into a nested context uncovered, which the exact pattern does not reach in every one of these formats. (c) is unavailable: `gcloud` and `kubectl` in later steps read the file the action writes, so suppressing it breaks the deployment. The action's own documentation prescribes exactly these ignore entries | Four files now carry the same two patterns. A parametrized case asserts all four, and also asserts that none of them re-includes the name with a negation |

### 86.3 Cloud Function invocation authority and deployable configuration (M11, m1)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.3.1 | Replace `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_member` with `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_binding`, whose `members` list is the complete set for the invoker role | (a) Keep `_iam_member` and add a removal step to the deployment script; (b) use `google_cloudfunctions_function_iam_policy`, which is authoritative for the whole policy; (c) keep `_iam_member` and rely on `--no-allow-unauthenticated` at deploy time | The finding's substance is that `_iam_member` is **additive**: it guarantees the named principal is present and says nothing about who else is, so a pre-existing `allUsers` invoker survives every apply. `_iam_binding` is authoritative for one role, which is exactly the scope of the defect — after apply, the invoker role holds the declared members and nobody else. (b) is authoritative for *every* role on the resource, so an apply would also remove bindings this module never declared; that is a far larger blast radius than the finding needs and could strip access this configuration is not the authority for. (a) makes the desired state depend on an imperative step outside the declaration, which is the property infrastructure-as-code exists to remove. (c) does not work at all, and the finding says so: the flag governs what a *deploy* grants, not what an existing policy already contains | `_iam_binding` will remove an invoker member added out-of-band, deliberately. If an operator has granted a service account invoke access by hand, the next apply revokes it unless it is added to the variable. `terraform plan` renders `members` explicitly, so the effect is visible before it is applied |
| 86.3.2 | Drive the function's name, entry point and source object from variables with validation, and delete the `HUMAN ASSISTANCE NEEDED` block | (a) Leave the generic `function-test` and `hello_world` values with the guidance block; (b) hard-code deployable values; (c) move the block's text into a comment | Generic placeholders in executable infrastructure are indistinguishable from a real configuration until an apply produces something nobody wanted, and a guidance block instructing a human to finish the file means the file is not finished. Variables with validation give a deployable default and refuse a malformed value at plan time — an entry point that is not an identifier, or an invoker member of `allUsers`, is refused before anything is created. (b) removes the placeholder and the configurability together. (c) keeps the deferral and hides it | Three new variables must be supplied or defaulted per environment. Both negative cases are verified: `entry_point=not-an-identifier` and `invoker_member=allUsers` are each refused by `terraform plan` |
| 86.3.3 | Keep `runtime = "python39"` byte-identical | (a) Advance it with the rest of the hardening | This is one of the five pin sites the AAP declares load-bearing, and §12 and row 12.1 already hold it. A round that touches the surrounding resource is exactly when a pin gets advanced by accident, so it is stated | None. A case asserts the pin, and the reachability of the pin is asserted by the same module that asserts the workflow's interpreter version |

### 86.4 The deployment script (M1, M2, M11)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.4.1 | Rewrite `scripts/deploy.sh` so it deploys the same artefacts the workflow deploys, rather than retiring it | (a) Delete the script and let `cd.yml` be the only deployment path, which the finding offers; (b) leave it and document that it is unused; (c) reduce it to a thin wrapper that invokes the workflow | The finding is that the script builds a Dockerfile that does not exist, targets a Kubernetes resource that does not exist, and deploys a function from a directory that does not exist — so it has never run successfully. Deletion is the cheaper fix and it was declined for one reason: a deployment path that exists only inside a hosted CI system cannot be exercised by an operator during an incident, and the two failure modes this review found in `cd.yml` — a migration ordering error and a liveness-only health gate — are precisely the kind of defect a second, readable implementation surfaces. Rewritten, it names the same Dockerfiles, the same Deployments, the same regional cluster and the same migration ordering, so the two paths agree. (b) leaves a script an operator may reasonably run, doing damage. (c) requires a CI credential to deploy, which inverts the point | Two paths now express one deployment and can drift. They are held together by naming the same inputs and by the contract tests; a case asserts the script and the workflow build from the same Dockerfiles |
| 86.4.2 | Run the migration as a one-shot pod built from the **new** image, before `kubectl set image`, with its spec derived from the live Deployment and an explicit success check | (a) Keep `kubectl exec` into a serving pod, which is what the script did; (b) run it after the rollout; (c) use a Kubernetes `Job` object; (d) run it from the operator's workstation against the database directly | The finding is that the migration ran *after* the rollout and *inside* a pod already serving traffic — so the new code served requests against a schema it did not yet have, and the migration inherited whatever image the old Deployment was running. Deriving the pod spec from the live Deployment with `jq` carries the environment, service account, image pull secrets and volume mounts across, so the migration authenticates to the database exactly as the application does and no credential is restated. The terminal phase is compared against `Succeeded` explicitly and anything else exits non-zero, because a poll that never observed a phase must not be read as success. (c) is the more idiomatic object and needs a manifest this repository does not carry; a pod with overrides needs no new file. (d) requires database reachability from outside the cluster, which the hardened Cloud SQL configuration deliberately removes | The `jq` transformation depends on the Deployment's shape, so a Deployment restructured beyond a single application container needs it revisited. It was verified against a real `jq` with a captured Deployment, producing a spec carrying `restartPolicy: Never`, the service account, the exact Alembic command array, and the env, envFrom and volumeMounts of the application container |
| 86.4.3 | Pass `--no-allow-unauthenticated`, **then** remove `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers`, **then** re-read the effective policy and exit non-zero if either survives | (a) Pass the flag alone, which the finding's guidance could be read as requesting; (b) flag plus removal, without re-reading; (c) rely on the Terraform binding alone | The finding is explicit that omitting the grant does not revoke an existing one, so the flag alone leaves a function that was public still public. Removal without verification is better and still assumes the removal took effect; a removal can fail on a permission the deploying identity lacks and `gcloud` can report success on a policy that was not what the operator believed. Re-reading the policy and failing the deployment converts an assumption into an assertion. (c) is the declarative control and correct, but the script must not depend on Terraform having been applied first | The check adds a `gcloud` read per deployment and will fail a deployment whose identity cannot alter the policy — deliberately, since silently deploying a publicly invocable function is the defect. Verified against captured policies: a public policy is reported as public, and private and empty policies report nothing |


### 86.5 The delivery workflows (M3, M4, M5, M10, m1, m4)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.5.1 | Gate deployment on the **whole** verification workflow with `uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml`, and add `workflow_call` to that workflow so the reference resolves | (a) Add the missing gates to `cd.yml`'s own verification job; (b) trigger on `workflow_run` completion; (c) require the checks through branch protection instead | The finding is that deployment was gated on a security subset — the dependency audit, Bandit and the security suite — with no full test run and no integration check. Restating the missing steps inside `cd.yml` would close the finding for today and reopen it on the next check added to CI, because two lists of gates drift by default. Calling the workflow makes the gate *definitionally* everything CI runs. (b) decouples them: a `workflow_run` trigger fires after CI regardless of its conclusion unless conditioned, and reads its result at a distance. (c) is worth having as well, but branch protection is repository configuration and not reviewable in this tree | The gate now depends on the frontend job too, so a genuine frontend failure blocks deployment. That is correct and is also why the frontend's unfixable read-only problems are handled by a ratchet rather than a hard gate — see row 35.5.5 |
| 86.5.2 | Build each image with `-f` naming its Dockerfile, and address the cluster with `--region` | (a) Add a `Dockerfile` to each context so the default resolves; (b) move the Dockerfiles into their contexts | The finding is that both builds omitted `-f` while neither context carries a default `Dockerfile`, so both would fail, and that the cluster was addressed with `--zone` when `google_container_cluster.primary` takes `location = var.region` and is therefore regional. Naming the Dockerfile is the smaller change and keeps every image definition in `infrastructure/docker/`, where Compose already resolves them. (a) and (b) would create or move files to avoid passing a flag, and would leave two definitions of each image or split them across two directories | A build context with a default `Dockerfile` added later would make `-f` look redundant. A case asserts no context carries one, so the flag stays load-bearing rather than becoming decoration |
| 86.5.3 | Probe `GET /health/ready` after the rollout, retrying, and print the liveness answer on failure | (a) Keep probing `/health`; (b) probe both and require both; (c) use `kubectl rollout status` alone | The finding is that liveness answers 200 whatever state the database is in, so a release whose database is unreachable was being declared healthy. Readiness is the probe that distinguishes them, which is also why row 35.1.1 keeps the route. Printing the liveness answer when readiness never succeeds separates "the process is not up" from "the process is up and the database is not", which is the first question an operator asks. (b) adds nothing, since readiness cannot answer unless the process is up. (c) reports that pods became ready by their own probe definition and asserts nothing about the release's own contract | The probe depends on the readiness route continuing to mean what it means. The test module imports `READINESS_PATH` from the application rather than restating the string, so a rename moves both together |
| 86.5.4 | Order the deployment job **build → authenticate → push**, so no credential file exists in the workspace while an image is built | (a) Keep authenticate → build → push and rely on the ignore rules alone; (b) set `create_credentials_file: false` and use a token | The ignore rules from row 35.2.1 are necessary and are not sufficient on their own: they prevent a credential from being *added* to a build context that respects them, and the stronger property is that the credential does not exist while any layer is created. The authenticating action's own troubleshooting guidance prescribes this ordering — checkout, compile, auth, push — for exactly this reason, and `docker build` needs no credential, so the reordering costs nothing. (b) was considered and rejected because later steps run `gcloud` and `kubectl`, which read the file | The ordering is a property of step positions and is easy to undo while editing. A case asserts every build precedes the credential exchange and every push follows it |
| 86.5.5 | Split verification into **four jobs that declare no `needs`** — backend, frontend, integration, infrastructure | (a) Keep one job and reorder its steps so the backend gates come first; (b) keep one job and mark the frontend steps `continue-on-error`; (c) two jobs, backend and frontend | The finding is that a step invoking `npm run lint` — a script `frontend/package.json` does not declare — failed the job before the dependency audit, Bandit, the two compensating-control guards and the security suite ever ran. Fixing the command alone closes the symptom and leaves the structure that caused it: with one job, *any* early failure still suppresses every later gate. Reordering (a) only chooses which gates get suppressed. (b) makes the frontend unable to fail at all, which is worse than the defect. Independent jobs mean each concern reports on its own, and it also let the integration and infrastructure gates be added with their own services and tooling rather than bloating a single job | Four jobs install dependencies separately, so the workflow does more total work. A case asserts no job declares `needs`, and seven parametrized cases assert every backend gate survived the split |
| 86.5.6 | Keep `node-version: '14'` byte-identical and add `npm install -g npm@9` before `npm ci` | (a) Advance the Node version, which would also address a known flagged finding; (b) regenerate the lockfile in a format the bundled npm reads; (c) replace `npm ci` with `npm install` | Measured, not assumed: `frontend/package-lock.json` is `lockfileVersion: 3`, which npm 7 introduced and which the npm bundled with Node 14 cannot read — so `npm ci` was a *second* command in this job that could not succeed. The pin is nonetheless an AAP §0.9.2 finding held for confirmation, and row 34.6.3 records that flagged findings are reported and not acted on; advancing it here would be fixing one unilaterally. Selecting a newer npm satisfies both: the registry confirms npm 9 accepts the 14 series from 14.17.0 upwards, alongside 16.13 and later and 18 and later, and the pin resolves to 14.21.3 — so it installs. (b) rewrites a committed lockfile to accommodate an EOL runtime, moving the problem. (c) abandons reproducible installs | Node 14 is end-of-life and this row keeps it, deliberately, with the reason recorded rather than the consequence hidden. A case asserts that a lockfile of version 2 or later is accompanied by an npm selection of 7 or later, ordered before the install, so the pairing cannot be half-removed |
| 86.5.7 | Gate ESLint as a **ratchet**: fail on any error-level problem outside one named exemption, and on any increase above a recorded warning budget | (a) `npm run lint` fixed to a hard `--max-warnings 0` gate; (b) `continue-on-error: true`; (c) omit the frontend lint entirely; (d) fix the offending frontend source | Executing the check first is what made this decision: ESLint reports eight warnings and one **error** — `src/services/paypal.ts` holds JSX in a `.ts` file and refers to `React` without importing it, confirmed independently by `tsc --noEmit` producing twelve errors in that one file. So the source genuinely does not parse, and `frontend/src/**` is read-only reference material here, which makes (d) unavailable and (a) a gate that can never pass — writing a step that cannot succeed, which is the very defect this finding raises. (b) is the usual escape and it is a gate that checks nothing. A ratchet is a real gate: a new error anywhere else, or a ninth warning, fails the job, while the recorded unfixable problems do not. The exemption names the file and the reason | The exemption and the budget are numbers that must be lowered when the source is fixed, and nothing forces that. Both were verified to bite: an injected error in another file fails, and a budget of seven against eight warnings fails |
| 86.5.8 | Replace the comment-only integration step with a gate that runs against a real PostgreSQL service and a served application | (a) Leave the placeholder; (b) assert only that the container starts; (c) run the existing pytest suite a second time and call it integration | The step was a `HUMAN ASSISTANCE NEEDED` block and two comments, which is a step that always succeeds while checking nothing — indistinguishable from a passing gate to anyone reading a green tick. The gate now applies both revisions, asserts exactly one administrator, steps both revisions back and reapplies them, imports the entrypoint, then serves the application and reads its contract over HTTP. Each of those is something the unit suite cannot establish, because each needs a database or a running process. (c) would duplicate cost and prove nothing new, since the suite already runs against SQLite fixtures | The gate is the slowest job and depends on a service container. Every step of it was rehearsed locally against a throwaway database first, and the contract block was then extracted from the workflow **verbatim** and executed against a live server, so what is committed is what was proven rather than an approximation of it |
| 86.5.9 | Generate the integration gate's `SECRET_KEY` at run time with `openssl rand -hex 32` | (a) Commit a fixed development key into the workflow; (b) supply it from a repository secret; (c) reuse the `.env.example` placeholder | The settings validator refuses a short key, a denylisted placeholder, and a key of too few distinct characters — measured here, when a 64-character key of one repeated character was refused for carrying fewer than twelve distinct characters. So (c) fails by construction, which is the validator working. (a) commits a key-shaped string, and a reader cannot tell a deliberately fake key from a leaked real one without checking. (b) is a secret this gate does not need, and every secret a workflow can read is a secret a workflow can leak | The key differs per run, so no token minted in one run verifies in another. Nothing in the gate spans runs |
| 86.5.10 | Add an `infrastructure` job running `terraform fmt -check -recursive`, `init -backend=false` and `validate` | (a) Leave Terraform unchecked in CI, as before; (b) run a `plan`, which checks more | Nothing in this repository checked the Terraform configuration, and §86.3 changes it — so the round that hardens the root module is the round that should stop it regressing. `-backend=false` needs no state and no credential, so the job runs on a pull request from any source. (b) requires credentials and a real project, and would make a configuration check depend on cloud access | `validate` does not catch a semantically wrong but syntactically valid configuration. Both commands were run locally and pass; `plan` was additionally run by hand during §86.3 and rendered 24 resources to add |
| 86.5.11 | Correct the `pip-audit` comment so each manifest names its own advisory registry | (a) Add the four development identifiers to `RESIDUAL_RISK.md`; (b) leave the comment | Found by cross-checking rather than by reading: of the fourteen suppressed identifiers, four appear nowhere in the file the comment names. Investigating rather than assuming showed the register is correct and deliberate — it scopes itself to the runtime manifest in its own words and points the development set at that manifest's own accepted-advisory section, where all seven are present. So the register was right and only the comment over-claimed. (a) would have duplicated a register that explicitly declines to cover that set, and would have made the register's own scope statement false | A reader must now follow two pointers instead of one. A case asserts every suppressed identifier appears in one of the two registries, so a future suppression cannot be added silently to neither |
| 86.5.12 | Keep the flake8 step as `cd backend && flake8 .` | (a) Change it to `flake8 backend scripts`, matching the form the README documented | This looked like an improvement and is a regression: `setup.cfg` carries `per-file-ignores` patterns for **both** invocation directories and its comment names "the CI step's `flake8 .`" as one of the two forms it exists to support. Changing the step would leave that comment describing something that no longer happens. The README was aligned to the workflow instead — row 35.7.2 | The two forms must both keep working. Both are run at every verification point in this round, and `setup.cfg` explains why in place |

### 86.6 Making the delivery surface verifiable (the round's structural fix)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.6.1 | Add `backend/tests/security/test_pipeline_contract.py` and `backend/tests/security/test_documentation_contract.py`, so the workflows and the documents' checkable claims are asserted by the suite | (a) Verify this round's fixes with throwaway scripts and commit none of them; (b) rely on review; (c) add the assertions to `test_deployment_contract.py`, which already covers Compose and the Dockerfiles | Measured first: a search of every file under `backend/tests` for any reference to a workflow, an ignore file or `cd.yml` returned **zero matches**. So six of this round's findings sat in files nothing in the repository read, which is why defects as plain as a missing `-f` survived. Ad-hoc scripts (a) are deleted at the end of a session and protect nothing afterwards — and Rule 1's traceability requirement cannot be met for these findings at all if no verifying test exists to cite. (c) was declined on subject matter: that module's authority is Compose and the image definitions, and its docstring says so; a workflow is a different contract with different authorities | Two more modules to maintain, and a workflow edit can now fail a test — which is the point. Both read their authorities rather than restating them: the readiness path from `backend.app.main`, the required settings from the `Settings` class, the cluster's shape from `main.tf`, the npm scripts from `package.json` |
| 86.6.2 | Verify both new modules by **mutation testing** — reintroduce each original defect, confirm the matching case fails, and restore the file byte-for-byte | (a) Accept that the cases pass on correct input; (b) hand-review the assertions | A contract test that passes on correct input and *also* passes on the defect it names is worse than no test, because it certifies the absence of a check. Each of the thirty-three mutations reintroduces a real defect from this review or a plausible regression of one: dropping `-f`, addressing the cluster by zone, removing the gate dependency, probing liveness, reordering the credential exchange before the build, chaining the frontend job ahead of the backend gates, linting through the missing npm script, restoring a comment-only step, restoring each placeholder contact, claiming a gate nothing automates. All thirty-three failed the intended case, and every mutated file was restored and byte-compared | The harnesses are throwaway and are not committed, so the property they establish — that each case bites — is recorded here and in the resolution report rather than enforced continuously. Restoration is asserted by byte comparison inside each harness, so a harness that failed mid-run could not leave a mutated file behind |
| 86.6.3 | Assert the pinned interpreter, the Node pin, every backend gate and every suppressed advisory identifier, not only this round's fixes | (a) Assert only what the findings named | The findings are evidence of what goes wrong unobserved in these files, not an exhaustive list of what matters in them. The interpreter pin is load-bearing in five places and §12 holds it; a workflow edit is exactly how it would be advanced by accident. The same reasoning covers the gates that a future job split could drop and the advisories a future suppression could hide | The module asserts more than the findings asked for, so a legitimate future change to any of those properties fails a test and must be made deliberately. That is the intended cost |

### 86.7 Documentation accuracy (m2, m3)

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 86.7.1 | Publish **no** contact address, and remove the placeholder from both documents rather than replacing it | (a) Invent or choose an address; (b) leave the placeholder with its self-describing caveat, as it stood; (c) point at a repository owner's profile | The finding offers two options — supply a monitored address, or remove the nonfunctional fallback — and only the second is available without fabricating something. There is no address this work can know to be monitored, and writing one that is not is the specific harm: it invites a reporter to disclose a weakness into a mailbox nobody reads while believing it was received, which is worse than publishing nothing. (b) is the state the finding rejects. What remains is better than what it replaces: GitHub's private vulnerability reporting needs no address, reaches whoever holds the repository, and cannot go stale — and the policy now says what to do if that route is not enabled, so removing the fallback leaves no dead end | A repository whose private reporting is disabled has no reporting route until an administrator enables it. The policy names the setting and the step. A case asserts the placeholder strings are absent *and* that the working channel is still described, so the removal cannot be repeated into an empty policy |
| 86.7.2 | Align the README's verification commands on the exact forms the workflow runs, rather than relaxing the check that compares them | (a) Loosen the comparison to match equivalent command forms; (b) leave the README forms and narrow the claim to "the same gates, invoked differently" | Writing the check before declaring the finding resolved exposed four real mismatches: the README omitted `--strict` from both `pip-audit` invocations, wrote `flake8 backend` where CI runs `flake8 .` from `backend/`, and wrote `alembic upgrade head` where CI runs it with `-c backend/alembic.ini`. (a) means building a hand-tuned table of which command forms count as equivalent — precisely the brittleness worth avoiding, and a table that would itself need maintaining. | 86.7.3 | Describe the environment-file resolution as implemented — a repository-root absolute default, an `ENV_FILE` override used as given, and an empty override reading no file | (a) Correct the literal to `env_file` pointing at the root; (b) delete the sentence | The document stated `env_file = ".env"`, which reads as a path relative to the working directory and is what a reader would act on. The implementation resolves an absolute path under the repository root precisely so the same file is read from the root or from `backend/`, and an empty `ENV_FILE` reads none — the form a container or a CI job wants. A one-token correction (a) would fix the literal and still omit the override and the empty case, which are the parts a reader needs. (b) removes guidance rather than correcting it | Three behaviours are now documented and must stay true. A case asserts the superseded literal is absent and that the override variable — imported from the configuration module, not restated — appears |

## 87. Identifier concordance for citations written before renumbering

This record grew one round at a time, and each round appended its decisions as a new
top-level section. Where two rounds arrived with sections of the same number, the later
one was renumbered so that no two sections share a number. That is why a citation written
inside one round can name a number this document no longer uses.

**Two rules describe every move.** The row suffix is preserved: a row cited as `35.36` is
row `81.36` today, with the same three digits after the section number. Only the section
prefix changed, and it changed by topic rather than by arithmetic — the round originally
numbered §35 was split, its performance and resource rows becoming §81, its
reconciliation and inventory rows §82, and its delivery-surface rows §86; the round
originally numbered §36 became §80; and §40's second-pass accuracy corrections became
§84.

The table below is exhaustive for the citations that still use a historical number,
across this log, `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`,
`docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`, `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md`,
`docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`, `SECURITY.md` and `README.md`. Each citation is left
as it was written rather than rewritten in place, for the reason §27's convention gives:
the sequence of positions is itself part of the account, and silently renumbering a
citation inside a superseded row makes that row look as though it had always said
something it did not.

Where a row reads **Not written**, the identifier is cited in the record but no row or
section of that number exists in this tree. Each such citation was written against a
longer draft of its section, which a later round consolidated. The topic column names
where the subject now lives, so the citation still leads somewhere.

### 87.1 The six rounds that all appended a section 89

Six rounds were reviewed and remediated concurrently, and each appended its
decisions to a record whose last section was 88. Five arrived numbered
§89 and two numbered §90, so the log carried five sections called 89 and two
called 90, and **forty row identifiers named two different rows each**. A
citation such as "row 89.5" resolved to one row about a database lock and
another about a delivered-surface measurement.

They are renumbered in the order they appear in the file, the first keeping 89.
Row suffixes are preserved exactly, so a row cited as `89.12` by the round that
became §94 is `94.12` today with the same suffix.

**These citations were rewritten in place, which is a deviation from the
convention stated above, and it is recorded here rather than taken silently.**
The convention leaves a historical citation as written because a concordance can
carry the reader from the old number to the new one. That is only possible while
the old number names one row. Here it named two, and a concordance mapping one
identifier to two rows disambiguates nothing, so the citation itself had to
carry which round it meant. Ownership was decidable without guesswork: no round
could see another's section, so every reference to an 89.x or 90.x row was
written by one round and names that round's own section.

Every affected citation was rewritten on that basis -- 234 inside this log,
including 52 forward references made from earlier sections, and 56 across
`docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`,
`docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md`, `docs/review/CRITICAL_DECISIONS.md`,
`SECURITY.md`, `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` and two test modules. After the
change this log defines 942 row identifiers with **no duplicate**, its top-level
sections ascend without a gap, and all 849 decision-log citations in the
repository resolve to a row or subsection that exists.

## 88. Consolidating the Kubernetes inventory onto one directory

Three inventories of the same cluster existed at once, and the effect was worse than
duplication. `infrastructure/kubernetes/` held a substitution-templated set that
`scripts/render_kubernetes_manifests.sh` renders and that both delivery paths apply.
`infrastructure/k8s/` held **two** further sets under different naming conventions — one
splitting each workload into `-deployment`, `-service` and `-hpa` files, the other
combining a workload and its Service in a single file — so four objects were declared
twice **inside one directory**: the `backend` and `frontend` Deployments and their
Services, with a different specification each time. Applying that directory with a glob
would have created each object twice, and which specification survived would have
depended on the order the files were read.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 88.1 | **Consolidate onto `infrastructure/kubernetes/` as the single inventory, and empty `infrastructure/k8s/` of manifests.** Rows 81.22, 82.3 and the inventory rows that name `infrastructure/k8s/**` are superseded in their path, not in their substance: the inventory they argued for exists, in one place | (a) Consolidate the other way, onto `infrastructure/k8s/`; (b) keep both and document which is authoritative; (c) deduplicate within `infrastructure/k8s/` and leave two inventories standing | The surviving directory is the one the renderer, `.github/workflows/cd.yml` and `scripts/deploy.sh` actually apply, so choosing it means the manifests that are validated are the manifests that are applied — the property (a) would have had to rebuild. (b) leaves a reader to discover by reading a workflow which of two contradictory `backend` Deployments governs, which is the defect rather than a description of it. (c) removes the intra-directory collision but keeps two statements of one cluster, so a change to one is a silent divergence from the other | The autoscalers and the ingestion schedule existed only in the retired directory and had to be carried across rather than deleted, which is a re-expression rather than a copy: see 88.2. `infrastructure/k8s/README.md` is kept as the record of where the manifests went, so a reference in an older document leads somewhere |
| 88.2 | **Carry the two autoscalers and the ingestion schedule across, and change the ingestion pod to read its credentials from mounted files** rather than from a synchronised Kubernetes Secret | (a) Drop them with the rest of the directory; (b) carry them across unchanged | (a) would delete the only declaration of a replica range and the only declaration of the scheduled ingestion workload, neither of which exists anywhere else. (b) would leave one workload consuming credentials through `secretRef` on a synchronised Secret while every other workload reads mounted files — so a value would be written into the cluster datastore for one pod's benefit, which is the exposure `30-backend-secrets.yaml` declares no `secretObjects` in order to avoid. The autoscaler minimums are the same tokens the Deployments declare their replica counts from, so applying both does not scale a workload down on arrival | The ingestion command is now a shell that exports six mounted files before it execs the task, so a mount failure surfaces as a named missing secret rather than as an application error. Three new renderer tokens carry the maximum replica counts and the schedule, each with a default |
| 88.3 | **Retire `scripts/render_manifests.sh`.** Row 82.7's decision — one implementation of the substitution pass, shared by both delivery paths — is upheld; the implementation that survives is `scripts/render_kubernetes_manifests.sh`, which is the one both paths invoke | (a) Keep both scripts; (b) keep the retired one and repoint both paths at it | It rendered only the directory that no longer holds manifests, so keeping it would leave an executable that silently renders nothing. (b) would mean rewriting the paths, the groups and every case that reads them to gain nothing | A reference to the retired name in an older row now names a script that is absent; this row is where that is recorded |
| 88.4 | **Declare every non-credential setting in `20-backend-config.yaml`**, taking it from fourteen entries to forty-two | (a) Leave the fourteen and let the rest fall back to the code's defaults; (b) declare only the settings that differ from their defaults | The standing manifest check asserts the key set equals `Settings.__fields__` minus the managed credentials, and it was passing against the retired directory's own configuration map while the applied one carried fourteen — so the check was guarding a file nothing applied. (a) leaves twenty-eight values undeclared in the deployed configuration, which is the opposite of the reviewability the inventory exists for. (b) makes the check impossible to state as an equality | Twenty-eight more values are now this repository's responsibility to keep correct. The check is what keeps them correct: a setting added to the model without a value here fails the build |
| 88.5 | **Hold the two standing repository checks as scripts under `.github/scripts/` and have the workflow invoke them**, rather than embedding either as a workflow step body | (a) Keep both inline in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; (b) move them into the test suite as cases | An embedded body cannot be run at a workstation, so a failure is only reproducible by pushing; and the manifest check's body was long enough that the workflow linter's own shell analysis stopped returning on it, which made the whole verification surface unusable until it was extracted. (b) would tie a repository-shape check to a Python test session and to the database fixtures the suite configures, and the secret-policy check is a shell program already | Two more executables to keep correct. Each is covered: `bash -n` and the workflow parse the shell one, and the manifest one prints the number of manifests it matched so a silent no-op is visible |
| 88.6 | **Index every delivered path in `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` section 4, 4.1 or 4.3, and publish the row count with what it counts** | (a) Leave the fifty-five later-round paths unindexed and keep the earlier count; (b) merge them into the plan's own table; (c) index them and publish no count | Rule 1 requires the matrix to be bidirectional with no gaps, and fifty-five delivered paths &mdash; the whole workload inventory among them &mdash; were reachable from neither direction, so the claim was disprovable by listing the changed files. (b) would break the 30 / 29 / 0 / 10 breakdown that other documents quote. (c) leaves a reader unable to check the completeness claim without recounting the tree | The published figures are measurements and go stale when a path is added. `test_operator_documentation.py` recomputes both from the tree and the document on every run, so staleness fails the build rather than surviving in prose |
| 88.7 | **Judge the frontend lint report against a recorded warning budget of eight, rather than on the linter's exit status.** The gate invoked the linter and let its exit status decide, which fails while any problem remains and passes once none does -- so it could not distinguish a warning introduced by a change from the eight `frontend/src` already carries. Measured: eight warnings and no error outside the one exempt file. | Demand zero warnings, which would fail every run against read-only source; keep the exit-status gate, which reports the same result whether or not a warning was added; exclude the unparseable file from the run, which hides the finding rather than exempting it. | The budget is a ratchet: the eight existing warnings pass and a ninth fails, which is the property a gate over source this change set may not edit can actually hold. The exempt file is exempted in the judgement rather than excluded from the run, so its parser defect stays visible in the uploaded report. The judgement is a script under `.github/scripts/` for the reason row 88.5 records. | The budget is a number that has to be revised deliberately when the read-only source changes; the failure message names the variable and asks for the reason, so a silent raise is as visible as a silent regression would have been. |

**The accepted total is eight, and both registers are named.** Rows 1.9 and 45.9
record that **Seven** advisories cannot be fixed, which was the runtime register alone
and is the figure each of those rounds measured. **Eight** advisories cannot be fixed
once the development manifest's one is counted with them: seven in the packages the
deployed image installs and one in the verification tooling, held in the *Runtime
register* and the *Development register* of
[`docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](../security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md) respectively, each with
its unreachable fix version and its compensating control. The two sets are disjoint, so
eight suppressions are eight distinct advisories rather than an overlap, and the
audit gate suppresses exactly those eight. The earlier rows stand as chronology; this
paragraph is the figure to quote.
