## 89. Concurrency at the database boundary, the bounds a migration runs under, and what a one-shot pod is given

Four defects in this round share one shape: a decision that reads correct in a single
session and is wrong the moment two sessions, or two kinds of statement, meet. A
subscription intent was created by reading for a reusable row and then inserting, with
nothing between the two steps to stop a second caller doing the same. A filter page was
offset and limited with no ordering, so the row a page boundary fell on was whatever the
plan happened to return. A duplicate webhook delivery arbitrated by waiting on a
uniqueness index, under a request-path statement timeout short enough to cancel that
wait. And the migration environment reached the database on the request path's terms,
so a schema statement was held to the bound a read is held to, while every value it
resolved fell back to a default when it was malformed rather than being refused.

Four more concern the one-shot pods either delivery path runs, and they share a
different shape: a statement about a workload that its own declarations did not hold to.
The administrator credential command was written to run under an identity granted two
values and imported a module that requires eight, so it could not start in the
deployment it exists for. Both one-shot pods were handed a credential neither reads. The
credential Job's name was composed in three places and the three did not agree, one of
them producing a name two characters past the length Kubernetes accepts. And the record
announcing that a credential was in place was written before the transaction carrying it
committed.

**Row 38.7 is superseded in one figure.** Its decision stands -- the provisioning job
runs as its own identity with its own provider class -- but it records that identity as
reading three secrets, which rows 89.7 and 89.8 reduce to two: the command no longer
reads the token-signing key, so the grant and the mount no longer carry it.

One more defect is a written number that the tree outgrew. The revision chain carries
three revisions and nine places still reversed it twice: both gate jobs, the readme's
verification row and its destructive-command warning, a fixture docstring, two
PostgreSQL cases, the security gate's reversal case and the deployment contract's count
assertion. Row 89.12 records how the number was removed from those places rather than
corrected in them.

The last of them is this log and the traceability matrix themselves. Four claims here
described a system that the rows above have since changed, and one described a schema
this work never had. Row 89.13 records how each is withdrawn.

**Rows 6.14, 15.4 and 81.10 are superseded in the claims named
here.** Each decision stands; what is withdrawn is a statement about the system that
another row has since made untrue.

* 6.14 decides to **reuse the most recent open intent** for an account and
  plan. That holds, and row 89.1 is what makes it hold when two creates overlap: until
  the account row was locked before the reuse read, two simultaneous creates each read
  no reusable row and each inserted one.
* 15.4 decides to **run the blocking session calls of the two `async def`
  subscription routes in a worker thread**, and that stands. Two statements in it are
  withdrawn. "No timeout applied, so nothing recovered without restarting the process"
  describes the state before that decision, not the delivered one: the engine has
  carried a 3-second `statement_timeout` since row 81.10, and row 89.3 is what makes
  the contended arbitration resolve within it rather than being cancelled by it. And
  "one read on the same path is still issued on the loop -- the ownership resolution
  inside the payment service" is no longer the case: `backend/app/services/
  paypal_service.py` resolves the order and checks its ownership through
  `run_in_threadpool`, so no statement on that path runs on the loop.
* 81.10's risk column states that "no statement in this service approaches" the
  3-second ceiling. Two did. The webhook arbitration waited on the delivery uniqueness
  for as long as the holder's provider call took, which row 89.3 addresses, and the
  index revision's DDL took 9.2 seconds over 1.2 million rows, which row 89.4
  addresses by giving a migration its own budget. The ladder rows 81.10 and 81.11
  establish -- statement 3 seconds, socket 4, probe 5 -- is unchanged and remains the
  request path's; the migration budget is a fourth number outside it, bounded by the
  migration job's own wall-clock deadline rather than by the probe.
* The traceability matrix's schema section counted **8 added and 37 pre-existing**
  columns, and listed `webhook_events.received_at` among columns added to a
  pre-existing table. Measured from `Base.metadata` and from revision `0001`: **11
  introduced and 34 pre-existing**, the 11 being 7 appended to two pre-existing tables
  and the 4 columns of the table the revision creates. It also described revision
  `0002`'s post-condition as a count, where the revision compares the ordered list of
  addresses holding the role against exactly one address.

**Row 81.39 is completed rather than superseded; 84.6.3 is superseded in one figure, and
rows 43.5.6, 82.16, 83.16 and 86.5.8 in one phrase.** 81.39's decision -- state the count
and the chain together so the two read as one fact -- stands, and of the two documents it
names, `docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md` §4 carries it while `README.md` was left
reversing twice; row 89.12 delivers the readme's half and adds the assertions that keep
both halves true. 84.6.3's decision to end the documented sequence at `alembic upgrade
head` stands; its alternative (a) names "the two downgrades", which is now one per
revision. The four pipeline rows describe the gate as applying and reversing "both
revisions", which was exact when the chain held two.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 89.1 | **Take a write lock on the owning account row before the reuse read** in the subscription-intent path, so two overlapping creates for one account resolve to one subscription row and one provider request identifier | (a) A partial uniqueness index over open intents per account, with retry and requery on violation; (b) a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on the account identifier; (c) `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` against such an index; (d) leave the read-then-insert and rely on the provider's own idempotency key to collapse the duplicates | The two steps that must not interleave are a read for a reusable row and the insert that follows it, and only a lock held across both makes them one decision. The account row is the natural subject: it is already loaded by authentication, every intent for the account is scoped by it, and locking it serialises exactly the callers that could collide while blocking nobody else. (a) needs a new index whose predicate has to name every status the application treats as open, so a status added later silently widens the gap it closes, and it still needs the retry path a lock removes. (b) locks a number rather than the row the invariant is about, and leaves a reader of the code to discover which number. (c) decides against uncommitted rows and would let two callers each believe they had created the only open intent. (d) makes the provider the authority for a decision this service is making, and leaves two rows in this database whatever the provider does with them | A create now waits for a concurrent create on the same account for as long as that create's provider call takes, which the outbound timeout bounds. Callers on different accounts are unaffected: the lock names one row. Proven on PostgreSQL by two overlapping creates that resolve to one row and one request identifier, with the second observed waiting on the lock the first holds |
| 89.2 | **Order the filter page by primary key before the offset and limit are applied** | (a) Order by creation time; (b) order in the application after fetching; (c) leave the ordering to the plan and document that pages are not stable | A page boundary with no ordering is whatever the plan returns, so a row can be seen twice or missed entirely across two adjacent pages -- a correctness defect that shows only under paging. The primary key is total, already indexed and never null, so it costs nothing and cannot tie. (a) is not unique, so it leaves the tie-break unspecified. (b) cannot work: the offset and limit are applied by the database before the application sees a row. (c) documents a defect rather than fixing it | The ownership expression the interface freeze names is untouched -- the ordering is applied after it, and the frozen line is byte-identical. Proven by reading the emitted SQL for the order clause and by asserting the same boundary row across repeated reads |
| 89.3 | **Arbitrate a duplicate webhook delivery with a bounded sequence -- a non-blocking read, then the insert, then a rollback-and-requery on any database failure -- and answer an unresolved delivery for redelivery** | (a) Raise the request-path statement timeout so the wait fits inside it; (b) give the webhook session its own longer statement timeout; (c) treat a cancelled wait as a duplicate without re-reading; (d) leave the single `IntegrityError` branch and let a cancellation surface as a server error | The wait on the uniqueness index is the arbitration, and the request-path bound can cancel it -- which is correct behaviour from the bound and left the route answering a server error for a case the constraint exists to absorb. A rollback followed by a re-read distinguishes the two outcomes the waiter needs to tell apart: the holder committed, so this is a repeat and is acknowledged; or the holder rolled back, so this delivery is still unsettled and the insert is attempted again. (a) weakens a control that protects every other statement in the service to accommodate one route. (b) puts two statement bounds on one connection pool and makes which one applies depend on the route. (c) would acknowledge a delivery whose record was never written, and the provider does not redeliver an acknowledged notification -- the delivery would be lost. (d) is the defect | The sequence retries a bounded number of times and then answers for redelivery rather than looping, so a database that is refusing every write produces a retryable answer instead of an unbounded wait. An unresolved attempt writes nothing. Proven on PostgreSQL under a deliberately short statement bound: the cancelled waiter resolves to a duplicate and acknowledges, and an unresolved delivery leaves no row |
| 89.4 | **Give a migration its own statement budget, `DB_MIGRATION_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, defaulting to 600 seconds with a ceiling of 3600**, rather than reaching the database on the request path's three-second bound | (a) Keep the single bound and raise it to something a schema change can live inside; (b) keep the single bound and have each revision lift it for itself; (c) apply no statement bound to a migration at all | A schema statement rewrites whatever the tables already hold, so its duration is a function of the data rather than of the query, and a bound sized for a request-path read cancels it. (a) would apply a minutes-long bound to every request-path statement, which is the control that stops a contended write holding a worker. (b) puts the bound inside each revision, so a revision added later inherits nothing and the guarantee holds only where somebody remembered it. (c) leaves a stalled schema statement running until the platform kills the pod, with nothing in the record saying which statement stalled. The wall-clock deadline on the migration job stays the outer bound and is above this budget, so a stalled statement is cancelled by the server while the job can still report why it failed. **Row 86.1.2 is superseded in its rationale, not its decision:** it argued for a transaction-local readiness bound on the grounds that the migration environment runs against the application engine, which it does not -- it builds its own -- and the case that rationale was protecting is now held by this separate budget | The value is declared in three places a deployment reads -- the environment template, the Compose environment and the cluster configuration map -- and the standing manifest check asserts the configuration map carries every setting the model declares, so an addition that reaches only some of them fails the build. Measured against PostgreSQL 13: the migration engine opens with `statement_timeout` reported as `10min` and `timezone` as `UTC`, and the three-revision round trip applies, reverses to base and reapplies with exactly one administrator. **The defect this closes was live, not hypothetical.** On a `listings` table of 1,200,000 rows occupying 262 MB, applying `0003` takes 9.4 seconds and creates six indexes; under the three-second bound the environment previously used, the same upgrade is cancelled by the server with `canceling statement due to statement timeout` and leaves no index behind, and a concurrent `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on that table cancels it at the lock wait under any bound shorter than the lock is held for. Under this budget all three cases complete once the lock is released |
| 89.5 | **Extract the database configuration contract into `backend/app/core/db_contract.py`, and have the settings class and the migration environment both hold a value to it** | (a) Have the migration environment import `Settings`; (b) restate each rule in the migration environment; (c) leave the environment's own resolution as it was | The environment reads the database credential and nothing else by design, so importing `Settings` would make a migration depend on the token-signing key and five provider credentials it has no use for. (b) is what stood, and the two statements had already diverged: the environment accepted any non-blank string as a URL where the settings class held it to a scheme, a host, a database name and the environment gate. A restated rule is a rule that drifts. The module reads no setting, opens no connection, reads no file at import and publishes no mutable state, so a one-shot command may import it with only the database URL in its environment | The contract is now on the import path of both the application and every one-shot command, so a defect in it reaches both. It is covered from both sides: the settings cases exercise the validators through the model, and the migration cases exercise them through the environment, including the refusals |
| 89.6 | **Refuse a resolved value the settings class would refuse, rather than replacing it with the default** -- an out-of-range, non-integer or blank bound, an unsupported URL scheme, and an environment name outside the accepted set | (a) Default a malformed value and record it; (b) validate the URL alone and keep defaulting the bounds; (c) leave the fallback in place | A silent fallback means the run proceeds under a value nobody chose, which is the failure mode the settings class was given validators to avoid, and the environment name is the worst case of it: it decides whether a local database scheme is accepted, so an unrecognised name would have been compared against the local one, found unequal, and quietly selected the stricter branch for a reason that had nothing to do with the deployment. (a) puts the fault in a log a migration run may not be watched through. (b) closes the case that carries a credential and leaves the cases that carry a bound. The refusal message names the setting and the rule and never the value, so it can be rendered where a credential must not appear | A deployment that carries a malformed optional bound now fails its migration where it previously ran. That is the intent, and the message says which setting and what range. Proven by driving each refusal through the environment and by perturbation: reinstating either fallback fails twenty-one cases |
| 89.7 | **Decouple the administrator credential command from the serving settings**: it resolves the database URL through the shared contract, builds its own session, and hashes through a new settings-free `backend/app/core/hashing.py`, so it imports neither `Settings` nor any module that reads it | (a) Widen the credential Job's grants so the command can build `Settings` -- mounting the token-signing key and the five provider credentials it never reads; (b) give the command its own settings class carrying only the fields it needs; (c) relax the settings validators so a partially configured environment builds | The Job mounts what the command reads, and the command read a module that reached `Settings`, which requires six credentials the Job does not mount and applies four non-local guards besides -- so the run failed at import in exactly the deployment it was written for. (a) inverts least privilege to accommodate an import: every future run of the credential step would hold the payment and email credentials. (b) is a second settings class to keep in step with the first, which is the drift row 89.5 exists to remove. (c) weakens a control that protects the serving path to fix a command. The role literal moves with it -- the command previously took it from the authorization module, and that module reaches `Settings` -- so the value is stated locally and asserted equal to the enum and to the grant revision's own literal | The command now builds an engine of its own, so a connection setting has two consumers. Both read it from the same contract with the same defaults. Proven by driving `python -m backend.app.core.admin_provisioning` in a subprocess whose environment is exactly what the Job mounts: it provisions, verifies and repeats idempotently against PostgreSQL, and reinstating the settings-bound import makes that same environment fail with the six missing credentials |
| 89.8 | **Withdraw the token-signing key from the credential Job's mount and from the identity's grants**, leaving the database URL and the seed password, and withdraw the shared rate-limit secret from both one-shot Jobs | (a) Leave both grants in place as a safety margin; (b) leave them and record that they are unread | Row 89.7 removes the only reason the credential step ever read the signing key, and a grant that outlives its reason is a grant nobody is accountable for. The rate-limit secret was never read by either one-shot pod: it carries the address of the store the serving pods share, and a migration and a credential write have no counter to keep. (a) treats an accessor binding as free, which is what least privilege denies. (b) leaves a reader unable to tell an unread grant from an unnoticed one. The mount and the IAM binding are changed together, because the binding is what enforces the boundary and the mount is only what consumes it | Two halves must agree, and a test asserts the mounted set equals the granted set in both directions. A future step that does need the signing key must add the grant deliberately, which is the intended cost |
| 89.9 | **Derive both one-shot Job names in the renderer, exposed as `job-name <group>`, and have every delivery path ask it** rather than composing a name at each site | (a) Validate the image tag more strictly so a composed name is always safe; (b) record the name once in each path and pass it forward; (c) put the whole tag in the name and accept the length | The workflow waited on `backend-admin-credential-` plus the first twelve characters of the tag while the manifest rendered the whole tag -- so the wait was issued on an object that had never been created, and a 40-character commit put the manifest's own name at 65 characters, two past the limit the API server enforces on an object name. A tag may also carry upper case, underscores and dots, all legal in a registry tag and none legal in an object name. One derivation in the file that renders the manifest is the only arrangement where the name applied and the name waited on cannot differ: it folds the tag to the accepted alphabet, shortens it to the accepted length, trims a hyphen the shortening left, and refuses a tag that leaves nothing usable. (a) constrains the release to please Kubernetes rather than converting between the two grammars. (b) is what stood in one path and still let the other compose its own. (c) cannot be done: the limit is the API server's | The renderer gains a mode that prints rather than renders, and the two Job manifests now carry a name token whose value no environment can override. Measured: a 40-character commit gives `backend-migrate-<sha>` at 56 characters and `backend-admin-credential-<sha truncated>` at exactly 63; `Release_2026.08.10_RC1` gives a valid lower-case name; a tag of only hyphens is refused |
| 89.10 | **Delete a previous administrator credential Job and confirm its removal before creating the new one**, in both delivery paths | (a) Shorten `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` so the completed Job expires sooner; (b) add the release run to the name so every attempt is a new object; (c) leave it and require an operator to delete by hand | A completed Job is retained for a day so its record can be read, and a Job's pod template cannot be changed in place -- so a reset on a tag that had already provisioned was refused by the API server, which is precisely the operation the reset variable exists to perform. (a) trades the audit record for repeatability and still fails inside the window. (b) makes the name unpredictable, which is what row 89.9 removes, and leaves an object per attempt behind. (c) makes the documented rotation procedure depend on a step the procedure does not mention. The migration Job is deliberately left alone: applying an identical specification for a tag is a no-op, and leaving a completed migration in place is the property its own manifest states | The delete is waited on and the absence re-read, so a deletion that has not finished stops the run instead of racing the create. A retained record of a previous provisioning for the same tag is lost when a reset is performed, which is the cost of making the reset possible; the record survives in the log the run emits |
| 89.11 | **Emit the record that says a credential is in place only after the transaction commits**, and mark every outcome record with whether the state it describes is durable | (a) Leave the record where it was and note the ordering in the message; (b) move the whole write into its own committed transaction; (c) emit nothing until the caller commits | The record was written after the flush and before the commit, so a rollback afterwards left an audit trail asserting a credential that the database did not hold -- and an audit trail is the one artefact that must not overstate. (a) is prose against a false claim. (b) would commit a credential before the post-condition that guards it had been re-asserted. (c) would lose the attempt, which is the record that tells an operator a refused run got as far as writing. So there are two records: the attempt, marked not durable, and the outcome, emitted after the commit with the administrator count re-read from the committed state. A commit that raises emits an error record instead, so the absence of a durable record is never silent | An importer that calls the function directly and commits itself gets the attempt record only; the command is the supported path and it emits both. Proven by perturbation: moving the record back before the commit, or restoring its original wording, fails the two cases that assert the ordering |

## 90. Comment and docstring reduction (fourth pass), and the pointers it moved

A fourth re-review read every comment and docstring in the fifty-nine processed files and
judged them on length and truthfulness rather than on placement. Three comments were
**factually false** about the code beside them. Thirteen module docstrings had grown to
between 206 and 1,105 words, twenty-eight public contracts restated their own mechanics at
length, and the test suite carried 544 comments, 253 `test_*` docstrings and 34 class
docstrings that named what the function name already said. The presentation carried forty
comments of the same kind.

The boundary applied is the one §54.17 set and §65 tightened, with one addition this pass
makes explicit: **a comment that restates its own identifier, its own heading or the line
beneath it earns its removal on redundancy alone**, independently of whether it states
rationale. That is why the presentation's eighteen numbered slide markers went — each named
the heading rendered two lines below it — and why a docstring reading "Returns the user's
role" above `def _role(user)` went with them.

Nothing was lost by removal. Every clause that carried reasoning is recorded here or was
already recorded in an earlier section, and every construct-to-construct mapping stays in
[`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md), which is the only place this project
records one.

### 90.1 Decisions behind this round's changes

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 90.1.1 | **Correct the three false comments in place rather than deleting them.** `core/authorization.py` claimed that returning the first unowned row lets `require_ownership` distinguish a refusal from an absence; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` claimed the development advisories are recorded only in the manifest and that the register covers the runtime set alone; `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` claimed the Function reads `cloud_function_source` and referred to a "whole policy above" that no resource declares | (a) Delete all three, since a comment that is wrong is worse than none; (b) correct the code instead, making each claim true | Each names a real construct a reader needs — the preference order, the register, the uploaded archive — so the fact was worth keeping once corrected. (b) is not available for any of the three: both ownership paths *must* answer alike, because answering differently is the enumeration oracle the remediation closed; the register genuinely holds both sets; and no IAM policy resource is wanted, since the invoker binding is what restricts the Function | A corrected comment is still a second copy of a fact, and can drift again. The three now name a construct or a document that a test resolves, so drift fails a case rather than surviving in prose |
| 90.1.2 | **Delete the presentation's eighteen numbered slide markers and re-key the cases that used them onto each slide's own rendered heading** | (a) Keep the markers, on the ground that they are navigation rather than rationale; (b) delete them and drop the twenty cases that addressed slides by label; (c) replace them with `id` attributes on each `<section>` | Each marker restated the heading two lines below it, which is the redundancy this pass removes. ## 91. Final reconciliation: the authority for current state

This is the round that consolidated this log. Four sections sit after it in this
file, written by rounds that reviewed other areas of the tree at the same time and
that this reconciliation integrated; §87.1 records why each of them arrived numbered
89 or 90. Where any earlier row disagrees with a row here about what the delivered
tree contains, the row here is correct and the earlier row stands as
chronology. Every claim below was
read back from the working tree by grep, by `git ls-files` and by `git diff` against
the baseline revision `a26f7fb`, rather than carried over from the round that wrote
it.

### 91.1 The scope revert: two confirmation-only findings were implemented and are undone

Row 34.6.3 decided to report the ten security-relevant issues found outside the
stated scope and to change nothing in response to any of them. Two later rows broke
that decision without ever withdrawing it, which left this log asserting both
positions at once. The tree now matches row 34.6.3 again.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 91.1.1 | **Row 80.3.1 is withdrawn and its change reverted.** The `terraform` block carrying `required_version` and pinned providers is removed from `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf`, and `infrastructure/terraform/.terraform.lock.hcl` is untracked and deleted. `.gitignore` now ignores that lock instead of re-including it | (a) Keep the pin and record the scope departure afterwards; (b) keep the pin and seek authorization for it; (c) remove the block but keep the committed lock | Item (6) of row 34.6.3 is the absent provider constraint, reported for confirmation rather than fixed. AAP §0.9.2 and §0.12.5 place it there, and a decision-log rationale is not an amendment to the AAP: the authority to close a confirmation-only finding is the user's, not this work's. (a) is what happened and is the defect — a boundary applied per finding stops being a boundary. (b) is unavailable from inside a commit. (c) leaves the pin in force, because a committed lock constrains provider selection on its own | The configuration resolves whatever provider major the registry last published, so two runs a week apart can validate against different resource schemas. That is the open finding, restated in the file's own "Open risks" block, and it is where the fix belongs once authorized |
| 91.1.2 | **Row 80.4.1 is withdrawn in its image half and its command half is re-expressed for the release that runs.** `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` carries `gcr.io/cloudsql-docker/gce-proxy:1.19.1` again, with `-instances=<name>=tcp:0.0.0.0:5432` and `-ip_address_types=PRIVATE`. The ambient-identity posture of that row is **kept**: no credential file is mounted and the instance name is still required | (a) Revert the image and leave the later release's flags in place; (b) revert the whole row, remounting the service-account key; (c) keep the upgrade and record the scope departure | Item (8) of row 34.6.3 is the superseded proxy image, reported for confirmation per row 16.10 and never authorized for upgrade. (a) leaves a command the running release does not accept, which is a stack that cannot start. (b) would reintroduce the mounted key AAP §0.5.1.5 removed, trading a scope breach for a security regression — the credential removal is an in-scope C-4 fix and is unaffected by the image question. (c) is the defect | The image remains a superseded release, which is the open finding. Its listener and address-type controls are expressed in that release's own flag spelling, so a future authorized upgrade must revisit both arguments — the same cost row 42.6.1 accepted |
| 91.1.3 | Restate the four contract cases that asserted the withdrawn constructs, rather than leave them asserting a state the tree no longer has | (a) Delete the cases; (b) mark them skipped pending authorization | A case that asserts a pin the AAP forbids is a case that fails the moment scope is honoured, so it has to move with the revert. (a) removes the guard that would catch a silent re-pin. (b) leaves a skipped case nobody reads | The cases now assert an absence and an exact image tag. An authorized upgrade fails them deliberately, which is the intended signal |

**Rows these two withdrawals restore to truth.** Each was accurate when written,
was contradicted by rows 80.3.1 and 80.4.1, and describes the tree again: row 16.10
(the proxy image tag stands), row 42.6.1 (the tag held while the address-type flag
was added), row 42.6.2 (the absent provider constraint and remote backend left
alone), row 83.21 (no provider constraint and no remote backend added), items 5 and
7 of §42.1's inventory, and row 34.6.3 itself. **None of the ten findings reported
for confirmation is fixed in the delivered tree.** Two remain incidentally changed
in state rather than by decision, exactly as row 34.6.3 already records: the
frontend lock file exists as a setup byproduct (row 23.2.3), and item (3), the
deprecated coroutine decorator, is held per row 12.1.

| 91.6.2 | Keep the seven development advisory identifiers in `backend/requirements-dev.txt` while the analysis lives only in the register | (a) Move the identifiers out too, leaving the manifest to point at the register; (b) restate each fix version and control in the manifest | A reader holding only the manifest needs to know what installing from it accepts, and the identifier list is exactly the set the audit gate suppresses, so naming it beside the pins keeps the two from drifting. (b) is the duplication Rule 1's single-source requirement forbids | The list has to be kept in step with the gate. `test_release_automation_contract.py` compares the two sets on every run |
| 91.6.3 | Restrict the Cloud Function invoker with the authoritative binding form, declaring no `_iam_member` resource and no policy resource for that role | (a) Use the additive `_iam_member` form; (b) manage the whole function policy | (a) adds the approved principal beside whatever is already there, so a public invoker left by an earlier deployment survives every apply. (b) owns every role on the function and would strip unrelated grants, and the provider does not support a policy and a binding managing the same function | The binding removes any member absent from its list, so a grant made deliberately outside this configuration is removed on the next apply |
| 91.6.4 | Hold the manifest settings-contract assertions in a tracked script under `.github/scripts/` and have the workflow invoke it | (a) Embed the assertions in the workflow step body | An embedded body cannot be run at a workstation and is not covered by the repository's own lint, so a failure is only reproducible by pushing. Row 88.5 records the same choice for the two standing checks | One more executable to keep correct; the workflow parse and the repository lint both cover it |
| 91.6.5 | Refuse an in-process rate-limit storage scheme in the deployment workflow, before any pod starts | (a) Let each pod fail its own startup validation | Every replica would fail with the same message at the same moment, which reports a configuration error as an outage. Refusing once, where the value is published, names it as configuration | The workflow now encodes the scheme list the settings module also encodes; the two are asserted against each other by test |
| 91.6.6 | Keep the deploy script's cleanup guard with its reachability note suppressed | (a) Drop the guard, since the handler runs only after the variable is set | The handler is reached through an `EXIT` trap, and a trap that runs after an early failure would dereference an unset variable under `set -u`. Suppressing the note keeps the analyser quiet without removing the protection | A future edit that moves the trap earlier needs the guard, and the suppression hides the analyser's warning that it does |
| 91.6.7 | Read the effective Cloud Function invoker policy back from the deployed function rather than inferring it from the flags the script passed | (a) Trust the flags | A binding added outside this script appears in the policy and in no flag, so the flags cannot answer the question the check exists to ask | One extra provider call per release |
| 91.6.8 | Draw generated passwords from a character set carrying no dollar sign, backslash, quotation mark or backtick, and express the acceptance set for `tr` with the hyphen last | (a) Use the full printable set and escape on write; (b) accept any character and validate only length | `docker compose` reads a dollar sign in an environment file as a variable reference and a backslash as an escape, so a password carrying either reaches a container as a different value from the one PostgreSQL was given. In a `tr` set a hyphen anywhere but last opens a range | The generated alphabet is smaller than the printable set, which the length compensates for |
| 91.6.9 | Pass `--no-password` on the administrator connection and run the access check before the virtual environment, the dependencies and the environment file | (a) Let `psql` prompt; (b) check access after the environment is built | A prompt inside a non-interactive script blocks forever. Checking last means reporting an unusable connection after creating a virtual environment and writing a file | An operator who expects a prompt gets a failure instead, which the message names |
| 91.6.10 | Write the database password into the environment template twice — literally for `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and percent-encoded inside the two URLs | (a) Reference one entry from the other | The two forms are genuinely different strings, and compose performs no encoding. A reference would ship one of them wrong | Three entries to keep in step, which the setup script writes from one prompt |
| 91.6.11 | Collapse the credential-file ignore block to one entry pair in each of the four ignore files | (a) Leave the three duplicate blocks in place and only reword their comments | The pattern was declared three times in each file, and row 82.23's parity claim between the four files was already false because the repository file carried five entries and the image files six. One pair each is what makes the parity claim checkable | The four files must be edited together for the parity to hold; `test_deployment_contract.py` exercises the effective exclusions of each |
| 91.6.12 | In the test suite: read the provider failure message from the module under test, name the readiness bounds independently of the application, accept both PostgreSQL URL variable spellings, isolate integration cases by database rather than by schema, and keep the scripted contention barrier beside the server-driven cases | (a) Restate each value in the test module; (b) accept one URL spelling; (c) isolate by schema; (d) delete the scripted barrier once the server-driven cases existed | A message restated in a test silently stops matching when the module changes it, while a bound restated independently is what makes the assertion able to fail. Both URL spellings are set by continuous-integration jobs. `backend/app/db/database.py` passes its own libpq `options` on every connection, which replaces any search path a URL carries, so a schema is not an isolation boundary here. The scripted barrier decides the outcome and is therefore deterministic, which the server-driven cases are not | The suite carries two contention mechanisms for one behaviour, and the integration path needs create-database privilege on the server it is given |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 91.7.1 | **State repository-delivered, locally verified and applied state separately, and never assert an issuer-side or deployment-side fact.** A document here may say a manifest is delivered, that a test passes and that a credential was removed from the tree. It may not say that nothing is deployed, that a credential is still live, or that a rotation has or has not happened | (a) Keep the shorter unqualified sentences; (b) drop the subject entirely | An unqualified "nothing is deployed" and "the credentials are still live" both read as verified facts, and this repository has no access to a cluster or to a provider console to verify either. (b) removes the warning that rotation is outstanding, which is the one thing a reader must not miss | The qualified form is longer and reads as less certain, which is the accurate reading. `docs/security/CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md` remains the runbook and states that the operation is irreversible and unexecuted here |

## 92. The provider seam's failure contract, the release path's build values, and four positions this log had left standing in contradiction

A code review of the API-to-external-integration seams found six issues. Two were
defects in delivered code, one was a deployment misconfiguration, and three were
this log and its siblings describing a tree that had moved on. The rows below
record every decision taken in answer, and — because Rule 1 treats an
unexplained deviation as a defect and an unwithdrawn contradiction as worse than
either — they also **withdraw four positions** this log had left standing.

**Why the corrections are as consequential as the code changes.** A reviewer
reading row 80.6.5 was told no ingestion trigger existed and was pointed at work
that had already been done, which pointed them away from the two risks the
delivered schedule actually carries. A reader of §82.4 was told secrets arrive
through a synchronised Kubernetes Secret consumed by `envFrom`, which is not what
the manifests declare, and would have looked for an object that does not exist
while rotating a credential. Neither is a documentation nicety: both misdirect the
person the document exists to serve.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 92.1 | **Do not implement a listing provider's real contract; make the declared one enumerable, make a mismatch fail loudly, and register the gap as open item O-9** | (a) Implement an identified provider's exact URL, method, authentication, pagination and response schema, as the review's guidance suggested; (b) implement a substitute third-party provider's contract; (c) leave the adapter and the documentation exactly as they were; (d) delete the adapter until a provider is agreed | The review is right that the adapter's request shape, parameter names and response fields were never checked against a provider, and right that a schedule multiplies that. (a) is refused on two independent grounds. The first is scope: AAP §0.6.1.2 enumerates this file's entire authorised change set — the credential into a request header, an explicit timeout, and the redacting logger — and AAP §0.9.2 excludes feature additions unrelated to security and directs that findings outside scope be reported for confirmation rather than fixed. The second is that there is nothing to implement: Zillow retired its public Web Services API in September 2021 and its official successor is an approval-gated RESO Web API requiring a multiple-listing-service membership or an approved partnership, so no self-serve specification exists to code against and guessing a more plausible shape would not make it verified. (b) is the same problem wearing a different name — choosing a provider is a licensing and cost decision with an owner, and it is not this one. (c) leaves a delivered integration whose far side has never been checked reading as working software. (d) would remove the only path by which the corpus is ever populated. What is left is the honest middle: publish the declaration so it is reviewable and changeable in one place, make every departure from it a loud failure so the first live call reports the difference, and register the gap where a reader looks for what was not closed | The adapter may not work against a real provider, and this remediation does not claim otherwise. The risk is now bounded rather than hidden: a mismatch fails on the first call naming the element that did not match, `DECLARED_PROVIDER_CONTRACT` is the single place to change, and O-9 tells an operator to close it before enabling the schedule |
| 92.2 | **Raise `ListingProviderError` carrying a stable `reason` for every provider read that produced no usable response, and keep an empty collection a success** | (a) Return an empty list and log, as before; (b) return a sentinel value the caller inspects; (c) return a result object carrying either listings or a failure; (d) raise, but reuse `ListingMappingError` | Seven distinct outcomes — an endpoint outside the allowlist, an oversized postal-code chunk, a transport failure, a refused status, an oversized body, an undecodable body, and a body that does not satisfy the declared contract — all produced the same value as a provider that answered and reported nothing. (a) is what the review found: an outage and a quiet market were indistinguishable, and the log record that named the difference had no consumer. (b) puts the burden on every caller to remember to check, which is the failure mode of every sentinel. (c) is the tidier design and is refused as disproportionate: there is one caller, and a typed exception with a stable `reason` field gives it the same information for a fraction of the change. (d) would conflate a whole read that failed with one record that could not be mapped, which are handled differently and counted differently. The distinction the raise draws is deliberately narrow: a provider that answered correctly and reported no listings still returns an empty list, because alerting on a quiet hour would train an operator to ignore the signal | A caller that previously received an empty list now receives an exception. There is exactly one caller and it is changed with this row. `reason` is a stable identifier rather than prose, so a log query selects a cause by field |
| 92.3 | **Roll back and re-raise at the ingestion task boundary, and give the in-process schedule its own catch-log-continue** | (a) Re-raise from both, so a failure ends the in-process schedule too; (b) keep absorbing in both, and signal failure some other way — a sentinel exit code, or a health file the CronJob checks; (c) re-raise only when a caller opts in through a parameter | The CronJob decides retry and failed-job history from the container's exit status, and `update_listings` absorbed every failure, so `asyncio.run(update_listings())` exited 0 and `backoffLimit: 2` never engaged. The two callers want opposite things and both are legitimate: a one-pass-per-process caller needs the failure, and `run_listing_updater`, which runs passes inside the serving process, needs the loop to survive one bad hour. (a) would make a single provider blip stop refreshing the corpus until the process restarted. (b) is an exit-status protocol invented to avoid using the one the platform already provides. (c) adds a parameter to express what the call site already knows. Putting the raise in the pass and the tolerance in the loop leaves each function's docstring true of it, and `asyncio.CancelledError` is re-raised so the background task still stops when cancelled | A failure now ends the pass, so a later chunk's failure discards the earlier chunks' writes rather than committing a partial refresh. That is the intended direction: a partial refresh that reported success was indistinguishable from a complete one |
| 92.4 | **Bind the CronJob's retry contract and the task's re-raise together in one test, rather than asserting either alone** | (a) Assert the manifest's `backoffLimit` and `failedJobsHistoryLimit` only; (b) assert the task re-raises only; (c) assert neither and rely on the code review | Either half alone is satisfiable while the property fails: a manifest can declare an attempt limit for a command that always exits 0, and a task can raise into a command that swallows it. `test_the_ingestion_schedule_can_observe_a_failed_pass` therefore reads the manifest for the attempt limit, the failure history, the concurrency policy and the restart policy, asserts the pass is the last thing the command `exec`s and that no `\|\| true`, `set +e` or handler follows it, and reads the task's own source for `db.rollback()` followed by `raise`. (c) is how the defect survived several rounds | The test reads source text for a control-flow property, which a sufficiently creative refactor could satisfy while breaking. It is paired with behavioural cases in `test_tasks.py`, and the process outcome was measured directly rather than inferred |
| 92.5 | **Read both frontend build values from the repository-variable context in the workflow, and derive the browser client identifier from the same `PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID` the manifests render** | (a) Move the manifest render to the secrets context instead, so both sides read `secrets`; (b) populate both namespaces and document that they must match; (c) pass the client identifier to the frontend build from a separate variable of its own | The workflow built the browser bundle from `secrets.PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID` and `secrets.REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL` while rendering the backend manifests from `vars.PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID`, and the README documents both as repository **variables** — so under the documented configuration the bundle was built with an empty client identifier and hosted checkout could not open. (a) is refused because neither value is a secret: the bundler inlines both into a published bundle, so storing them as secrets misrepresents what they are and invites the assumption that the PayPal *secret* could travel the same way. (b) is the defect restated as a procedure: two namespaces holding one value drift, and nothing detects it. (c) has the same flaw one level down — two variables for one PayPal application. One expression on both sides makes divergence impossible rather than unlikely | Both values must now be present as repository variables, and a deployment configured before this change fails its preflight naming the variable to set. That is the intended direction: the previous behaviour was to publish a bundle that could not transact |
| 92.6 | **Pass the frontend build arguments from a per-workload table in `scripts/deploy.sh`, and refuse an empty value before anything is built** | (a) Special-case the frontend inside the build loop with an `if`; (b) always pass both arguments to every image; (c) pass them and let docker decide | The script built every image through one generic loop and passed no build argument at all, so the manual release path published a bundle with neither value. (a) puts image-specific knowledge inside a loop written to be image-agnostic, and the next image with a build argument repeats the problem. (b) passes arguments the backend image does not declare, which docker warns about and which misstates the contract. (c) is the trap the whole finding rests on: docker accepts an empty `--build-arg` silently, so the failure surfaces to an end user rather than to the release. A table beside the existing Dockerfile and context tables keeps the loop generic, and the check runs in `read_inputs` so it fails before an image is built rather than after one is published. The names are read into an array through a quoted here-string and carried in the function's own positional parameters, because the repository's shell audit refuses any unquoted expansion and the nested-quote idiom for a possibly-empty array is one | `usage()` now lists two more required inputs. A release that omits either stops with the name of the missing value rather than publishing a bundle that cannot transact |

The gate's consequence sentence is unchanged, so the reviewer's action is the same one |
## 93. The seam review: password semantics, delivered-surface truth, and two release seams

A review of the boundary between this backend and the read-only frontend, and of the
documents that describe the delivered surface, raised sixteen findings. Five are repairs
inside `frontend/src/**` that this change set may not make, and the closing paragraph of
this section records where each is already accounted for. The remaining eleven are seams:
places where two artifacts stated one fact differently, or where a document had gone stale
against the tree it describes. Every row below is a choice a competent engineer could have
made differently, and three of them withdraw a position this project previously published.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 93.1 | **Record the password-length divergence as a documented seam and change neither side.** The browser validator counts UTF-16 code units (`frontend/src/utils/validators.ts:19` declares the floor, `:26` applies it); the request schema counts Unicode code points for the same twelve-character floor (`backend/app/schema/user.py:8`, applied at `:68`) and UTF-8 bytes for the seventy-two-byte ceiling (`:9`, applied at `:58`). Three units, one field. Measured, with `Aa1!` as the class-satisfying prefix: four astral emoji give 12 code units, 8 code points and 20 bytes, so the form accepts and the server refuses on the floor; eighteen give 40, 22 and 76, so the form accepts and the server refuses on the ceiling; and `Aa!` followed by nine U+0967 DEVANAGARI DIGIT ONE gives 12 code points and 30 bytes, which the server accepts and the form refuses, because the server's digit predicate is Unicode-aware and the browser's `/\d/` is ASCII-only. The four character-class patterns are otherwise character-identical, `backend/app/schema/user.py:15-20` against `frontend/src/utils/validators.ts:20-23` | (a) Change the browser validator to count code points and UTF-8 bytes, so both sides judge one field the same way; (b) relax the server's floor and ceiling to agree with UTF-16 code units; (c) leave the divergence unrecorded, as the previous revision of this log did | (a) is the repair a reader reaches for first, and it is the one change this set may not make: the plan's §0.9.2 places everything under `frontend/src/**` out of scope, and §0.6.1.7 lists that file as a read-only reference whose role is to establish the documented twelve-character policy, not to be a target. (b) moves the server to meet the client, which §0.1.2 forecloses in the same terms it freezes the login response shape and every route path &mdash; and the byte ceiling in particular is the guard §0.2.2.3 requires *because* pre-hashing was rejected, so relaxing it would either truncate a credential silently or surface the hashing library's own `ValueError` as a server fault. (c) is the finding itself: Rule 1 treats an unexplained deviation from an obvious reading as a defect, and "both sides enforce twelve characters" is exactly the obvious reading this seam departs from | A password composed of astral characters can be accepted by the form and refused by the request, so the user sees a submitted-then-rejected error rather than an inline one. The refusal is a 422 carrying the generic invalid-request body and creates no account, which is asserted by `test_login_lockout_and_rate_limit.py::test_a_registration_password_beyond_the_byte_ceiling_is_refused`, `::test_a_login_password_beyond_the_byte_ceiling_is_refused`, `::test_a_password_at_the_byte_ceiling_is_accepted`, `::test_the_byte_ceiling_counts_bytes_and_not_characters` and `::test_a_password_failing_the_policy_floor_is_refused`. Every ASCII password &mdash; the case the twelve-character policy was written for &mdash; is judged identically by both sides, because the three units coincide on ASCII |
| 93.2 | **Collapse the credential-file block to one canonical pattern pair per ignore file, in all four files rather than the two the review cited.** `.gitignore`, `.dockerignore`, `backend/.dockerignore` and `frontend/.dockerignore` each carried the same block two or three times; each now carries `gha-creds-*.json` and `**/gha-creds-*.json` once, under one explanation | (a) Leave the repetition, which changes no behaviour; (b) delete the later copies and keep only the root-anchored pattern; (c) fix the two files the review named and leave the other two | The repetition is not inert: three copies in one file mean a future narrowing of one copy is invisible against the other two, and a reader must reconcile them before trusting any. (b) stops matching the path at depth, which is the case the authenticating action actually produces when it writes into a working subdirectory, so the pair is the minimum that holds &mdash; `git check-ignore -v` resolves `gha-creds-1234.json` through the anchored pattern and `backend/gha-creds-abc.json` and `a/b/c/gha-creds-x.json` through the recursive one. (c) leaves the same defect in two files that share one root cause, which is how a single edit becomes four divergent ones | A reader who remembers the block from one of its old positions finds it once. Behaviour is unchanged and is asserted rather than described: `.github/scripts/check_secret_policy.sh`, `test_delivery_surface_contract.py::test_the_credential_name_is_ignored_everywhere` &mdash; which requires the anchored and recursive pair in each of the four ignore files &mdash; and `test_release_path_contract.py::test_the_generated_credential_file_is_ignored_everywhere` judge the property, not the wording |
| 93.3 | **Read the two public frontend build values from `vars.*`, and refuse the run when either is blank.** `.github/workflows/cd.yml:256-257` reads `vars.REACT_APP_API_BASE_URL` and `vars.PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID`, and the step at `:134` names the missing variable and stops before any image is built | (a) Keep both as `secrets.*`; (b) declare each in both namespaces so either provisioning works; (c) make the switch without a preflight | The same setting was already read as `vars.PAYPAL_CLIENT_ID` at `:553` for the function deployment, so one workflow read one value from two namespaces and at most one of them could be populated. Neither value is a secret: both are compiled into a bundle served to every visitor, and treating a public value as a secret is what let the mismatch survive review. (b) doubles the provisioning surface for one value and leaves the reader to work out which wins. (c) leaves the original failure mode intact, because an unset `vars.*` expands to the empty string and the build would succeed while producing a bundle whose API base is blank; the preflight was exercised over all four populated-and-blank combinations and refused three | An operator who had provisioned these as repository secrets must move them to variables. The preflight names which one is missing, so the diagnosis is one line of log rather than a bundle that fails in a browser |
| 93.4 | **Give the Compose redirect URLs their own override names,** `COMPOSE_PAYPAL_RETURN_URL` and `COMPOSE_PAYPAL_CANCEL_URL` at `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml:85-86`, defaulting to the origin Compose actually publishes | (a) Keep the generic `PAYPAL_RETURN_URL` and `PAYPAL_CANCEL_URL` names; (b) drop the Compose defaults and require both values; (c) change the published frontend port so the generic values become correct | The generic pair is documented at `.env.example:515-516` with a development origin on port 3000, while the Compose frontend publishes port 80 &mdash; so an operator with a populated environment file had a correct default silently replaced by one pointing at a port nothing listens on, which was reproduced by evaluating Compose's own interpolation before and after the change. (b) makes the documented one-command bring-up fail on a value the file can supply correctly on its own. (c) changes a published port to accommodate a documentation value, inverting which artifact is authoritative. The alias convention already exists in this file and is asserted by the alias table in `test_deployment_contract.py`, so the fix reuses a mechanism rather than inventing one | Two further names an operator may set. Both are documented in the Compose section of `.env.example` at `:713-714`, beside a cross-reference to the generic pair they override, and the alias table asserts each is both consumed by the Compose file and documented in the template |
| 93.5 | **Publish exactly one current measurement of the delivered surface, and label every earlier figure as a superseded snapshot rather than overwriting it.** The identity is `59 + 27 + 56 - 17 = 125` delivered paths, being 95 created and 30 modified, with `125 + 9 + 17 = 151` reverse-index rows | (a) Update each of the four standing figures in place; (b) keep the largest and delete the rest; (c) publish a range instead of a number | Four different totals &mdash; 86, 91, 93 and 141 &mdash; stood in one document at once, so a reader could not tell which to check and each was disprovable by measuring the tree. One identity, recomputed from the tree and from the document on every run by `test_operator_documentation.py`, is checkable. (a) destroys the record of what each round measured, which §27's convention establishes this log does not do. (b) and (c) leave a figure nobody can reproduce | The snapshot register is longer than a single number would be. The whole 141-to-125 gap is accounted for arithmetically &mdash; seventeen paths withdrawn by the manifest consolidation of §88, and `.terraform.lock.hcl` counted where it previously was not &mdash; so the register is reconciliation rather than narrative |
| 93.6 | **Reconcile the plan-entry figure to the plan's own `30 + 29 + 0 + 9 = 68`, and state that section 2 of the matrix renders 69 rows for those 68 entries** | (a) Restate the figure as 69 with ten read-only references, matching the rendered row count; (b) leave both figures standing and let a reader choose | §0.6.1 of the plan is frozen, and a document that describes the plan may not renumber it. `backend/app/api/router.py` is rendered inside the application-core group because that is where a reader looks for it, and is counted once, as a reference, in the read-only table &mdash; so row count and entry count differ by exactly one by construction. (c) erases which half changed and when, and §27 records that this project supersedes rather than rewrites | One more open item to carry, and every document quoting the count of open items moved from eight to nine. `test_documentation_citations.py` asserts the register's identifiers are O-1 through O-9, so an item added without being indexed fails the build |
