| 93.17 | **Recolour the closing slide's lead line for its dark background, reusing the value that block already applies to its bullets.** The navy closing slide overrode its heading and its bullets and not its lead line, which kept the light-surface `--blitzy-text` at `#333333` and rendered at 1.30:1 against `#1A105F` &mdash; measured in a browser and sampled from the rendered pixels, with the heading and bullets on the same slide measuring 16.36:1 | (a) Leave it, since every automated check over the deck passed; (b) give the lead line a token of its own; (c) drop the lead line from the closing slide | The sentence is the one-line takeaway on the last slide and it was invisible to a viewer, while the bounds, overflow, bullet, word-budget and declared-token checks all passed &mdash; which is how it survived to a review. (b) introduces a second value for body text on the same background, and the two are then free to drift. (c) deletes a sentence the closing slide exists to carry and that `test_operator_documentation.py::test_the_deck_closing_offers_review_rather_than_release` requires | One more rule to add for any further text element the closing slide gains. `test_deck_contract.py::test_the_dark_closing_slide_recolours_every_text_element_it_carries` reads which elements the slide actually carries and requires a colour rule for each, so a fifth element without one fails rather than renders unreadably |

**Five of this review's sixteen findings are repairs inside read-only frontend source, and
none is closed here.** They are the authentication client's import of a symbol its module
does not export and its use of a path and response fields this backend does not serve; the
absence of any bearer-token transport alongside a profile route that does not exist; the
payment client's use of the Billing Subscriptions interface against a Checkout Orders
backend, together with an undeclared dependency in `frontend/package.json`; the
subscription interface whose fields do not match the response and which is not exported;
and the implementation half of the password divergence row 93.1 records. Each is already
accounted for &mdash; rows 29.7 to 29.10, rows 73.7 to 73.10 and row 80.6.3 here, and open
items O-5 and O-6 in [`docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](../security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md) &mdash;
and the plan's §0.9.2 is the clause that keeps them there. The opposite repair, moving this
backend to meet the client, is foreclosed by §0.1.2, which freezes the login response shape
and every route path. Row 93.1 closes the one obligation this change set does own from that
set: the deviation is now recorded, which is what Rule 1 requires of it.
**Rows 84.1.1 through 84.1.3, and row 42.4.3, are superseded on their figure.** They
recorded a development register of seven and a published total of fourteen, and both
were accurate for the manifest shape of their round. Six of that seven were
`pip-audit`'s own dependency tree, reported because the manifest declaring the
instrument was the manifest being audited. Row 93.1 below moves the instrument to
`backend/requirements-audit.txt`, which no audit reads, so the development register is
one and the total is eight. Those rows' *reasoning* stands — two registers, counted
separately, each stating its manifest — and only their counts are withdrawn.

**Four further rows quote the same withdrawn figure and are superseded on it alone:**
row 43.5.5, on auditing each manifest in its own step; row 80.8.2, on reproducing the
gate commands in `SECURITY.md`; row 86.5.11, on correcting the audit comment; and the
`SECURITY.md 2` row of §35.2's correction table. Each says *fourteen* where the gate now
suppresses *eight*, and row 80.8.2 additionally describes a contract test asserting the
count is exactly fourteen — that assertion now reads eight. Their decisions are all
still in force: the two audited manifests are still audited in separate steps, the
policy still reproduces both invocations verbatim, and each step's comment still names
only its own register. Only the quantity moved. One row is **not** superseded despite
using the word: the *fourteen-pattern reachability measurement* in
[`RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md) counts search patterns rather than advisories,
and that figure is unchanged.

Finding F-13 of the earlier review — *fourteen advisories suppressed against a register
covering seven* — is recorded as it was found, because a finding is a statement about the
tree at the time it was raised. What changed is its resolution: the earlier round closed
the gap by registering both sets and publishing fourteen, and this round closes it
again, and better, by removing six of them from the measured surface altogether.

## 94. The release path, the toolchain and the audited surface

This round answers a review that returned NOT APPROVED on the whole project. Its
findings are addressed in the order the work had to happen: the release path and the
toolchain first, then what the dependency audit measures, then the cloud footprint,
then two database invariants, then the configuration contract and the published
record. Every row below is a decision a competent engineer could reasonably have
taken differently.

### 94.1 What the dependency audit measures

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.1.1 | **Declare the audit instrument in a manifest of its own, `backend/requirements-audit.txt`, install it in the gate and audit it with nothing.** The audited surface is `backend/requirements.txt` and `backend/requirements-dev.txt`; the instrument is the tool that reads them. | (a) Leave `pip-audit` in `backend/requirements-dev.txt` and keep accepting its six transitive advisories, which is the shape the review found and rejected; (b) replace the instrument with a scanner whose own tree carries no advisory; (c) advance the interpreter so the six fixes become installable; (d) suppress the six by identifier and describe them as tooling in prose. | The review's own resolution names this first: isolate the audit toolchain so vulnerable scanner dependencies are not part of the project development manifest. It is also the only option that changes the *measurement* rather than the *accounting* — measured after the split, `pip-audit --strict -r backend/requirements-dev.txt` reports one advisory in one package where it reported seven in five, and no `--ignore-vuln` flag anywhere names one of the six. (a) leaves a frozen requirement broken. (b) trades a known instrument for an unmeasured one and would have to be re-argued from scratch. (c) is forbidden: the interpreter pin is a hard constraint at five sites. (d) is the accounting this round exists to correct — six of the seven accepted advisories were not this repository's supply chain at all. | The instrument's own tree is now unaudited, so an advisory in it is not reported by this pipeline. What bounds that is recorded in *The audit instrument's own tree* of [`docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md): the instrument is in no image, is exercised only by its own invocation against a manifest in this repository, and reads no request. The specific hazard to watch is a runtime dependency being laundered into the tooling manifest to leave the audited set; the runtime audit suppresses neither `requests` nor `urllib3`, so it fails if either returns, and `test_no_withdrawn_development_suppression_returns` fails if any of the six is added back to an ignore list. |
| 94.1.2 | **Depart from the `backend/requirements-dev.txt` file schema's seven-entry limit by splitting one entry into a third manifest**, keeping all seven tools pinned at exactly the versions that schema names. | (a) Hold the seven-entry shape literally and leave the finding open; (b) drop the instrument from the repository and run it ad hoc, unpinned. | The schema's two requirements are jointly unsatisfiable under the interpreter pin: it requires `pip-audit` to be declared in that manifest, and it requires an audit of that manifest to report no advisory outside the documented set. Something had to give, and the review's resolution authorises exactly this — "obtain a separately authorized change to the frozen requirement". What the schema is protecting is preserved in full: the same seven tools, the same exact pins, the same absence from every image, and `httpx` still pinned identically to the runtime manifest. Only the file boundary moves. (b) would unpin the instrument, which is the opposite of the toolchain immutability this round establishes elsewhere. | A third manifest is a third file an installer has to know about. Every documented install command and the gate itself name all three, and the new manifest's own header states why it exists. |
| 94.1.3 | **Keep the one remaining development advisory accepted rather than raising the test framework**, and record it in the *Development register* with its measurement. | (a) Raise `pytest` to its fix version; (b) remove the framework's advisory from the audited surface by some further split. | `pytest==9.0.3` and every later release declares `Requires-Python >=3.10` and is refused under CPython 3.9.25, measured with `pip install --dry-run --no-deps`. (b) would be the accounting trick that (a) of row 94.1.1 was rejected for: the test framework genuinely is this repository's development surface, and hiding it would make the register less honest rather than more. | One advisory stays accepted, in a package that is in no image and reads no request. It closes with the interpreter migration recorded at row 1.9, and with nothing else. |

### 94.2 The release path and the toolchain

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.2.1 | **Require four facts of the triggering run rather than one** — the run passed, it was a push, it was on the release branch, and its head repository is this repository — carried in the same single conditional job every other job reaches. | (a) Keep the conclusion check alone; (b) revert the trigger to `on: push` with an in-workflow gate, which is the shape the workflow's own file schema describes literally; (c) add a second conditional job for provenance. | `workflow_run` fires for every completed run of the named workflow, and the run it starts holds this repository's write token and release credentials, which the triggering run need not have held. A pull request opened from a fork produces a successful run, so the conclusion alone is not provenance. The trigger's own branch filter matches the triggering run's head branch, which on a fork is the fork's branch name, so a fork branch named for the release branch satisfies it — `head_repository` is the term that does not. (b) would discard the reusable-gate design that the delivery contract now asserts in depth. (c) would put the guard in two places that could disagree. | The guard hardcodes the release-branch name, matching the trigger's own filter; renaming the branch means changing both, and the contract test names the branch so the omission fails rather than silently admitting nothing. |
| 94.2.2 | **Pass the released commit into the reusable gate as an input, resolved once into a single workflow-level value every checkout reads.** | (a) Remove the re-run entirely and rely on the already-passed triggering run, which the review offers as its second option; (b) repeat the expression at each of the six checkouts. | A reusable workflow runs the definition its caller holds and checks out the caller's revision unless told otherwise, so the gate was re-verifying the default branch rather than the commit being released. (a) is defensible but leaves the deployment with no verification of its own artefact; re-verifying the exact commit is stronger and costs one input. (b) invites drift as checkouts are added. | An added checkout that omits the reference would read the wrong revision; `test_the_gate_verifies_the_commit_the_deployment_releases` asserts every checkout in the gate resolves the one value. |
| 94.2.3 | **Pin the two tag-referenced actions at the current release of the major each already used, rather than advancing to the next major**, and pin the Terraform binary to the exact release the configuration is verified with. | (a) Advance to `actions/setup-node` v7 and `hashicorp/setup-terraform` v4 while pinning; (b) leave the tags and keep the exemption; (c) declare no `terraform_version` and let the action resolve whichever release it prefers at run time; (d) keep the contract's exemption set and empty it rather than deleting it. | The finding is mutability, not staleness: a full commit is the only immutable reference, and it is obtainable for both without changing behaviour. A major bump is a separate behavioural change the minimal-change constraint excludes and would need its own argument. (b) was the previous position, and the ground it rested on — that the commits were not derivable here — is disproven: both resolve from `git ls-remote --tags --refs`, and the method reproduces the `actions/setup-python` pin already in the file exactly. (c) would leave the binary that plans and validates the infrastructure chosen by the action at run time, which is the same mutability one layer down; `terraform_version: 1.15.8` names the release this configuration is verified against here, and it clears the 1.11 floor the ephemeral input variables and write-only secret arguments need. **The clause that said it "satisfies the definition's own `required_version >= 1.11.0`" is withdrawn by row 96.1.1: the configuration declares no `required_version`, deliberately, and the floor is a property of the constructs it uses rather than a constraint it states.** (d) would leave a hook in the contract with nothing in it, and an empty exemption invites a refill. | The pinned releases age, and nothing detects that automatically. The exemption set that previously allowed a tag is deleted rather than emptied, so the contract is unconditional over both workflows and a tag reference fails the build. |
| 94.2.4 | **Pin the bootstrap installer to one exact version declared once at workflow scope**, and inventory it as a comment in the development manifest rather than as a requirement line. | (a) Repeat the version at each install site; (b) add `pip==26.0.1` as an eighth manifest entry; (c) drop the upgrade and use whatever the runner provides. | Five jobs install a manifest and each bootstrapped an unpinned latest installer first — a package outside both audited manifests executing ahead of the audit itself. One declaration cannot drift; five can. A requirement line would place the installer inside the audited set it is the tool for, and would exceed the manifest's declared entry list. (c) makes the version a property of the runner image, which is not reviewable from this repository. | The pin has to be revised deliberately as releases appear. `test_the_gate_installs_one_pinned_bootstrap_everywhere` fails if any install drops it. |
| 94.2.5 | **Move the documented line-number citation to the line the construct now occupies and record the line it left as withdrawn**, rather than arranging the workflow so the original number stayed true. | (a) Order the workflow's new steps so the cited construct keeps its original line; (b) drop the line numbers from the review artefact and cite constructs only. | Pinning the bootstrap installer added lines above the runtime pin in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, so the citation the review artefacts carry moved from line 88 to line 113. The standing convention at rows 43.5.7 and 80.7.1 is that the citation follows the code: the numbers stay, because a reviewer performing a mandated check benefits from the exact line to open, and `backend/tests/security/test_documentation_citations.py` asserts each one against the file. (a) would let a document's line number decide the shape of a workflow, which inverts that. (b) is the convention the decision log and the traceability matrix already follow for claims about the current tree, and row 43.5.7 records why it is deliberately not extended to the review artefact. | The citation is coupled to a line in a file this round edited repeatedly; the assertion is what makes that safe, and the abandoned line is held in `WITHDRAWN_CITATIONS` so a reverted edit cannot quietly restore it. |

### 94.3 The PostgreSQL verification path

Found while enabling the production-dialect database locally to de-risk the two
revisions this round adds. Three cases asserted the state of a *fully reversed*
migration chain after a *counted* number of reversals, and the count was two — the
length of the chain when they were written. The chain has been three revisions since
`0003` was added, so two reversals stop one revision short, and the assertions that
follow describe a schema that has not been reached.

This was not a dormant local-only defect. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` names the
integration database and sets the variable that turns an absent server into a failure
rather than a skip, and `backend/tests/conftest.py` accepts both of that job's variable
names as aliases — verified by reading the alias tuples rather than assumed, after an
initial reading suggested the names did not match. So the cases ran in the pipeline and
failed there. Measured locally with the server named: **1 failed, 3425 passed** before
these rows, **3426 passed with nothing skipped** after.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.3.1 | **Name the revision each reversal reverses down to — a revision identifier or `base` — wherever the assertion that follows describes a fully reversed chain**, rather than counting steps back from the head | (a) Raise the count from two to three; (b) derive the count from the revision inventory at run time; (c) leave the cases skipped locally and treat the pipeline failure as environmental | (a) restores the assertion for exactly as long as the chain stays three revisions, and this round adds two more, so it would be wrong twice more before the work is finished — the defect is the counting, not the number. (b) computes the right number but states the intent less clearly than naming the target, and couples every case to an inventory helper. (c) is not available: the pipeline sets the variable that makes an absent server a failure, so these cases were red rather than dormant. A named target says what the assertion means and is indifferent to how many revisions sit above it | A named target reverses several revisions in one invocation, so it does not by itself prove each reverses independently. That property is asserted separately and more strongly by the two cases row 94.3.3 keeps, which step one revision at a time and read the recorded revision after each |
| 94.3.2 | **Assert that no table the chain created remains, rather than asserting the legacy pre-revision shape**, in the case whose fixture applies the revisions to a database created for that case | (a) Keep the legacy-shape helper and have the fixture write a preceding schema first; (b) relax the legacy-shape helper to tolerate absent tables | Revision `0001` records whether it created the tables it found missing, so its downgrade drops them when it created them and removes only the added columns when they already existed. The fixture migrates an empty database, so the create path is the one taken and an empty schema is the correct inverse — measured: reflection after the reversal returns `alembic_version` alone. Asserting the legacy shape there asserted a state that revision is right not to leave. (a) would change what the case covers, and the alter-in-place path is already covered by the cases that write a preceding schema. (b) would weaken a helper three cases share, so a genuine failure to restore the legacy shape would stop being detected in the two cases where that shape is the correct expectation | The assertion is a negative over a named table set, so a table added to the schema without being added to that set would not be checked. The set is the same constant the positive shape assertion reads, so the two cannot drift apart |
| 94.3.3 | **Leave the two cases that read the recorded revision after each single reversal counting steps**, and extend them by one step as each revision is added | (a) Convert them to named targets for consistency with row 94.3.1; (b) collapse them into the full-reversal cases | Their subject *is* one-step-at-a-time behaviour: one asserts the recorded revision after each reversal, the other asserts that the first reversal removes the indexes and leaves the administrator, the second returns the administrator to the default role and leaves the columns, and only the third removes what `0001` added. Converting them would delete the only assertions that each revision reverses independently, which is the property row 94.3.1 gives up. Their docstrings state the step count, so the count is asserted rather than incidental | Each is a place a new revision must be extended, and forgetting one fails the case rather than passing it silently — the reversal would stop above `base` and the recorded revision would not match. That is the safe direction to fail |


### 94.4 The function's source artefact and its authorization

The configuration held **two** source objects in the same bucket. One was named
for the content digest of an archive Terraform packaged from the committed
function directory, and the function read it. The other sat at the fixed name
`function-source.zip`, took its bytes from a path on whatever machine ran
Terraform, and was what `scripts/deploy.sh` deployed — after checking only that
something existed at that address. So the artefact released was not provably the
artefact this repository builds, and the invoker binding governed a function
built from bytes the configuration never saw.

Separately, the function is authorized off by default, while the delivery
workflow verified its invoker policy unconditionally. `gcloud functions
describe` fails when nothing was created, and the step runs under
`set -euo pipefail`, so the default configuration failed its own verification.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.4.1 | **Keep one source object, the content-addressed one, and delete the fixed-name object together with `cloud_function_source_archive`, `cloud_function_source_object` and the orphaned `cloud_function_source_archive_object`** | (a) Keep both objects and point the release script at the digest-named one; (b) keep the fixed name and delete the digest-named object; (c) keep both and document which is authoritative | Two objects cannot both be the artefact, and whichever the script deployed, the other was dead weight that a future reader would reasonably treat as live. (b) reintroduces the defect it would appear to fix: a fixed name can be overwritten, so the name stops identifying the bytes, and `source_archive_object` would no longer change when the function changes — the function would not be redeployed on a source change. (c) leaves an arbitrary local path as a deployable artefact, which is the path-traversal shape of the finding rather than a naming preference. The orphan was read by nothing at all and its description claimed it was applied as `source_archive_object`, which was untrue | The archive is now packaged only by Terraform, so an operator cannot substitute a locally built zip — deliberate, and the reason the packaging directory `var.cloud_function_source_dir` remains an input. `test_the_terraform_function_contract_matches_the_release_script` asserts the deleted resource and all three deleted variables stay absent, and `test_the_function_reads_a_source_object_this_configuration_creates` asserts exactly one bucket object exists |
| 94.4.2 | **Publish the object's name and its base64 MD5 as outputs, and have the release script compare the digest the bucket reports against the digest Terraform reported before deploying** | (a) Keep the existence check; (b) have the script run `terraform output` itself; (c) pin the object generation in the `gs://` address; (d) have the script rebuild the archive and compute the digest locally | An existence check proves only that the name is occupied, which is exactly what the fixed-name object made cheap to abuse. Comparing digests proves the bytes. The digest is carried as an output because `google_storage_bucket_object.md5hash` and `gcloud storage objects describe --format="value(md5_hash)"` are the **same base64 encoding**, so the comparison needs no re-encoding — the archive data source's `output_md5` is hex and would have needed converting in shell. (b) would require the release host to hold Terraform state, which is a much larger privilege than deploying. (c) is stronger against replacement between check and deploy but relies on `gcloud functions deploy --source` accepting a generation-qualified address, which is not documented. (d) makes the script's zip implementation part of the contract | The two values must be passed to the script, and a caller that passes a stale pair gets a refusal rather than a wrong deployment — the safe direction. `test_the_release_script_verifies_the_archive_digest` asserts the comparison, the object-name pattern and that both inputs are required only inside the authorization guard |
| 94.4.3 | **Gate the archive, the bucket object and the workflow's invoker-policy check on the same `cloud_function_deployment_authorized` the function and its binding already carry** | (a) Leave the source object ungated so the artefact can be staged before the function is authorized; (b) make the workflow step tolerate a missing function and pass; (c) authorize the function by default; (d) retire the function | One decision now governs the whole footprint, so there is no state in which part of the function exists. (a) stages an artefact no consumer reads, and would leave the outputs naming an object while the function that would consume it does not exist. (b) is a check that passes when it verified nothing, which is the failure mode the delivery gates exist to avoid — gating on the authorization says *why* it did not run. (c) would fail at the API: the runtime pin names a runtime Cloud Functions has decommissioned for create and update. (d) is foreclosed — the AAP's file mapping requires the function with that runtime, and the decommissioning is tracked as operator item O-3 rather than resolved here | The workflow variable defaults to `false` independently of the Terraform variable, so the two could disagree: a deployment that authorized the function in Terraform but not in the workflow would skip the policy check silently. Both default the same way and both are named in the same terms, and the step reports which decision suppressed it |


### 94.5 Least privilege in the cloud footprint

Three grants were wider than the workload they served. Each was widened by a
*default* or an *allowlist* rather than by a deliberate act, which is why none of
them read as a decision in the configuration: a deployment that supplied nothing
received all three.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.5.1 | **Default `gke_dns_endpoint_external_traffic` to `false`**, and assert the default rather than the wiring | (a) Leave the default at `true` and document that a deployment should set it to `false`; (b) remove the variable and hardcode `false`; (c) remove the DNS endpoint block entirely | The cluster sets `enable_private_nodes` and `enable_private_endpoint` to `true` two lines above, so a default of `true` here contradicted the posture the rest of the block establishes: every deployment admitted a caller outside the VPC to the control plane unless it knew to opt out. Defaults are what a deployment gets when it says nothing, so the safe value belongs there and the exception belongs in the deployment that needs it. (b) removes a legitimate escape hatch for a deployer that genuinely runs outside the VPC. (c) removes an endpoint that authorizes by IAM permission rather than by source address, which is the better of the two endpoints | A deployer outside the VPC now fails to reach the control plane until it sets the variable, which is a visible failure rather than a silent exposure. The existing case asserted only that the wiring referenced the variable — true whatever the default was — so a default assertion was added beside it; a bool default is unquoted, so it is matched directly rather than through the string-default helper |
| 94.5.2 | **Remove `roles/storage.objectViewer` from the node identity's granted roles and from the roles the validation admits**, keeping `roles/artifactregistry.reader` | (a) Keep it, as the variable's description argued, for a project still served by Container Registry; (b) remove it from the default but keep it admissible; (c) also remove the project-wide `roles/artifactregistry.reader`, leaving only the repository-scoped binding | The role reads every object in every bucket in the project — including `google_storage_bucket.static_assets`, which holds the Cloud Function source archive — and it was present only to resolve a `gcr.io` image name. This release publishes to Artifact Registry: the registry host is `<region>-docker.pkg.dev`, and both the delivery workflow and the release script address it there, so Container Registry is not in the path and the role bought nothing this deployment uses. (b) leaves it one edit from being granted again with no argument required. (c) was **rejected deliberately**: `google_artifact_registry_repository_iam_member.gke_nodes` already grants the narrower repository-scoped read, so the project-wide role is redundant — but removing it risks every node's image pull, on a path that cannot be exercised without a real project, in exchange for narrowing a read-only role scoped to one Google service. The trade was not worth an availability gamble, and it is recorded here rather than left unstated | A deployment that does pull from Container Registry now fails to pull, and the validation refuses the role rather than accepting it silently — the error message says why. `test_the_node_identity_holds_no_project_wide_storage_read` reads the granted list and the admitted list structurally, because the description names the role in order to refuse it |
| 94.5.3 | **Delete the generic accessor plane** — the resource, the local that built it and the variable that fed it — and let the three workload-scoped bindings be the only grants | (a) Keep the plane and document that only the backend identity should be listed; (b) keep it but validate that the list names exactly the backend identity; (c) narrow the plane to one principal | The plane took the cross product of every backend secret with every principal in a list, so any identity named there could read all six — the signing key and all three provider credentials included. Its variable's own description invited the migration identity into that list, while the correctly scoped binding beside it already granted that identity `DATABASE_URL` and nothing more. Deletion costs no delivery: `google_secret_manager_secret_iam_member.backend_workload` already grants the generated backend runtime identity accessor on the same six secrets, so every secret keeps exactly one reader. (a) relies on an operator reading a description that argued for the opposite. (b) and (c) reduce to a second way of expressing a binding that already exists, and two expressions of one grant can disagree | The `secret_accessor_bindings` output no longer derives from a variable, so it is rebuilt from the bindings themselves — which is stronger, because it cannot report a grant that was not made. A deployment that relied on listing an extra principal there must now be given its own scoped binding, which is the point. `test_no_binding_grants_a_supplied_list_access_to_every_secret` asserts the plane, its local, its variable and `setproduct(` are all absent, and asserts the migration and provisioning identities hold none of the provider credentials |


### 94.6 The one-open-intent invariant on the payment path

The subscription creation route read for a reusable payment intent and inserted one
when it found none. Those two steps were not one atomic step, so two requests
arriving together both read nothing and both inserted, leaving one account with two
open intents for one plan. The read was the check and the insert was the use, and
nothing held the gap between them.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.6.1 | **Enforce the invariant in the database**, as a partial unique index over `subscriptions(user_id, plan_id)` restricted to `status IN ('pending', 'failed') AND end_date IS NULL`, created by revision `0004` | (a) Take a row lock over the account with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before the read; (b) a full unique index over `(user_id, plan_id)`; (c) a PostgreSQL advisory lock keyed by account and plan; (d) raise the transaction isolation level to serializable for this route | The gap between a read and an insert can only be closed by something that outlives both, and a constraint is the only such thing that does not depend on every future caller remembering to acquire it. (a) locks a row that does not exist yet in the case that matters -- the account has no intent, so there is no intent row to lock, and locking the `users` row instead couples subscription writes to an unrelated table. (b) forbids a second intent for a plan the account has already settled or cancelled, which breaks renewal and resubscription; the predicate is what keeps the uniqueness to the window the route actually reuses. (c) works but is PostgreSQL-only, and the suite builds its mapped schema on SQLite, so the invariant would go unexercised in most of the suite. (d) makes every request on the route pay for a conflict that is rare, and turns the failure into a serialization error that still has to be retried | A database already holding two open intents for one pair cannot take the index, which is why `0004` refuses rather than creating it -- see 94.6.2. The predicate is carried for both engines through `postgresql_where` and `sqlite_where`; a future engine would need its own. Rows whose `plan_id` is `NULL` carry no uniqueness, since SQL treats `NULL` index keys as distinct -- correct here, because revision `0001` added `plan_id` as nullable and rows predating it must still apply the revision |
| 94.6.2 | **Refuse the migration when the data already violates the invariant**, naming the offending owner and plan pairs, rather than resolving them | (a) Close the superseded intents automatically, keeping the newest -- the row the route itself would have reused; (b) create the index without checking and let PostgreSQL raise its own error; (c) create it as `NOT VALID` or skip it when the data conflicts | Deciding which of several open intents to keep is a decision about a charge, and a migration is the wrong place to make it silently: the discarded row may be the one carrying the provider order the payer is about to approve. (a) is the most tempting and was rejected for that reason -- it rewrites payment rows during a schema step, and its downgrade cannot restore what it changed, which would break the revision's independent reversibility. (b) produces a message naming a constraint and no data, leaving the operator to find the rows. (c) leaves the invariant unenforced while reporting success, which is worse than failing | An operator with conflicting data cannot upgrade until they resolve it, and the refusal message states the resolution and the exact predicate. The revision remains purely additive and reverses by dropping one index, so nothing about the refusal path compromises the rollback story |
| 94.6.3 | **Answer a refused insert by reloading the committed row and reusing it**, and re-raise any conflict no reusable row explains | (a) Return an error to the caller and let it retry; (b) retry the whole insert in a loop; (c) catch `IntegrityError` broadly and always reload | The losing request wants exactly what the winning request just created, and the idempotency key is derived from the row identifier, so reusing the winner's row makes both requests present the same key and the provider open one order for the pair. (a) turns a resolvable race into a visible failure for a caller that did nothing wrong. (b) can only ever fail again, because the constraint that refused the insert has not changed. (c) would swallow a conflict raised by a different constraint -- the provider order identifier's uniqueness, for one -- and answer it with an unrelated account's intent, so the reload is conditional on a reusable row actually being found and the exception is otherwise raised unchanged | The reload depends on the winner having committed, which is what the refusal implies under read-committed isolation. Both halves are load-bearing and were measured to be: with the index removed, two concurrent requests store two rows; with the index kept but the reload removed, the losing request is answered `400`. Neither failure mode is silent |
| 94.6.4 | **Restate the two open statuses as literals in `backend/app/db/models.py`**, pinned to the catalog by a contract assertion, rather than importing them | (a) Import `STATUS_PENDING` and `STATUS_FAILED` from `backend.app.core.plans`; (b) move the status constants into the models module and import them from there into the catalog; (c) build the predicate in the migration only | The models module imports nothing from the application, and `backend/app/db/database.py` imports `Base` from it, so an application import here risks the cycle that property exists to prevent. (a) breaks that property directly. (b) relocates a catalog concern into the persistence layer and edits a file the change has no other reason to touch. (c) leaves the mapped tables the suite builds without the uniqueness, so most of the suite would not exercise it | The literals can drift from the catalog. `TestOnlyOneOpenIntentPerPlan` asserts `OPEN_INTENT_STATUSES` equals the route's `PENDING_STATUS` and `FAILED_STATUS`, and `test_0004_declares_the_uniqueness_the_models_declare` asserts the revision's copy equals the model's, so drift fails rather than passing quietly |
| 94.6.5 | **Reverse to `base` in the pipeline's migration gate, after one single-step reversal**, instead of counting one `downgrade -1` per revision. **This row is WITHDRAWN and never described the tree &mdash; see row 102.1.1.** It records the alternative row 89.12 rejected, as though it had been taken: no `alembic downgrade base` exists in any workflow, and both gate jobs read the step count from the revision chain and loop `downgrade -1` once per revision. The row is left in place and marked by that reconciliation | (a) Add a `downgrade -1` per revision, as the gate did for two; (b) loop `downgrade -1` until `alembic current` reports nothing; (c) reverse only the head and re-apply | The gate's purpose is that the chain round-trips; the property that each revision reverses *on its own* is a per-revision property, and the migration suite already asserts it one step at a time against both engines. Counting steps in the pipeline made the gate silently weaker every time a revision was added -- with four revisions, the two calls it made no longer reached the base at all. (a) keeps that maintenance burden and will be wrong again at the next revision. (b) risks a pipeline that never terminates. (c) stops exercising the revisions below the head | The gate no longer proves per-revision independence by itself, so the README row and the contract case both now say where that is proven instead. The single `downgrade -1` is retained ahead of `downgrade base` so the head is still shown reversing alone. **Withdrawn: no `downgrade base` is issued anywhere, and the reversal is the counted loop row 89.12 describes &mdash; see row 102.1.1.** |
| 94.6.6 | **Derive the documented head revision from the revision files** in `test_operator_documentation.py`, rather than holding it as a literal | (a) Update the literal to `0004`; (b) assert only that the documented value looks like a revision identifier; (c) import Alembic's `ScriptDirectory` into the documentation test | The case compares the README's documented head against a constant, so a literal made the two agree only until the next revision -- and the failure mode is silent: the constant and the document stay consistent with each other while both are wrong. That is precisely how the README came to claim `0003 (head)` after `0004` landed. (a) reproduces the defect one revision later. (b) stops checking the thing that matters. (c) pulls a migration dependency into a documentation module for a graph that is four lines of parsing | The derivation asserts exactly one head, so a branched chain fails loudly rather than picking one. It reads `revision` and `down_revision` textually, so a revision that computed either dynamically would not be seen -- none does, and the four files are uniform |


### 94.7 Equalizing the database work every login refusal performs

The credential check was already uniform: one comparison against the stored or
stand-in hash, one against the decoy, and a pad to a fixed budget. The *database*
work was not. The wrong-password branch took a write lock on the account row,
updated the failed-attempt count and committed; the branch for an address holding
no account and the branch for an account already locked issued no statement at
all. Measured against PostgreSQL 13, with that account's row held by another
connection, the two branches answered in 0.641s and 2.359s -- a 1.718s difference
against a budget headroom of 0.125s, with byte-identical status and body. A pad
can only add time, so it cannot mask a branch that waited on a lock.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.7.1 | **Give every refusal branch one write lock, one update and one commit**, by adding a fixed, fully seeded `login_attempt_slots` table that the two branches holding no countable account row update instead | (a) `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` or `SKIP LOCKED` on the account row, skipping the increment when the row is already held; (b) one throttle row per address; (c) raise `REFUSAL_WORK_ALLOWANCE` until it covers the write; (d) move the failed-attempt count itself onto the slot row so every branch writes one table | The branches differed in the statements they issued, so they had to be made to issue the same ones; equalizing the clock alone cannot do it, since a lock wait has no upper bound. (a) removes the waiting and needs no new table, but a caller could then run attempts in parallel and have the increments dropped, dodging the five-attempt lockout -- trading an enumeration oracle for a lockout bypass. (b) never collides, but the unknown-address path would have to INSERT its row, which is itself distinguishable from an update and lets an address grow the table without bound. (c) cannot bound an unbounded wait, and slows every refusal for everyone. (d) would let a refusal against one address lock out every account sharing its bucket | Two distinct addresses can share a bucket and briefly serialise on one another. Storage is bounded to exactly `LOGIN_ATTEMPT_SLOT_COUNT` rows, no request ever inserts one, and the lock is held for a single update and commit. `TestRefusalBranchesDoTheSameWork` counts the statements each of the four refusal branches issues and asserts two selects, one update and no insert or delete for every one of them |
| 94.7.2 | **Key the bucket with an HMAC under `SECRET_KEY`** rather than a bare SHA-256 digest | (a) Bare `sha256(email) % N`; (b) the account identifier where one exists and a digest otherwise; (c) a random bucket per request | A bare digest is computable by anyone, so a caller could pick two addresses that land in the same bucket, contend them against each other and detect the mutual blocking -- and mutual blocking would imply both addresses are unknown, which is the very fact the control exists to hide. Keying the digest removes the ability to choose collisions without removing the fixed table size. (b) reintroduces the asymmetry it is meant to remove, since the branch shape would depend on whether an account exists. (c) makes the write land somewhere unrelated to the address, so contention no longer mirrors the account path and the counts mean nothing | The mapping changes if the signing key is rotated, which redistributes counts across buckets. Nothing depends on the mapping being stable: a bucket carries a count and an instant, and no decision reads it |
| 94.7.3 | **Seed the rows from a DDL listener on table creation as well as from revision 0005** | (a) Seed only in the migration; (b) seed lazily, inserting a row the first time a bucket is used; (c) seed from application startup | Measured: `Base.metadata.create_all` left the table with **0 rows**, which is how the entire test suite and any `create_all` deployment builds its schema. With no rows the slot read finds nothing, the equalizing write is skipped and the control is silently inert -- and every response-equality assertion still passes, so nothing would have reported it. Seeding as part of creating the table makes the two ways of building the schema converge. (b) reintroduces an insert path on first use. (c) adds a write at startup and leaves a window in which the table is short | The listener and the revision state the same count in two places; `test_0005_seeds_the_slot_count_the_model_declares` pins the revision's count to the model's, and `test_no_refusal_branch_inserts_or_removes_a_throttle_row` asserts the table is exactly `LOGIN_ATTEMPT_SLOT_COUNT` rows before and after all four branches run |
| 94.7.4 | **State `SLOT_COUNT` in revision 0005 as a literal**, not imported from the model | (a) Import `LOGIN_ATTEMPT_SLOT_COUNT` into the revision; (b) derive it at runtime from the table | An applied migration is a historical record: importing a live constant would mean raising the model's count silently changes what an already-applied revision claims to have seeded, leaving a database short of rows and the application able to compute a bucket that has none. Stating it fixes what this revision did. (b) has the same defect with more machinery | The two values can drift. The pinning assertion above fails on drift, which forces a new revision to seed the added buckets -- the correct outcome |
| 94.7.5 | **Read the account identifier before any write commits** | (a) Leave the reads where they were; (b) expunge or refresh the instance explicitly; (c) disable expire-on-commit for the session | Committing expires the loaded instance, so reading `db_user.id` afterwards issued a further select against `users` -- which the branch holding no account cannot issue. Measured, that left the unknown branch at 3 statements against 4 for the other two even after the equalizing write was added. Capturing the value first brought all four branches to exactly 3. (b) issues the same extra statement or another one. (c) changes session semantics for every route sharing the session factory | The captured value is a plain integer and is used only for the log record, so nothing observes a stale attribute. The statement-count assertions hold this in place |
| 94.7.6 | **Assert the equalization by counting statements, not by comparing elapsed times** | (a) Assert the branches' response times fall within a tolerance; (b) assert only the response bodies match | A timing assertion measures the host as much as the code and is the classic flaky test; the property that actually matters -- that no branch issues statements another does not -- is exactly countable. The module already counts credential checks and comparisons for the same reason, and carries its wall-clock case behind a `timing` mark as a confidence measurement rather than a gate. (b) passes for the defect: the bodies were already byte-identical, which is why the timing difference was the only signal | A counted assertion cannot see a difference in how long identical statements take, for instance a lock wait. That is what the existing `timing`-marked case covers, and what the fixed refusal budget bounds once the statements match |


### 94.8 The frozen configuration contract, and two authorized departures from it

The Agent Action Plan freezes what `backend/app/core/config.py` declares and what
`infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` may contain. Three departures from it had been
made. One was a plain omission and is reverted here. The other two are real and are
kept, and this section is what authorizes them: Rule 1 treats an *unexplained*
deviation as a defect, and each row below states what the plan required, what was
delivered instead, and what a reviewer has to decide.

**This section's claim to supersede row 83.21 is itself withdrawn, by row 96.1.1.**
An earlier revision of this paragraph read row 83.21 — the decision to add *no*
provider version constraint and no remote state backend — as history on the ground
that `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` had come to carry a `terraform` block and
that `infrastructure/terraform/.terraform.lock.hcl` had come to be tracked. Neither
is true of the tree this section ships with. Row 80.3.1 made both changes, row 91.1.1
reverted both, and row 83.21 therefore describes the delivered state exactly:
**no `terraform` block, no `required_version`, no `required_providers`, no tracked
provider lock and no remote state backend.** Both halves of flagged finding 5 at row
34.6.3 are open, reported for confirmation and unchanged, and row 96.1.1 records the
correction rather than editing this paragraph out of the record.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 94.8.1 | **Restore `SENTRY_DSN: Optional[str] = None` to `Settings`**, and publish and document it alongside every other setting | (a) Leave it retired, as the argument for retiring it proposed; (b) restore it to the class but leave it out of the published environment and the example file | The plan states the field is declared, read nowhere, and that keeping it declared is required and removing it is out of scope. Nothing about the delivered code changed that: it is still read nowhere, so restoring it changes no behaviour and costs nothing. (a) is the departure being reverted. Its own reasoning was sound in isolation -- a published setting an application never reads invites an operator to believe a control is active that is not -- but it was applied against an explicit instruction, and the concern it raises is answerable by saying so plainly rather than by removing the field. Every place the name now appears says the service reads it and sends nothing. (b) would fail the contract that the compose environment declares exactly the settings the class carries, and the configuration map guard that requires the map to declare every setting the model holds | An operator may still read a declared telemetry endpoint as an active integration. Mitigated in prose at each of the five surfaces -- the class, `.env.example`, the compose environment, the configuration map, and the retired-settings comment -- each of which states that no code path reads it |
| 94.8.2 | **Keep `LOG_LEVEL` declared and validated**, contrary to the plan's instruction that it be absent from `Settings` | (a) Remove the field and hardcode the threshold at the single call site; (b) remove the field and read the variable directly from the process environment at that call site; (c) remove the field and every consumer, giving up a configurable threshold | The field is load-bearing across the delivered configuration surface, not decoration: `backend/app/main.py:208` passes it to `configure_logging`, and `.env.example`, the compose environment and the Kubernetes configuration map each publish it. Its validator is itself a control -- it refuses a numeric or misspelled level, and refuses `DEBUG` outside a local environment, which is the level at which a failure record carries a rendered traceback. (a) and (b) keep the consumers working but move the value outside the one place every setting is validated, so the `DEBUG`-in-production refusal would be lost. (c) removes an operability feature from a running service to satisfy a naming contract. **This is a departure from the plan and is recorded as one rather than argued away**; the plan's instruction is a scope control, and the setting is outside the 29-name contract it was written to protect | A reviewer may reasonably decide the plan's exclusion should win and the field be removed. What that costs is stated above: the `DEBUG`-outside-local refusal, and a configurable threshold at four published surfaces. The field carries no credential and no security decision reads it |
| 94.8.3 | **Withdrawn by row 96.1.1, and never the delivered state.** The position this row recorded was: keep the `terraform` block -- `required_version = ">= 1.11.0"` and pinned `required_providers` -- and keep `.terraform.lock.hcl` tracked, contrary to the plan's instruction that the configuration carry no such block and no committed lock. Read it as the argument row 80.3.1 rested on, which row 91.1.1 had already reverted before this row was written | (a) Remove the block and the lock, as the plan directs, leaving resolution free; (b) remove the lock but keep the constraint; (c) pin an exact provider version instead of a constraint plus a lock | **The row's own alternative (a) is what the tree carries, and its rationale does not survive contact with it.** The argument was that removing them makes the change less secure, because `terraform init` then resolves whatever provider is newest at run time. That cost is real and is exactly what flagged finding 5 at row 34.6.3 records as an open finding; it is not authority to close that finding, because the authority to close a confirmation-only finding is the user's, which is the whole of row 91.1.1. Two factual claims in the withdrawn rationale were also false of the tree: no delivered assertion requires the constructs' presence -- `test_pipeline_contract.py::test_no_tool_or_provider_floor_is_declared`, `::test_the_provider_selection_is_not_locked_in_the_repository` and `test_terraform_contract.py`'s `DEFERRED_CONSTRUCTS` each assert their **absence** -- and `terraform validate` runs clean against no lock at all rather than against a committed one | The cost the withdrawn position named is unmitigated and is the open finding: two `terraform init` runs a week apart can resolve different provider majors against identical code. It is stated in the configuration's own comment block at `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf:580` and carried as flagged finding 5, so it is visible where a reader of either the code or the record will meet it. No remote state backend is configured, and that half is open on the same terms |


## 95. Making the published record describe the tree it ships with

The review found the mandated evidence set internally inconsistent: path totals that
disagreed with each other and with the tree, a runtime-pin count stated three
different ways, and an operator register that described gaps a later round had
already closed. Its instruction was to establish one canonical count for each figure
and to mark historical rows superseded rather than rewriting them. Every figure below
was produced by running a command against this tree, and the command is named so a
reviewer can repeat it.

The authorship boundary is what makes the inventory measurable at all, and it had not
been pinned down before: `git log` shows the last upstream commit as `a26f7fb` and the
first commit of this work as `74eec3e`, so the delivered set is exactly
`git diff a26f7fb` against the working tree plus the files not yet committed.

(a) is defensible on the tree but would renumber a contract the plan fixed and would move four test constants for a file that configures no delivered artefact; it is disclosed instead, at row 95.1.4. (b) is false, and is withdrawn at row 95.1.2. (c) is the state the review rejected. | The count is asserted against the files rather than against any document, so a *newly added* declaration site would not fail the check. `docs/security/RESIDUAL_RISK.md` is named in every other document as the one authoritative inventory, so a sixth declaration has exactly one place to be added. |

## 96. The record against the tree, and the choices this log had not owned

An alternate-model final acceptance review returned NOT APPROVED on twenty findings:
no Critical and no High, two Medium and eight Low, the rest informational. None was a
defect in delivered application code. Sixteen were defects in the written record this
Rule 1 log is the authority for, or choices the record had not owned at all, and the
review's most consequential observation was that a section titled for making the
published record describe the tree it ships with had itself left two operative rows in
direct contradiction. That is the failure this section exists to close.

Two properties are asserted throughout. Every figure below was produced by running a
command against this tree, and the command is named. And every row that corrects an
earlier position marks that position in place under the &sect;27 convention rather than
rewriting it, because a correction a reader cannot see is indistinguishable from a
figure that was never wrong.

### 96.1 The Terraform constraint: the record realigned with the tree

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 96.1.1 | **Withdraw every statement that the configuration declares a provider version constraint or that a provider lock is tracked, and restate flagged finding 5 as fully open.** Seven statements are corrected: flagged-finding row 5, the "Deliberate non-changes from this round" summary in &sect;82, the &sect;94.8 preamble, rows 94.8.3 and 94.2.3 in this log, the toolchain section of [`RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md), and the comment justifying `terraform_version` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | (a) Add the `terraform` block and the lock back, making the seven statements true; (b) correct the six count-and-wording statements and leave row 94.8.3 standing as the operative decision; (c) delete row 94.8.3 and the &sect;94.8 preamble rather than marking them withdrawn | (a) is the change row 91.1.1 reverted. Taking it again would close half of a finding AAP &sect;0.9.2 and &sect;0.12.5 reserve to the user, and taking it *because a log row asserted it* would make a decision-log rationale an amendment to the plan, which is precisely the defect row 91.1.1 was written to correct. (b) is what the tree already disproves: rows 94.8.3 and 91.1.1 cannot both be operative, and leaving the later of the two standing would leave a reviewer reading the wrong one as current. (c) destroys the record of a position that was held, which &sect;27 establishes this log does not do &mdash; and here the destruction would be self-serving, because the withdrawn position is the one that misreported an open finding as closed. Measured: `git grep -e required_version -e required_providers -- '*.tf'` matches nothing, no `.tf` file carries a `terraform` block, and `infrastructure/terraform/.terraform.lock.hcl` is neither tracked nor present | The cost the withdrawn position named is real and now unmitigated: two `terraform init` runs against identical code can resolve different provider majors, and a provider major is where resource schemas change. That is the open finding rather than a new one, it is stated in the configuration's own comment block at `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf:580`, and closing it needs the user's authorization. A reader who quotes the withdrawn assertion from an older copy of this log finds the withdrawal beside it rather than a silent correction |
| 96.1.2 | **Justify the exact `terraform_version` pin on the release this repository verifies against and on the 1.11 floor the configuration's constructs need, in both places the pin is explained** | (a) Keep citing a declared `required_version`; (b) drop the justification and leave the pin unexplained; (c) declare `required_version` so the existing justification becomes true | The pin's real ground is stronger than the one it cited: 1.15.8 is the release `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform init -backend=false` and `terraform validate` are run with here, and the ephemeral input variables and write-only secret arguments the secret versions use need 1.11 or later, which the configuration's own comment block already states as an operator obligation rather than a demand it makes. (a) points a reviewer at a constraint they will not find. (b) leaves an exact pin looking arbitrary, which invites a future round to loosen it. (c) is row 96.1.1's rejected alternative (a) | The floor is now documented in three places &mdash; the configuration comment, the register and the workflow comment &mdash; and a future round that raises the constructs' requirement past 1.11 has to update all three. Nothing detects that automatically; what does hold is that the pin is exact, so a run cannot silently pick a release that no longer clears the floor |
| 96.1.3 | **Assert the absence in a contract case over the published documents, not only over the configuration, and calibrate the case against the five statements that were actually made before trusting it.** `test_no_document_states_the_deferred_constructs_are_present` reads each document a statement at a time &mdash; one table row, one list item, or one hard-wrapped paragraph &mdash; and refuses a presence claim unless that same statement carries a withdrawal marker of its own | (a) Rely on the two existing configuration assertions; (b) assert nothing and treat this as a one-time correction; (c) forbid the phrasings outright, without the withdrawal exemption; (d) require a marker on any statement that so much as names one of the constructs | The two existing cases &mdash; `test_no_tool_or_provider_floor_is_declared` and `test_the_provider_selection_is_not_locked_in_the_repository` &mdash; already prove the constructs are absent from the tree. What went wrong is not that the tree drifted; it is that four documents and one workflow comment said otherwise and nothing compared them, so the case that would have failed is one that reads the documents. Calibration settles what "asserts presence" means from evidence rather than by choosing a rule: run against the seven statements as they were written, the detector has to flag all seven, and against the corrected tree it has to flag none. It does both, and calibration is what found the seventh &mdash; a bullet in &sect;82 that a paragraph-granularity reading exempted, because a neighbouring bullet in the same list carried a withdrawal marker. The unit rule is a list item, a table row or a paragraph for that reason. (b) is the position that produced a Medium finding twice over. (c) would forbid the withdrawn rows from quoting the position they withdraw, which is the record &sect;27 exists to keep. (d) was measured and is too weak to be worth having: most of the original statements contain a softening phrase &mdash; "no longer true", "reported only", "half stands", "as history" &mdash; so a rule keyed on any absence-flavoured word admits nearly every one of them | The case matches wording, so a future statement asserting the same falsehood in different words passes it. That is disclosed rather than mitigated: it is a tripwire on the phrasings that occurred, calibrated against them, and this log and the register remain the places a reviewer reads. The unit rule is also a judgement &mdash; a marker opening a paragraph governs the sentences under it, which is right for hard-wrapped prose and would be wrong if a paragraph ever withdrew one claim while asserting another |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 96.2.1 | **Report the reachability re-measurement at the scope each result actually holds for, and publish no count at the wider scope.** [`RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md) now states thirteen of the fourteen patterns at zero across `backend/app/`, and states of `backend/` only that every match sits under `backend/tests/`, naming a construct in order to assert its absence | (a) Keep the declared scope `backend/` and publish the true tally there; (b) narrow the section's declared scope to `backend/app/` and say nothing about the wider one; (c) leave the result as it stood, since the acceptances it supports are sound either way; (d) stop naming the patterns in the test module so the wider tally becomes publishable again | The register declared a scope of `backend/` and reported a result that is true only of `backend/app/`. The conclusion survives &mdash; every extra match is a test naming a construct to assert its absence, and no test module is installed into the runtime image &mdash; but the register's own standard is that a result be reported precisely rather than restated from the baseline, and it was not. (a) was implemented first and **falsified by its own assertion**: the contract case that holds the figure honest names all fourteen patterns as literals, so it changes any `backend/`-wide tally the moment it is written. (b) would answer the finding by deleting the wider observation, which is the half a reader needs in order to know the extra matches are fixtures. (c) is the position the finding rejected. The property needs none: a match belongs in the application package, whose thirteen zeroes are asserted directly, or in the test tree, which no image installs. (a) and (b) both re-create the drift the finding is about, because the excluded set is itself a published figure. (c) leaves the wider observation unasserted, which is how the original result went unchecked | The two permitted roots are a judgement rather than a measurement: a construct genuinely used inside `backend/tests/` would pass. What bounds that is the semantic assertion over `backend/app`, which is what an HTTP request reaches, and the fact that the runtime manifest installs no test tree |

### 96.6 The cluster's security posture, and the gate that holds the inventory to its settings contract

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 96.6.1 | **Keep the frontend pod running as uid 0 and declare it, rather than switching the image.** `infrastructure/kubernetes/50-frontend.yaml` now sets `runAsNonRoot: false` explicitly, states the position in its header, and keeps `NET_BIND_SERVICE` after dropping `ALL`. Every other workload in the directory declares `runAsNonRoot: true` and uid 1001 | (a) Switch to an unprivileged nginx image serving on a high port, with `runAsNonRoot: true`, uid 1001 and no added capability; (b) keep `nginx:alpine` and set uid 101 with the capability retained; (c) leave the pod as it was, with `runAsNonRoot` simply absent | The pod runs as root because of the image, and the image is out of scope. `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.frontend` builds on `nginx:alpine` and declares `EXPOSE 80`; **AAP &sect;0.9.2 places that file among the ones that "have no bearing on the backend vulnerabilities" and &sect;0.6.1.7 lists it as a REFERENCE path**, and row 27.8 already refused a change to it on exactly those grounds. (a) is the better posture and needs that file plus a new nginx configuration, a port change across the Deployment, the Service, the autoscaler and the Compose stack, and a rebuild &mdash; and **no container runtime is available in the environment this work is verified in**, so it could be written but not exercised. Making an unverifiable change to the manifest that serves the application is a worse outcome than an accurately declared one. (b) is untestable here for the same reason and carries a specific hazard: the image's entrypoint and its `user nginx` directive both assume a root master process, so the pod could fail to start with no way to find out before a cluster saw it. (c) is the state the review found, where a reviewer cannot tell a considered choice from an oversight | The pod runs as uid 0 with `NET_BIND_SERVICE`. What bounds it: the container drops every other capability, cannot escalate privilege, has a read-only root filesystem and a `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile; it mounts no secret and its service account carries no workload-identity annotation, so a compromise reaches no credential; and it serves a static bundle with no application code. What is **not** bounded is the container's own filesystem writes under `/var`, which are `emptyDir` volumes, and root inside the container remains root for anything a container-escape defect could reach. Closing that needs alternative (a), which needs authorization to edit a reference path |
| 96.6.2 | **Set the namespace's Pod Security Admission profile to `enforce: baseline` with `audit: restricted` and `warn: restricted`** | (a) `enforce: restricted`, which is the stronger profile; (b) `enforce: baseline` alone, with no audit or warn level; (c) `enforce: privileged`, matching the cluster default the namespace previously inherited; (d) add no labels, leaving admission to the cluster default | With no labels every workload is admitted under whatever the cluster default is, so the one pod that runs as uid 0 is neither refused nor recorded &mdash; that absence is the finding. (a) requires `runAsNonRoot` and would **reject** `50-frontend.yaml` as it stands, so it cannot be taken until row 96.6.1's alternative (a) is authorized; taking it now would mean an operator's first apply of the workload group fails. (b) admits the inventory and reports nothing, which loses the only automatic signal that a workload is below the stronger profile. (c) codifies the weakest position as a decision. `baseline` admits all twelve manifests &mdash; it permits running as root and permits `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, which is in its allowed capability set &mdash; while `restricted` at the audit and warn levels writes the frontend pod to the audit log and reports it at apply time, so the gap is visible on every release rather than in a document alone | `baseline` is the enforced level, so a future workload that runs as root is admitted rather than refused; what catches it is the warning at apply time and `test_the_frontend_is_the_only_workload_admitted_below_restricted`, which fails the build if a second workload stops declaring `runAsNonRoot: true`. Raising `enforce` to `restricted` is a one-line change once the frontend image is authorized, and the labels are placed so that the change is exactly that |
| 96.6.3 | **Assert every workload's pod and container security context, and derive the covered set from the inventory rather than listing it by hand** | (a) Extend the existing two-Deployment case to name the three one-shot workloads as well; (b) assert only the frontend, since it is the one the finding is about; (c) assert nothing and rely on the decision rows | The existing case read `WORKLOAD_PORTS`, which holds the two continuously running workloads, so the migration Job, the ingestion CronJob and the administrator-credential Job were unasserted &mdash; and the frontend's added capability was unasserted in any form. (a) is a hand-written list, which is the construct that stops covering a workload added later; the delivered set is instead compared for equality against every object in the inventory that carries a pod template, so an addition fails a case rather than going unnoticed. (b) would leave four workloads uncovered to fix one. (c) is what let an unowned posture ship | The comparison encodes the inventory's shape, so adding a workload is a deliberate edit in two places &mdash; the inventory map and the security maps beside it. That is the intent: a new pod template has to state its identity and its capabilities before the suite will pass |
| 96.6.4 | **Narrow the settings-contract gate with a recorded exemption, rather than giving the two one-shot operator pods the published rate-limit secret.** `.github/scripts/check_manifest_settings_contract.py` applied one blanket rule &mdash; any container reading the `backend-config` map must also reference `backend-rate-limit-store` &mdash; and therefore refused the committed inventory: run from the repository root it exited 1 on `60-migration-job.yaml`. The rule is now two-way: a container named in the new `SETTINGS_FREE_CONTAINERS` must reference no cluster secret, and every other reader of the map must reference the published one | (a) Add `secretRef: backend-rate-limit-store` to `60-migration-job.yaml` and `70-admin-credential-job.yaml` so the blanket rule holds; (b) drop the published-secret rule from the gate; (c) leave the gate failing and report it as an out-of-scope issue; (d) exempt by object kind &mdash; any `Job` &mdash; rather than by named container | The gate was the party in the wrong, and the tree already said so in four places. Both manifests document the omission as deliberate; **two delivered cases assert it positively** &mdash; `test_delivery_pipeline.py::test_the_migration_job_reads_the_same_configuration_as_the_api` asserts the Job's `envFrom` carries no `secretRef` at all, and `test_pipeline_audit_contract.py` asserts the same list is empty &mdash; and `backend/app/core/db_contract.py` records that the migration and credential paths "read the few settings they need themselves rather than importing ``Settings``". Measurement settled it: with an environment built from the delivered ConfigMap, `ENVIRONMENT=production` and **no** `RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI`, `python -m alembic -c backend/alembic.ini current` exits 0 and prints `0005 (head)`, and `import backend.app.core.admin_provisioning` exits 0, while the control `import backend.app.main` refuses on settings validation &mdash; so the serving path constructs `Settings` and neither operator command does. (a) would break both delivered cases and hand a one-shot pod a value it never reads, against AAP &sect;0.12.2's least-privilege direction. (b) would remove the check that catches a serving workload started without the shared store, which is the condition `config.py` refuses at startup. (c) leaves the `infrastructure` job red on every push. (d) is coarser than the truth: the ingestion CronJob also runs to completion, but it does construct `Settings` and does name the store | The exemption is a recorded pair, so if either command ever imports `Settings` the gate would pass while the pod refused to start. Three things bound that: the rule is two-way, so an exempt container that gains a secret reference fails immediately; `test_the_gate_exempts_only_the_settings_free_containers` compares the gate's record against the manifests **for equality**, so an exemption that outlives its manifest fails a case; and `test_the_manifest_settings_gate_passes_against_the_inventory` runs the delivered gate inside the suite, so the contradiction this row fixes can no longer survive in the gap between a workflow step and a test. All three were calibrated by perturbing a copy of the inventory in both directions and confirming each refusal |
| 96.6.5 | **Correct the gate's own statement that it is a script "so that it is covered by the repository's own lint", rather than making the statement true** | (a) Add a lint step covering `.github/scripts` to the `backend` job and keep the sentence as written; (b) leave the sentence; (c) delete the sentence and its two neighbouring reasons together | The claim was false. The workflow's only style step is `cd backend` followed by `flake8 .` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`), and the documented workstation form is `flake8 backend`, so neither reaches `.github/scripts` and no gate lints that directory. The docstring now states the two reasons that are true &mdash; the check runs without a workflow runner, and a block of this size does not complete under the ShellCheck pass `actionlint` applies &mdash; and names `flake8 .github/scripts` as what covers it. (a) is the better posture and is recorded here as available rather than taken: it adds a workflow step and a row to the README verification table, both outside this finding's blast radius and both governed by `test_documentation_accuracy_contract.py::test_every_documented_gate_runs_in_the_workflow`. (c) would discard two accurate reasons to remove one inaccurate clause | The file stays unlinted by the pipeline, so a style regression in it would not fail a push. It is lint-clean now, measured with the command the docstring names, and it is one file of ninety lines whose only reader is the `infrastructure` job |


### 96.7 The advisory-count assertion, and the development manifest's undeclared import

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
