## 97. The performance and resource-control review: client identity and the pool's failure mode

A final performance and resource-control review returned FAIL on two findings out of eleven
in-scope surfaces and roughly six hundred runtime checks: **F-1**, that the credential rate
limit is defeated by varying an `X-Forwarded-For` header, and **F-2**, that connection-pool
exhaustion is returned to a client as an unhandled HTTP 500 after a ten-second stall with no
`Retry-After`. Three further observations were informational. Nine surfaces passed, and the
review recorded explicitly which behaviours were correct and were not to be changed; both
lists are honoured below.

Two properties hold throughout this section. Every figure is one this round produced by
running something against this tree or against the installed packages, and the command or the
measurement is named. And where the review's suggested repair and the delivered repair differ,
the row says so rather than presenting the delivered one as the only option considered.

### 97.1 F-1: which address a request is counted against

The finding, as behaviour: twelve consecutive login attempts for one non-existent address,
each carrying a different `X-Forwarded-For` value, were all answered `401` and none was
throttled &mdash; against a policy of five per minute. The same twelve with one fixed
forwarded value were answered `401` five times and then `429` seven times, carrying
`Retry-After`. So the limit works; what defeats it is that the key changes.

The review located the cause below the application and this round confirmed it twice over. The
application's own `client_address` in `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py` is correct: at the
shipped `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` of `0` it returns the peer address from the ASGI scope and does
not read the forwarded header at all. What changes the scope is the ASGI server.
`inspect.getsource` over the installed `uvicorn` 0.39.0 shows `Config.__init__` defaulting
`proxy_headers` to `True` and `forwarded_allow_ips` to `None`, which falls back to
`os.environ.get("FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS", "127.0.0.1")`; `Config.load` then wraps the application
in `ProxyHeadersMiddleware`, whose `__call__` replaces `scope["client"]` with the header's
value whenever the connection's own address is trusted. The server's access log records the
substitution in the clear: every one of the twelve requests was logged from
`198.51.100.<n>:0`, and the port of `0` is that middleware's own signature.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 97.1.1 | **Add `--no-proxy-headers` to every invocation of the application this repository ships or documents**, so the ASGI server leaves `scope["client"]` as the address the connection was made from and `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` is the only setting that decides which address a limit is counted against. Five invocations carry it: `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile.backend`, `infrastructure/kubernetes/40-backend.yaml`, the documented command in `README.md`, and both invocations in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | (a) Change `client_address` to prefer the peer address; (b) set `--forwarded-allow-ips` to an empty or unroutable value instead of disabling the handling; (c) set the `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` environment variable to a value the server trusts nowhere; (d) leave the invocations alone and raise `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` so the application selects from the right-hand end of the chain | (a) cannot work and would break a correct control: once the server has overwritten `scope["client"]`, the real peer is no longer in the scope for any application code to prefer, and the review lists `client_address` among the behaviours that are correct and must not change &mdash; two delivered cases in `test_rate_limit_store.py` encode that behaviour as the contract, including that two forwarded values resolve to one key at zero hops. (b) leaves the handling installed and turns a security property into a value that has to stay correct; the flag removes the middleware from the stack instead. (c) is (b) delivered through an environment variable, which is a fifth place to keep right and is not visible in the command a reader sees. (d) misreads the chain: with the server rewriting the scope there is no chain left for the application to select from, only the single value the server chose. Measured after the change on the same twelve-request probe: `401` five times then `429`, with `Retry-After` present | An operator who genuinely terminates TLS at a proxy and needs the forwarded chain honoured now has to do two things rather than one &mdash; pass `--forwarded-allow-ips` with the exact proxy addresses and raise `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` to the same hop count. That pairing is stated in both places the setting is read, the README table row and the `.env.example` block, and the wildcard form is named as the thing not to reach for. The failure direction if only one is done is the safe one: every caller collapses onto the proxy address, so the limit applies globally rather than not at all |
| 97.1.2 | **Assert the flag on every invocation from the module that already owns each surface**, rather than adding a module of its own: `test_delivery_pipeline.py` for the image command, the deployment command and both continuous-integration invocations, and `test_operator_documentation.py` for the documented command and for the pairing statement in the README row and the `.env.example` block | (a) A new contract module of its own, covering all five surfaces in one place; (b) assert it in `test_rate_limit_store.py`, beside the keying behaviour the flag protects; (c) assert only that the string appears somewhere in each file | (a) was written first and then withdrawn. It reads well, but it introduces a delivered path, and a new path moves the counted totals in [`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) &sect;2.9, &sect;2.10, &sect;4.3 and &sect;6.1 together with `MATRIX_REVERSE_ROWS` and `LATER_ROUND_PATHS` &mdash; six figures to keep in agreement for a case that fits inside two modules that already read these files. The withdrawal is recorded here rather than left invisible. (b) puts filesystem scanning into a unit module about in-process storage, against the repository's own convention that a `*_contract` module reads files. (c) is too weak to hold: the flag appears in prose in both documents, so a substring match would pass a file that documents it and does not carry it. What is asserted instead is token membership in the parsed command, with a floor on how many invocations must be found so a reader that stops matching fails rather than passing over an empty set | The Dockerfile carries its command as a JSON array and the deployment carries it inside a shell block continued with a backslash, so the parser normalises both before reading tokens. If a future invocation is added in a form neither reader recognises, the per-source floor catches it in the file it was added to; an invocation added to a file listed in neither module would not be seen at all, which is the residual gap and is why both modules name the files they cover |

### 97.2 F-2 and INFO-3: what happens when the connection pool runs out

The finding, as behaviour: driving the public listings collection at 60 concurrent
connections produced 38 answers of **HTTP 500 after a 10.44 s stall**, with a body of
`{"detail":"Internal server error","request_id":"..."}` and **no `Retry-After`**; at 100
concurrent it was 73 of them and the median response was two stacked ten-second waits. The
ladder below 40 was clean, no connection leaked, and the peak server-side connection count
sat at 16 throughout. Separately, the review classified every traceback in the server's
error stream and found **179** blocks of `Exception in ASGI application`, **all 179** ending
in the same pool timeout and no other exception class anywhere — so the failure was not
merely being mapped to a 500, it was reaching the server unhandled, and the multi-frame
traceback it wrote bypassed the redacting logger that every other failure travels through.
That is INFO-3, and it has the same cause.

Two measurements settled the shape of the repair. The pool's ceiling was `size 5 + overflow
10`, because `_pool_args` named neither bound and the pool's own defaults applied. The
number of requests admitted to run a statement at once was **40** — the event-loop library's
default worker-thread count, read from the installed `anyio` 4.12.1 — and every route that
reads the database either is synchronous or hands its work to those threads. So 25 admitted
requests could be waiting on a pool that had nothing to give, each for the full
`DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, before any of them could be refused.

**The second of those two measurements is a correct account of the finding and an incorrect
account of the repair.** Rows 97.2.3 and 97.2.4 below decided to lower that thread count to
`DB_POOL_SIZE`. That was implemented, driven under load, and found not to remove the stall —
capping threads does not bound how many connections are wanted. §97.4 records the
measurement that falsified it and the mechanism delivered in its place. Rows 97.2.1 and
97.2.2, which decide the refusal itself, are unaffected and are delivered as written.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 97.2.1 | **Answer a pool timeout with 503 and `Retry-After`, from a handler registered for the pool's own exception class**, carrying `CAPACITY_DETAIL` and the request identifier and nothing else | (a) Widen the catch-all handler to inspect the exception and branch on it; (b) catch the timeout in each route or in the session dependency and raise an `HTTPException(503)`; (c) keep the 500 and add `Retry-After` to it; (d) map it to 429, reusing the throttling shape the service already has | (a) and (c) both leave the failure travelling to the catch-all, and that is the half of the finding a status change would not fix: the framework routes the `Exception` key to its outermost error layer, which answers and then **re-raises**, which is where the 179 raw tracebacks come from. A handler registered for a specific class is placed in the inner layer instead, which does not re-raise — so one registration closes F-2 and INFO-3 together, and the response travels back out through the security-header, cross-origin and request-identifier layers rather than having to set those itself, which the catch-all does by hand. (b) would put the same `try` in nine places and would still miss the dependency's own checkout. (d) says the caller sent too many requests, which is untrue and would collide with the limiter's own headers. Narrowness was verified rather than assumed: the pool's class is **not** a subclass of the interpreter's `TimeoutError`, so registering it cannot capture the outbound provider or listing-provider timeouts, which have their own answers | A 503 is retryable, so a client that retries immediately and repeatedly adds load to a service that is already at capacity. `Retry-After` is what bounds that, and its value is the configured wait rather than a guess. The body names no pool figure, so an operator diagnosing capacity reads the structured record rather than the response |
| 97.2.2 | **Derive the `Retry-After` value from `DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, rounded up with a floor of one second**, rather than introducing a setting for it | (a) A new `CAPACITY_RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS` setting; (b) a fixed literal; (c) an HTTP-date form rather than seconds | The wait a request just spent is also the longest a request still in flight can be holding the connection it is waiting for, so the configured wait is the honest hint and needs no second value to keep in agreement with it. (a) adds a setting that can be set to disagree with the timeout, and every setting is a name that has to be published in five places. (b) goes stale the moment the timeout is tuned. (c) is permitted by the specification but the limiter already emits the seconds form, and one form across both refusals is what a client parses once. The floor matters because the timeout accepts a fractional value: a configured 0.25 s would otherwise render as `0`, which some clients read as "retry now" | The hint is as good as the configured timeout is. An operator who sets a very long timeout gets a very long hint, which is correct but may be longer than a load balancer's own budget |
| 97.2.3 | **Superseded as a statement of final state — see §97.4. The worker-thread cap this row decided was implemented, measured under load, and withdrawn; requests in flight are bounded instead. The two pool bounds and their defaults of 10 and 5 stand and are delivered.** The position below was true when this round ran. Cap worker threads at `DB_POOL_SIZE` at startup, and state both pool bounds in configuration, with defaults of 10 and 5 that keep the ceiling at the 15 the pool's own defaults produced | (a) Raise the pool to at least the worker-thread count of 40 and leave the threads alone, which is the review's first suggestion; (b) cap the threads at the full ceiling of `DB_POOL_SIZE + DB_MAX_OVERFLOW`; (c) add an admission-control middleware bounding requests in flight; (d) change nothing here and rely on the 503 alone | (a) was rejected on a measurement of the deployment rather than a preference: `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` provisions the database at the `db-f1-micro` tier with no flag raising its connection limit, and the renderer defaults to two replicas with a horizontal autoscaler above that, so 40 per process is more connections than the server accepts. The defaults chosen instead keep the per-process ceiling at exactly what it was, so no deployed database sees more demand than before. (b) creates a narrow deadlock window and is the reason the cap is the persistent bound rather than the ceiling: the framework runs a synchronous generator dependency's entry, the endpoint and its exit as **three separate** units of threaded work, so a request whose handler has returned still holds its connection while it queues for the thread that will close its session. Leaving `DB_MAX_OVERFLOW` unclaimed by admitted requests is what covers that overlap. (c) is a new layer on the request path for a property configuration can express. (d) leaves every refusal costing a full ten-second stall first, and the stall is part of what the review called defective | The cap is process-global and lowers what the whole process admits, not only its database work. Two consequences are accepted and stated: the credential routes pad each refusal to a fixed budget and hold a thread for it, so the number of refusals in flight is now bounded by `DB_POOL_SIZE`; and the liveness route had to move off the threads for the cap to be safe, which row 97.2.4 covers. The cap is only ever lowered and only for a URL whose pool has a ceiling, so a SQLite configuration — the test suite's — is untouched |
| 97.2.4 | **Stands as a decision and is delivered; its premise is superseded — see §97.4. The handler is a coroutine. What made that necessary is no longer a thread cap but the admission bound, which the liveness path is exempt from.** Answer the liveness route on the event loop rather than in a worker thread, by making the handler a coroutine | (a) Leave it synchronous and raise the thread cap enough to spare one; (b) exempt the route from the cap; (c) leave it synchronous and accept the queueing | The route reads nothing and waits on nothing — it returns a constant — so it needs no thread, and with the threads capped at the pooled connection count a synchronous liveness route would queue behind the database-bound requests holding them. An orchestrator reading a timeout on **that** route restarts the pod, which would turn a capacity event into a restart loop. Nothing observable changes: the path, the status and the body are identical, and no test asserted the handler was synchronous — the one case that asserts a route runs off the loop names the readiness route, which stays synchronous because it does read the database. (a) reintroduces the mismatch the cap exists to remove. (b) is not expressible: the cap is a property of the thread pool, not of a route | The handler is now a coroutine, so any future work added to it would block the event loop rather than a worker thread. It returns a constant, and the readiness route beside it is where database-dependent work belongs |
| 97.2.5 | **Stands as a decision and is delivered; one sentence of its rationale is superseded — see §97.4. Where it says the alignment makes a real pool timeout hard to provoke, read the admission bound.** Verify the refusal through the assembled application as well as in isolation, driving the readiness route with its database read made to fail | (a) Assert the handler by calling it directly with a constructed request; (b) provoke a real pool timeout by configuring a pool of one; (c) assert only the isolated probe application | (a) would not show that the security, cross-origin and request-identifier headers reach the response, which is the property that follows from where the handler is registered rather than from what it returns. (b) is the one thing the alignment makes hard to do on purpose: with threads capped at the pool's persistent bound, an admitted request finds a connection waiting, so the timeout stops being reachable through normal traffic — which is the point of the change, and is why the runtime evidence for the refusal comes from a configuration that defeats the alignment deliberately. (c) leaves the middleware property unasserted. The readiness route is used because it is the one route whose database work can be made to fail on demand, and its own 503 reports a status where the capacity refusal reports a detail, so the two answers are distinguishable | The case substitutes a module-level function, so it depends on the route resolving that name at call time. That is how the route is written, and a refactor that bound the name earlier would fail the case rather than pass silently |

### 97.3 The informational observations, and what each was worth

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 97.3.1 | **Record, and do not act on, the absence of response compression** | (a) Add the framework's compression middleware; (b) add it for the listings collection alone | Nothing in the plan requires compression, and the review raised it as an observation of what is configured rather than as a departure from a requirement. Adding a middleware would widen the request path for a property no requirement names, which AAP &sect;0.1.2 forbids, and every compression layer interacts with the body-size cap that &sect;0.4.4 relies on as a named compensating control | A collection response is larger on the wire than it would be compressed. The page size is capped at `MAX_PAGE_SIZE`, so the size is bounded whatever a caller asks for |
| 97.3.2 | **Record, and do not act on, rows beyond the absolute offset ceiling being unreachable through the collection routes** | (a) Raise `MAX_PAGINATION_OFFSET`; (b) add keyset pagination beside the offset form | This is the intended behaviour of the bound rather than a defect in it: finding H-5 is that the collection must not return the whole corpus, and the pair of `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` and `MAX_PAGINATION_OFFSET` is what delivers that. (a) weakens the control the review confirmed effective. (b) is a new capability, and the review itself passed the pagination surface | A caller cannot page past the ceiling. That is the control working; a corpus consumer needs a filtered query rather than a deeper offset |

### 97.4 The first repair for F-2, and the measurement that withdrew it

**Rows 97.2.3 and 97.2.4 record the first repair. It was written, it passed the whole suite,
it was driven under load, and it did not work.** This section records the measurement that
falsified it and the mechanism delivered in its place. It follows the convention §27
established and §35.1 reused: the earlier rows are marked in place and keep their own
chronology rather than being rewritten into agreement. Cite them for what that round decided
and cite here for what is true in the delivered tree.

Rows 97.2.1 and 97.2.2 — the 503, the handler registered for the pool's own class, and the
`Retry-After` derived from `DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` — are untouched by this and are
delivered as written.

**What the first repair achieved, and what it did not.** With worker threads capped at
`DB_POOL_SIZE`, the ladder that produced the finding was re-driven against 20 000 seeded
rows. The 500s were gone, every refusal was a 503 carrying `Retry-After`, and the server's
error stream fell from 179 `Exception in ASGI application` blocks to none — so rows 97.2.1
and 97.2.2 were doing their work. But the stall the review called defective survived, and
throughput did not merely degrade, it collapsed:

| Concurrency | With the thread cap | With the admission bound |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 547 × 200, 54.4 req/s, p50 63 ms | 659 × 200, 65.7 req/s, p50 63 ms |
| 15 | 735 × 200, 72.5 req/s, p50 203 ms | 725 × 200, 71.1 req/s, p50 203 ms |
| 40 | 684 × 200, 65.7 req/s, p50 547 ms | 674 × 200, 64.2 req/s, p50 563 ms |
| **60** | 92 × 200 **+ 13 × 503**, **4.7 req/s**, **p50 10 703 ms** | **626 × 200, no refusals**, 58.2 req/s, p50 859 ms, max 1 860 ms |
| **100** | 60 × 200 **+ 40 × 503 + 42 client read timeouts**, **2.2 req/s**, **p50 31 203 ms** | **528 × 200, no refusals**, 46.9 req/s, p50 1 422 ms, max 2 828 ms |

**Why capping threads cannot work.** Row 97.2.3 already names the mechanism, for a different
purpose: the framework runs a synchronous generator dependency's entry, the endpoint and its
exit as **three separate** units of threaded work. Cap the tokens at ten and ten endpoints
run — but the sessions waiting to be *closed* queue behind them in the same first-in
first-out thread queue, and each of those still holds a pooled connection. The number of
connections wanted is therefore not the number of endpoints running; it is that plus a
backlog with no bound on it. It exceeded the ceiling of fifteen, the eleventh checkout
blocked for the full `DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, and the closers that would have freed the
connections could not be scheduled because the blocked endpoints were ahead of them. A thread
cap bounds how many handlers run. It does not bound how many connections are outstanding, and
the pool cares only about the second.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 97.4.1 | **Bound requests in flight rather than worker threads. `RequestAdmissionMiddleware` in `backend/app/main.py` admits at most `admitted_concurrency(settings.DATABASE_URL)` requests into the router at once; a request that waits its whole allowance is refused with the same 503 the pool refusal returns.** Worker threads go back to the library's own default. Rows 97.2.3 and 97.2.4 are the position this supersedes | (a) Keep the thread cap — falsified above; (b) raise the pool to at least the worker-thread count of 40, which was the review's first suggestion and row 97.2.3's alternative (a); (c) acquire the bound inside the session dependency `get_db` rather than in a layer; (d) convert `get_db` and the endpoints to an asynchronous driver so entry and exit are not separate threaded units; (e) implement the layer as a `BaseHTTPMiddleware` subclass, as three of the existing layers are | The bound is provable rather than hopeful, and the proof is a property of where the framework closes a dependency. Read from the installed `fastapi` 0.125.0: `routing.py` creates the dependency exit stack **inside** the per-route ASGI application — `async with AsyncExitStack() as request_stack: scope["fastapi_inner_astack"] = request_stack` — and `solve_dependencies` is handed that same stack, so `get_db`'s session is closed before the route's own ASGI call returns. A layer that awaits the downstream application therefore encloses the session's entire life. At most `bound` requests are inside it, so at most `bound` sessions are open, so at most `bound` connections are wanted. With the shipped 10 against a ceiling of 15 the pool cannot block, and the two paths §97.4.2 exempts draw on the remainder. Measured at the database rather than inferred: `pg_stat_activity` sampled every 50 ms through a concurrency-100 run peaked at 11 sessions, one of which was the sampler's own — exactly the bound, against a review baseline of 16. (b) stays rejected for the reason row 97.2.3 gave, which was a measurement of the deployment and not a preference: `infrastructure/terraform/main.tf` provisions the database at `db-f1-micro` with no flag raising its connection limit, and the renderer defaults to two replicas under a horizontal autoscaler, so 40 per process is more connections than the server accepts. (c) reproduces the defect being fixed: `get_db` is a synchronous generator run in the thread pool, so waiting for a slot there occupies a worker and re-creates the same inversion. (d) is a driver migration across every endpoint, which no finding asks for and which the frozen SQLAlchemy 1.4 pin of AAP §0.4.1 does not make cheap. (e) cannot hold the bound: `BaseHTTPMiddleware` runs the downstream application in a task group of its own and returns once the response has *started*, so the exit stack can outlive the layer — a plain ASGI class awaits the whole call and is the only shape that encloses teardown | The ceiling on useful concurrency is now explicit and low: at 100 concurrent callers the median response is 1.4 s rather than 63 ms, because 90 of them are queueing. That is the arithmetic of a bounded system and is the intended trade — a queue with a stated bound and a retryable refusal in place of an unbounded queue that ends in a 500. An operator who wants more concurrency raises `DB_POOL_SIZE`, and the `.env.example` block and README row say so together with the warning to raise the database's own limit with it |
| 97.4.2 | **Register the gate as the innermost layer, and exempt `/health` and `/health/ready` from it** by naming them in `UNGATED_PATHS` | (a) Register it outermost, ahead of the request-identifier layer; (b) register it between the host check and the rate limiter; (c) gate every path including the probes; (d) exempt the probes by checking for them inside the router instead | Innermost means the rate limiter and the body-size cap both sit outside it, so a request they refuse never spends a slot — a 429 or a 413 costs nothing from the budget that protects the database. It also means the 503 travels back out through all six outer layers, which was verified on a live refusal: the response carried `retry-after`, all six entries of `SECURITY_HEADERS`, `cache-control: no-store`, `x-request-id` and `traceparent`. (a) and (b) both put the gate outside layers that refuse cheaply, so a throttled caller could exhaust the budget without ever reaching a route. (c) is the dangerous one: an orchestrator restarts a pod whose liveness probe times out and removes one whose readiness probe fails, so a saturated gate holding the probes would turn a capacity event into a restart loop — the exact failure row 97.2.4 was written to avoid, arriving by a different door. Under a concurrency-150 load against a bound of one, the exempt probes answered 200 in 3–68 ms for liveness and 8–36 ms for readiness, against container timeouts of 5 s. (d) puts the exemption where the gate has already held the request, which is too late | Two consequences are accepted and stated rather than left to be discovered. First, the readiness probe reads the database and is not gated, so it needs a connection no admitted request is entitled to; the gap between `DB_POOL_SIZE` and the ceiling is what covers it, which is why `DB_MAX_OVERFLOW` is not left at zero and why the boundary case asserts the admitted count is below the ceiling by exactly it. Second, the framework reads a request body before it opens a session, and that read happens inside the gate — so a client trickling a body slowly holds a slot without holding a connection, and `bound` such clients can starve the database-backed routes. What bounds that today is `MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES`, `MAX_REQUEST_BODY_CHUNKS` and the per-address rate limits, plus the two exempt paths keeping the pod visible and drainable to its orchestrator; no request-read deadline exists anywhere in this service and adding one is a control no finding names. An operator terminating traffic at a proxy should set a body-read timeout there |
| 97.4.3 | **Resolve the bound per event loop, through an `anyio` `RunVar` holding an `anyio.Semaphore`**, created on first use rather than at construction | (a) A module-level `anyio.Semaphore` created at import; (b) a `contextvars.ContextVar`; (c) a `threading.Semaphore`; (d) create it in a startup hook on the application | The layer is constructed before any event loop exists, and an `anyio` semaphore's waiters belong to the loop that awaited them, so the object cannot be built at import and cannot be shared between loops. A `RunVar` is the library's own answer to exactly that: one value per running loop, resolved lazily. It also keeps the suite honest — the framework's test client starts a blocking portal, and `testclient.py` reuses one only while the client is entered as a context manager, so a bound shared across loops would behave differently under test than in the server. Verified by a case that reads the bound's identity through two clients and requires the two to differ. (b) is wrong in a way that would have looked right: a `ContextVar` is copied into each task, so every request would have created a bound of its own and the layer would have admitted everything. (c) blocks the event loop while waiting, which is the defect this whole section is about. (d) would work for the server and not for the suite, where most probes never run a startup hook | A future deployment running more than one loop in one process gets one bound per loop rather than one per process, so the per-process ceiling would be the product. Nothing in this repository runs that arrangement — `uvicorn` is invoked without `--workers` in all five commands, and a worker there is a process rather than a loop |
| 97.4.4 | **Set the allowance for a slot to `DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`**, the same value the pool would have waited | (a) A new setting of its own; (b) a short fixed allowance such as one second; (c) no wait at all — refuse immediately when the bound is reached | One configured value answers one question — how long may a request wait for database capacity — and the gate is now where that wait happens instead of the pool, so introducing a second value would only create something to disagree with the first. It also keeps the `Retry-After` of row 97.2.2 honest without a second derivation. (a) adds a name that must be published in five places for no new expressiveness. (b) would refuse callers the queue was about to serve: at the shipped bound the measured ladder drains 100 concurrent callers in under 1.5 s at the median, so a one-second allowance would manufacture refusals out of a healthy queue. (c) turns every burst above the bound into a refusal and gives up the queueing that produced the 46.9 req/s at concurrency 100 | A refused request has still waited the allowance before being refused, so the worst case for one caller is that wait plus its own service time. That is the same budget the pool spent, now spent where it can end in a retryable answer instead of a 500; measured against the deliberately tiny configuration, the worst single response was 3.7 s with an allowance of 1 s |
| 97.4.5 | **Prove the delivered mechanism at runtime in two configurations — the shipped one, and one small enough to force refusals.** Row 97.2.5's decision to verify through the assembled application stands; the sentence in it that calls a real pool timeout hard to provoke *because of the thread cap* is superseded here, and reads the same way of the admission bound | (a) The shipped configuration alone; (b) the forced configuration alone; (c) unit cases alone | The shipped configuration shows the property that matters — 3 212 requests across five rungs with no 500, no 503 and no client timeout, a worst single response of 2 828 ms where the review measured two stacked ten-second waits, and a database-side peak of exactly the bound. But a configuration where nothing is ever refused cannot show the refusal, so a second server was run with `DB_POOL_SIZE=1` and a one-second allowance and driven at 150 concurrent: 476 refusals, every one a 503 with `Retry-After: 1` and a body of exactly `CAPACITY_DETAIL` and the request identifier, 476 matching `WARNING` records naming the path, the bound and the allowance, no traceback in any of them, and the error stream still 202 bytes of server banner. (a) leaves the refusal unproven, (b) proves an answer nobody will meet, and (c) cannot show either the header set or the database-side count | The forced configuration is not one anybody should deploy, and the figures from it should not be read as capacity guidance — it exists to make a refusal reachable. Notably it produced **no** pool-exhaustion record at all even with a ceiling of one, which is the clearest statement of what changed: with the gate in force the pool is no longer the thing that runs out, so row 97.2.1's handler is now the answer for the ungated readiness path rather than the everyday one, and its own runtime evidence stays the case that makes that route's read fail on demand |



## 98. The browser-facing response surface, and the contract the schema publishes

A read-only product-frontend continuity review exercised the running service through a
real browser across ten modules and 412 cases. It returned FAIL, and the reason is worth
stating precisely because it is not a defect in this remediation: **every one of its six
failed cases, its single Critical and all of its Major findings sits in read-only
`frontend/src/**` source**, and it recorded *"Regressions attributable to the backend
security remediation: ZERO"* alongside a full pass on all seventeen of its
browser-verifiable AAP requirements. It failed on its own second gate &mdash; that no
unresolved blocker hides required coverage &mdash; because the product React application
does not compile, so the product's five screens render nothing and could not be exercised.

Four of its informational findings are defects in files this remediation owns, and this
section records their fixes. The remainder are deferred, each against a clause that
excludes it, in &sect;98.3.

Two properties hold throughout. Every figure below was produced by running a command or a
browser against this tree, and the command is named. And each fix was proved to be the
thing that changed the behaviour, by a calibration that disables it and observes the old
behaviour return &mdash; because a case that would pass either way verifies nothing.

### 98.1 The response headers a browser receives

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 98.1.1 | **Remove `ambient-light-sensor=()` from the `Permissions-Policy` header and withdraw the `ambient-light-sensor` half of row 12.9.** The other thirteen tokens are untouched | (a) Keep the token and keep row 12.9 standing; (b) keep the token and add a note to the README that one console warning per HTML page load is expected; (c) remove the token and edit row 12.9 in place | Row 12.9 held the token on two grounds and a later review disproved both. Its first ground &mdash; that every change must trace to a named finding &mdash; expired the moment a review named this one. Its second, that the token "is ignored by browsers that do not recognise it", is factually wrong and was measured: an A/B control on a throwaway server showed this Chrome build emitting `Error with Permissions-Policy header: Unrecognized feature: 'ambient-light-sensor'.` when served a header containing the token, and emitting nothing when served this application's corrected thirteen-token value. So the cost was not zero, and the benefit is: the feature the token denies exists in no browser that would honour the denial, which is precisely why the parser rejects the name. (a) leaves a header that provably makes a browser complain on every page it governs. (b) documents a defect instead of fixing a one-token string. (c) destroys the record of a position that was held, which &sect;27 establishes this log does not do | The remaining thirteen tokens are the whole of the policy's enforcement, and no test pins the string, so a future round could remove an enforcing token without a case failing. What bounds that: the header cases iterate `SECURITY_HEADERS.items()` and assert every entry reaches every response including the error paths, so the header cannot go missing, only become weaker. Nothing here detects a weaker one |
| 98.1.2 | **Expose the throttle policy to a cross-origin caller's own code, by naming the four headers the limiter writes in `expose_headers`.** `CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS` is built from `RATE_LIMIT_HEADERS + (RETRY_AFTER_HEADER,)` rather than restated | (a) Say nothing and let a browser client keep guessing its back-off; (b) name the four headers as literals in `main.py`; (c) expose every header the service sends; (d) move the policy into the response body so no header need be exposed | The limiter writes `Retry-After` and the three `X-RateLimit-*` headers onto every refusal, and a browser hides all four from page JavaScript, because only six CORS-safelisted response headers are readable without an explicit grant. Measured in a real browser from the one allowed origin: before, three headers readable; after, seven &mdash; the three safelisted ones plus exactly these four. So the control the service already implements was unusable by the only client the frozen contract permits, and a client that cannot read `Retry-After` retries blind. (b) is the drift this repository has been bitten by before: the exposed set and the emitted set would be two lists to keep equal, and `test_the_exposed_set_is_the_headers_a_refusal_carries` exists because deriving it makes them one. (c) contradicts the explicit-lists posture AAP &sect;0.5.1.5 requires and would publish `x-request-id`, the security headers and `server` to any allowed origin's script. (d) changes a response body the refusal contract fixes, to avoid adding a header | Four header names become readable by script on an allow-listed origin. Each is policy metadata the server chose to send about the caller's own request; none carries user data, a credential or a server internal. The blast radius is bounded by the origin allowlist, which is unchanged, and by the derivation: a header the limiter stops writing stops being exposed |
| 98.1.3 | **Never emit `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` on a response that carries no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`**, enforced subtractively in `SecurityHeadersMiddleware` | (a) Leave it, since a browser blocks the read regardless; (b) replace the framework's cross-origin middleware with one of our own; (c) set `allow_credentials=False` and lose the credentialed flow; (d) strip it in each handler that builds a response itself | A refused preflight answered `400` carrying `access-control-allow-credentials: true` and no origin header, because the framework builds its preflight headers before deciding whether the origin is allowed and then adds the origin conditionally. The header is read only beside the origin header, so on its own it says nothing true: it advertises a credentialed relationship with an origin the service just refused. (a) is correct about the browser and wrong about the signal &mdash; a reviewer reading the response cannot tell a refusal from a grant by its headers alone. (b) is a large change to a control the same review passed on 22 of 22 cases. (c) breaks the frozen `localStorage` bearer flow. (d) is the construct that misses the next handler; `_cors_headers` already pairs the two correctly for the handler outside the middleware stack, and one invariant at the outermost layer covers every response either way. The helper runs before the documentation-policy branch, because that branch rebuilds a response from the headers this one leaves | The invariant deletes a header, so a future change that legitimately needed the credentials header without an origin header would be silently undone. No such case exists: the Fetch specification gives the header meaning only in the presence of the origin header. Two cases assert the pairing in both directions, and a third asserts the allowed preflight still receives both |

### 98.2 What the published schema is allowed to claim

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 98.2.1 | **Publish the refusal body this service actually returns.** Every `422` in the generated document now references a new `ErrorResponse` component &mdash; an object with one required string member `detail` &mdash; and the generator's `HTTPValidationError` and `ValidationError` components, which nothing then references, are removed | (a) Leave the document as generated; (b) change the runtime to return the generated shape; (c) declare the response per route in each endpoint module; (d) rewrite every non-2xx response, not only the refusal status | The generator publishes a `422` whose `detail` is an **array** of per-field objects carrying `loc`, `msg` and `type`. This service returns `{"detail": "Invalid request"}` &mdash; one fixed string, which is the non-disclosure property row 13's rows delivered. So the published contract was wrong about every refusal, and a client generated from it mis-parses all of them. (a) leaves a document that misdescribes the surface it documents. (b) reopens the disclosure the fixed detail closes, publishing field names, positions and validator identities to any caller. (c) touches four endpoint modules to state one fact that is true of all of them, and the next route added would omit it. (d) was measured and rejected as a different untruth: the `500` envelope carries `request_id` alongside `detail`, so a blanket rewrite would publish a body that route does not return. The alignment therefore names one status &mdash; the one the generator emits and the one the finding is about | The alignment post-processes a document the framework generates, so a future framework release that changes where the refusal is declared would leave it in place unaligned rather than failing. What bounds that: `test_at_least_one_refusal_is_published` fails if the set it asserts over becomes empty, `test_no_published_reference_dangles` fails if a removed component is still pointed at, and `test_the_returned_refusal_matches_what_is_published` reads the body from a live route rather than restating it, so the published description and the returned body cannot drift apart in either direction |
| 98.2.2 | **Hold the aligned document on the application and align once**, by wrapping the generator rather than replacing it | (a) Align on every request; (b) generate the document from scratch with an explicit call to the framework's builder; (c) align at import time | (a) rebuilds nothing but re-walks the document per request on a route a documentation viewer fetches on every load. (b) restates the title, version, route list and every other argument the framework already derives from the application, so an argument gained by a future release would be silently dropped. (c) would read the route table before the router is mounted. Wrapping keeps the framework as the source of the document and this module as the source of one correction to it, and the correction is idempotent, so applying it twice leaves the document as the first application did | The cached document is the framework's own cache slot, so a future round that clears it gets the alignment reapplied rather than losing it &mdash; which is the intended direction. A round that replaces `app.openapi` again would displace this wrapper; `test_the_schema_route_serves_the_aligned_document` reads the served document rather than the function, so that would fail here |

### 98.3 Findings deferred, each against the clause that excludes it

Every row below answers a finding the review raised. None is fixed, and each names the
clause that withholds the authority to fix it. The precedent is settled rather than new:
row 34.6.3 decided to report the findings discovered outside the stated scope and change
nothing, &sect;91.1 **reverted** two later changes that had closed two of them, and row
91.1.1 states the principle this section applies &mdash; *"a decision-log rationale is not
an amendment to the AAP: the authority to close a confirmation-only finding is the user's,
not this work's."*

Independently measured for this round: across the 35 commits this remediation carries,
`git log --author=agent@blitzy.com --name-only -- frontend` lists exactly two paths,
`frontend/.dockerignore` and `frontend/package-lock.json`. **Nothing under
`frontend/src/**`, and neither `frontend/package.json` nor `frontend/public/index.html`,
was ever touched by this work** &mdash; which is the evidence behind every "pre-existing"
classification below.

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 98.3.1 | **Leave the product React application uncompilable.** The review's single Critical: `#root.innerHTML.length` is 0 on all five product routes, from thirteen distinct blockers &mdash; two dependencies absent from `frontend/package.json`, two extension-less store modules, twelve bare `'frontend/src/...'` specifiers, six modules that do not exist, seven `api.ts` exports that are referenced but not exported, JSX inside a `.ts` file, a React 17 render call on React 18, and no stylesheet at all | (a) Fix the thirteen blockers; (b) fix only the two absent dependencies, as the cheapest step; (c) rename `services/paypal.ts` to `.tsx`, which is the single hard parse failure | AAP &sect;0.9.2 places **"Everything under `frontend/src/**`"** out of scope as read-only reference material, and separately excludes `frontend/package.json` and `frontend/tsconfig.json` as files that "have no bearing on the backend vulnerabilities". Every one of the thirteen blockers sits in one of those. (b) and (c) are also refused on a second ground that (a) shares: neither makes the application compile, because the other blockers remain &mdash; so each would spend authorization this work does not have and still leave `#root` empty | No end user reaches this backend through the product UI. That is the single largest production-readiness risk in the repository and it is entirely outside this remediation's authority. It needs its own authorized work item, and the review's own suggested fix list is the specification for it |
| 98.3.2 | **Do not add a `token` alias to the login response.** The review's finding that the read-only client destructures `response.data.token` while this service returns the frozen `{access_token, token_type}`, so the stored token is `undefined` on every login | (a) Add `token` alongside `access_token`, which AAP &sect;0.1.2 permits since fields may be added; (b) change the client to read `access_token` | This is item 1 of the ten findings row 34.6.3 reports for confirmation, is registered as **O-5** in [`RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md) and as **C1** in [`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) &sect;11, and the review's own suggested fix says it "requires confirmation per AAP &sect;0.12.5". (a) is permitted by the frozen-shape clause and still refused, for the reason row 91.1.1 gives: permission to add a field is not authorization to close a finding reserved to the user, and taking it *because a log row argues for it* is the defect &sect;91.1 exists to correct. It also buys nothing measurable &mdash; the application does not compile, so no login it fixed could ever run. (b) edits read-only frontend source | Authentication through the product client remains broken. The backend half is verified correct: the review read the frozen two-key body on five different accounts |
| 98.3.3 | **Do not add a `GET /user/profile` route,** which the read-only client calls and which answered `404` four times in the review | (a) Add the route; (b) remove the call from the client | The route exists in no revision of this service. (a) is new product capability, which AAP &sect;0.9.2 excludes outright &mdash; *"No new product capability is introduced"* &mdash; and the Minimal Change Clause forbids. (b) is `frontend/src/services/api.ts`, out of scope by the same clause. Registered as **C2** in [`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) &sect;11 | A product screen shows an error where a profile belongs. Nothing in this service is wrong |
| 98.3.4 | **Leave the client's filter-creation call as it is:** a camelCase body this service's request contract would refuse, sent with no `Authorization` header, answered `307` then `401` | (a) Accept the camelCase shape as an alternative contract; (b) attach the bearer token and map the body in the client | Two independent client faults, both inside `frontend/src/services/api.ts`, which AAP &sect;0.9.2 places out of scope; this is the other half of **C2**. (a) would widen a request contract to accept a shape no documented client sends, weakening the field allowlist that closes H-6, in order to accommodate a caller that would still fail on the missing credential. (b) is the correct repair and is a frontend change | Filter creation through the product client cannot work. The review verified the endpoint itself end-to-end on 47 cases with a byte-verbatim harness |
| 98.3.5 | **Leave `users.last_login` and `filters.last_used` unwritten.** Both columns are declared, both are projected by their response models, and both are `NULL` after the operation that would set them | (a) Write `last_login` on a successful authentication and `last_used` when a filter is read; (b) remove both columns from the response models | The `last_login` half is already recorded: row 33.10 holds it as "pre-existing and named by no requirement", and the review confirmed it independently by reading the original pre-change `auth.py`, which never wrote it either. The `last_used` half is registered here for the first time and has the same standing. (a) is a behaviour addition AAP &sect;0.9.2 excludes as a "feature addition unrelated to security", and it is named by no AAP requirement and by none of the plan's twenty findings. (b) removes fields from a response, which AAP &sect;0.1.2 forbids in the same clause that permits adding them | Two projected fields are always null, so a consumer cannot distinguish "never used" from "not recorded". Neither is read by any authorization or audit path: the audit trail AAP &sect;0.12.2 requires is the structured logger, the seed revision's own record, this log and the traceability matrix |
| 98.3.6 | **Leave stored input encoded on output rather than sanitised on input,** and leave `criteria[].field` shape-validated rather than allowlisted against column names | (a) Sanitise on input, stripping or rejecting markup; (b) allowlist `criteria[].field` against the columns a filter may name | The review classified both as observations rather than defects and verified the safety property for each: every payload it stored rendered as inert text with `childElementCount 0` and produced zero dialogs across six injection cases, and a repository grep found nothing that resolves `criteria[].field` into a column or an attribute. (a) destroys the user's literal data, and output encoding is the correct layer. (b) rejects values the published contract accepts by design &mdash; the contract publishes `pattern=^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*$` &mdash; so it is a breaking contract change no AAP requirement names, and the `operator` allowlist already guards the primitive that would matter | Any *other* consumer of `filters.name` or `criteria[].value` &mdash; a different client, an email template, a report export &mdash; must encode independently. And if a future consumer ever resolves `criteria[].field` into a column, the allowlist becomes necessary. Both are recorded here as the condition under which the position changes |
| 98.3.7 | **Do not self-host the documentation viewers' assets,** which load from external content-delivery networks and would render unstyled in an egress-filtered deployment | (a) Vendor the viewer bundles and serve them from this application; (b) inline them into the documentation HTML | This is the one deferral where fixing the finding would **break** a control rather than merely exceed scope. Serving a vendored bundle requires mounting a static-file handler, and `StaticFiles` is one of the fourteen reachability patterns [`RESIDUAL_RISK.md`](RESIDUAL_RISK.md) holds at zero **because** "no static-file handler is mounted anywhere in the service" is the named compensating control for accepted advisory PYSEC-2026-2281, whose fix requires an interpreter AAP &sect;0.1.2 pins away. Taking (a) would reactivate that advisory, fail the reachability guard in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, and fail `test_thirteen_reachability_patterns_are_absent_from_the_application`. (b) has the same effect by another route and additionally breaks the per-page policy, which admits an inline script only by the digest of its own content | In a deployment with no egress the documentation pages render unstyled. They are a developer surface, `DOCUMENTATION_ENABLED` governs whether they are published at all, and no API response depends on them |
| 98.3.8 | **Change nothing for the shared-host and test-instrument observations** | (a) Namespace ports and databases in committed configuration; (b) fix the accessibility and overflow items the review found in its own harness | Neither is product code. The port and database collisions the review met are properties of several agents working one host concurrently, and it isolated itself and cleaned up; this round did the same, taking port 8110 and a database named for its clone. The harness observations are explicitly the review's own instrument, which it then deleted. Its two "latent product analogues" &mdash; a bare unstyled table in `ListingTable.tsx` and no expiry check in the client's `auth.ts` &mdash; are both in read-only `frontend/src/**` | Nothing in the delivered tree. The isolation practice is a convention rather than a mechanism, so a future round must namespace its own resources deliberately |

## 99. The test-suite review: two mechanisms per property, one budget, and one blind spot

A final test-suite and test-infrastructure review returned FAIL on six findings: no
Critical and no Major, two Minor and four informational, and no defect in delivered
application code. Five of the six are properties of the suite rather than of the
service, and the sixth is a fact about what the static analyser reads that no
artefact had recorded.

Two properties are asserted throughout. Every figure below was produced by running a
command against this tree, and the command is named. And every change this round makes
is additive to a file the plan already delivers -- five test modules and this log -- so
no path enters the delivered set, and the inventories and totals in
[`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) are unchanged rather than restated.


### 99.1 The timing marker's coverage-equivalence claim

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.1.1 | **Close the gap the claim describes by adding a counted case for the wait, rather than narrowing the claim.** `_RecordingClock` replaces the module-level `time` the security module reads, so a case states elapsed time as data and reads back the interval the helper asked to sleep for. `test_it_sleeps_out_the_time_still_left_on_the_budget` asserts the interval is the remainder rather than the whole budget, `test_a_refused_login_sleeps_out_the_refusal_budget` and `test_a_credential_check_sleeps_out_the_credential_budget` assert each caller reaches the helper with its own budget on all four stored-hash shapes, and two further cases pin the not-waiting branch at and past the boundary | (a) Narrow the marker description to the properties it actually held for; (b) remove the `timing` mark so the wall-clock cases can never be deselected; (c) delete the wall-clock cases and keep only counted ones; (d) leave it and record an exception | Row 43.4.6 registered the marker with the note that deselecting it loses no coverage of the control, and the review measured that false for one property. Measured here first, to confirm the report rather than assume it: with `if remaining > 0:` replaced by `if False:` in `_pad_until`, `pytest backend/tests/security/test_login_throttling_and_timing.py -m "not timing"` exited 0 with 54 passed, while the two marked cases exited 1 with 2 failed. The decomposition row 43.4.6 introduced was sound in half: `test_every_path_is_held_to_the_floor` counts that the check reaches the helper and the equalisation count in `TestRefusalBranchesDoTheSameWork` counts that every refusal branch does, so removing the *call* was already caught; nothing unmarked caught the helper ceasing to *wait*. (a) makes the record true by lowering what it promises, and that promise is the reason `-m "not timing"` is documented as a supported way to run the suite on a noisy host. (b) puts a wall-clock reading back into the mandatory set, which row 31.13 refused on measurement. (c) discards the only end-to-end evidence. Re-measured after the change: the same mutation exits 1 with six unmarked failures | The new cases read a replaced clock, so they cannot see a wait that a real `time.sleep` refused to perform; the marked cases remain the only end-to-end evidence of that, which is why both mechanisms are kept. The intervals are asserted exactly rather than within a tolerance, which is safe only because the readings are chosen so the arithmetic is exact in binary floating point. |
| 99.1.2 | **Correct the two docstrings that stated the claim in the singular, and leave `setup.cfg` byte-identical** | (a) Reword the marker description as well; (b) leave all three as they were; (c) move the claim out of `setup.cfg` and into this log | The claim was made in three places: the marker description at `setup.cfg`, the module docstring of `test_login_throttling_and_timing.py`, and the docstring of `TestRefusalBranchesTakeTheSameTime`. Closing the gap makes the marker description true as written, so (a) would be churn on a line whose content a contract case reads. The two docstrings said "the counted case" of a single mechanism and now name both, because a reader deciding whether to deselect the mark needs to know what still covers the control. (b) leaves two statements understating the coverage they describe. (c) removes the statement from the file a contributor reads when they run the marker | Three copies of one claim still exist, and a future change to the decomposition has to reach all three. The marker description is the one a contract case reads, so a divergence there is caught; the two docstrings are not asserted. |

### 99.2 The developer setup script's subprocess budget

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.2.1 | **Give a full run of the script its own 300-second budget as `SCRIPT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, and keep the 60-second `SHELL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` for the parse and the declaration block** | (a) Raise the single constant to 180 for every shell case; (b) make the budget an environment input; (c) shorten the case so the run stops before the step that builds a virtual environment; (d) leave it, since the configuration the review used is not the one CI runs | The two budgets cover different work. A parse and a run of the declaration block are text operations that finish in a fraction of a second -- measured at 0.06s and 0.10s -- while `test_the_script_asks_for_no_administrator_it_has_no_use_for` runs the script far enough to build a real virtual environment, measured at 29.56s idle. The review reported it failing under `pytest -n 8`, and that was reproduced here without installing the parallel runner by running eight concurrent copies of the same case: every one passed and each took between 59.58s and 61.38s, so the old ceiling is crossed by the contention a parallel run creates rather than by any defect. (a) relaxes the two text checks as well, and those are where a genuinely hung shell should be reported quickly. (b) adds an input to document in the README and to keep in agreement with the workflow. (c) stops exercising the branch the case exists for, which is the checkout that is already configured. (d) leaves a correct case one busy host away from red | A run of the script that genuinely hangs now takes five minutes to report rather than one. The two sub-second checks still report in one minute, so the slow path is the only one that waits. |

### 99.3 What counts as a delivered path

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.3.1 | **Read the delivered set from what is committed against the baseline or staged in the index, and treat a path git does not track as scratch.** `_delivered_paths` skips a porcelain line whose status is `??`, the new `_status_path` resolves a rename to its new path, and the assertion message now names the document and tells the reader whether to add a row or leave the byproduct untracked | (a) Widen the byproduct prefix and suffix lists; (b) exclude only paths git ignores; (c) skip the case when the working tree is dirty; (d) document the constraint and leave the helper | `test_every_delivered_path_is_reachable_from_the_file_side` unioned `git status --porcelain` into the delivered set, so any untracked path outside a fixed list failed it in a working tree while CI, which runs on a fresh checkout, stayed green. Reproduced here with an untracked scratch directory: `AssertionError: not indexed: qa-scratch-probe/`. A commit is assembled from the index, so a path that is genuinely delivered is staged before it is committed and is still caught -- measured in both directions: with the scratch present the case now passes, and `git add` of a new unindexed path fails it again with the new message. (a) is a list that grows with every future tool. (b) is narrower than it looks, because `git status --porcelain` does not report an ignored path at all, so the paths that actually failed the case were the ones nobody had ignored. (c) makes the case unrunnable exactly while a change is in progress, which is when it is worth running. (d) leaves a reader following documented instructions into a failure | A path that is neither committed nor staged is not asserted against the index, so the window in which a new deliverable is unindexed is the moment before it is added. The rename branch is exercised by a direct check of the helper rather than by a rename in this tree. |

### 99.4 Two branches of the redacting logger that no case reached

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.4.1 | **Cover the unquoted mapping value and the base-logger fallback with cases that read the substituted text and the resolved logger back.** `TestMappingValuesCarryingNoQuotes` and `TestTheBaseLoggerIsReachable` in `test_settings_and_redaction` | (a) Assert only that the credential is absent from the output; (b) leave both uncovered as defensive depth; (c) reach them indirectly through a logger call rather than through the exported function | A serialised mapping does not have to quote its value -- a number, a boolean and a null are written bare -- and the accessor's fallback decides whether a record enters the governed tree at all or reaches the root logger, which carries no redacting handler. (a) is the weaker assertion the rest of the module already makes, and it cannot distinguish this rule replacing the value from a different rule catching it; each new case therefore asserts the exact substituted text, and one asserts the fallback logger carries the handler by name. (b) leaves two reachable branches of a credential filter unexercised. Measured before: `logging.py` at 743/148/80% for this module with 546-549, 1868 and 1871 missed. After: 743/142/81% with all of them executed | The mapping cases assert against one placeholder and one alphabet, so a change to either has to be reflected here. |
| 99.4.2 | **Keep the skip-value guard on the unquoted branch, and exercise it through the module's own skip set** | (a) Leave the guard's line uncovered and record it as unreachable; (b) delete the guard, since nothing can reach it; (c) change the redaction placeholder so the branch becomes reachable in normal use | The guard is unreachable with the shipped values, and provably so: the bare value alphabet is `[^\s,}\[\]]+`, which admits no bracket, while the placeholder is `[REDACTED]`, so substituted text can never re-enter the branch; and the pattern requires at least one character, so the emptiness half cannot fire either. (b) removes a check that becomes load-bearing the moment either value changes, inside the one module whose purpose is that a credential never reaches a stream, and the quoted branch beside it needs the same check today. (c) changes a published output to move a coverage figure. `test_a_skipped_unquoted_value_is_emitted_unchanged` therefore adds a bracket-free token to `_SKIP_VALUES`, which is the value the branch consults, and asserts both halves: the skipped value is emitted unchanged and a real sentinel in the same shape is still replaced | The case reaches a private module value, so it asserts the branch's behaviour rather than a shape a caller can produce against the shipped placeholder. That is the property worth holding: the branch stays correct if the placeholder or the alphabet changes. |

### 99.5 The ingestion task's provider seam

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.5.1 | **Drive one ingestion pass with nothing stubbed but the transport the HTTP library sends on.** `TestTheRealProviderSeamIsDriven` in `test_tasks` asserts the request's method, the postal code it carries, the credential header, the credential's absence from the URL and the query, the per-request timeouts, the rows the real field mapping stored, the off-domain address it discarded, a second pass refreshing rather than duplicating, and a refusing provider reaching the task as `ListingProviderError` with no row written | (a) Leave the split as it was, since `test_services` covers the adapter; (b) stop patching `fetch_listings` in the existing cases; (c) patch the adapter's internals rather than the transport | Every other pass in that module replaces `fetch_listings`, the boundary the task calls, so the adapter behind it never ran from there: measured, `test_tasks` alone covered `zillow_service.py` at 131/62/53% with the whole request, decode and mapping block 269-367 missed. (a) is defensible on coverage and silent on integration -- the two layers agreeing about the shape of a record is exactly what a per-layer test cannot show. (b) would rewrite cases whose purpose is to count what the task does with a given result, and would make each of them depend on a provider body. (c) leaves the request assembly, the streamed read and the bounded body untested from this side. After the change the same measurement is 131/20/85%, and what remains missing there is the individual error and truncation branches `test_services` covers | One more place that has to be updated if the provider contract changes. The case reads the delivered `PROVIDER_FIELD_SOURCES` mapping rather than restating it, so a change to the mapping's keys surfaces as a discarded record rather than as a silent pass. |
| 99.5.2 | **Build the stand-in client with the delivered factory's own timeout rather than with the setting** | (a) Pass `settings.HTTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, as the sibling helper in `test_services` does; (b) assert nothing about the timeout in this module | Passing the setting makes the assertion true by construction: the case builds the client, so it is reading back its own argument. Reading the timeout from `_client()` makes the recorded request carry whatever the delivered factory configures, which turns this module into a second and independent gate on the outbound timeout. Measured: with both timeouts removed from the adapter, the suite reported one failure -- `test_the_client_factory_carries_the_configured_timeout` -- before this change and two afterwards, in two different modules | The case now depends on the factory being callable at collection-adjacent time; it opens and closes a real client to read one attribute, which issues no request. |

### 99.6 What the static analyser does not read

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 99.6.1 | **Record that the zero-Medium static-analysis result no longer depends on the outbound timeout being present, and name the cases that do gate it** | (a) Say nothing, since the command passes and the control is present; (b) reshape the provider call into a form the analyser's check recognises; (c) add a text guard to the workflow asserting the timeout argument is present | AAP &sect;0.3.3 attributes the single Medium finding this work started from to the analyser's missing-timeout check at the Zillow call site, and &sect;0.8.2 makes `bandit -r backend/app -ll` exiting 0 a success criterion. The adapter now issues its request through `httpx.Client(timeout=...).stream(...)`, a shape that check does not analyse: measured, with both timeouts removed the command still reports "No issues identified" and exits 0. The criterion is therefore satisfied by the delivered code but is no longer evidence for this particular control, and a reader entitled to think otherwise is the failure being closed. (a) leaves that inference standing. (b) would trade a bounded streaming read for an unbounded buffered one to satisfy a scanner, which is a worse control for a better report. (c) adds a text rule for a property the suite already asserts behaviourally, and row 96.8.6 records the precedent for stating a verification caveat rather than reshaping the command around a tool's limitation. What gates the control is `test_the_client_factory_carries_the_configured_timeout` in `test_services` and, since row 99.5.2, `test_the_request_carries_the_credential_in_its_header` in `test_tasks` | The whole gate on this control is two test cases. Deleting either lowers assurance with no signal from the scanner, which is why both are named here and why the second was made independent of the first. |
