## 100. The runtime review: a variable contract that refused a plan, and a documented secret boundary the manifests contradicted

A runtime quality pass over the infrastructure and configuration surface returned two
findings, both Minor, both defects in what a file *says* about the configuration rather
than in what the configuration does. Neither weakens a control &mdash; in the second case
the applied posture is the stronger one &mdash; and that is precisely why they matter
under Rule 1: a reviewer establishes the boundary from the description, so a description
that contradicts the tree is believed in preference to it.

Two properties hold throughout this section. Every figure was produced by running a
command against this tree, and the command is named. And each of the two findings is
closed twice: once by correcting the statement, and once by a contract case that refuses
the statement's shape, calibrated by restoring the delivered defect and requiring the
case to fail.

### 100.1 The Terraform variable contract

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 100.1.1 | **Give `database_private_network` a default in the form `gke_network` already uses, and describe it as retained for a deployment that supplies its own VPC.** Its description had claimed it was "applied as settings.ip_configuration.private_network on `google_sql_database_instance.main`" | (a) Wire the variable into the instance so the description becomes true; (b) delete the variable; (c) leave it required and correct the description alone; (d) leave it as it was, since `terraform validate` passes | The variable was **required and read by nothing**: measured, `terraform plan -refresh=false` with every other input supplied fails with "No value for required variable ... on variables.tf line 703", so a deployment was refused over a value that reaches no resource. (a) is the one option that would weaken a control: `main.tf:264` takes the private network from `google_compute_network.primary.id`, and `test_terraform_contract.py::test_the_cluster_and_the_database_share_one_network` resolves the cluster's and the database's network expressions to the same **created** resource &mdash; a variable reference would make that resolution fail and would restore exactly the class of misconfiguration row 82.8 closed, a database on a VPC the pods cannot reach. (b) removes a declared input, which is an interface change no finding asks for and which rows 12.3 and 82.26 decline for the ten cosmetic names on the same ground. (c) leaves the plan-time refusal in place, which is the operative half of the finding. (d) is the defect: `validate` and `fmt` resolve no variable values, so nothing in the pipeline reports this before a deployment does. Measured after the change: the plan with the input omitted and the plan with it supplied are **byte-identical across all 72 resources**, which is the direct evidence that the value reaches nothing | The default is a self-link naming a network this configuration does not create, so a reader could mistake it for the network in use. Three things bound that: the description says in its first clause that the input is retained rather than applied, the sibling `gke_network` carries the same default for the same reason, and the plan proves the instance takes its network from the created resource. A deployment that was passing a self-link is now silently ignored rather than validated &mdash; it was already ignored, and this round is what says so |
| 100.1.2 | **Correct the four descriptions that attributed an application to the wrong input, and the two that named a resource this configuration does not declare, rather than making the claims true by wiring each variable** | (a) Wire each variable into the property its description named; (b) delete the six variables; (c) correct only the four the finding enumerated; (d) leave the singular/plural resource names, as typographical slips | Each of the six is a second spelling of an input a resource already reads: the private-services range and prefix by `var.private_service_access_range_name` and `var.private_service_access_prefix_length`, the store size by `var.rate_limit_store_memory_size_gb`, the engine version by a literal on the instance, and the subnetwork by the created resource the cluster references. (a) would give one property two sources of truth in five places and, for the subnetwork, would replace a resource reference with a name comparison &mdash; the same weakening row 100.1.1 refuses. (b) is the interface change rows 12.3 and 82.26 decline. (c) would leave a description naming `google_compute_global_address.private_service_access`, which does not exist, beside two the round had just corrected. (d) treats an address a reviewer cannot resolve as cosmetic; the whole finding is that a description is what a claim is checked against | Six descriptions now say what a resource reads rather than what the variable does, which is longer prose to read at the point of declaration. The compensating property is that each names the input actually applied, so the reader is one hop from the truth rather than at a dead end |
| 100.1.3 | **State that `google_redis_instance.rate_limit` fixes `redis_version` as a literal, and move `rate_limit_store_version`'s default from `REDIS_7_0` to `REDIS_6_X` so the declared default is the version created** | (a) Wire the variable into `redis_version`, keeping its `REDIS_7_0` default; (b) wire it with the default lowered to `REDIS_6_X`; (c) correct the description and leave the default at `REDIS_7_0`; (d) delete the variable | An operator setting this input got silence: the resource creates `REDIS_6_X` whatever the value, and the default disagreed with the literal, so the file contradicted itself in two directions at once. (a) changes the planned engine version, which is an infrastructure change made to satisfy a sentence. (b) is defensible and was weighed: it would make the description true and change nothing planned. It was refused because it moves a fourteenth attribute into variable control, where the measured property of this configuration is that thirteen security-relevant attributes are literals and `ingress_settings` is the only variable-driven one &mdash; a property a reviewer checks, and one worth more than a description's convenience. (c) leaves the self-contradiction the finding names. (d) is the interface change | The input remains inert, so an operator can still set it and see no change &mdash; but now the description says so in its first sentence and the default states what is created. Raising the engine version is a one-literal change in `main.tf` if a deployment needs it |
| 100.1.4 | **Withdraw row 37.1's claim that `database_private_network` was removed, and row 42.2.6's claim that cross-variable validation ties `gke_network` to it, marking each in place under the &sect;27 convention** | (a) Correct the two rows in place so they read as though they had always described the tree; (b) delete them; (c) leave them, since both record decisions that still stand in substance | Row 37.1's risk column stated the variable "was removed, so a deployment that was passing a self-link must stop", and row 42.2.6 described an equality check between the two network inputs. Neither is true of the delivered tree: the variable is declared at `variables.tf:703` and was required until this round, and no cross-variable validation exists &mdash; row 82.8 replaced that design by creating the VPC. Two operative rows about one variable, contradicting each other and both contradicting the tree, is the failure &sect;96's own preamble named. (a) destroys the record of what was believed, which &sect;27 establishes this log does not do. (b) is the same destruction. (c) leaves a reader landing on either row taking it as current &mdash; and the first of them would tell them a required input does not exist | Two more withdrawal markers in sections a reader may reach first. `test_documentation_contract.py::test_each_withdrawn_claim_names_the_row_that_made_it` now requires both rows to be named in a section at or after &sect;89, so a withdrawal cannot be added without the row it withdraws being reachable from it |
| 100.1.5 | **Correct the two `main.tf` comments that named `var.backend_kubernetes_namespace`, `var.backend_workload_namespace` and `var.backend_workload_service_account` as the inputs the workload-identity principal is composed from** | (a) Leave the comments and record the divergence here; (b) change `local.backend_workload_principal` to read the inputs the comments named; (c) delete the comments | `main.tf:913` composes the principal from `var.workload_identity_namespace` and `var.backend_kubernetes_service_account`, and the plan confirms it: the member is planned as `serviceAccount:<project>.svc.id.goog[apartment-finder/backend]`, where `apartment-finder` is `var.workload_identity_namespace`'s default and `var.backend_workload_namespace` defaults to `default`. So the comments named inputs whose values do not appear in the value they describe. (b) would change a planned IAM member to satisfy a comment. (c) removes an accurate description of the construct along with the inaccurate attribution. (a) is Rule 1's own prohibition read backwards: a comment states what a construct does, and one that misstates it is corrected rather than annotated elsewhere | Correcting them made three inputs genuinely unreferenced, which row 100.2.2 records and the unread inventory now carries. A reader of an older copy of `main.tf` finds different variable names in that comment with no marker; the comment states what the code does, and unlike a decision it is not a position this log preserves |
| 100.1.6 | **Correct the README's two "no default" paragraphs to thirteen, keep `database_private_network` named there as an input that carries a default, and replace the "Private services access, and a shared VPC" prerequisite row** | (a) Leave the count and add a footnote; (b) drop the variable's name from the README entirely; (c) leave the prerequisite row, which concerns Terraform rather than this repository | The README stated fourteen inputs with no default in two places and named this one among them, so following it produced a `-var` a plan no longer wants. Measured: thirteen variables declare no default and every one is read in code. The prerequisite row asserted that "the Terraform variables enforce that the cluster and the database sit on the same network" and that "the network itself is an input" &mdash; three clauses, all false since row 82.8: `main.tf` creates the VPC, the subnetwork, the reserved range and the peering, and both the cluster and the database attach to what it creates. (a) publishes a figure and then contradicts it. (b) would remove the name a reader searches for when they meet the variable, and `test_operator_documentation.py` requires it to be reachable. (c) leaves a reader provisioning a network the configuration will create anyway, under a heading that says this repository cannot satisfy it | The replacement row names the one thing that genuinely is a prerequisite &mdash; the `servicenetworking` API being active before the apply reaches the peering &mdash; so the table is shorter by nothing but says less than it did about topology. That is the intended direction: the topology is now the configuration's own, and `main.tf`'s prerequisites block is where it is described |

### 100.2 The contract cases that hold the variable contract to the tree

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 100.2.1 | **Assert the three properties in the contract suite the `backend` job already runs, and do not add a `terraform plan` step to the `infrastructure` job** | (a) Add a `plan` step with a committed placeholder tfvars file; (b) add a `plan` step reading values from repository secrets; (c) add `plan` with `-var` defaults invented in the workflow; (d) rely on a deployment surfacing it, as before | A plan needs values for thirteen inputs, eight of which are credentials whose validators refuse a placeholder shape &mdash; the signing key by strength and denylist, the store address by scheme and by placeholder segment, the DSN by marker &mdash; so (a) has no committable value that is both safe and acceptable, which is the argument row 82.6 makes for the manifest tokens. It would also put credential-shaped content in a tracked file, which `.github/scripts/check_secret_policy.sh` scans for. (b) gives a pull-request workflow access to production credentials to check a variable declaration. (c) is (a) with the values hidden in YAML. (d) is the finding. The defect class &mdash; an input a plan demands that no resource reads &mdash; is decidable from `variables.tf` and `main.tf` alone, needs no credential and no network, and `test_every_variable_without_a_default_is_read_by_the_configuration` decides it in the gate that already runs on every push | A contract case reasons over the configuration's text, so it cannot catch what only a provider can: a value the schema rejects, or a resource that fails at apply. That boundary is unchanged by this round and is what the deployment's own `plan` is for. What is closed is the one class the finding names |
| 100.2.2 | **Read variable references from the configuration's code alone, treating a reference inside a comment as prose rather than as a read, and grow the recorded-unread inventory from seventeen to twenty** | (a) Keep the textual comparison over the whole file; (b) keep it and exempt the three names by hand; (c) strip comments but leave the inventory at seventeen, letting the case fail | The comparison read `var.` anywhere in `main.tf` and `outputs.tf`, so the two comments row 100.1.5 corrected were the only thing standing between three unapplied inputs and the report that exists to name them &mdash; a case whose docstring promises that "a variable added and left unread is reported rather than ignored" was answering yes because prose mentioned it. (a) leaves the loophole in the case that is supposed to close it. (b) is an exemption list that grows silently. (c) leaves the build red. Measured after the change: sixty-five inputs are read in code, twenty are not, and all twenty carry defaults so none can refuse a plan | The comment stripper is line-based and drops anything after `` #`` on a line, so a `var.` reference in a trailing comment is no longer counted; measured, none exists, and one added later would be reported as unread, which is the safe direction. The inventory is three entries longer and each entry is a name a future round may delete once tidying is authorized |
| 100.2.3 | **Assert description accuracy as two rules &mdash; every provider address a description names is declared, and every description claiming a value is *applied as* a property *on* a block names a block that reads it &mdash; calibrated against the configuration before being trusted** | (a) Assert only the addresses resolve; (b) assert only the application claims; (c) require every description to name its consumer, so an unread input must say so in a fixed form; (d) assert nothing and rely on review | The two rules divide the finding cleanly: the singular/plural names are unresolvable addresses, and the four misattributions are application claims. (a) admits `applied as memory_size_gb on google_redis_instance.rate_limit` for an input that resource never reads. (b) admits an address that resolves to nothing. (c) would impose a phrasing on eighty-five descriptions to police twenty. (d) is what let six statements ship. Calibration settles the clause's shape from evidence: the application pattern matches **24** claims across the file, including nested properties written as dotted paths, and every one resolves to a block that reads its input; the address rule checks **60** addresses. Both were run against each delivered defect restored one at a time &mdash; six perturbations, six refusals, six controls green | The clause matches wording, so a description asserting an application in other words passes it, and a description that says nothing at all is not required to. That is a tripwire on the phrasings that occurred rather than a proof of accuracy, and it is disclosed as such: the prose remains a reviewer's subject, and these cases keep the two shapes that were wrong from returning unnoticed |

### 100.3 The documented secret boundary

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 100.3.1 | **Rewrite the six-secret class's comment to name the two workloads that mount it and to cross-reference the two narrower classes that are declared**, and correct the migration Job's citation of its own mount | (a) Change the manifests to match the comment, mounting the six-secret class from all three pods; (b) correct only the sentence the finding quotes; (c) leave both, since the applied posture is the stronger one | The comment said the class's readers were "the backend Deployment, the migration Job and the administrator credential Job", and that a narrower class holding `DATABASE_URL` alone "is not declared, because the migration runs under the backend workload identity". Measured from the YAML, every clause is false: `40-backend.yaml` and `65-ingestion-cronjob.yaml` mount it; `60-migration-job.yaml` mounts `backend-database` from `35-migration-secrets.yaml` under its own service account; `70-admin-credential-job.yaml` mounts `backend-admin-credential`; and `main.tf:775` grants the migration identity exactly one secret. (a) would take a real entitlement from one secret to six to make a sentence true &mdash; the finding's own impact note is that the applied configuration is the stronger posture. (b) leaves the "is not declared" paragraph, which is the half that misleads: a reviewer auditing from this file concluded no narrower class existed and that the migration identity held all six, the exact opposite of the tree. (c) is the defect, and its cost is a security reviewer reaching the wrong conclusion from the right file | The comment now carries filenames, which is more to keep in step than prose labels were &mdash; and that is what makes it checkable: row 100.3.2's cases compare those filenames against the mounted volumes, so a workload that stops mounting the class fails the build rather than leaving a stale sentence |
| 100.3.2 | **Assert the boundary in both directions from the committed comments and the mounted volumes, comparing manifest filenames rather than prose labels** | (a) Assert only that each workload cites the class it mounts; (b) assert only that each class names its readers; (c) match prose labels such as "the backend Deployment"; (d) assert nothing and rely on the corrected comments | The defect had two shapes and each direction catches one: a class naming readers it does not have, and a workload attributing its mount to the wrong file. (a) would have passed the six-secret paragraph, which cited no workload at all. (b) would have passed the migration Job's citation. (c) matches a label a reader cannot follow and a case cannot resolve, and the labels are what the defective text used. (d) is where the round started. The negative direction is deliberately narrow: another workload may be named in the declaring file, and must then be named beside the class it does mount, so a cross-reference and a sequencing note are both admitted while a bare attribution is not. Calibrated with five perturbations &mdash; the pre-round paragraph restored verbatim, a planted attribution of the migration Job to the six-secret class, each of the two reverse citations removed, and the pre-round migration citation restored &mdash; and all five are refused | The comparison is textual, so a citation could be present and the sentence around it still wrong; and the negative direction keys on the word "mount", so an attribution phrased without it passes. What the pair does guarantee is that the set of workloads a class names and the set that mount it agree, and that no workload sends a reader to a class it does not mount &mdash; which is the property the finding was about |
| 100.3.3 | **Name the ingestion CronJob's delivery class in its own header, and say why that pod reads all six credentials** | (a) Leave it, since the class is visible in the volume below; (b) name the class without the reason; (c) narrow the CronJob to a class of its own | The CronJob was the workload the six-secret comment omitted, and its header described the mount path without naming the class, so the file that mounts the widest class was the one file not saying so. (c) is a real option and was weighed: it is refused because the task imports the application's settings model, which refuses to construct unless every managed credential is present &mdash; measured, its container exports all six before the task starts &mdash; so a narrower class would produce a pod that cannot start. (b) leaves the reader to discover that by reading `config.py`. (a) leaves the omission the finding names | The stated reason is a property of the settings model, so a future change that lets the ingestion path construct settings without every credential would make the sentence stale while the mount stayed wide. That is the point at which alternative (c) becomes available, and this row is where a reader should look for it |
## 101. The browser QA round: the deck's runtime behaviour, and four backend surfaces

A browser QA round returned FAIL on seventy-five findings against the executive
presentation and the backend surfaces a browser reaches: no Critical, eighteen Major,
thirty-four Minor and twenty-three informational, over six hundred and twelve executed
cases. Fifty-two fall inside this repository's scope; the remainder are third-party
viewer bundles, read-only frontend source, or environment observations, and the reason
each is out of scope is recorded in the round's own non-changes table below.

Two properties are asserted throughout. Every figure below was produced by driving the
running artifact in a real browser and reading the value back, and the reading is named
rather than the intent. And every row that corrects an earlier position marks that
position in place under the &sect;27 convention, because a correction a reader cannot
see is indistinguishable from a figure that was never wrong.

This round's finding-to-change mapping is carried in §101.3 rather than in
`docs/security/TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`, because that document's published change
figures are pinned by a contract test against the presentation's own change map, and
this round moved none of them: every file this round touches was already inside the
counted set.

### 101.1 Decisions of this round

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 101.1.1 | **Remove `ambient-light-sensor` from the `Permissions-Policy` header** | (a) Keep it, as row 12.9 decided; (b) keep it and suppress the console category; (c) replace it with the feature name browsers do implement | Row 12.9 declined this token on one stated ground: no finding named it. A browser round has now named it, so the ground no longer holds. The directive is inert &mdash; it restricts nothing, because no browser implements the feature it names &mdash; and every browser that parses the header reports it once per document load, on all three backend HTML surfaces at all four tested viewports. Removing it costs no restriction and removes the report. There is no feature name to substitute: the sensor permission was withdrawn from the specification, not renamed. The remaining thirteen directives are unchanged. | A future browser that revives the feature would find it unrestricted. The header denies every other sensor and capture feature to every origin, and a revived feature would need a named directive whatever this row decided. |
| 101.1.2 | **Carry the retry window in the throttled response body, under `retry_after_seconds`, read back from the response's own `Retry-After` header** | (a) Leave the wait in the header alone; (b) compute the wait independently in the body; (c) publish the window's reset epoch in the body instead; (d) also emit the rate-limit headers on admitted and refused-credential responses so a caller sees its remaining allowance | A refused caller was told to slow down and not for how long: the three-word body carried no wait, and the value existed only inside a raw header dump where a reader must know to look. The header is written by the limiter *after* the body has been rendered, so the body is rendered a second time once the value is known and `Content-Length` corrected &mdash; which is why the value is read back from the header rather than computed twice, so the two can never disagree. The reset epoch is already published as a header and is a less useful number to a client than a duration. Alternative (d) is refused in its own right: see row 101.2.1. | The body is rendered twice on the refusal path only; every admitted response is untouched. A header that is absent, non-numeric or negative leaves the body at its original shape, so `detail` is present on every throttled reply whatever the limiter reported. |
| 101.1.3 | **Replace every documentation-generator cross-reference in the published schema with prose, and extend that beyond the two descriptions the round named to every description the schema publishes** | (a) Fix only the two named descriptions; (b) strip the roles in a custom `openapi()` hook at serialisation time; (c) drop the affected descriptions entirely | The viewers render a description verbatim and resolve no markup, so a role reached the reader with its own punctuation intact and read as broken documentation, while a dotted package name additionally published this application's internal module layout to anyone who fetched the schema. A scan of the whole published surface found the same construct in eleven further places the round's reproduction steps did not reach &mdash; four model descriptions the viewers render in exactly the same panes &mdash; so fixing only the two named would have left the finding reproducible. A serialisation hook would hide the construct from the schema while leaving it in the source for the next description to copy. The descriptions carry information worth keeping, so they are rewritten rather than dropped, and each internal constant is replaced by the public field name or by the bound the schema already publishes machine-readably beside the field. | Prose can drift from the values it describes. Every value the prose previously named by constant is now either a published field name or a published numeric bound, so the schema itself carries the authority and a contract test asserts no role, module path or configuration attribute returns. |
| 101.1.4 | **Publish one credential example, shared by the registration and login bodies** | (a) Publish no example, as before; (b) publish a different example per endpoint; (c) publish an example that omits the password; (d) relax the password policy so a synthesised value would validate | With no example the viewer synthesised one from each field's own constraints, producing an address of random punctuation and the literal word `string` for the password &mdash; valid JSON, so nothing warned the reader, and refused the moment it was sent. One example serves both endpoints because both accept the same two fields, and the published value satisfies the stricter of the two contracts in full: twelve characters or more, one of each required class, and inside the byte ceiling. A password-less example would still fail on Execute. Relaxing the policy to suit a documentation viewer inverts the priority. | The example is a plausible-looking credential in a published schema. It is not a credential: no account exists for it, and it is asserted to be accepted by its own contract rather than by any account. |

### 101.2 Deliberate non-changes from this round

| # | Left unchanged | Why it was not changed | Risks |
|---|----------------|------------------------|-------|
| 101.2.1 | The rate-limit headers on an admitted or credential-refused response, so a caller cannot see its remaining allowance before it is refused | The round suggested emitting them so a client could warn before the wall. Publishing a per-address allowance countdown on the credential endpoints hands an attacker the pacing signal that makes credential stuffing efficient: it converts a blind budget into a measured one. AAP §0.5.1.2 makes the credential endpoints uniform by design and §0.12.2 admits no new disclosure, and an existing contract test asserts these headers are absent from an admitted response. The refusal itself now carries its wait, which is the part a legitimate client needs. | A legitimate client discovers the limit by being refused once. It is then told exactly how long to wait. |
| 101.2.2 | Field-level detail in a validation refusal: every rejected body still answers `{"detail":"Invalid request"}` | AAP §0.6.2 fixes the after-state of the handlers as returning generic errors and §0.5.1.5 requires handlers that do not leak internals; §0.9.2 excludes feature additions. The round's own text declines it for the credential endpoints. The concrete case it reported &mdash; a reader who cannot tell which field a pre-filled body failed on &mdash; is instead removed at its source by row 101.1.4, which makes the pre-filled body valid. | A client with a mistyped nested key must consult the published schema rather than the refusal. The schema publishes every field, bound and required flag. |
| 101.2.3 | The diagram edge stroke at `#999999`, measured at 2.849:1 against white | Rule 2 fixes the presentation theme's `lineColor` at that value literally, and a contract test asserts it. The two contrast defects that were inside this repository's authority &mdash; the risk-class node stroke and the subgraph border &mdash; were fixed, from 2.513:1 to 11.145:1 and to a painted 12.63:1 in light and 13.08:1 in dark forced colours. | Connector lines remain lower-contrast than the shapes they join. The shapes, their borders and every label meet the threshold, so no information is carried by the lines alone. |
| 101.2.4 | The title slide's secondary text, reported at 3.233:1 | Measured against the surface that actually paints, the ratio is 7.218:1 and 7.017:1. The reported figure was taken against the bare gradient at a point the contrast scrim covers, so it measured a colour no reader sees. The scrim is unchanged and its contract test is untouched. | None. Recorded so the figure is not re-derived from the report. |
| 101.2.5 | Eighteen sections in the presentation, against prose elsewhere describing sixteen | Rule 2 fixes the permitted band at twelve to eighteen and a contract test asserts both ends, so eighteen is compliant. | A reader comparing the two numbers sees a discrepancy. The band, not the prose, is the authority. |
| 101.2.6 | Arrow-up and arrow-down navigating the presentation rather than doing nothing | This is the framework's own behaviour under the linear navigation mode the round asked for: the two keys alias onto the single linear axis, which is what linear mode means. Verified by boundary clamping &mdash; up is inert on the first slide and down on the last &mdash; and the vertical controls are themselves absent, which was the reported defect. | A reader expecting a two-dimensional grid finds none. There is none to find. |
| 101.2.7 | The `.reveal ` selector prefix on one rule of the presentation's forced-colours block, which the other fifteen carry | The diagram library injects its own cluster styling from inside the rendered graphic, at identifier specificity and later in the cascade. Prefixing would raise the rule to three classes and it would still lose to an identifier, so the rule wins on `!important` instead, which outranks a normal declaration whatever its specificity. Measured winning in both palettes. | The block's prefix convention has one documented exception. A contract test asserts the block remains the stylesheet's last rule, which is the property the convention exists to protect. |
| 101.2.8 | Diagram node labels overrunning their own node borders by up to 4.86px per side | A pre-existing consequence of the library sizing its boxes from fallback font metrics before the web font paints. Measured on the untouched diagram as well, where the worst case is larger at 5.71px per side, which establishes it as pre-existing rather than introduced. Nothing is clipped, no two nodes overlap, and no label is unreadable. | Labels sit tight to their borders. Recorded rather than fixed, because the fix is a font-loading change to a third-party renderer. |
| 101.2.9 | Everything under `frontend/src/`, the frontend dependency manifest, and the third-party viewer bundles the documentation routes load | AAP §0.9.2 designates the frontend source read-only reference material and excludes the manifest explicitly; the viewer bundles are not in the AAP's file map and their routes are published only when the environment is local. One genuine client-side defect was found &mdash; the authentication service reads a response field the backend does not return &mdash; and is reported here rather than fixed, because fixing it means editing read-only source. | A real client defect stands. It is named, and its fix is a one-line change in a file this round may not touch. |

### 101.3 Traceability for this round

| Finding | Behaviour that was wrong | Change | Verified by |
|---------|--------------------------|--------|-------------|
| Header directive | An inert directive drew one browser report per document load | Row 101.1.1 | The served header carries thirteen well-formed directives and not the withdrawn one; asserted on both the published constant and a served response |
| Throttled body | A refused caller was not told how long to wait | Row 101.1.2 | The body equals `detail` plus the integer the response's own `Retry-After` header carries, and `Content-Length` matches the re-rendered body |
| Published descriptions | Generator roles and internal module paths reached the reader verbatim | Row 101.1.3 | A scan over all eleven published operations and fifteen schemas returns zero roles, zero module paths and zero configuration attributes, and the patterns are shown to match what was removed |
| Absent example | A pre-filled credential body was refused the moment it was sent | Row 101.1.4 | Both models accept their own published example unedited, the example meets the registration policy, and the registration route answers `200` to it sent verbatim |

## 102. The runtime verification round: the release path executed, the guard measured, and the record realigned

A runtime verification pass returned FAIL on thirty-one findings: one Critical, five
Major, twenty Minor and five informational. None was a defect in delivered application
code, and none touched a frozen interface. One was a defect in a release script that
made every successful deployment report failure, two were guards that could not fail,
and the rest were statements in the published record that a reader could disprove by
running the command beside them.

Two properties hold throughout. Every figure below was produced by executing something
against this tree &mdash; a stub-instrumented run of the release script, a mutation
matrix in a throwaway repository, an audit against a manifest, or a slug computed the
way GitHub computes it &mdash; and the instrument is named. And every row that corrects
an earlier position marks that position in place under the &sect;27 convention rather
than rewriting it, because a correction a reader cannot see is indistinguishable from a
claim that was never wrong.

### 102.1 The migration gate: one operative decision, and a row that recorded the rejected one

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 102.1.1 | **Withdraw row 94.6.5 and leave row 89.12 operative**, marking 94.6.5 in place, and correct the one sentence in [`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) that repeated its claim | (a) Delete row 94.6.5; (b) edit it in place so it reads as the delivered design; (c) leave both rows standing and let a reader choose; (d) change the gate to match row 94.6.5, reversing to `base` after one single-step reversal | Rows 89.12 and 94.6.5 record opposite designs, and only one is in the tree. Measured before this round: `git grep 'downgrade base'` matched three prose sites and no workflow &mdash; row 89.12's rejected alternative, row 94.6.5, and one sentence in [`TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md`](TRACEABILITY_MATRIX.md) that has been corrected here &mdash; while both gate jobs read the step count with `len(list(chain.walk_revisions()))` and loop `alembic downgrade -1` once per revision, then read the base back from the database as `remaining == ['alembic_version']` with `stamped == 0`. `test_deployment_contract.py::test_the_gate_applies_and_reverses_the_migrations` asserts exactly that shape for every reversing job: the chain-derived count, one literal reversal call, the loop around it, and the base check. (a) and (b) erase the record that a position was held, which is the value this log carries across rounds. (c) leaves a reader taking the later row as current, which is the defect. (d) would take the gate to the design row 89.12 rejected with a stated reason: a single command cannot name which step failed and does not distinguish a revision whose downgrade is not independently reversible. The matrix sentence is corrected rather than marked, because it describes the workflow rather than recording a decision &mdash; the distinction row 91.5.5 draws | A reader meeting row 94.6.5 in isolation sees a withdrawn position; it is marked and names this row. The gate's own limitation that row 94.6.5 observed is real and unchanged: reaching the base does not by itself prove each revision reverses alone, which is why `test_migration_gate.py::test_each_revision_reverses_and_the_chain_re_applies` walks the chain a step at a time and both the readme row and the contract case say so |
| 102.1.2 | **Correct the workflow comment above the gate to describe the counted loop it introduces**, in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | (a) Leave the comment, since no gate reads a comment; (b) delete it; (c) implement what it claimed | The comment asserted that the gate targets `base` "rather than counting steps", five lines above the derivation that counts steps, so the two contradicted each other inside one step and the false half was the one a reader meets first. (a) leaves a reviewer with a comment that disagrees with the code beneath it, which is how row 94.6.5 came to be written. (b) removes the statement of intent that says why the loop exists. (c) is row 102.1.1's rejected alternative (d). The mirrored gate in the same workflow already carried an accurate comment and is left byte-identical, so the two now agree | A comment is prose and no gate reads it. What bounds the drift is that the mechanism it describes is asserted by the contract case named in row 102.1.1, so the code cannot move away from the corrected comment without failing a test |

### 102.2 The release path, executed rather than read

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 102.2.1 | **Keep one `cleanup` function and one EXIT trap in `scripts/deploy.sh`**, adding a module-scope `HEALTH_FORWARD_PID` beside `KUBECONFIG_FILE` that `probe_health` assigns and the single trap acts on | (a) Keep the nested `cleanup` and declare `forward_pid` global; (b) keep the second trap but give it a global variable; (c) save and restore the outer trap around `probe_health` with `trap - EXIT`; (d) kill the port forward inline at the end of `probe_health` and install no trap | A bash function definition is global while `local` is not, so the nested `cleanup` permanently replaced the top-level one and then read a variable that had left scope: under `set -Eeuo pipefail` the EXIT trap aborted on an unbound variable, and the kubeconfig the outer `cleanup` exists to remove was never reached. Measured with a stub-instrumented harness against a copy of the previous script: exit status 1 after printing that the release completed, `deploy.sh: line 991: forward_pid: unbound variable`, one leftover `tmp.*` kubeconfig, and "closed the port forward" never printed. Against the delivered script, same harness: exit 0, zero leftover kubeconfigs, both messages printed. (a) and (b) leave two functions of the same name in one file, so which teardown runs depends on whether `probe_health` was reached. (c) makes correctness depend on restoring a trap on every exit path, including the failing ones. (d) loses the teardown precisely when it matters, which is when the probe fails | The kill is best-effort: the trap tests the variable, ignores a `kill` failure, and clears it, so a forward that has already exited is not an error. A forward whose process identifier was reused by another process would be signalled &mdash; bounded by the identifier being cleared as soon as it is acted on, and by the forward being started and stopped inside one function |
| 102.2.2 | **Split the render-token inventory into required, admin-only and defaulted arrays, and add a pre-flight `assert_manifest_tokens` that dry-renders every manifest before any credential is acquired** | (a) Add the two missing names to the flat `OPERATOR_RENDER_TOKENS` array; (b) leave the validation to the renderer, where it already exists; (c) move the existing failure earlier without changing what it checks | Two tokens the manifests require without a default &mdash; `BACKEND_GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL` and `ADMIN_PROVISIONER_GCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL` &mdash; were in neither the operator array nor the renderer's defaults, so a run reached `apply_prerequisites` and failed there, after cluster credentials had been acquired and a kubeconfig written. Measured on the manifests: 33 distinct tokens, 18 defaulted, 2 derived by the renderer, 5 exported by the release script, leaving 9 the operator must supply &mdash; 8 always and 1 only when the administrator credential is provisioned. (a) fixes the export but keeps the failure late and keeps one array carrying three different kinds of token. (b) is what stood: the renderer does refuse, but only when it is asked to render, which happens after credentials. (c) would move a check that did not cover the two missing names. The pre-flight asks the renderer, so the renderer stays the single authority for the required set and the two cannot drift | The pre-flight renders every manifest twice per run, once to `/dev/null` and once for real. Measured with each of the 8 always-required tokens omitted in turn: exit 1 naming the missing token, with zero `gcloud` invocations recorded in the trace &mdash; the property the change exists to establish |
| 102.2.3 | **Print the token lists in `--help` from the same arrays the validator reads**, rather than restating them in the usage text | (a) Extend the static usage heredoc with the missing names; (b) point the reader at the renderer instead of listing anything | The usage listed 7 required inputs and omitted 8 mandatory ones, which is the drift a restatement always ends in. Deriving the text from the arrays makes the printed contract and the enforced contract the same object. (a) is the restatement that drifted. (b) leaves an operator running two commands to find out what one command needs. Measured: `--help` exits 0, prints 77 lines, and names all 29 checked inputs, with the admin-only token marked conditional | The usage now depends on array ordering for readability. `test_release_automation_contract.py::test_the_release_script_prints_its_usage_and_exits_zero` asserts every accepted input appears, so a name dropped from an array fails rather than quietly disappearing from the help |
| 102.2.4 | **Capture the selector's file list into a variable and test the status before rendering**, in `scripts/render_kubernetes_manifests.sh` | (a) Add `set -e` inside the function; (b) check the output for emptiness instead of the status; (c) validate the selector against a literal list at the top of `main` | A command substitution inside a here-document discards the exit status of the command it runs, so `files_for`'s refusal was swallowed and an unrecognised selector printed its message to standard error and exited 0 with empty output &mdash; a delivery path could therefore apply nothing and be told it succeeded. (a) does not change how a substitution's status is read. (b) conflates "no such selector" with "this selector legitimately matches nothing". (c) duplicates the list the function already holds. Measured against the previous script: `bogus` exited 0, now exits 1 naming the accepted selectors; `prerequisites` renders 11805 bytes byte-identically before and after; `99-absent.yaml` exits 1; no arguments exits 2; `job-name migration` exits 0 | One more local variable holds the whole list in memory. The lists are five to nine paths, so the cost is nil |
| 102.2.5 | **Renumber the runtime-pin citation to `scripts/deploy.sh:889` and record the previous location as withdrawn**, in the test module and in both citing documents | (a) Leave the citations and accept that they point at a neighbouring line; (b) stop citing a line and cite only the construct; (c) reorder the release script so the pin keeps its line | The teardown and pre-flight changes added lines above the pin, moving `--runtime python39` from line 768 to 889, and two documents plus one test module cite it by line. (a) leaves a reviewer landing on unrelated code, which is the defect row 89.14 closed for the model references. (b) is the better long-run shape and is what row 89.14 adopted for constructs, but the pin inventory's value is that a reviewer can open one line and see the pinned runtime. (c) subordinates the script's structure to a citation. Row 94.2.5 is the precedent: the withdrawn location is listed rather than deleted, so a reviewer holding an older copy finds the move recorded | Every future edit above line 889 moves it again. What bounds it is that `test_documentation_citations.py` reads the line and asserts the pin is on it, so a stale citation fails the build rather than misleading a reader |

### 102.3 The two guards that could not fail

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|
| 102.3.1 | **Apply the placeholder test to the matched connection string rather than to the whole `git grep` line**, in `.github/scripts/check_secret_policy.sh` | (a) Exclude paths whose name contains `example` and scan the rest; (b) require a marker comment on the same line as a documented connection string; (c) narrow the connection-string pattern so a placeholder cannot match it | `git grep -n` emits `path:line:content`, so a line-level inverse match tested the path as well as the value, and the token `example` in `.env.example` exempted that file wholesale &mdash; the guard's own promise is that the example file is scanned like any other. A real password committed there passed. Measured on the delivered tree: 7 connection-string matches, and every one carries its placeholder marker inside the matched value, so narrowing the test to the value leaves the tree green while closing the hole. (a) inverts the promise into an exemption list. (b) puts the burden on whoever writes the next example. (c) cannot be done without also failing to see the real credentials the guard exists to catch. Measured with an 11-case mutation matrix in a throwaway repository, delivered against previous: a real connection string in `.env.example` 1 against 0, in `infrastructure/docker/example-compose.yml` 1 against 0, in a notes file 1 against 1, a documented placeholder 0 against 0, and a real string under `backend/tests/` 0 against 0 | The value-level test admits a line that carries a real credential *and* a placeholder marker inside the same connection string. That requires a deliberately crafted value, and the four markers are literal strings the guard names |
| 102.3.2 | **Pass `--no-index` to `git check-ignore` for the tracked required paths**, and record the caveat in &sect;4.3 of [`CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md`](CREDENTIAL_ROTATION.md) | (a) Leave the check and rely on the tracked state; (b) test the ignore rules by parsing `.gitignore`; (c) drop the check | `git check-ignore` skips paths present in the index, so the check that a required path is not ignored could never fail for a tracked path &mdash; a widened rule over `.env.example` passed. Measured: the ignore rule appended over the tracked example file returns 1 with the flag and 0 without it. (a) is the defect: the guard reported a property it had not tested. (b) reimplements the ignore grammar. (c) removes a control that catches a rule widened by hand. The runbook's own verification prescribes the same technique, so the caveat belongs beside it | The flag makes the check answer about the rules rather than about the tree, which is the question asked. A path that is both ignored and untracked is still caught by the neighbouring check, which is left as it was |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|

(a) contradicts the tree. (b) is for a position that was decided, not for a figure that was superseded and then restated by omission &mdash; the distinction row 91.5.5 draws, applied here to four descriptive sentences. (c) is what allowed the drift: the figure is now asserted from the module's own suppression tuples by `test_release_automation_contract.py` and by `test_residual_risk_guards.py` | The rows in this log that carry the old figure stay as they are, so a reader grepping for *fourteen* still finds it in withdrawn rows and in the two register sentences that narrate the change. That is the intent of &sect;27 rather than an oversight |
| 102.4.2 | **Restate &sect;1.2 of the runbook in the three categories the credentials actually fall into** &mdash; committed and exposed, exposed through logs only, and new and never exposed &mdash; and correct the exposed count from three to four | (a) Correct the count alone; (b) keep two categories and treat the listing-provider key as committed; (c) move the log-only credential out of the exposed group entirely | &sect;3 of the runbook and [`../../SECURITY.md`](../../SECURITY.md) both name four exposed credentials while &sect;1.2 said three, and the fourth &mdash; the listing-provider key &mdash; was never committed: it travelled in URL query strings and was printed to standard output. So the dividing question is where a value was disclosed, not whether it was committed, and a two-way split cannot express that. (c) would tell an operator a disclosed credential needs no revocation. Both halves are asserted: `test_operator_documentation.py` reads the opening for the corrected count and reads &sect;4.1 for the scoped claim, and each of the seven credential sections keeps the same four headings so the shape is uniform |
| 102.4.3 | **Qualify the administrator-credential claim to the process argument list, and prescribe a form that keeps the value out of the history file** | (a) Delete the claim; (b) keep it and change the prescribed command to one that reads the value from a file; (c) leave it, since the argument-list half is true | The prescribed form is an environment-assignment prefix, which a shell records in its history verbatim and which is readable from the process environment, so the claim covered one channel and asserted two. (b) is the right shape and is what the prescribed alternative now is &mdash; sourcing a mode-0600 file with history disabled around it &mdash; but the environment-prefix form is what an operator running one command will reach for, so both are given with the difference stated. (c) publishes an overstatement in the one document whose purpose is incident response | The history-safe form is three more lines for an operator to run, and disabling history is per-shell. The claim now names the channel it covers, so a reader can decide for their own shell |
| 102.4.4 | **Remove the trailing `--` from every history sweep in the runbook and state that the sweep is read from its output**, recording that a clean sweep returns 123 | (a) Keep the `--` and correct only the exit-code sentence; (b) keep the sweep and drop the status claim; (c) replace the sweep with `git log -S`, which reports a status a reader can use | Measured in a scratch repository, the documented form was not merely reporting an inverted status &mdash; it was searching nothing: everything after `--` is a pathspec, so the revisions were handed to `git grep` as paths, and the command was silent and returned 123 both when the value was present and when it was absent. Without the `--`, the same measurement prints one line per commit carrying the value and returns 0. So (a) would have documented an accurate status for a command that cannot find anything. (b) leaves an operator with no criterion. (c) searches diffs rather than commit contents, which is the reason this sweep exists. A **third** occurrence of the same defect was found by grepping the tree during verification rather than from the finding, in the section that inventories the refs before a rewrite, and is corrected with the other two | The pass condition is now "prints nothing", which a script cannot test by status alone; the runbook says so at each sweep and states 123 as the clean status. `xargs` still returns 123 for any child failure, so an operator scripting this must read the output, which is what the instruction requires |
| 102.4.5 | **Compute heading anchors the way `github-slugger` computes them** in `test_security_documentation.py`, and correct the five links that a collapsing rule had hidden | (a) Correct the five links and leave the helper collapsing whitespace; (b) remove the em dashes from the five headings so both rules agree; (c) drop the fragment check | The helper collapsed runs of whitespace to one hyphen, while `github-slugger` replaces each space individually &mdash; so for a heading separated by an em dash between two spaces, GitHub emits two hyphens and the helper emitted one. The consequence ran both ways, and both were measured over the seven documents: two links in the runbook were correct and the suite called them broken, and two fragments in the register were broken and the suite called them fine. (a) leaves the suite unable to see the second class at all. (b) edits headings to suit a test, and the em dash is the register's own convention for a qualified heading. (c) removes the check that catches a link going nowhere. The rewritten helper also reads only ATX headings and skips fenced blocks, so a shell comment inside an extracted command can no longer supply an anchor that masks a broken link, and it applies GitHub's duplicate-heading suffix | The helper now encodes a third party's slug algorithm, and a change to that algorithm would make it wrong. It is calibrated against the delivered documents in both directions, and a sweep over all 219 relative links and fragments in the seven documents reports zero broken. Two assertions that had encoded the withdrawn three-exposed-credentials figure are updated with it, one of them gaining a negative guard so the withdrawn wording cannot return unnoticed |

| # | Decision | Alternatives considered | Rationale | Risks |
|---|----------|------------------------|-----------|-------|

(b) makes the script unusable unattended, which is how the developer setup is run in a container. (c) is (a) with a different guess. (d) leaves the one command a new contributor runs first exiting 1 with the explanation in a different file. The prerequisite is now documented where a reader meets it |
| 102.5.2 | **State the pipeline's two pytest invocations with their flags, rather than claiming it runs the same command** | (a) Change the workflow to a single call so the claim becomes true; (b) drop the *Enforced by* detail and name only the job | The readme said the `backend` job ran "the same suite with coverage instead of `-q`" and, for the security path, "this exact command". The two partitions exist so coverage accumulates across them, and (a) would trade that for a sentence. (b) removes the detail that lets a reader reproduce the gate. Both flag sets are now quoted in the row and asserted against the workflow | The flags are restated in prose and could drift from the workflow. What bounds it is that they are quoted exactly and the workflow's step names are quoted with them, so a reader can diff one against the other in two greps |

(a) and (b) each remove the property that the delivered inventory is measured against the tree as it stands, which is the reason the case exists. (c) is the finding. (b) leaves a reader unable to tell which scope the acceptance rests on | The register's acceptances rest on a scope narrower than the whole backend tree, which is now stated rather than implied. The measurement behind it is one grep, and it is quoted |
| 102.6.4 | **Remove the duplicated invocation rules rather than reconciling them**, leaving one statement of each | (a) Keep all of them and make the wording identical; (b) keep the paragraph and drop the bullets | The `-r <manifest>` rule was stated three times &mdash; once as a paragraph and twice as a bullet &mdash; and the `--strict` rule twice, and the introductory sentence promised three details above six bullets. Duplication is not harmless in a policy: two of the three `-r` statements differed in scope wording, so a reader could not tell which was authoritative. (a) preserves the redundancy that caused it. (b) would lose the `--ignore-vuln` half, which is the part that distinguishes the diagnostic form from the gate. Four bullets now carry four distinct rules and the sentence says four | A future edit could reintroduce a duplicate. The count sentence and the bullet count are asserted together, so a fifth rule added without updating the sentence fails |
| 102.6.5 | **Label the safe-harbour section as proposed and not in force, in the same form as the response-target table**, and keep its limits as statements of scope | (a) Delete the section until item 4 is settled; (b) leave the undertaking published; (c) fold the limits into owner item 4's table cell | The section opened "Good-faith research that stays within the limits below will not be pursued by this project" &mdash; an unqualified legal undertaking &mdash; while item 4 of *Owner action required* records that safe-harbour terms need legal input and are the owner's decision, and no such decision exists. The response-target table two sections earlier is the model: it is labelled "Proposed target, not yet in force". (a) would lose five limits that are useful independently of any undertaking: they tell a reporter where a third-party defect belongs, that `frontend/` findings are recorded rather than patched, and that the shared login-throttle row is deliberate. (b) publishes a commitment nobody authorized, which is the failure the whole *Owner action required* section exists to avoid. (c) buries operational scope inside a table about legal decisions | The section now says two things at once &mdash; no undertaking is in force, and these limits describe today's scope &mdash; which is more to read than one sentence. Both are stated in their own paragraph, and the heading carries the qualification so a reader who reads only headings still sees it |
| 102.6.6 | **Point the response-target paragraph at item 1 as the prerequisite that establishes both of its conditions**, and name item 2 as the one that would set the targets | (a) Leave "one of the two prerequisites"; (b) restate the two conditions as one | The paragraph said neither condition &mdash; something receives the report, someone is accountable for reading it &mdash; holds "until an operator completes one of the two prerequisites above", which cannot be true of both: completing one of two leaves one outstanding. Item 1 is in fact what establishes both, since it is enabling private reporting *and* confirming a test report was read. (a) leaves an operator unable to tell which item unblocks the schedule. (b) would lose the distinction between a channel existing and a person reading it, which is the distinction the paragraph is making | The item numbers are referenced by number in four places in the policy. They are stable because the table is the owner-action list and no row has been added or removed here; the count sentence above it now agrees with it at four |
| 102.6.7 | **Have the bootstrap's closing message state what remains rather than asking for an edit that is not needed**, naming the five provider placeholders | (a) Leave "Please update the values in .env file."; (b) remove the message; (c) change the readme to match the message | The script printed a general instruction to update the file, and the readme states this route produces a file the application starts against without further editing. Both cannot be right. Measured by driving `configure_env_vars` in a scratch repository: the written file carries a generated 64-character `SECRET_KEY`, a generated `ADMIN_SEED_PASSWORD` and the template's five `CHANGE_ME` provider placeholders, and the next step rewrites the three database entries. So the message now says nothing needs editing by hand, names what the next step writes, and names the five values no bootstrap can supply along with when each must be set. (a) sends a developer looking for an edit to make. (b) leaves the placeholders undiscovered until a provider call fails. (c) would make the readme's supported route sound unfinished when it is not | The message enumerates five names that live in the template, so adding a sixth provider credential means updating it. What bounds the cost is that a non-local environment refuses a placeholder at startup, which the message also says |

(c) is the treatment row 89.14 chose for the model references, and is wrong here: the value of a pin inventory is that a reviewer can open one line and see the pinned runtime, which is why the table names both a path and a line | The numbers move whenever the surrounding file grows above them, as entry 4 did this round from 768 to 889.
